#3217. Apple says memory costs and Siri AI will weigh on holiday quarter profit margins

Following today’s earnings report, Apple held its quarterly earnings call, during which the company discussed the impact of rising memory costs on its profit margins and warned of additional pressure from Siri AI expenses during the holiday quarter. Here are the details.

Over the past few quarters, Apple has repeatedly warned that rising component costs would put pressure on its profit margins. Last quarter, gross margin was 50.1%, up from 49.3% in Q2. However, that included a roughly two-percentage-point benefit from tariff refunds.

Today, Apple reported that its gross margin fell to 47.9% in Q4 2026, with product gross margin dropping to 37.2%, down from 40.1% in the previous quarter. That represented a 2.2-percentage-point decline in company-wide gross margin and a 2.9-percentage-point drop in product gross margin.

Against the backdrop of record September quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh explained that tariff refunds once again provided some relief, though not enough to offset the impact of rising memory costs. He also noted that, excluding the impact of tariff refunds, the sequential decline in gross margins would have been roughly one percentage point, primarily due to higher memory costs:

“We saw strong performance in many services categories with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services, and advertising, and a September quarter record in music. Company gross margin was 47.9%, and products gross margin was 37.2%. These both included a benefit from tariff refunds, which had a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point in the September quarter. When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs.”

Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon, with the company forecasting gross margins of between 45% and 46% for Q1 2027.

He attributed the expected decline primarily to higher memory costs, alongside the impact of the ongoing Siri AI rollout.

When asked to elaborate, Parekh explained that Siri AI will affect Apple’s margins in two ways. First, running the service will increase cloud costs. Second, Apple will have to spread out the recognition of some revenue from devices that include Siri AI over their lifetimes, rather than counting it all at the time of sale.

This, he added, is an accounting practice Apple already follows for other services bundled with its devices, such as Maps, Siri, and iCloud:

“Consistent with how we’ve always accounted for Maps, Siri, and iCloud, for the devices we sell that include these bundled services, we defer a portion of the revenue and recognize it over the life of the device.”

Meanwhile, CEO John Ternus described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” adding that Apple expects the cost of purchasing memory components to continue rising beyond the December quarter.

Ternus said recent price increases across the Mac, iPad, and iPhone lineups would help offset some of those costs, alongside existing inventory purchased at lower prices and savings on certain non-memory components. He also warned that the benefits of carrying lower-cost memory inventory would diminish over time. Apple did not say whether it expects to raise product prices yet again to compensate.

#3216. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3215. Apple forecasts its biggest revenue quarter ever despite supply constraints

During today’s earnings call following its fiscal Q4 2026 report, Apple said it expects its December quarter “to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company.” Here are the details.

Apple today reported its fiscal Q4 2026 results, with revenue climbing 12% year over year to $114.5 billion and net profit reaching $30.71 billion. This marked September-quarter records on both fronts, despite supply constraints on iPhone, Mac, and iPad, as well as rising memory costs.

During the conference call following the earnings report, Apple acknowledged that higher memory costs were putting pressure on its profit margins, while also warning of limited supply-chain flexibility, stronger-than-expected demand for Mac and iPad, and ongoing shortages of the new iPhone Duo.

Still, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh was very clear about what the company expects from the next fiscal quarter, which includes the holiday shopping season:

We expect our December quarter total company revenue to grow between 7 and 10% year over year, which reflects our best view of constrained supply. We expect this to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company.

If this pans out, Apple’s fiscal Q1 2027 revenue should fall between $153.82 billion and $158.13 billion, adding between $10 billion and $14.4 billion in revenue compared to the year-ago quarter.

Beyond revenue, Parekh also shared Apple’s expectations for several other financial metrics during the December quarter:

Parekh noted that “third-party licensing and foreign exchange” will be the primary headwinds for the Services revenue, while higher memory costs and “some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI” are expected to put further pressure on the company’s gross margins.

Finally, Apple cautioned that its outlook “assumes that global tariff rates, policies, and their application remain in effect as of this call, and the global macroeconomic outlook does not worsen from today.“

#3214. Clorox (CLX) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Net sales surged 33% despite $240M in input cost inflation, 2.5x historical average.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

The Clorox Company (CLX +2.16%) reported first-quarter results that exceeded management's expectations despite an increasingly difficult inflationary environment. Management reported significant net sales growth driven by the integration of the GOJO acquisition and favorable year-over-year comparisons following a prior-year software transition. The company updated its full-year outlook to account for approximately $240 million in projected input cost inflation, which is roughly 2.5 times higher than its historical annual average. Leadership emphasized a focus on volume-led growth, margin recovery through productivity initiatives, and the strategic transition to a new chief executive officer in early 2027.

Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to The Clorox Company Fiscal Year 2027 First Quarter Earnings Release Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this call is being recorded. I would now like to introduce your host for today's conference call, Ms. Lisah Burhan, Vice President of Investor Relations for The Clorox Company. Ms. Burhan, you may begin your conference.

Lisah Burhan: Thank you, Jen. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. On the call with me today are Linda Rendle, our Chair and CEO; and Luc Bellet, our CFO. Please note that our earnings release and prepared remarks are available on our website at thecloroxcompany.com. Linda will share a few opening comments, and then we'll take your questions. During this call, we may make forward-looking statements, including about our fiscal year 2027 outlook. These statements are based on management's current expectations but may differ from actual results or outcomes. In addition, we may refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures.

Please refer to the forward-looking statements section, which identifies various factors that could affect such forward-looking statements, which have been filed with the SEC. In addition, please refer to the non-GAAP financial information section of our earnings release and the supplemental financial schedules in the Investor Relations section of our website for a reconciliation of non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures. I'll now turn it over to Linda.

Linda Rendle: Thanks, Lisah, and thank you for joining us today. We entered fiscal year '27 focused on steadily improving performance and market share while navigating continued input cost pressures. We made good progress in the first quarter, delivering better-than-expected results through strong execution and some favorable timing benefits. Importantly, the underlying trajectory of the business continues to move in the right direction with steady progress in organic sales growth and market share. At the same time, we continue to advance the priorities that will strengthen our performance over time.

We are improving superiority and innovation across our portfolio, integrating GOJO to unlock the full potential of Clorox Purell ProCare, continuing to evolve our portfolio and advancing our transformation efforts from a period of significant investment toward one of optimization and value creation. Together, these priorities are focused on building a stronger business that delivers more consistent profitable growth. While we are encouraged by the start to the year, we recognize that the operating environment remains challenging and uncertain. Consumers continue to seek value. Competitive activity remains elevated and increased commodity and transportation costs are putting additional pressure on margins.

We have a strong track record of managing cost pressures, and we're taking balanced actions to mitigate their impact while continuing to invest in improving our top line trajectory. The pace of that improvement will be driven in large part by our continued progress on superiority. Our updated outlook reflects these realities, along with the actions we're taking to mitigate their impact. Our focus remains on strengthening brand superiority improving the consistency of our performance and creating sustainable value over time. As you saw in our announcement on Thursday, the Board has appointed Fabian Garcia as Clorox's next CEO.

Through the process, I've had the opportunity to get to know Fabian, and I've been impressed by both his experience and his perspective on our business. He is an accomplished global consumer product leader with a strong track record of building brands, evolving portfolios, developing talent and delivering disciplined growth. Between now and January, I remain fully focused on executing our strategy, delivering our commitments and maintaining momentum while supporting a smooth transition and helping Fabian hit the ground running. With that, we'll open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question today will come from Peter Grom with UBS.

Peter Grom: Great. Linda, if this is your last earnings call, I just wanted to say thank you for everything and best wishes moving forward.

Linda Rendle: Thanks, Peter. I appreciate that.

Peter Grom: Yes. Thank you, Linda. So maybe just to start, just on the commodity outlook, the commentary in the prepared remarks is very helpful. But just given how volatile the external environment is, can you unpack the underlying assumptions embedded in the updated guidance? Is there anything you can share on the phasing of that cost pressure as we think about the balance of the year?

Luc Bellet: Sure. I can take that, Peter. So as you've read in our prepared remarks, we now expect input cost inflation for the fiscal year to be about $240 million. And that's about $40 million more than we expected at the beginning of the year. This -- the increase is mainly driven by just a range of commodities as well as transportation costs. And so for perspective, the $240 million is about 2.5x higher our historical annual average rate. Now what I would say is while oil remains an important variable, it's important to recognize that inflation we're dealing with is broader than energy alone, right? And so we're seeing -- commodities, we're seeing resin being a significant driver.

We're also seeing inflation across a wide range of commodities. Beyond commodities, we are seeing inflation in broader areas of supply chain, including supply -- supplier cost increase as well as transportation and other logistic costs. Now from an oil standpoint, we are assuming that the Brent annual average price would be around $100. But again, keep in mind that the inflationary pressures are proving much more persistent and extend beyond the oil headline. From a phasing standpoint, we expect inflation will be more pronounced in the first half and -- than in the second half. And then in the second half, we'll also see many of our mitigation actions stacking up and starting ramping up over time.

So that's why you're seeing an imbalance between the front half gross margin and the second half gross margin.

Peter Grom: That's really helpful. And then second, you noted some of the moving pieces around 2Q organic sales including a shipment comparison and some merchandising and timing dynamics that will push organic sales to be flat to minus 2%. And I know it all depends on where you fall within these ranges, but at first glance, it seems like that would imply a return to growth in the back half of the year to kind of get to flat to up slightly. Maybe first, am I thinking about that the right way? And if so, can you maybe unpack what drives the confidence that this will improve in the back half of the year?

Luc Bellet: Sure. Maybe let me actually just get us grounded in the full year then talk about the phasing of both halves and I can briefly touch on the timing for the second quarter. So for the full year, our organic sales growth rate is expected to be 3.5% to 4.5%, and that includes about 3.5 points of benefit from lapping the ERP transition. So essentially, our guidance is organic sales growth, excluding the impact of the ERP, is flat to plus 1% for the full year. As you mentioned, from a phasing standpoint, we expect organic sales growth, excluding the ERP to be down slightly in the front half and up slightly in the back half.

Now the way to think about it, there's a little bit of noise, especially in the front half between organic growth and consumption. But -- and some of it is driven by the Kingsford trough, some of it is driven by some of the ERP lap. But if you really look at the annual retail consumption, it's essentially flat in the front half and then becomes up slightly in the back half. And as a reminder, last fiscal year, we started in low -- negative low single digits. And so we've been improving sequentially to the front half of this year and continue to improve in the back half of this year.

So essentially, while we're not where we want, you could see that the outlook assumes that the business is moving in the right direction, reflecting steady progress on market share and consumption. So that's for the phasing. Now specifically to the second quarter, most of it is really reflecting timing and relapping dynamic. If you exclude that, again, you get to what I mentioned, which is U.S. retail consumption about flat and then for our Pro and international business being outside contributors.

Operator: And we'll take our next question from Anna Lizzul with Bank of America.

Anna Lizzul: Thank you for the question. And Linda, congratulations on your amazing career at Clorox. We will all miss you.

Anna Lizzul: I was wondering here if you could elaborate more on the mitigation efforts in light of the cost outlook. Just how much of the mitigating actions are coming from cost savings? And then how confident are you in your ability to take that incremental pricing you mentioned in the second half of the fiscal year? And also you noted your category growth on top line is within your expectations, is that still around flattish as you kind of started the year here?

Luc Bellet: Anna, I'll just take your first question on some of the mitigating actions and then Linda can just add anything and talk about the category growth. So as you -- given the inflationary outlook, as we talked about last quarter, we're leaning strongly in a holistic margin management set of tools. And the majority is still going to come -- margin recovery is still going to come from productivity and cost savings. We have actually really strong cost savings plan this year. First quarter, we're off to a good start. This was one of the highest cost savings -- quarterly cost savings on record.

But we are also going to implement targeted pricing in the front half and some in the back half as well as some RGM initiatives. And some -- most of those will actually play out more in the back half than in the front half. As you think about the recovery, I guess I've mentioned 2 things. The first is balance. We're really going to continue to pay some actions thoughtfully and balance rebuilding the margin while maintaining and accelerating the progress we're making on market share. And then the second is that we have confidence. We're confident in our ability to rebuild margin over time.

We have a strong track record of doing so successfully in a much more challenging environment. And we actually feel that we have a much stronger set of tools and capabilities today. And as we look at our pipeline, and the actions that are ahead of us, we feel confident in our ability to bring margin over time. Now for the fiscal year, I was stating to Peter, like, it's going to take time and some of this is going to phase in the back half. And so we're seeing gross margin compression on average for the full year, but we'll expect to exit the year with much stronger gross margin.

Linda Rendle: On the category side, Anna, we continue to see the category in line with the expectations we set for the year. And that was certainly true in the first quarter. And as the fundamentals of the category are playing out as we've expected. So recall, we said the category flat to up 1, was certainly within that range this quarter. And moving forward, we're seeing consumers continue to behave in ways that we expect lots of value-seeking behavior, buying larger sizes, smaller sizes, delaying purchases, et cetera, but in line with what we expect we've seen competitive activity generally in line with what we expect. Retailer activity, again, generally in line with what we expect.

So no indication that our assumptions on category won't hold up for the year. And then I would just note, because we continue to expect that in the back half, that implies that we would see better share performance in the back half of the year as well.

Operator: And our next question will come from Robert Moskow with TD Cowen.

Robert Moskow: I was hoping for a little more detail on where specifically you're seeing the market share improvement that you talked about, like what categories are you seeing some momentum? Where are you gaining share right now?

Linda Rendle: Sure, Robert. So when we talk about market share improving, we're looking at an aggregate number, but I can break that down by category as well. So if you look at Home Care, which is our largest business, we have continued share momentum on that business with a very strong quarter, up over 0.5 share point and that is in large part due to great activation on innovation as well as our back-to-school merchandising. We saw strong share growth in Brita, that also was correlated to our back-to-school, back-to-college merchandising and broad-based strength across promotions as well as innovation. Hidden Valley grew almost 2 share points this quarter.

And I think you all know that, that category was under a lot of pressure due to the cyclospora outbreak and category was down, we had -- saw weeks that were down strong double digits. But Hidden Valley, given we are a condiment used on more than just salads, was able to win and deliver strong execution. So very strong share growth in Hidden Valley. I know Burt's Bees was about flat, Glad Trash, about flat. So a number of the businesses showing positive share momentum. The continued story on Litter, although we have some green shoots that we're happy about as the plans come in, and we are still far from the place we want to be on share.

That continued to be a drag from a company perspective. And then the final note is on Kingsford, while the category continues to be under stress, given weather, et cetera, we did see a very strong Labor Day for Kingsford, delivered very strong high single-digit growth for that period as well as share growth. So that's a good indicator that as we have made some adjustments on execution, it bears well for fiscal year -- or excuse me, season year '27 for Kingsford, but that business also highly event dependent and share you have to win the key holidays to do that, and it was a good indication that Labor Day delivered.

Robert Moskow: Okay. And a quick follow-up. You said that you have good line of sight for synergies for GOJO, and it's moving faster than you expected. At some point, do you think you can raise your accretion estimate for first year on that?

Luc Bellet: I can take that, Robert. So first on the accretion and then maybe -- and then I'll talk a little bit about the synergies. So at the time of the acquisition, we had estimated that the adjusted EPS impact on year 1 will be about neutral. And we revised this to positive, right? We didn't share any specific. And this is really a factor of 2 things. First, the base business is actually continuing performing very well. And second, we're actually just progressing very nicely on integration and started accelerating some of the synergies.

If you remember from a cost synergy standpoint, we had estimated about $50 million and our initial estimate assumed that we would capture that mostly in year 2 and 3. And because the good news is we're -- now have, like, line of sight to the entire $50 million, which gives us great confidence that we will get at least that and potentially more. But in addition, because we've been making the progress on integration, we're able to actually start seeing some of those later in the first year, which is in fiscal year '27.

So net, I think we feel really good about the progress of both the base business as well as the integrations and that's starting showing up in our financials.

Operator: And our next question will come from Andrea Teixeira with JPMorgan.

Andrea Teixeira: So, Linda, congratulations on your amazing career at Clorox and wish you all the best in the next chapter. I was hoping to -- if you can elaborate a little bit more on what you said about some of the categories where you were able to get -- regain share with basically a lot more merchandising and also potentially promotions. As you think about recovering -- continuing to recover in the path of getting growth -- organic sales growth in the second half. Can you talk about like how you're planning those actions?

And then if there is anything in particular that you're counting on in terms of like additional phasing of innovation that would give us confidence that this path is going to materialize?

Linda Rendle: Sure. Thanks, Andrea, and thanks for your comments. So if you look at the share results, first, I want to acknowledge that fiscal year '26 was certainly really noisy for the company. We underwent our ERP transition, which is never easy, had a bit of bumpiness in part of that. And so a lot of the businesses were facing not only a heightened competitive environment, a weakening consumer, but they were also focused on just operational execution and ensuring that we were able to deliver to retailers and keeping stock, et cetera.

And so a lot of what you're seeing is us getting back to executing with excellence, now that, that noise is well behind us, delivering on our superiority plans, which we invested incrementally behind this year, as well as ensuring that we execute with excellence behind merchandising. And I just want to make sure that I'm clear, the merchandising that we have in the system is the typical merchandising we do just executed very well. So back-to-school, we always have strong promotional activity during that time. The team actually made a bet on back-to-school that it would occur a little later this year, given the consumer stress that it was under that was a good bet.

We actually saw the timing of consumers' consumption move to later on that, and we were prepared for it. So I would just want to make sure I note this is not us investing a lot in extra merchandising or price reduction outside of targeted activities we've taken, but just executing the things we have to do with excellence. So as we move into the back half, there's a few more things that will enhance what we've seen in the front half, and that is most of our innovation launches in the back half. And that happens throughout Q3 and Q4.

And we have one of our strongest innovation plans on record this year, and we're hoping it will be a record year on innovation. And we've seen good retailer sell-in. And many of these innovations had very, very strong consumer testing behind them. So we go in with a lot of confidence that, that innovation will work. In addition, some of the innovation is building on current platforms that have been successful like Clorox PURE, the allergy removing platform that we have. So we already know we have success in market, and we can turn that success into additional areas that those products can deliver on for consumers.

The other thing I would note is, as Anna mentioned, we expect the category continue to be in line with our expectations. But we are seeing consumers continue to focus on value. And at the beginning, we talked about the fact that we saw consumers stocking up more or buying a smaller size, but we are also seeing them begin to shift their behavior in terms of timing, like I mentioned for back-to-school. So those are the things we're watching really closely as we execute in the back half. But we feel like we have them well handled and well managed.

But those are the things that are kind of as we look to executing that are on our mind, ensuring we deliver our superiority plans, delivering on innovation, executing with excellence against merchandising and new distribution and then watching the consumer really closely as they continue to navigate a difficult environment.

Andrea Teixeira: Linda, this is super helpful. Can you talk about like the pricing magnitude that you including? And I think Luc had said some selective pricing, and you said that in the prepared remarks as well. What is, number one, the magnitude, the number two, the timing of the pricing? And if, three, this list pricing is more selective with innovation?

Linda Rendle: I'll start, and I'll hand it over to Luc, if there's any more detail that he wants to provide, particularly as it comes to gross margin, although I think you walked through the bridge of the beginning. So on pricing, we've implemented already this year, targeted pricing across all 4 of our reporting segments. And we looked at those very carefully to decide where the biggest impact was from a commodity perspective. So Glad, for example, is one that is heavily based off of resin pricing and so we took a price increase on Glad Trash. That was a good magnitude, high single-digit price increase that we implemented in July.

It took a little while for it to get passed through. So you're starting to see it in the data now at the end of September and then some other targeted pricing actions against those 4 segments. As you would expect, given the environment and the fact that we're seeing additional cost pressures across the industry, it's logical to assume that we will take additional pricing in the back half and that's what we're working on right now. And of course, as Luc has said many times in the past, those actions take a while to see them show up in margins.

So you see the impact from the increase in cost, and it takes a couple of quarters to start to see those mitigating actions. But we'll use the same principles that we did for their first round when evaluating these price increases, going where we're seeing the most commodity pressure, ensuring that we have superiority plans. And to your point, Andrea, timing it when we can with innovation and product improvements so that we balance what Luc mentioned at the beginning, which is our top line and superiority trajectory alongside recovery margins.

Luc Bellet: I guess the only thing I would add, and maybe that's what you were referring to, Andrea, is that we -- in our outlook and our gross margin and our top line outlook also reflects some targeted investments we're making to improve superiority in some brands. And those investments can come in the form of actually lower prices, either through trade or price pack architecture and the Litter business is one of those. Or in other cases, it could be in the form of higher cost where we're really doubling down to step up the product benefit and performance to further strengthen the proposition as part of the innovation in the back half.

That is all contemplated, and that's what you would expect us to do as part of that balancing.

#3213. When Electric Cars Were for Women

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3212. Apple stock drops nearly 3% after hours following Q4 2026 results

Apple shares fell as much as 4.43% in after-hours trading on Monday during the company’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, before recovering some of those losses later in the evening. Here are the details.

Apple today reported its fiscal Q4 2026 results, with a 12% increase in revenue, another 12% increase in net profit, and record revenue from its Services category, following its first sequential quarterly decline in 15 quarters.

The results also included a 17% increase in iPhone revenue and a 24% increase in Mac revenue, but an 8% decline in Wearables, Home, and Accessories revenue, which Apple attributed to “a difficult compare against the launch of the Watch SE 3 and the AirPods Pro 3 in the prior year,” and a 10% decline in iPad revenue, which Apple attributed to supply constraints and a similarly difficult comparison against last year’s A16-powered iPad launch.

During the conference call, Apple CEO John Ternus, CFO Kevan Parekh, and COO Sabih Khan fielded questions from analysts about rising memory costs, recent hardware price increases, and ongoing supply constraints, including those affecting the iPhone Duo.

The executives also offered a mixed outlook for the holiday quarter, with Apple expecting its highest quarterly revenue ever, but slower year-over-year growth, lower profit margins, and continued shortages of Mac and iPad models.

After ending the regular trading session down 1.83%, Apple shares initially climbed 0.5% to $340.00 following the earnings release. However, as the conference call progressed, the stock reversed course, falling to $323.33, or 4.43% below Monday’s closing price. Shares then recovered some of those losses, ending the after-hours session at $328.81, down 2.81%.

Of course, post-earnings after-hours trading doesn’t necessarily reflect how a stock will perform during the next day’s regular session, so it remains to be seen how investors will react when markets reopen on Tuesday after digesting tonight’s news.

#3210. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3209. Apple to require 18+ age ratings for dating apps and AI romantic companions

Apple today announced new age rating requirements coming to the App Store, covering apps with location-sharing features, as well as dating and relationship features. Here are the details.

In an update to its Developer News blog, Apple today announced that starting November 16, developers will be required to declare whether their apps include location-sharing or dating and relationship features when completing the age rating questionnaire in App Store Connect.

When completing the age rating questionnaire in App Store Connect, you’ll need to declare whether your app includes:

The company added that “apps that include Dating and Relationships receive a minimum age rating of 18+,” while “apps that include Shared Location may not have an impact on their minimum age rating in some regions.”

Apple notes that in Brazil, local regulations require an A16 rating for apps with location-sharing features and an A18 rating for those with dating and relationship features. However, developers can request a lower official rating from Brazil’s Ministry of Justice and Public Security if they believe their apps qualify, such as those designed to let parents and children share their locations.

Finally, Apple said developers must provide these declarations when submitting an app update or changing their age rating questionnaire, with all apps required to complete them by January 12, 2027.

Oncology portfolio surges 35% as Ziihera launches and Xywav sustains momentum.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Jazz Pharmaceuticals plc (JAZZ -0.71%) reported record quarterly revenue driven by growth in the oncology portfolio and sustained demand for the sleep medicine franchise. Management raised full-year revenue guidance to reflect commercial execution across multiple products in the U.S. and Europe. The company launched Ziihera for first-line gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma, establishing a source of potential long-term growth in the HER2-positive cancer market. The acquisition of Actio Biosciences expanded the rare epilepsy pipeline with a precision therapy candidate, ABS-1230. The company utilized its cash flow to exhaust a share repurchase program and authorized a new repurchase plan to continue its capital allocation strategy. President and Chief Executive Officer Renée Galá stated that the results demonstrate momentum in advancing practice-changing medicines while maintaining a disciplined approach to capital allocation.

How are you thinking about the trajectory of the product, just given the data that was recently presented? Thanks.

Samantha Pearce: Yeah. Thank you for the question. Yes, there are a few different dynamics in relation to Zepzelca. Obviously, we had the removal of the second-line monotherapy indication at the end of September that was aligned with the FDA. That does not affect our full approval in first-line maintenance segment, and that segment accounts for about 30%-40% of our total revenue. Now, we did see strong competitive data in first-line maintenance presented at ESMO, as you mentioned. IMDELLTRA, as we know, is very strong data. So, I think it's good news that there are more options. A couple of years ago, when the Imfinzi data came out, that was the first new data in this space for decades. #3207. Apple recently notified users in 99 countries of potential mercenary spyware attacks

Apple reportedly sent notifications to users in 99 countries warning of potential mercenary spyware attacks, as German authorities investigate reports that lawmakers and government officials may have been targeted. Here are the details.

A couple of reports from The Financial Times and TechCrunch today offer complementary details about a new wave of Apple threat notifications warning users that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware.

As we’ve covered before, Apple periodically sends out threat notifications to users it believes may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks. The company doesn’t disclose who may be behind the attacks or confirm whether a device has been compromised, but advises recipients to take the warnings seriously and seek expert assistance.

You can learn more about Apple’s recommendations for protecting against mercenary spyware, including how to enable Lockdown Mode, here.

Back to today’s reports, The Financial Times says that German lawmakers and government officials began receiving threat notifications from Apple last Thursday, prompting the country’s Federal Office for Information Security to issue an urgent warning over the weekend.

The agency advised recipients to “assume their device is no longer secure,” while the German government said it was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously” and “working flat out to investigate the circumstances of the incident.”

The FT noted that German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius declined to say whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among those affected, and added that the attacks reportedly exploited a “zero-click” vulnerability, allowing attackers to compromise devices without any interaction.

Knowledge of their targets’ phone numbers was all that the hackers needed to carry out the attack.

As it reported on the alerts, TechCrunch noted that “others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple,” including Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, who shared his alert on X.

It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries.

Mortada also noted in his tweet that he had previously been targeted by Pegasus spyware in 2017 and 2021, and that he does not know who was behind the latest attempt or whether it was connected to an investigative documentary he directed.

#3206. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."
