Can you just walk through, like, Alex, like you talk to so many of these customers. Like, do they come into a boot camp, just they're not -- they're trying to understand their AI path and then they leave and they're actually a customer? Like, can you just walk through, like, just from your perspective?

Alexander Karp: Well, I mean what's really shifted on the front line is, like, there used to be this long walk-up to people, like, talking to us and then you do a pilot and then you try to get a long pilot, and then you kind of lock that in because the same way you lock in, like, hire all these salespeople so that the market believes you're going to have sales kind of thing. Now it's much more -- people are -- it's super heterogeneous. So some people -- everybody basically comes in on the spectrum of what I have doesn't work now, and I've heard what you have does work. That's usually where it starts.

They also strongly believe and are quite tired of what they believe the reality is, my IP is in danger, and I'm getting no value. It's like -- and this is -- when we started talking about sovereignty, this was kind of -- this was something that was being expressed, they felt, but they didn't know how to articulate. Now it's something they articulated and they've gone from anger to action. It's like they've gone from thinking, hey, I'm not in a great marriage, to I'm at the divorce. And like, they come.

And then what's very special now is they're surrounded by people who've had the same journey, and the time line from interaction to them buying pilots or going into production is completely shifted. And so what, like, Ryan and I are seeing on the front line in commercial is this much quicker interaction, much quicker to deployment, shorter duration of the contract, but then an ability to expand that contract dramatically. Because as soon as you go in there and you show them that you can, for example, train open-weight models in our Ontology, those models are valuable and you have beyond frontier capacity without losing the alpha, you just are hooked.

What we have to do internally is figure out how to re-resource our company to focus exclusively on those people because we don't have even the bandwidth to do that. So -- but that's because, like, every single time we go into the conference, like in the past, you would be -- we go into a conference and people are like warm leads turn into hot leads. This is like first date into bed kind of thing. Maybe that's not the right metaphor for this, but it's like -- it's a very different jam.

It's like we've -- put this way, we've gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team kind of thing. I mean, not that I did that. But this is like a completely different jam of, like, what's going on. And then it's also different on our end because we know we can deliver on use cases no one else can deliver on. So like even today, we're going over a use case after use case with like a supermajor, like, one of the most important companies, and I'm going to go see them.

And basically, it's like I'm going to -- instead of saying, hey, which is like, let's just get started. You have this crucial problem for your business. We know we can deliver on this in weeks. This will change the trajectory of your business. And it's, in a weird way, it's much, much closer to what we were doing in the beginning in the U.S. government, where we're like, hey, we're just going to get started. We knew we could prove it with PG and then we -- but it's like at a much more massive scale. So instead of being, like, $250,000, it's like $25 million to start.

And honestly, the general vibe is if this actually works, it's worth of infinite value, and it will work. And quite frankly, I do not see how other offerings are going to work because this is both product and artistry. It's not -- that's why these numbers are so bombastic. It's not like some static, like when Shyam's on the front line doing implementations or Ryan is structuring these -- I mean, Ryan was so busy in the last couple days of last quarter, he couldn't get out of his car. We were like -- I was about to send over a bottle, so he could, like, take care of nature.

It was like -- it's like that on the front line. Like, I'm not even -- I'm not exaggerating. It's like -- I'm like, Ryan was on his way to work and, like, he had to pull over. He drives a fancy car. I mean, look at that. It's -- but he literally had to pull over. And that's just what's going on. And -- but again, I know like the primary focus of your interest here is financial, but there's the flip side. The other stuff is not working. That's part of -- it's not just that our thing is unique.

It's -- there's a very strong sense in the market that these other approaches, fake deploy codes, token, raw usage, lightweight companies reselling tokens, software companies that are reselling tokens and accounts as revenue, people are just tired of it. And I'll tell you, last not least, the taste of the market is shifting. Like, people really do grow to like what works. I mean, look at the success in the Department of War. It's like, that was -- we shifted the taste. That's what's happening in U.S. comm. That's what's explaining the numbers. And that's what -- if you like people watching this, you should come to one of our AIP Sovereign.

Ana Soro: Our next question is from Gil with D.A. Davidson.

Gil Luria: I want to build on that conversation you had with Dan. You talked to him about one type of CEO, the one that comes to you with an urgency around sovereignty. But as reading the Anthropic S-1 will tell us about half of their customers work directly with Anthropic. So when you have a -- which means there's a lot of CEOs that haven't gotten the message. To your point, you're in the first inning of this conversation. When you get a CEO that's still unconvinced, what kind of analogies and metaphors can you use to help them understand the importance of this diffusion layer, orchestration harnesses coming from you and not directly from the lab?

What kind of examples do you have to provide them to understand the risk?

Alexander Karp: There's 2 parts to your question, which is, like, the person who's not convinced or not yet convinced, and then what do we do? The weird thing here, though, is we really cannot satiate demand. So this is a market that is growing so rapidly. We don't need the people who aren't convinced. We really don't. And by the way, and again, I say this every time, Dario is someone I get along very well with. I think he's one of the most important business people of my generation, if not multiple generations. They are also selling our product because people interact with them. And again, some people want that approach.

But a lot of people are super concerned about their alpha being transferred to them. And the results -- even the results they talk about are often already in our application layer. We work very effectively with Anthropic and the Department of War and at AIG and all over the place. But again, the primary -- what they are doing is increasing the size of the market. What we're doing is servicing the market that's gotten real. And we are actually in a symbiotic relationship with them commercially because they're growing a market that's probably much, much bigger than it will be -- than it is today.

And we're taking advantage of the market where you really need delivery, where delivery also includes. Now if there is somebody -- we don't -- we really do convincing in the government space, like, we've been on the front line, like, certain agencies didn't want to adopt, and we knew the war fighters would die if they didn't adopt. So we went to convince them. In commercial, our real approach is, hey, enjoy the one you're with until you just -- you find out it's not the one you want. There are very, very, very few times where we're trying to go and compete and take their customer away. It really is not happening.

And conversely, once you go Palantir, you don't go back. And that's just -- that's how it is. And you see it in our numbers, which is -- so it's -- this is a very different thing. I don't know at what point we become competitive with each other. But at this point in the U.S., the market for us is insatiable. And it's insatiable and growing and growing and growing. There's 2 ways to look at our numbers. One is to say we are just sublime at what we do. Another way is to say we're very unique and the market is exploding around us. I'm much more in the latter camp.

Like, I don't -- we are a creative colony. We're not perfect. But the market is exploding around us, and they are helping it explode. And the only area where we do anything that looks competitive is we are spending a lot of time educating clients, partners that may -- that are non-partners around the risks of using closed models without an application layer. That's the one thing we do, do actively. So -- but we're not really saying, hey, you're going to -- the value creation, people know we own. It's certainly an industry, I think less on Wall Street.

Actually, honestly, I think on Wall Street, I don't mean you, but I think really what happened on Wall Street is everybody invested in these firms early, bless you guys. It's hard to see the reality when you're getting rich on something that's not actually working the way you think it is. And the reality is, though, in industry, people realize when it gets real, you need us. And that market is much larger than we can service.

Ana Soro: Our last question is from Brad with Deutsche Bank.

Brad Zelnick: Congrats on another rocket ship quarter. Alex, in your shareholder letter, you said that you see Palantir as the pioneers of a genuine and viable anti-war movement. Can you expand on what that means and what it might mean for your government business?

Alexander Karp: Well, one of -- and I'll let Shyam talk about this. I'll go back to the beginning of our Palantir PG. And we built products that would protect civil liberties and stop terrorism for the very simple reason that you don't want to do one or the other. If you don't stop terrorism, you're going to get a radical fringe on the right. If you stop terrorism without rights, none of us want that. Okay. You could say it's an anti-terror product or you could say it's a product for social cohesion.

It's this product for -- our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that, in fact, it's not worth going to war and also to create social cohesion because we're going to bring back our troops healthier, safer, non-damaged and that makes our society much more effective. And I would say as a person, not as, like, Palantir, I grew up as a lefty. I don't actually like war. I want to avoid war. I do not support wars. Sometimes they are necessary. And when they are necessary, America and its allies need the very, very, very best tools. And we have competitors, adversaries and enemies out there.

They need to know our stuff works. The way to stop a war is for them to know these things work. And also, part of the problem that we've had in an AI discussion in this country is we do have a rival and adversary on the battlefield. I happen to respect their culture quite a bit, China, but it is us or them. And they have a dynamic, interesting super high IQ scaled culture that is doing exceedingly well at AI. And we've got to make sure we're the leaders.

And somehow, we have to drag our European and other allies with us, which is going to be hard because they're going to have to also learn how these things work, and that probably means a real interaction with the leader of the sovereign movement, not some fake bureaucratic thing made up by people who have no idea what they're talking about and think you can regulate these things like a telecom industry when, in fact, this is galvanizing a new transformative technology that is transforming every part of society and transferring our numbers and everything it touches.

Ana Soro: Thank you. Alex, as always, we have a lot of individual investors online.

Alexander Karp: Somebody else has got to talk.

Ana Soro: Is there anything -- anyone would like to say before I end the call?

Alexander Karp: Maybe you guys can say a couple words. Shyam, would you like to say?

Shyam Sankar: Well, I mean, you spoke about deterrence really well. I guess I would just add that, of course, the objective is to deter conflict. Deterrence is not something you accomplish by hope. You actually have to build it brick by brick. And so on one end, in the foxhole, that's about having a capability that's 10x, 100x better than your adversary. Should they choose to fight, they're going to lose, and therefore, they should not choose to fight. And on the other end, it comes down to the factory floor. Deterrent conflict, as we've seen with Russia and Ukraine, is really about your ability to produce the materiel.

And we are in a period where we need to reinvent how we do production. We've gone through 30, 40 years of essentially deindustrialization in the nation beyond just our defense industrial base. And the work that we're doing with war machine and working with commercial and private and public sector companies in order to enable production using a modern American manufacturing stack. These are 2 parts of the same coin here. And I think it comes down to, yes, freedom driven through the foxhole, but also prosperity, the growth of the American economy on the back of that.

Alexander Karp: Do you want to say something? Would you like to talk about your greed afterwards?

Ryan Taylor: I'll just add, the Sovereign AI revolution, we launched this last quarter and the felt version on the ground is -- and what we're seeing at Sovereign AI boot camps when we actually show and don't tell is the momentum and the urgency of customers that get it and see it, adopting quickly, moving quickly, moving with urgency because they realize how much it matters. And we're feeling that on the ground, and we're at the very beginning of this, and we only see that continuing and expanding from here.

Shyam Sankar: And because I can't help myself, I'll say one more thing, going back to Gil's question. I mentioned this earlier in my comments, but it really is the case that I think one of the conceits that the labs don't have right and that perhaps the customers who don't quite yet realize that the return is not there, is that the atomic unit of the enterprise is not the knowledge worker. You can make people more productive and generate no actual return on investment. If you're measuring the inputs, it can feel really good to see that productivity of the person. You actually -- the atomic unit is the workflow.

And having a platform like AIP, where you're already managing your supply chain or your S&OP or your key enterprise processes, the exhaust of those processes then enable you to go through the post-training loop to have a model that's better than frontier at that. We give you the tools to elegantly integrate your people, your AI and the software to actually drive objective, quantifiable value against the workflow. This is the compounding loop that the customers who are coming to us in the Sovereign Bootcamps really understand.

Just at our most recent DevCon down in Miami, we had a customer who, on their stack in production as a hackweek project, built a production-ready model that's better than frontier for their use case in the 48 hours. Single person, in the 48 hours that was DevCon. So the proof is everywhere on this.

David Glazer: And I guess to add 2 financial metrics to leave you with, I'd say, 2 years ago on net income and to today, we've 8x-ed our net income over the last 2 years, which I am incredibly proud of as well as everything else that was said. And also, as we look at sort of this year to basically guide to almost $5 billion in cash flow for the full year is, I think, something we all can be excited about.

Alexander Karp: And to close, I just -- the people who invested in us early, many of them were investing their own money and would otherwise be called retail, and many now and recently have reinvested in us. The sovereign revolution is a metaphor for your interaction with Palantir. And the fact that we've been able to help you and you've been able to help us in your own wealth creation and in our journey and that you've defended us against what obviously now look like ridiculously stupid and malicious, incredibly hard-to-understand attacks is something that we will never forget.

And part of the delivery here, part of what motivates me is helping to make sure we are fighting for you and, quite frankly, making sure that the people that made fun of you and made fun of us are suffering. And I'm very proud of that, and I'm very proud to have all of you along with us, and thank you for that support.

Ana Soro: Thank you. That concludes today's call.

#3204. SCOTUS sets hearing date for Apple’s appeal in Epic Games case

The U.S. Supreme Court has officially scheduled oral arguments in Apple’s appeal in its long-running legal battle with Epic Games. Here are the details.

Back in 2020, Epic Games sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store for introducing an alternative in-app payment system through a remotely activated update.

The following year, despite ruling in Apple’s favor on nine of Epic’s ten claims, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled that Apple could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment options outside the App Store.

As a result, Apple changed its rules to allow external purchase links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on transactions completed through them, along with restrictions on how those links could be presented.

Epic challenged Apple’s implementation, and the district court agreed. In April 2025, Judge Rogers ordered Apple to remove those restrictions and stop charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store, finding the company in civil contempt for violating the original injunction.

Since then, Apple has allowed developers to direct users to external payment options in the US App Store without charging a commission, while continuing to challenge the contempt ruling.

After unsuccessful attempts before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, Apple eventually took its case to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to review whether Apple could be held in contempt for violating the “spirit” of an injunction, even when its text did not specifically prohibit the conduct in question.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only review the civil contempt ruling, not how much, if anything, Apple can charge developers for purchases made outside the App Store. That issue is being handled separately by the district court, after the Ninth Circuit overturned the blanket ban on commissions in December.

Earlier today, the Supreme Court’s official docket for the case was updated with a date for oral arguments.

According to the filing, Apple and Epic Games will present their arguments before the Supreme Court on Monday, January 11, 2027, though both sides have already outlined many of their arguments in recent filings.

In September, Apple filed its opening brief with the Supreme Court, arguing that the contempt ruling should be overturned because the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit it from charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store.

In its brief, Apple cited multiple court decisions to support its argument that a party cannot be held in civil contempt unless an injunction clearly prohibits the conduct in question.

A few days after Apple’s filing, the US Department of Justice and several legal and business groups also submitted briefs supporting at least part of the company’s argument.

The DOJ, however, also argued that the lower courts were right to hold Apple in contempt over some of its restrictions on external purchase links, including a requirement that developers use what Apple called “plain buttons,” which could not have contrasting backgrounds.

With the hearing now scheduled, the case is one step closer to a final decision from the Supreme Court. However, both sides still have some paperwork to submit before then, as Epic Games has until November 13 to file its brief responding to Apple’s arguments, while Apple’s reply is due December 14.

#3202. Bioventus (BVS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Pain treatments drove 3% revenue growth as management targets $100M+ for nerve stimulation.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Bioventus Inc. (BVS -1.31%) reported third quarter results characterized by modest top-line growth and expanded profitability margins as management continues to execute its strategy across four primary growth drivers. The company focused on accelerating revenue in peripheral nerve stimulation, platelet-rich plasma, ultrasonics, and international markets while maintaining operating discipline to offset increased strategic investments. Management noted that significant cash flow generation enabled the company to achieve a financial milestone by reducing net debt to below $200 million. During the call, the company confirmed that its ongoing review of strategic alternatives remains active following prior expressions of interest, though no specific timeline for a conclusion was provided.

Generally Accepted Accounting Principles or GAAP. We generally refer to these as non GAAP or adjusted financial measures. And now I will turn the call over to Robert.

Robert Claypoole: Good afternoon, everyone, and thanks for joining our call today. Bioventus continued to build on its positive momentum in the third quarter. Delivering a solid financial performance and encouraging leading indicators across our growth drivers. These results reinforce our conviction in our ability to create sustainable long term value for shareholders. Before going through the details on the third quarter, I will take a moment to provide a brief update on the strategic review we disclosed on our Q2 earnings call. With the assistance of our advisers, we continue to evaluate a range of strategic options for the company. We are not able to provide further details at this time, and we will not be answering any questions regarding the strategic review. 1, accelerating long term revenue growth with increased investment in the 4 growth drivers peripheral nerve stimulation, platelet rich plasma, ultrasonics, and our international business, 2, increasing earnings even with a higher level of investment in these 4 growth drivers; and 3, continuing to strengthen cash flow and enhance capital allocation optionality. Let me expand on each priority starting with accelerating long term revenue growth. Overall, third quarter revenue grew 3%, led by strong growth of 6% in pain treatments. This performance was partially offset by softness in bone graft substitutes down 6% for the quarter, reflecting strong underlying momentum within each of the growth drivers.

Let me highlight a few examples of the progress we are achieving with the growth drivers starting with platelet rich plasma, where momentum continues to build with sequential growth in the number of capital placements. Even more encouraging is the meaningful ramp up in disposable reorders. During the third quarter, revenue from PRP disposable kits exceeded revenue from capital placements. Which is an important indicator of future growth. We are pleased to see the growing adoption of our customizable solution and its potential to displace competitive offerings. This agreement broadens the addressable market and creates an additional avenue for growth as we continue to build commercial momentum. Next, our PNS business continues to gain traction strengthening our confidence in both the market opportunity and the vast potential for our product offering. Physician feedback is very encouraging as clinicians gain more experience with Talisman, providing further validation of our differentiated technology and launch strategy. Key performance indicators reinforce this progress. Trial to permanent conversion rates are exceeding plan, the time from trial to permanent implant placement has shortened, and the number of physicians trained grew by more than 50% quarter over quarter. Collectively, these trends point to growing physician engagement and improving conversion efficiency.

Key drivers for continued revenue growth acceleration. We have also strengthened PNS leadership and commercial capabilities by hiring a best in class marketing leader, expanding our commercial infrastructure, equipping the team with more effective competitive selling and targeting tools, and increasing our presence at key medical congresses and industry meetings. Learning within the initial launch phase combined with these investments position us to accelerate market adoption and capitalize on this significant growth opportunity. Turning to Ultrasonics. We saw very strong double digit revenue growth this quarter. Investments in marketing and surgeon training are driving increased surgeon adoption. We expect this momentum to continue into the fourth quarter paving the way for further growth acceleration in 2027. Finally, international revenue accelerated 16% in Q3. As we begin to see the impact from talent additions, and the team's successful focus on select markets. We are encouraged by the speed of execution the depth of the opportunity pipeline, and our customer win rates. We expect to deliver strong double digit growth in the fourth quarter, and for the full year. Turning to our second priority, increasing earnings even as we invest in future growth drivers. The third quarter again demonstrated the underlying earnings power and resilience of BioVentes' business.

Despite increased investment in the growth initiatives, we delivered an adjusted EBITDA margin of 20%, an improvement of 70 basis points compared to the prior year period. Looking ahead, we now expect full year adjusted EBITDA margin to be above the prior year level. Reflecting our ability to balance strategic investment with operating discipline. With strong operating performance, and significant interest expense savings, we delivered adjusted EPS of $0.17 in the quarter. Which advanced 13% versus the prior year. And on a year to date basis, adjusted EPS has increased by 18%, underscoring our continued ability to grow earnings while investing in the opportunities that will drive long term value for shareholders.

As we close out the year, we expect to see sequential acceleration in revenue growth and earnings while continuing to increase our investments to drive growth, and deliver on the full year adjusted EPS guidance we provided the beginning of the year. This reflects the strength of our business model. Supported by the earnings power generated from solid revenue growth, our stable peer leading gross margin, and the disciplined focus on operating expense management. Turning to our third priority, accelerated cash flow. We delivered another strong quarter with cash from operations of $21 million. This strong cash generation funded the repayment of $19 million of our term loan, bringing year to date term loan repayments to $65 million.

This enabled us to achieve an important financial milestone of lowering net debt at the end of the quarter to below $200 million Overall, we continue to execute on our strategic priorities. Driving increased conviction in our strategy and growing confidence in the strength of the portfolio and investment approach, as we build Bioventus into a leading $1 billion med tech company that delivers exceptional value for customers, employees, shareholders, and all other stakeholders. She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

#3200. Advanced Energy (AEIS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Revenue surged 50% year-over-year to $696.4 million; non-GAAP EPS more than doubled.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Advanced Energy Industries, Inc. (AEIS -2.19%) reported record third quarter financial results that exceeded management's guidance ranges for revenue, gross margin, and earnings per share. Management reported sequential revenue growth in all target markets and raised the 2026 total revenue growth outlook to approximately 40%. The company is scaling its 500,000 square foot Thailand facility to become the largest factory in its global network while advancing strategic initiatives in 800-volt data center solutions and leading-edge semiconductor power systems. Management indicated that operational performance and supply chain resilience have become competitive advantages in securing new design wins at advanced nodes.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Advanced Energy Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce Edwin Mok, Vice President of Strategic Marketing and IR. Please go ahead.

Yeuk-Fai Mok: Thank you, operator. Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to the Advanced Energy Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. With me today are Steve Kelley, our President and CEO; and Paul Oldham, our Executive Vice President and CFO. You can find today's earnings press release and presentation on our website at ir.advancedenergy.com. Before we begin, let me remind you that today's call contains forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially and are not guarantees of future performance. Information concerning these risks can be found in our SEC filings. All forward-looking statements are based on management's estimates as of today, November 2, 2026, and the company assumes no obligation to update them.

Any targets beyond the current quarter presented today should not be interpreted as guidance. On today's call, our financial results are presented on a non-GAAP basis unless otherwise specified. Detailed reconciliation between our GAAP and non-GAAP results can be found in today's press release. With that, let me pass the call to our President and CEO, Steve Kelley.

Stephen Kelley: Thanks, Edwin. Good afternoon, everyone, and thanks for joining the call. We delivered a record third quarter with revenue and earnings above the high end of guidance. Strong factory execution enabled us to meet increased customer demand. Total revenue grew over $120 million sequentially. Revenue in each of our target markets grew sequentially and year-over-year. Earnings per share more than doubled from a year ago, largely due to higher volume and operational leverage. Over the past year, we invested in capacity expansion and strategic piece part inventory. These investments are enabling higher revenue, increased profitability and greater customer satisfaction. In 2026, our execution and supply chain resilience have become competitive advantages.

Our new flagship factory in Thailand is beginning to generate revenue. Multiple data center customers have already qualified the factory and semiconductor customers are expected to follow shortly. Our Thailand production lines are being brought up by subject matter experts from around the world. After recently visiting the factory, I have no doubt that Thailand can become the largest and most efficient factory in our network, a true flagship. In addition, we continue to increase output at our factories in the Philippines, Malaysia and Mexico. We are expanding our footprint and becoming more efficient in all 3 locations.

The result is that we are on track to expand our total revenue-generating capacity to over $5 billion by the end of 2028. Demand is strong across all of our target markets. We are benefiting from significant market tailwinds across Semiconductor, Data Center and I&M. In addition, we believe that our new products will drive market share gains. In Semiconductor and Data Center, customers are projecting that demand will continue to strengthen through 2027 into '28. In Industrial & Medical, we experienced our fourth consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth, a trend we expect to continue into 2027. Now let me provide some color on each of our markets.

In semiconductor, we delivered another record quarter with year-on-year growth of over 60%. Increased investment in leading-edge wafer capacity is driving record demand for AE products. Our operational performance in this market has been solid, and we've been recognized by major customers for our ability to keep pace with increasing demand. During the quarter, we won several plasma power designs for advanced node processes, the culmination of multiyear design efforts. We believe that these wins will accelerate our growth as leading-edge processes begin to ramp their production in 2027. We secured 2 additional wins in semiconductor test, the latest in a series of test-related wins.

The power required to test AI chips and modules has increased meaningfully, driving the need for high power density, high-efficiency custom solutions from Advanced Energy. We expect our new plasma power and system power products to drive market share gains over the next several years. In Data Center computing, revenue grew almost 50% year-on-year. Increased demand and factory execution drove the outperformance. Our business with hyperscale customers continues to strengthen with multiple new programs driving revenue growth this year and into 2027 and '28. We also expanded our growing list of second-wave customers with several new wins secured in the third quarter. We expect that revenue from second-wave customers will add to hyperscale revenue beginning next year.

At the OCP Global Summit last month, we showcased our 800-volt power distribution board. With industry-leading power density, efficiency and reliability, our modular solutions can be customized rapidly to meet the evolving requirements of 800-volt architectures. We also highlighted our liquid-cooled power technology, which can be applied in both 50-volt and 800-volt systems, providing customers with optionality as they transition to higher-powered racks. Looking to 2027 and beyond, we expect Data Center revenue will continue to grow substantially, driven by 3 factors: growth from next-generation hyperscale programs, revenue from second-wave customers and the eventual ramp of 800-volt solutions. In Industrial & Medical, revenue grew sequentially and year-over-year.

Factory execution continues to improve, allowing us to meet growing demand and work down our overdue backlog. We expect robust market conditions to continue into 2027. In the Distribution channel, which accounts for roughly half of I&M revenue, distributor resales continue to outpace our sales into the channel. In the third quarter, we secured multiple design wins in medical imaging, life sciences, test and measurement, and mil/aero applications. In September, we launched our Defiant Future Family of ruggedized power supplies for aerospace and defense applications, which we expect will generate significant revenue for AE in the coming years. To expand our customer reach, we continue to invest in digital marketing.

Today, an increasing number of our I&M design wins originate as web leads, and some of those wins have turned into multimillion dollar opportunities. In Telecom & Networking, revenue grew sequentially as AI-related applications drove increased customer demand. Now for some closing thoughts. We are executing well to meet increased demand across all of our target markets. As a result, we have increased our 2026 growth outlook to around 40%. Looking ahead, based on customer forecasts and feedback, we believe that strong investments in AI data center and leading-edge wafer capacity will continue through 2027 into '28. We are expanding capacity by ramping up our Thailand factory as well as increasing output at our other factories.

We believe that we have enough capacity to deliver sizable upside over the next several quarters, assuming adequate supply of key components. We will continue to invest heavily in R&D. We believe that these investments will enable us to deliver differentiated products to our customers and gain share across all of our target markets. Leveraging increased product value, improved manufacturing efficiency and higher volume, we have line of sight to over 43% gross margin. Finally, we remain active in pursuing potential acquisitions, which make strategic and financial sense. Paul will now provide more detailed financial information.

Paul Oldham: Thank you, Steve, and good afternoon, everyone. In the third quarter, we delivered record financial results that exceeded the high end of our revenue, gross margin and EPS guidance ranges. Revenue of $696 million increased more than 50% year-over-year and earnings of $3.65 per share more than doubled. Gross margin improved 300 basis points year-on-year to 42.1%, contributing to record operating income. Operating margin reached 24.4%, the highest level in recent years. And we generated operating cash flow of $66 million while continuing to invest in strategic inventory to support expected customer ramps. Now let's review our third quarter financial results in more detail.

Total revenue of $696 million increased 21% or $122 million sequentially, well above the high end of our guidance range. Solid execution allowed us to meet increasing customer demand and capture upside to our guidance. Semiconductor revenue was a record $322 million, up 16% quarter-over-quarter and 64% year-over-year. Strong demand for leading-edge equipment, increasing etch and deposition intensity and expanding system power revenue continued to drive robust growth. Data Center computing revenue of $256 million was also a record, up 34% sequentially and 49% year-over-year. Increasing customer demand and the initial ramp of new programs are driving higher revenues.

Industrial & Medical revenue was $91 million, up 13% from last quarter and 27% from last year as we increased output to support growing customer demand. Telecom & Networking revenue was up 13% sequentially and 15% year-over-year to $28 million, driven by AI-related programs. Gross margin in the third quarter was 42.1%. Excluding the benefit of Q2 tariff refunds, gross margin expanded 140 basis points, driven by higher volume and manufacturing efficiency. Operating expense of $123 million was within our guidance range and increased slightly quarter-over-quarter due to R&D program spending and higher variable costs. With strong top line growth, gross margin expansion and OpEx leverage, our operating margin expanded 760 basis points year-on-year to 24.4%.

As a result, third quarter operating income increased 118% year-over-year to reach a record $170 million. Depreciation was $12.2 million, and our adjusted EBITDA was $182 million. Other income was $8 million, up from $5 million in Q2, mainly due to a full quarter of higher-interest income and lower-interest expense following our convertible note offering in Q2. For Q3, our non-GAAP tax rate was 15.7%, in line with our guidance. Third quarter earnings were $3.65 per share, up meaningfully from $2.74 last quarter and $1.74 a year ago. Turning now to the balance sheet. Following the end of Q3, we redeemed the remaining $136 million of our 2028 convertible senior notes, including unwinding the related note hedge and warrants.

Since the settlement occurred on October 2, this remaining debt and related cash are included on our Q3 balance sheet. As a result, total cash and equivalents were $1.42 billion and net cash was $159 million, both up from Q2. Inventory days decreased 1 day sequentially to 144 and turns stayed at 2.5x. We expect inventory turns to remain around these levels over the next few quarters. Days sales outstanding decreased 2 days to 61 days and days payable outstanding decreased 4 days to 81 days. Q3 net working capital was up 1 day to 124 days. As a result, Q3 cash flow from continuing operations was $66 million.

During the third quarter, we paid $4.1 million in quarterly dividends and invested $31 million in CapEx to support the production ramp in our factories. For the full year 2026, we now expect capital investments to be towards the low end of our $180 million to $195 million range on timing of expenditures. However, we will continue to invest at an elevated level throughout 2027 as we add capacity towards our target of over $5 billion in annual output. Following the 2028 convertible note redemption, we resumed our opportunistic share repurchase program. And in the month of October, we repurchased approximately $30 million of our common stock at around $241 per share. Turning now to our guidance.

Demand continues to strengthen across our markets with initial production of several new product programs contributing to revenue growth. As a result, we are forecasting fourth quarter revenue to be approximately $735 million, plus or minus $25 million. We now expect 2026 total revenue to grow around 40%, up from our previous target of low to mid-30%. Driven by increased customer demand, Semiconductor revenue is now projected to grow over 60% year-on-year in the second half, up from the prior outlook of 50%. Our outlook implies semiconductor product revenue, excluding service, will grow by around 45% in 2026. Following a strong Q3, we expect fourth quarter data center computing revenue to increase further.

As a result, we are raising our 2026 data center revenue growth to the high 50% range. In Industrial & Medical, we continue to expect year-on-year revenue growth for the next few quarters. And in Telecom & Networking, revenue is expected to moderate slightly after the stronger Q3. We expect Q4 gross margin to be in the 42% to 42.5% range. We expect Q4 operating expenses to increase to $126 million to $128 million due primarily to investments in new products. We expect other income to be approximately $8 million and continue to target a tax rate in the 16% range over the next several quarters.

As a result, we expect Q4 non-GAAP earnings per share to be $3.90, plus or minus $0.30 on 41.2 million shares outstanding. Our Q4 guidance puts us on a run rate to exceed our 2030 target model, 3 years ahead of our original plan. Let me finish with some concluding comments. We are executing well to meet a strengthening demand environment across our markets. After strong growth in 2025, we are on track to deliver 40% revenue growth and over 90% earnings per share growth in 2026. Current customer forecasts suggest 2027 revenue growth will be robust, and we continue to expect earnings per share to grow faster than revenue.

With higher-value new products still ramping and plans to further improve manufacturing efficiency, gross margin is on track to reach and eventually surpass our target of over 43%. Our strategies continue to position Advanced Energy for growth and increase our resilience in all market conditions. These strategies include diversifying into an expanding set of growing markets centered on our core competencies in precision power conversion, investing in leading-edge technologies and platforms and expanding our customer reach through our digital platform. In addition, we are building out a scalable best-in-class manufacturing footprint, strengthening our supply chain, investing in inventory to mitigate risk and fortifying our balance sheet with low-cost capital.

As a result, we are well positioned to gain share and outgrow our markets. With that, we will now take your questions. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question is from Krish Sankar with TD Cowen.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan: Congrats on the great results. Steve or Paul, my first question is, given your guidance very impressive. It looks like sequentially semi grows probably mid-single digits, Data Center probably grows like 10%. I'm just wondering, are those in the ballpark? And given the visibility you have, any thoughts into quantifying semi and data center power supply growth in 2027?

Paul Oldham: Yes. I think you're in the right ballpark for Q4 sequential numbers. I think that's in the right range and consistent with the overall number we gave. For 2027, we think that growth will continue to be robust. I think last quarter, we said we expect it to be over 20%. Directionally, we think that's probably around 30% at this point. Generally, we'd expect that to have sequential growth as we go through the year. But as you know, it's not linear necessarily based on supply constraints and product transitions. Having said all that, it's a pretty strong demand environment and demand growth could likely be higher than that number.

But we also -- there is some uncertainty regarding supply, which makes it difficult to give really actual specific guidance for 2027. But directionally, that's how we're thinking about it.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan: Got it. And just as a follow-up, within the 30% range for next year, how to think about Data Center and Semi and I&M?

Paul Oldham: Well, I think, again, we're not giving any guidance by market at this point, but you can look at relative growth from this year. You can also look at comments made externally about projected WFE growth and Data Center growth. Obviously, I&M will grow slower than those, and we expect Telecom & Networking to be about flat. So we're not breaking it down at this point just because it's looking forward into the next year. But I think you can get a pretty good idea of how that breakdown could look.

Operator: Our next question is from Matthew Prisco with Cantor Fitzgerald.

Matthew Prisco: On the Semi side, can you maybe offer some color on what type of visibility you're seeing today? And maybe how do the discussed wins impact your ability to grow versus WFE in '27?

Stephen Kelley: Yes, Matt, this is Steve. I think the visibility we have into '27 from our semi customers is excellent. They've given us detailed forecast for the entire year. And as we look into '28, we don't have a forecast by part type, but we have directional guidance that it continues to go up from '27. So I think it's quite good. For us, we're benefiting from 2 things. One is obviously the market surge. And most of that is coming from our older products, and we're executing on that, and that's benefiting our top line and our bottom line. But in addition, we're starting to see new products become a significant factor.

So, as we look into '27, we believe that more than 10% of our semi revenue will come from new products. So those new products basically are the way we're going to gain share over the next 5 years. And most of those new products are going into advanced logic and memory processes. In addition, we have the new products on the system power side, where we've been designed into a variety of tester, burn-in and process equipment applications.

Matthew Prisco: Great. And then maybe over to the Data Center. How are you thinking about those second-wave ramps and the magnitude of contribution there in 2027 based on current conversations?

Stephen Kelley: Yes. So on the second-wave ramps, again, let's go back, I'll just define it for folks. These are basically all the customers we have for data center products, except for the hyperscalers. These encompass enterprise, networking, neoclouds, et cetera. And we believe that over time, that altogether, these second-wave customers could generate more than $300 million in yearly revenue. That's not going to happen next year, but we think by '29, that's the case. So, I would say every quarter that goes by, we add to our roster of second-wave customers. So, we're qualified in the early shipment phase for multiple second-wave customers. And some of that's in Thailand and some of it's in the Philippines.

A lot of great opportunities. What I can say as we look into '27 is that we have a relatively small amount of revenue in our forecast for the second-wave customers because we don't understand at this point which of those customers will ramp the volume and which may be constrained by other factors. So, we have some in our forecast, but we're not dependent on second-wave revenue to meet our outlook for '27.

Operator: Our next question is from Scott Graham from Seaport Research Partners.

Scott Graham: So, I was just wondering, Steve, when you talk about we see strong growth in '27, '28. You're saying '28 is a growth year in that statement as well for Semi and data centers, right?

Stephen Kelley: Yes, I was commenting on Semi in particular, when I made that statement. But we do believe that's the growth year for data centers as well.

Scott Graham: Okay. All right. So even though you can't put a number on it, '28 should be another growth year for your 2 largest segments. Okay. Two most important segments for growth. So, the other question I had is more of a on math, if you don't mind, Paul. Was there like a credit -- a non-GAAP credit that rolled through the earnings this quarter for taxes?

Paul Oldham: Yes. There was actually a charge in taxes on a GAAP basis associated with the deferred tax asset that we had to write down a bit because we were able to lower our long-term tax rate in one of the jurisdictions. So that was -- we treated that as a onetime GAAP-only item. And so that's why our GAAP tax rate was higher at almost 24%, 23.7% versus our non-GAAP tax rate.

Scott Graham: Okay. So if I were to reverse the sign on that number, essentially take a 30% hit on what your charges are, that would be like $0.30, $0.35 a share swing. You're not saying that the non-GAAP is $0.30 to $0.35 higher because of that, are you?

Paul Oldham: I mean we reported our non-GAAP number, which you see there. And in the tax, if you look at the difference between the GAAP tax rate and the non-GAAP tax rate, the GAAP tax rate was 15.7% and the non-GAAP tax rate was 23.7% -- I'm sorry, the other way around, non-GAAP was 15.7% and GAAP was 23.6%. And that was entirely a function of this onetime charge for deferred noncash charge for deferred tax asset that we wrote down because we're getting a lower rate in the future in one of our jurisdictions.

Operator: Our next question is from Elizabeth Sun with Citi.

Yiling Sun: I guess my first question is in the longer term for Data Center. I think you've talked about hyperscalers growth to talk about second-wave of customers. And at OCP, you showcased some -- as David mentioned as well, like you showcased some solutions for 800 direct to server. So, I'm just curious, after moving to 800 volt, is there any opportunities to expand -- further expand your customer base beyond hyperscalers and second-wave customers like neoclouds or enterprise?

Stephen Kelley: Yes. Thanks for the question, Elizabeth. Yes, you're right. At OCP, we had a number of products on display. Probably the most important one was something called the Power Distribution Board, which is designed for customers who are moving to 800 volts or to somewhere in between. So, we see a lot of customers who are looking for transitional solutions where they may need to accommodate multiple power supplies, multiple different supply voltages. And so, our Power Distribution Board is interesting because it's modular and it's easily customizable. It's basically a mix and match approach to 800 volts and the interim solutions. What it features is best-in-class efficiency. We have 98% efficiency, best-in-class power density, 350 watts per cubic inch.

And then we can customize mechanicals, EMI performance and obviously, firmware. We also offer liquid cooling. So this is something that we're importing from our plasma power group. And so we've got a pretty versatile solution for customers. And those customers include hyperscalers as well as second-wave customers. So, there's quite a bit of interest in this modular approach to 800 volts.

Yiling Sun: That's great to hear. And on gross margin, I think Paul used to guide exiting this year at 42% and then next year, 43%. It seems like you are hitting 42% earlier than expected this year. I'm just curious, how should we think about gross margin trajectory for next year? And are you able to reach this 43% mark earlier than expected? And maybe like a rule of thumb is that 50% flow-through is a good way to think about it?

Paul Oldham: Yes, you're right, Elizabeth. We are hitting a little bit sooner. In fact, we guided Q4 now to 42% to 42.5%, so actually over 42% that we said last quarter. At this point, we still think we have an exit rate of 43% next year. That could be slightly higher or could come a little earlier. It will depend on volume. And you're right, it's just under 50% leverage to gross margin sort of in the high 40s would be the drop-through rate.

Yeuk-Fai Mok: Our next question is from James Ricchiuti with Needham & Company.

Stephen Kelley: Jim, are you there? Jim, your line is breaking up. Can you try again?

James Ricchiuti: Yes. Is this any better?

James Ricchiuti: Terrific. Yes, question is about Thailand. And I'm wondering, Steve, if you could talk to how many customers or data center customers are qualified, -- how many hyperscalers, how many of the next tier. But it sounds like you're seeing pretty good. You're making good progress there. So if you can give us any color on that.

Stephen Kelley: Yes, I'd be happy to, Jim. I was just out there a couple of weeks ago, and I saw products coming off the line for 2 different data center customers. So, they're already qualified. In addition, we'll have 2 of our top semi customers qualified in the next 2 to 3 months. So, we're starting out very strong in Thailand. It's a pretty impressive factory, quite frankly. It's 500,000 square feet on a single floor. So it's by far our biggest factory. The people I met were pretty amazing. We have subject matter experts from around the world who are helping to bring that factory up to speed. We're employing our best-in-class techniques from around the world there.

Warehouse is huge. And it's a linear flow. So, it's warehouse to assembly to test, to shipment. So, it's really a show place. And I think all customers will be eager to be qualified in that factory as soon as possible.

James Ricchiuti: All right. You alluded to supply chain. Obviously, that's a topic for a lot of folks. What -- are you experiencing any supply chain constraints across Semi, Data Center or for that matter, I&M?

Stephen Kelley: Yes. The short answer is yes. But the longer answer is we've been encountering supply chain issues for most of the year, but we've had pretty effective mitigation techniques. We put in place some strategic inventory based on our experiences during COVID, and our team is pretty good at chasing parts. And we've also put in place surge capacity because what we found is many of these constrained parts don't get delivered until the, let's say, the last 4 to 6 weeks of the quarter. So, we need to really push our production in the last [Technical Difficulty] some of that supply chain constraint that we won't be able to mitigate.

And so we built that into our forecast for the fourth quarter and for '27. And so we see the problem areas being isolated components, particularly ICs. We see some constraints on PCBs and also specialty ceramics.

Operator: Our next question is from Shane Brett with Morgan Stanley.

Shane Brett: My first question is on Data Center and your CPU opportunity. At your June quarter 2024 earnings, you talked about having 50% to 60% more dollar content in AI racks than we do with conventional server racks, which is still a lot of content. Is this still a valid metric in assessing your CPU opportunity? If not, how should I think about your content for CPUs versus AI accelerators? And could this sort of CPU or agentic AI opportunity become a meaningful tailwind for your data center business in 2027?

Stephen Kelley: Yes. Thank you, Shane. I would say as power supply makers, we view any reason to build an additional rack is a good thing for us essentially. So whether it's a GPU or a CPU or some other type of chip, it generally drives more demand for power supplies and other power delivery products in these racks. So, I think CPUs are a good thing for us.

Shane Brett: Got it. For my follow-up, I want to ask about semi. In prior cycles, market share between subsystems is more due to their customers' performance. But just given the pace of revisions in this WFE up cycle, it does feel as though there will be a few suppliers that can't keep up. You've clearly put yourself in a great position, but do you think there will be share gains to come from readiness as well as scale, so kind of drivers beyond just technology wins?

Stephen Kelley: Yes, Shane, that's an excellent question. And we have seen that actually because during COVID, I think we performed well from both a supply chain standpoint and an execution standpoint. And so, I think that's benefited us over the past 2 to 3 years as we've been working with key customers to design in new products because they know that we could build these products over time. And that's an important part of the equation. I think today, what we're seeing is that we're out executing many of our peers, and we like to continue to be in that position.

We've been recognized by some of our customers for our ability to keep delivering to their upside requirements over the past 9 months. And so we're happy about that, and we think it's going to help us win new slots in the Semiconductor segment.

Operator: Our next question is from Steve Barger with KeyBanc Capital Markets.

Steve Barger: Steve, it's really great to hear Thailand progressing so well. It seems like manufacturing capacity is going to be back ahead of demand in both DC and semi. So my question is, does engineering bandwidth again become the scarcer resource? And are there any attractive programs today that you're being selective about as you manage those return on engineering resources?

Stephen Kelley: Yes, Steve. I think engineering resources have always been the critical path for us, whether it's Semiconductor or Data Center. I think for us, adding capacity is not that difficult. Most of the machines that we buy are available within 3 to 6 months. The biggest hurdle was just building Thailand, and now that's open. And so I think we've got capacity which will get us through 2029 easily. So, on the capacity side, I think we're good. I think from an engineering standpoint, yes, there are opportunities that we can't address because of engineering bandwidth. But what we see are an increasing set of opportunities from our subset of hyperscale customers.

We continue to broaden our participation there, and our performance is helping us win more of those customers essentially. In addition, we have this long list of second-wave customers where we're getting design wins partially due to the technology, but also because they see our factories and like what they see.

Steve Barger: Got it. So, the factory is actually becoming kind of a competitive advantage for new product wins?

Stephen Kelley: Yes, I think it is. And after visiting the factories a couple of weeks ago, I could see where a customer would be pretty impressed by what we've done in Thailand and the improvements we made in the Philippines. I think they're world-class factories.

Steve Barger: Got it. And then you said the pace of distribution sales is outpacing your sales in I&M, which seems like a good sign. I know you've had a lot of design wins in recent quarters where you were just waiting for purchase orders to come through. Does it feel like that momentum is shifting more in your favor, broadly speaking, in I&M? And does -- I mean, are you thinking about this in terms of multiple years of double-digit growth given the share gains and new product wins that you've locked in?

Stephen Kelley: Yes. I think in I&M, that's a distinct possibility. So, we've gone through quite a transformation in our Industrial Medical business. 4, 5 years ago, we had some commodity business that was nestled in there Industrial & Medical. That's all been eliminated. So, everything you see today, all the growth is coming from high-margin new products. And so, we're getting a little bit of a tailwind, obviously, as the market recovers from the post-COVID inventory hangover. But most of what you're seeing from Advanced Energy and our outperformance is based on these new product wins we've been able to secure over the past 2 years.

So, we're pretty happy with the rate of growth in industrial application in particular, as well as semiconductor applications where they're using basically industrial medical products. And finally, we also see some interesting things happening in Medical. And so we're pretty happy with what's happening in I&M, and we see this trend continuing where we continue to grow sequentially for the foreseeable future.

Operator: Our next question is from Mehdi Hosseini with SIG.

Mehdi Hosseini: A couple of follow-ups from me. Steve, based on what your Semi OEM have reported, it seems like WFE in '27 could be closer around $200 billion, which implies a 30% to 35% year-over-year growth. What I want to ask you is a reference to your comment that 30% of your semi-cap revenue in '27 is driven by new product. And given what your OEM have communicated, does that imply that your revenue in '27 will be much stronger than what your OEM are guiding for WFE growth? And I have a follow-up.

Stephen Kelley: Yes. Okay, Mehdi. First, let's go back to the new product statement. What I said was that in 2027, we expected more than 10% of our Semi revenues to come from new products, which is our starting point on new products. I think at your larger question, with the WFE and so forth and are we growing as fast as WFE. If we go back to '26 and assuming that our current guidance in Q4 is accurate, if we strip out our service business, the actual growth in our product revenue in Semiconductor is roughly 45%. So it's higher than the overall Semi growth rate because service just doesn't grow at the same rate as the product revenue does.

As we look at '27, we think we're going to grow as fast or faster than WFE. But more importantly, over time, with all these design wins that have been confirmed over the past few months, we think we could really outpace WFE over the next 5 to 10 years based on what we've been able to secure for leading-edge memory and logic applications.

Mehdi Hosseini: Got it. And Steve, sorry, I missed the 10 -- I confused the 10% with the 30%. But going back to the semi-cap, I can't stop thinking about the post-COVID and there was a mismatch of components for your OEM that had a ripple effect for subcomponent suppliers. And you did have a backlog given the shortages. And actually, some of the same customers are experiencing the same mismatch. To what extent are you working with your OEM customers to plan for this growth into '27 and avoid mismatches or avoid any delay in complete system shipment?

Stephen Kelley: Okay. So just to clarify, you're talking more about downstream supply constraints that our customers may have as opposed to supply constraints that we have in building our boxes. Is that the question?

Mehdi Hosseini: Remember back in '22, '23, you didn't have enough power management PMIC components. Your semi-cap OEM customer also had mismatches. So, the mismatch was throughout the semi-cap supply chain, but it was more acute among your OEM customer. And I want to see what you're doing in collaboration with your OEM customer to avoid some of the challenges from back then.

Stephen Kelley: Yes. So basically, with our large OEM Semi customers, we ship into JIT bins. And so we -- our customers give us a target, basically a low and a high. And there we're allowed to ship into those bins as long as we keep the quantity within the low and the high targets. And so, what I can say is we've been keeping up there. That's why we've been recognized for our ability to keep up with our customers' demands. But I don't think we're close to the high end of those JIT bin limits. So, there's room for us to ship more, and that's something we could do. I would say we're a bit cautious.

We don't want to get too far over our skis. We want to make sure the customer has sufficient product from AE, but we don't want them to build too much inventory because we don't want to go through a correction phase.

Operator: Our next question is from Quinn Fredrickson with Baird.

Quinn Fredrickson: Steve, you mentioned showcasing liquid-cooled power technology solutions for 800-volt OCP. Our impression is you may have been included in NVIDIA's MGX liquid-cooled reference architecture. Just any color on what that might mean for you, if so?

Stephen Kelley: Well, it's always nice to be included in something like that. And we value NVIDIA as obviously a key technology partner. And hopefully, other people look at that and realize Advanced Energy has some pretty advanced liquid cooling technology, and we're ready to deploy it. So yes, I think it's great that we are recognized by NVIDIA as a technology partner.

Quinn Fredrickson: Okay. And then as we're thinking about your growth versus WFE for '27, you mentioned calculating it ex service in '26. Is there any reason to believe the service business could see better growth in '27 than what you've seen here this year where it seems like growth has been a little light of typical? And if so, why would that be the case?

Paul Oldham: Yes. If you think about service, it's really largely based on installed base, and there's some trade-off between repair and non-break fix depending on where you're at in the cycle. So, the simple answer is we would expect service to, kind of, grow in that mid-single digits to 10% every year pretty much. So, we're not counting on a big service growth rate next year. Similarly, if we ever went into a downturn or when we do, that will continue to grow. So, I think you could assume the similar relationships next year to this year.

Operator: Our next question is from Brian Chin with Stifel.

Brian Chin: Sorry, I was hopping between calls. So apologies if there's any backtracking here. But maybe firstly, on data center. In terms of the '27 commentary, it does sound like you're more constructive on data center growth in addition to semi-cap next year. Did I hear correctly that you expect strength from hyperscalers beyond your largest hyperscaler customer next year? And if so, can you expand upon that?

Stephen Kelley: Yes, Brian. I did mention that we have 2 significant customers in hyperscale. We haven't given out that number before. So very, very good that you picked that up. But yes, we're seeing strength with those 2 customers. Obviously, the revenue there could be complemented by revenue from second-wave customers as well, but we're not counting on the second-wave revenue to meet our outlook for next year. But yes, demand is very strong. In fact, we're actually having to air ship some of our power supply units because we can't keep enough in stock at the customer hub. That gives you some flavor for where we're at in the data center market.

Brian Chin: I appreciate that. And then maybe on the semi-cap side of the business, clearly some strong tone in terms of the positioning over the next several years. Can you provide any more sort of granularity about maybe wins or kind of progress specifically on the oxide etch market in terms of maybe memory or other applications?

Stephen Kelley: Yes, I'd love to. So, we've been talking about eVerest, eVoS and NavX for the last few years. And the good news is we just won some major slots here just in Q3. And this is across the board, eVerest, eVoS and NavX. And these are high-volume opportunities, which will begin to ramp next year. So, we think conductor etch, the new products begin to ramp next year as some of these leading-edge processes start to ramp. And then, we see our dielectric wins starting to ramp in '28. In addition, we've won key slots in deposition.

And the common theme, I think, for all these wins is that this new technology is required at the advanced nodes to maintain or improve throughput and to maintain and improve yield. And so there continue to be a strong pull from customers. And the other thing we've noticed is once we win one design at a customer, it starts to multiply. And it multiplies across different processes. And in addition, sometimes there's an opportunity to back integrate the technology. So, going to more recent nodes if the end customer is having any issues with throughput or yield.

So, we think we're in a very good spot with these new products, and we think that they're going to form the basis for significant market share gain over the next 5 years.

Operator: Our last question is from David Duley with Steelhead Securities.

David Duley: You partially answered this, but I was just, kind of, wondering what the key reason was that your Semi business' growth rate accelerated in the back half of this calendar year. It's, I think, 60% or higher in both Q3 and Q4, and you've just raised your guidance for the year to up substantially more than it was before. So, could you maybe rank order what the key reasons are? Is it you're just catching up with customer demand or you're out executing your competitors or share gains?

And then I guess as a follow-up is, would you expect this, kind of, year-over-year growth to continue into the first half of next year given they're pretty easy comps in the first half?

Paul Oldham: Yes, I'll take a cut at that, David. And Steve can fill in any other color. I think the first thing is we are seeing stronger demand in the second half. And if you remember, we started off this year a little slower. We had tougher comps a year ago, and we said we expected semiconductor demand to accelerate in the second half. And that's exactly what we're seeing. In our case, we think we're keeping up with customer demand. And so, that's resulting in higher numbers, both sequentially and year-over-year. And year-over-year comps are a little bit easier, so that's helping. We do think that we've been successful and been recognized for being able to keep up with demand.

And so we're not seeing those headwinds because of our strategies around inventory and capacity. Those things are helping. Going into next year, we haven't guided exactly for how those revenue growth rates would look. But you would anticipate that if you had sequential growth in that market, even a little bit, you'd still have a pretty significant year-over-year growth. And so I think you could see that for another quarter or so.

Stephen Kelley: I think the only thing I'd add is that I think we're also benefiting from increasing etch and dep intensity and also benefiting from the fact that most of the investment going into leading-edge logic and DRAM processes where we tend to have more content.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's conference call. You may disconnect your lines at this time. We thank you again for your participation.

#3199. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

Scotto noted that WMB stock has underperformed due to backlash related to data centers and investor anticipation of another Power Innovation project. She expects the company to announce at least one more project before the end of this year, potentially with a new customer and a contract duration of 15 to 20 years, which would be a positive catalyst for the stock.

Scotto ranks No. 175 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been profitable 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.2%. See Williams Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

EOG Resources, a crude oil and natural gas exploration and production company, will hold its third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 6. At a quarterly dividend of $1.02 per share, EOG offers a dividend yield of 2.75%.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on EOG Resources stock and increased his price target to $185 from $175. The analyst expects the company's Q3 cash flow per share to exceed the Street's consensus by 13%, driven by better-than-expected production.

Byrne expects crude oil production, excluding the UAE, to reach 551 Mboe/d, which is at the high end of guidance (546-551 Mboe/d) and above the Street's projection of 548 Mboe/d, driven by continued growth in the Utica.

Furthermore, Byrne expects cash operating expenses to come in at $10.27 per barrel of oil equivalent, below the midpoint of guidance of $10.05 to $11.35, helped by lower lease operating expenses. Overall, the analyst expects EOG to deliver free cash flow of $2.65 billion, supporting another quarter of buybacks near the minimum 70% shareholder return threshold and implying about $1.5 billion in share repurchases.

"As a first indication of the '27 plan, we expect EOG will message another year of mid-single-digit (~3.5%) growth on a flat capital budget (~$6.55bn), which is above the Street modeling 1% oil growth at $6.6bn," said Byrne.
