Late last week, a report popped up about a new Android phone exploit the security researcher dubbed "SMS of Death." Per the report, the attack, tracked as "CVE-2026-58882," lets malicious actors disrupt cellphone service or crash Android phones by overloading them with a repeating crafted SMS text message.

The denial-of-service flaw can even interrupt ongoing calls, including emergency calls, without requiring you to open the message. Apparently, the Android operating system processes the message before it even reaches your text message inbox, meaning you wouldn't immediately understand what caused the phone to crash.

Researcher Mark Blah says that even if you reboot your phone, the hacked message "stays queued and is retried on every boot, so the phone can crash on startup until it is cleared (recovery below)."

Upon finding Blah's report, Tom's Guide reached out to Google because the report claimed that Google had deemed it a "non-priority." Google has not yet responded to our inquiries.

However, some Android phones may already have the exploit patched.

Blah's report found that the exploit affects Android versions 12 up to 16 and was discovered on multiple devices, including Pixel 9s and Samsung Galaxy phones.

It appears Google patched the exploit in the October 2026 Android security update (if you haven't updated your Android phone, you should). However, that's only for Android versions 14 through 17. It does not appear to be available for any devices still running Android 12 or 13.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Per Blah, the flaw uses an improper validation of a header length in the Android WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu function. Attacks send a malformed WAP Push message to the targeted phone.

When this message is translated, it turns into a negative value that Android attempts to allocate memory for, which triggers a NegativeArraySizeException that crashes the com.android.phone process.

That process manages cellular functions, which disrupts connectivity and disconnects calls. This causes repeated crashes because the network tries to redeliver the malicious messages, which stack up and force Android to process each one. It only takes 20 bad messages to cause the crash.

Per the Google fix, the crash is prevented by catching the exceptions triggered by the attack messages. Then the patch deletes the messages from the SMS database to prevent them from looping.

Android security updates are generally automatically installed on supported devices. So you should already have them.

However, availability does depend on the phone maker and network carrier. So you should check your phone to see if the October patch has been applied. A restart may be required to complete the installation.

For the most part, this isn't an attack you can do anything about, but based on the patch notes and Blah's report, it doesn't seem to be widely deployed; instead, it appears to target individual phones. Since a working proof-of-concept of the exploit has been released, the best thing you can do is make sure you keep your phone up to date.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Samsung's advertisement features a sliced green apple that rolls right along through the entire Galaxy Z Fold line.

Samsung’s new Galaxy Z Fold 8 advertisement makes a direct jab at Apple’s iPhone Duo for its late arrival into the foldable phone market. In an Instagram video, Samsung’s “Slice” ad shows off an apple (the fruit, not the company) that’s chopped into pieces before one slice rolls along past the Galaxy Z Fold lineup, spanning from 2019 to 2026’s Z Fold 8.

It’s not unusual for phone-makers to bash Apple for bringing features and hardware ideas to the iPhone long after they’ve been available on Android devices. Samsung’s $1,900 passport-style Z Fold 8, which debuted in July, has a similar shape to the $1,999 iPhone Duo that debuted in September.

Samsung has also had years to optimize its One UI 9.0 software overlay for foldable phones, with plenty of options that take advantage of the phone’s larger and smaller displays. While the Duo does run Apple’s iOS 27, my colleague Abrar Al-Heeti noted in her review that third-party apps and services are still being optimized for different screens. The Duo is breaking new ground on iOS as Apple’s first foldable phone, but that also gives rivals like Samsung the opportunity to poke a little fun at Apple in their advertising.

Samsung’s ad ends by touting that the Z Fold 8 is thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo, which Samsung was able to achieve in part by using a new display tech called Flex Titanium and higher-capacity silicon-carbon battery tech.

While it’s fair to say that the iPhone Duo is late to the party, the company has a history of catching up quickly with its competitors. Apple began including wireless charging with 2017’s iPhone 8, years after other Android rivals. Now, Apple has helped develop the Qi2 wireless charging standard with faster speeds and magnets, and last spring the iPhone 17 Pro won CNET’s Lab Test of fastest wireless charging.

But until Apple’s new foldable phone is firmly established, I wouldn’t be surprised to see other foldable phone-makers like Google or Motorola creatively slice up Apple for waiting until 2026.

Turning to our segment results and outlook. The Government Operations delivered a strong quarter with good operating performance across business lines, driving Adjusted EBITDA margin of 22.6%, reflecting the continued benefit of improved efficiency, operational discipline and higher manufacturing volume. In Naval Propulsion, we booked our annual fuel contract for $189 million and are actively negotiating the next multiyear pricing agreement. In Special Materials, our defense fuels enrichment and high-purity depleted uranium programs continue to ramp, driving the majority of Government Operations revenue growth in the quarter.

For defense fuels, we are designing an HEU enrichment facility in Erwin, Tennessee, and industrializing centrifuge technology in our Oak Ridge facility. We remain on track to test a prototype centrifuge by the end of this year. On HPDU, as part of our $1.6 billion contract to produce 300 metric tons of high-purity depleted uranium annually, we initiated construction of a new large-scale facility in Jonesborough, Tennessee, that will drive meaningful revenue growth in the fourth quarter and through 2027. Our technical services teams once again boosted earnings in the quarter with outperformance on key programs, including Hanford and Savannah River, among others.

From a business development standpoint, we were selected to provide a conceptual design for a lithium processing facility at the Y-12 National Security Complex in support of strategic deterrence. We expect the down selection for the next phase of this program in the first half of 2027. Further, our technical services team is rapidly adopting AI to drive site performance and generate operating efficiencies. This further differentiates TSG as we develop new growth opportunities in that business to augment our base of predictable core earnings. Moving to Advanced Nuclear. It was a busy quarter for operations and business development. We completed the core barrel assembly for Project Pele.

And just a few weeks ago, we hosted Energy Secretary Chris Wright at the BWXT Innovation Campus to see our progress firsthand before we deliver the reactor to Idaho National Laboratory next year. We also secured new wins for the BWXT advanced nuclear reactor called BANR. We were selected for the U.S. Army's Janus Program that aims to install more than 20 microreactors of various sizes across 5 military bases. We are working through the first phase of the contract, including final site selection at Fort Campbell, initiating nuclear regulatory processes and TRISO fuel production. In parallel, we are working with our partners to fully define the program's costs, execution approach and operating plan.

In addition, BANR was selected by Prodigy Clean Energy for its transportable nuclear power plant project in Belledune, New Brunswick, Canada, our first international microreactor win. This is an excellent example of cross-segment collaboration as it brought together capabilities from our advanced nuclear teams from Lynchburg and commercial power and Kinectrics teams from Ontario, which will supply chain development and licensing services to Prodigy, highlighting the benefits of our broad capabilities across the nuclear value chain. And lastly, we entered into a multiyear agreement to supply an initial allocation of 1 metric ton of TRISO fuel to Antares, our first large-scale commercial customer.

This fuel will be manufactured in Lynchburg on the same TRISO production line used for Project Pele, the Antares Mark-0 criticality demonstration reactor and others. We will also manufacture TRISO for the Janus Program on that line. These awards are tangible proof of BWXT's leading position in the advanced nuclear market as we uniquely combine microreactor technology, TRISO fuel manufacturing and life cycle services into a differentiated integrated offering. Turning now to Commercial Operations. Organic revenue increased 15% and total revenue grew 25%, driven by double-digit growth in commercial power, Kinectrics and medical, along with contribution from the PCG acquisition. During the quarter, we completed the expansion of our Cambridge facility and began utilizing new sections of the plant.

The expansion increases our heavy component manufacturing capacity by about 50% and will improve operating efficiency and throughput as we execute on our deep backlog associated with CANDU life extensions and SMR projects and other new awards. In the United States, we are finalizing design details for a new commercial manufacturing facility for large steam generators and reactor pressure vessels. The expansion will complement our existing operations and amplify our role as a super merchant supplier of critical, highly engineered nuclear components. We intend to make a final investment decision by the end of the year. In Europe, we are also seeing high interest in nuclear power, particularly in markets where energy security is a national priority.

I recently met with government officials and business leaders in Poland, where there is a strong appetite for nuclear power to address their energy security and decarbonization goals. Specific to BWXT, there is a meaningful opportunity to deploy microreactors there and participate in the SMR supply chain. Any decision to invest in manufacturing capacity in Poland would be backed by firm orders and appropriate government partnerships. Commercial nuclear demand is precipitating rapidly on a global scale now, and we continue to expect to convert that demand into firm orders in 2027 and in the years to come as the trickle becomes a flood. With that, I will turn the call over to Mike.

Michael Fitzgerald: Thanks, Rex, and good evening, everyone. I'll begin with total company financial highlights on Slide 4 of the earnings presentation. Third quarter revenue was $953 million, up 10% year-over-year, including 7% organic growth. Strong Commercial Operations performance was complemented by steady growth in Government Operations. Adjusted EBITDA increased 19% to $180 million, driven by double-digit growth in both operating segments, partially offset by higher corporate expense as we continue to invest for the future. Adjusted earnings per share increased 26% to $1.26, driven largely by higher operating income as nonoperating benefits from lower interest expense and a lower tax rate were partially offset by lower other income.

Third quarter free cash flow was $151 million, reflecting strong earnings, favorable advanced billings and disciplined working capital management. Given our year-to-date performance, we raised the low end of our 2026 free cash flow guidance, resulting in a revised range of $350 million to $360 million. We continue to expect capital expenditures of approximately 6% of revenue in both 2026 and 2027. These investments are focused on expanding our manufacturing capacity, scaling fuel capabilities and supporting programs where we see significant long-term demand. Our improving credit profile, including Fitch's inaugural investment-grade rating and Moody's positive outlook revision reinforces the strength of our financial position and provides flexibility as we execute on our disciplined capital allocation strategy.

As we discussed at Investor Day, our top capital allocation priority is investing in attractive organic growth opportunities, maintaining the capacity to pursue disciplined acquisitions and return capital to shareholders when appropriate. We continue to view balance sheet flexibility as an important competitive advantage as BWXT executes on its next phase of growth. Moving to the segment results on Slide 6. Government Operations revenue increased 4%, driven by growth in Special Materials and Advanced Nuclear, partially offset by modestly lower Naval Propulsion revenue from reduced materials procurement compared with a strong prior year quarter.

Adjusted EBITDA was $144 million, representing a margin of 22.6% and up 22% from last year, supported by strong operational performance, productivity improvements and higher technical services equity income. As we look ahead, we remain focused on sustaining productivity improvements in our established businesses while scaling special material programs, supporting our expectation for Adjusted EBITDA growth broadly in line with revenue in 2027. Turning to Commercial Operations. Revenue increased 25%, including 15% organic growth, driven by increases in commercial power, Kinectrics and medical plus the contribution from the PCG acquisition, which closed in early July.

Growth in commercial power and Kinectrics reflected the continued strength of our Canadian components manufacturing and services businesses as well as increased engineering services revenue in the United States. Adjusted EBITDA in the segment grew 17% to $41 million. Adjusted EBITDA margin in the quarter was 13.2% as higher volume and good execution more than offset mix and continued investments to scale the business for future growth. Turning to our consolidated guidance for the remainder of 2026 and our preliminary outlook for 2027. In 2026, the assumptions in our operating guidance are unchanged. We anticipate Adjusted EBITDA of approximately $667 million and adjusted earnings per share to be $4.72 to $4.77, both at the midpoint of the previous guidance ranges.

Looking ahead to 2027, our preliminary outlook reinforces the financial trajectory outlined at Investor Day. We expect high single-digit to low double-digit growth in Adjusted EBITDA and adjusted earnings per share. Importantly, we expect this growth to be driven by continued expansion in our core businesses, increased contributions from Special Materials and ongoing improvements in operational execution and productivity. 2026 has been an exceptionally strong year, and we have a solid foundation for continued earnings growth in 2027, primarily supported by our existing businesses and programs with additional opportunities as new programs and commercial awards progress. Within Government Operations, we expect high single-digit to low double-digit revenue and Adjusted EBITDA growth.

Special Materials will remain a significant growth driver, complemented by increased Naval Propulsion and Advanced Nuclear activity. We expect continued productivity improvements and operational execution to help offset the margin mix effects associated with scaling new programs. In Commercial Operations, we expect high single-digit organic revenue growth and low single-digit total revenue growth due to the planned medical divestiture, which is on track to close later this year. Organic revenue growth will be supported by our components manufacturing and services businesses. We also expect Commercial Operations Adjusted EBITDA margins to improve by 50 to 100 basis points, reflecting higher volume, continued operational improvements and better absorption of growth investments, resulting in high single-digit Adjusted EBITDA growth.

From a cash perspective, we expect another year of solid generation in 2027 with free cash flow anticipated to be flat to slightly higher compared to 2026. While earnings growth should support increased operating cash flow, we expect continued investments in working capital and capital expenditures to support the significant growth opportunities across our business. We remain focused on disciplined cash conversion and capital deployment as we execute our long-term growth strategy. Importantly, our preliminary 2027 outlook remains consistent with the longer-term financial framework presented at Investor Day and reinforces our confidence in achieving our 2030 targets. Overall, we had a solid quarter.

Our focus on operational excellence, converting our bid pipeline into firm awards and driving profitable growth, combined with our strong balance sheet and disciplined capital allocation strategy positions us well to deliver another strong year in 2027. With that, I'll turn it back to Rex for closing remarks.

Rex Geveden: Thanks, Mike. To date, 2026 has been an excellent year for BWXT, and I'm excited about what lies ahead. As we close, I will leave you with 3 thoughts. First, our core businesses continue to deliver strong predictable performance, providing the foundation for our long-term growth. Second, the opportunities we discussed at Investor Day are blossoming. We are securing new contracts, executing on strategically important programs and investing in the industrial capacity needed to grow the business. And third, our focus remains on execution. We recognize the significant opportunities ahead of us and know that long-term value creation depends on converting those opportunities into profitable growth and strong cash generation.

BWXT is exceptionally well positioned to do that, and our performance this quarter underscores our confidence in the 2030 financial targets we established at Investor Day. With that, we look forward to your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Matt Akers with BNP Paribas.

Matthew Akers: I wonder if you could touch on a little bit more on the Government Operations margins. It was a really good quarter. And I know you guys -- you called out the equity income, I think even excluding that was pretty good. So if you could just kind of talk through kind of the big drivers there.

Michael Fitzgerald: Yes. So thanks, Matt. Look, we're really, really proud of kind of the execution that we're performing within Government Operations. We've seen a significant increase in our overall margin from our expectations at the beginning of 2026. I think when you get down to it and really what's happening is we're seeing a substantial increase in the efficiency of the volume of the work that we performed specifically in our naval nuclear business. So those contracts are performing very well. We're very focused on managing our volume so that it's highly efficient work. And we're seeing the results of that. So excited to see that.

I think if you look at some of the newer programs that we've talked about, no major changes there. I think that the growth on those programs, they're performing well, but they're in early stages. And as we've discussed before, we don't take large margin adjustments on those until we get further along from a progress standpoint. So what you're seeing is really excellence in the efficiencies of our core business. And certainly, it's great to see.

Matthew Akers: Yes. And then -- was there backlog acquired as part of the PCG deal? It looks like your commercial backlog is up a bit. And if so, can you talk about what that is, sort of how that runs off and how that fits in with your plan to kind of use that capacity for BWXT work?

Michael Fitzgerald: Yes, that's right. I mean, so when we announced the PCG deal, what we had said at the time was that there was still -- most of that business, I think, 75% to 80% of that business was still in the kind of naval work and ultimately, the rest is commercial. We had close to $500 million in backlog associated with that transaction. So that came on to the books associated with that. That will burn off over a period of time. I mean the thing that's encouraging is we're seeing growth in the PCG business.

But as we stated before, a lot of the -- if you look at the capacity, we thought that the factories were about 50% unutilized and that we could, with some modest maybe CapEx investments, be able to get another 50% of that. So we still want to continue to see that government work continue to be performed, and we'll see some growth in that, probably at a low single digit. But where we're able to do the commercial work is going to be in tapping into that unutilized capacity that currently exists at the site.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Bob Labick with CJS Securities.

Bob Labick: Great. Congratulations on another strong execution and continued great outlook. I wanted to dig into your capital allocation comments between today a little bit and then some from the Analyst Day or Investor Day as well. I think to maintain the 2 to 3x leverage by 2030, you'll be spending, I think, somewhere between $3 billion and $4 billion going forward. And you just reiterated, you want to spend this on attractive organic opportunities as kind of first thing you want to spend it on. So could you maybe tell us the top priorities, maybe 3, 4, 5 opportunities out there? And then how much of that $3 billion plus spending is necessary to reach your revenue and EBITDA numbers?

Or how much is upside? How should we think about that capital allocation?

Michael Fitzgerald: So one of the things that we laid out is that we had -- if you looked at kind of the slide from our Investor Day, it actually showed that amount of kind of additional capital. So the way I would think about it is the 2030 targets are really anchored to the 5% to 6% core CapEx spending that we've discussed from a target standpoint. We also stated that we didn't need any specific M&A per se to be able to hit those 2030 targets. So I would think of that as additional deployment opportunities above and beyond the core business and what we laid out there from a 2030 target standpoint.

With that said, I think we're seeing opportunities out there. However, we've made it very clear that when there's not organic opportunities or when there's not additional M&A targets that we would return that capital to shareholders as appropriate. So I still think there's a real possibility for that. If you look in our 2027 guidance, we'll do some modest share repurchases, consistent with our prior practice of offsetting dilution. But we are focused on kind of the -- those capital allocation priorities as stated. When you look at from a priority standpoint, we want to continue to build off the momentum that we've been seeing. So we've talked about capacity investments that we've made across the business.

We certainly have talked about Special Materials, and that's been a great part of our growth story. And then I think you'll hear more around we're seeing a lot of some traction happening with our microreactor business with the program Janus win and BANR being selected in Canada as well. And so excited to see that market. And hopefully, there's some additional opportunities there.

Operator: Your next question is from the line of Tomo Sano with JPMorgan.

Tomohiko Sano: Maybe just on Commercial Operations. Your full year guidance calls for roughly 45% growth in this business. Given where you are through Q3, that implies a pretty big step-up in Q4. Is there something specific a large order or revenue recognition event driving that acceleration, please?

Michael Fitzgerald: Nothing unusual to call out. We've always experienced some ramp in the fourth quarter as we look at just kind of the timing of that overall from an execution standpoint. You are -- we are also seeing there will be contribution from PCG as well. So if you look at that on over a year-over-year basis, you're going to see some additional growth there. But I don't think anything unusual from a fourth quarter perspective.

Tomohiko Sano: And just a follow-up on PCG acquisition. It's been a few months since you closed the acquisition. How is integration tracking? Are you seeing the synergies and cost benefits you expected on schedule?

Michael Fitzgerald: Yes, absolutely. Actually, the integration is going very, very well. We did not -- if you remember, the thesis around this transaction was not necessarily revenue synergies. We did see some opportunities on the cost side, but we didn't put out any specific targets related to that. However, I would say we're finding a lot of opportunities and the team has been getting very involved in how we can really address this from a U.S. commercial market standpoint. So I'm very pleased with the progress that we've made, and they've been a great addition to the overall company.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Jeffrey Campbell with Seaport Research.

Jeffrey Campbell: Your recent press release concerning rumors of Poland investment was explicit in saying that such a decision would require firm orders of sufficient size to transact. Should we assume the same structure applies to beginning construction of a new U.S. commercial heavy component facility?

Rex Geveden: No, Jeff. I don't know, that U.S. facility does not depend on firm orders. That said, there's so many things in the pipeline that we're certainly compelled to go ahead with that U.S. plant. The Poland situation had to do with some discussions around how much demand we think will precipitate for microreactors and small modular reactors in Poland. And there were certainly gigawatt scales of demand that we discussed. But no, we're going ahead with the U.S. plant regardless.

Jeffrey Campbell: Okay. Great. One of the things that impressed me in the Investor Day was the potential remuneration from your exposure to CANDU. Recently, I read that AtkinsRealis, the state of Indiana and Hoosier Energy had partnered to evaluate up to 6 gigawatts of CANDU reactors for that state. So high level, what do you think about CANDU potentially finally making inroads into the U.S.? And is it reasonable to assume BWXT could potentially be a component supplier to this project if it ever materializes?

Rex Geveden: Yes. Maybe to put some things in context, Jeff, if you look back at the history of CANDU and there were about 30 CANDU units delivered globally, 20 in Canada itself. And so 10 or so that went to other places, South Korea, China, India, Romania and Argentina. So -- and that's with -- that's 30 large plants compared to a total global installed base of about 600. So let's say it captured 5% of the international market over the course of those years. And maybe that's a reasonable assumption going forward. I certainly would hope and certainly, the Canadians hope that they can build some -- can build an international market from CANDU and have a real export capability.

And I think that's feasible. And I certainly do hope that they can export into the U.S. And if they do, we will certainly be in that supply chain, probably supplying fuel, major components, feeders, all the things that we normally do, we would do for that. And that's the purpose of Canada's investment in the CANDU industrial supply base is to be able to create an industry there that's durable and has export qualities to it.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Marc Bianchi with TD Cowen.

Marc Bianchi: I want to ask first on the '27 outlook. It looks like you upgraded the EBITDA growth expectation a little bit from the Investor Day. Could you talk a little bit about that?

Michael Fitzgerald: Yes. I think, look, we're seeing some -- we've had really strong performance in the underlying margin for this year. We're seeing some continued momentum as we go into 2027. So I would think of it as kind of a refinement of our expectations, nothing material, but we feel confident in ultimately getting to high single to low double digit, both on adjusted EBITDA as well as EPS.

Marc Bianchi: Okay. Is that more coming from government side of the business, just given the beat in 3Q here?

Michael Fitzgerald: I think we look at this from different scenarios. So we'll run multiple scenarios. I think it's fair to assume that our government business will continue to perform very well. As mentioned, we're kind of coming off of that -- some of those older pricing arrangements. And so we're starting to see that come into the financials as we execute successfully on those programs. But I would say we're also seeing continued momentum in commercial. So it's positive across the board.

Marc Bianchi: Okay. And then if I could just ask one more. On the potential orders for commercial, there's -- I think everybody sort of read the news around we've got this DOE long lead up program for large reactors and then there's a Department of Commerce track for 8 reactors, and there was an announcement, I guess, it's several weeks ago about the Korean program there. Like which one of those feels like we could get a quicker hit? And maybe do you think that BWXT is equally positioned for both of those programs or maybe more weighted to one than the other? Just curious for any color you can provide.

Rex Geveden: Yes, Marc, I'll add some color there. I think in my opinion is that the SMR opportunity is a bit ahead of large reactor opportunity. That's just my feel for it. We're certainly in active discussions with Westinghouse and GE on all of that. So I think you'd see -- we'd see more activity in our order book. I think first from the Darlington project, units 2, 3 and 4 up there. I think closely following that would be the TVA opportunities, the 10 reactors there, 5 at Clinch River and then 5 at Bellefonte, I think. And then with the APs to follow that would be my guess.

Now all those discussions are active, and I think all of that represents opportunity for us, but that's how I see the sequencing. And I said at the beginning of this year that I expected us to have new orders for U.S. reactor plant builds in -- by the end of this year. And I still think that's a possibility for us, but certainly no later than about the first half of the next year.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Scott Deuschle with Deutsche Bank.

Scott Deuschle: Mike, can you walk through what's been driving the relatively slow organic growth at Government Operations year-to-date? And maybe just kind of what the headwinds have been? And has the revenue cadence surprised you at all? Or is it consistent with how you thought the year would play out?

Michael Fitzgerald: No, I would say it's consistent. One of the things as we came into 2026 we were going to see a larger ramp on the -- on the newer programs, but specifically on the HPDU program as we get on to the third and the fourth quarter. And so we're continuing to see that. We did discuss, I think, a little bit last quarter how we were performing actually really well on that program. And because of that, it was lower revenue just because we had really strong margin performance, which under a percent complete model actually results in lower revenue. So no surprises.

I think those programs are performing well, and we'll continue to see them into '27 as well.

Scott Deuschle: Okay. And then, Rex, if the first U.S. AP1000 builds ultimately get funded by South Korea as opposed to another funding source, is that a negative as it relates to your content opportunity on those initial builds? Or is the funding source not expected to influence supplier content allocations?

Rex Geveden: I think it's hard for me to say on that one, Scott. I would say that it's our expectation that we will have to go and compete with Doosan and IHI and all the usual suspects when those opportunities come up. That said, I think there's going to be plenty of opportunity for all the players there because there's actually still not that much capacity globally for these kind of components. So we'll compete and hopefully get our share and make a great business out of it.

Scott Deuschle: Is Westinghouse typically the one deciding who gets the content or someone else?

Rex Geveden: No. I mean it's my expectation that Westinghouse will be making those decisions.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Jeff Grampp with Northland Capital Markets.

Jeffrey Grampp: Rex, sticking on the new build topic. From your guys' perspective, what are kind of the main gating item or items keeping new build projects from reaching an FID? Is it predominantly finance and kind of structuring things related to that? Or are there other particular items that you guys see that kind of holding things up from getting a couple of projects across the finish line here?

Rex Geveden: Yes, I'm not in those discussions, but what I'm hearing about is it has to do with the allocation of risk. How much are the hyperscalers going to take, how much of the utility is going to take, if that applies, how much is the government going to take? Are there any backstops and how much will the technology provider itself take? And so I think it's about -- we've been hearing this concept that everyone bleeds, but no one bleeds to death as it relates to any overruns or risks in the project. So I think it's about the distribution of risk.

I don't think it's so much about financing because in the case of the 10 X-300s and certainly those 10 AP1000s and then that second tranche, those are going to be funded through the sovereign investments from South Korea and Japan, as I understand it. So I think it's less about financing. It's more about allocation of risk.

Jeffrey Grampp: Got it. I appreciate those details. And for my follow-up, can you touch on BWXT's capabilities to handle multiple awards of projects for larger nuclear new builds if this accelerates into the coming years, how does your ability to scale compare to the business opportunities you guys are seeing? And maybe where does that rank in terms of, I guess, the list of worries on a given day for you guys in terms of just capacity to meet the demand that's out there?

Rex Geveden: Yes. Well, good problem to have. I would say we've been trying to anticipate all that. We, of course, just increased our production capacity by about 50% at Cambridge, Ontario. We literally just completed that expansion under budget, slightly under budget and about on the original schedule. So we're prepared there. Of course, the PCG acquisition was around that thesis. That, as Mike said in an earlier question, we think that, that asset is about 50% underutilized, and we can build some capacity there for medium reactor components. And then the U.S. plant that we've been talking about for the past couple of quarters is intended to deal with that demand.

So I mean, we're stacking them up we're stacking up our capacity. We're certainly one of the largest players in the world, and I think we'll be prepared for it.

Operator: Your next question is from the line of Mark Shooter with William Blair.

Mark Shooter: Congrats on the quarter. And Rex, I heard you mention that you'll have a prototype test of the DUECE centrifuge by end of the year. I was wondering if you can give us some color on the metrics you'll be judging it by. And speaking of the NNSA program, I know we also talked about the potential of widening that scope to include unobligated LEU and HALEU enrichment. So I was wondering if you could tell us how you're thinking about that now.

Rex Geveden: Yes. Sure thing, Mark. What we're doing, of course, in that program is taking technology developed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and taking it into industrializing that technology and building production capacity and ultimately, a demonstration cascade at our plant in Oak Ridge. And so I certainly can't cite the particular success criteria for that demonstration. It is just a demo. And what we're doing, of course, is trying to reduce the complexity, exercise the supply chain and be able to build an unobligated system. So I think sort of just spinning that thing will be the proof that we're looking for, and we'll be building certainly many more units in the future.

As it relates to the opportunity in between the technology transfer and the high enriched uranium scope that we have at our Erwin, Tennessee plant, we are certainly pursuing adding low-enriched uranium and high-assay, low-enriched uranium to the scope. Those discussions are ongoing. I can't offer any details on that, but it's certainly in our sights, and we hope to add it.

Mark Shooter: That's great. Switching gears on to the other fuel, TRISO. Congrats on the Antares win. And so you'll be supporting Antares, Project Pele, Project Janus and also from the Lynchburg facility. So can you remind us what capacity increases are needed today to meet those commitments? And what level of fuel contracting do you need to see to require an expansion past Lynchburg?

Rex Geveden: Yes, I'll offer some details there, Mark. We were able to produce a couple of hundred kilograms a year on that Lynchburg line, and that's enough capacity for fully fueling the core of the Pele reactor and some other things that we did, the Antares demo and a couple of other customers that we actually haven't -- that we haven't disclosed. Through some technology changes and some capacity we can add and from some operational improvements, we can at least quadruple the output of that facility. That's our Lynchburg plant that I'm talking about, not the greenfield. So that gives us quite some capacity for the near term.

I think in terms of making the larger investment decision and getting to multiple megatons of -- sorry, multiple metric tons of capacity, say, at a Wyoming plant, we're going to need to see 2 things. We need to see larger demand precipitate first with our partner, Kairos, for the Hermes reactor. That one as an anchor tenant will consume a lot of TRISO and then others, right, multiple BANR orders, for example. So we need the precipitation of concrete, significant demand in the future. And we also need to see HALEU become available commercially. And those are 2 important gates, and we'll get those -- we'll get to that decision as that becomes clearer.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Laurence Alexander with Jefferies.

Laurence Alexander: Just a simple one on Commercial Operations. The margin improvement expected for '27, how important is that? I mean, given the range of the growth opportunities you're evaluating and the incremental investments to support that, do you need that kind of -- is that sort of a flexible part of your bridge for next year?

Michael Fitzgerald: Yes. Sorry, I'm not sure I follow. So from a -- we are seeing some margin improvement as we look into 2027. That's -- there's a large mix. If you kind of remember what commercial, we have kind of a services business component that we have ultimately the components margin. So that's just on the components manufacturing. And then we also will have the kind of the contribution of PCG that would continue. So different margin mix profiles. I think we're seeing some substantial growth in the underlying revenue base for the components business.

That will -- that is offsetting some of the headwinds that were associated with the divestiture of Medical, which was a higher growth -- higher kind of margin business as well. So I think when you blend all that together, I mean, we're not seeing anything unusual. The margin continues to perform well, and we're seeing a slight uptick primarily as a result of just kind of overall mix and growth in different aspects of the business.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Andre Madrid with BTIG.

Andre Madrid: You had mentioned it before that maybe the gating factor in seeing more commercial orders convert was kind of the allocation of risk. Do you expect tomorrow's midterm elections to potentially, I guess, complicate those conversations any further? Or is that not really a concern?

Rex Geveden: I don't think it's a big concern, Andre, because those deals are constructed outside the framework of congressional appropriations and authorization and they don't come through the President's budget request. So in some ways, it's outside that whole system. It obviously relates to the tariff deals that were done and the sovereign investments that were made to offset the threat of tariffs. So I think those deals go forward regardless. And all that said, and I've said this often, I've been in the seat for 10 years and through multiple administrations and support for nuclear has only gotten stronger and stronger. It's bicameral, it's bipartisan. It makes sense for so many different reasons.

And so just about everyone lines up behind nuclear now. So I don't expect a lot of impedance here.

Andre Madrid: Got it, Rex. That's helpful. And staying on that point of commercial order flow, I mean, you said that you were expecting something to start -- some of these to start picking up in the latter part of this year, but definitely no later than the first half of next year. I mean, given the back-end weighted nature of your 2030 targets, I mean, at what point does the pace of commercial order flow start to become a concern? If we don't see, I guess, a specific number of awards come in, in the first half of next year, does that kind of put risk on the long-term guidance that you guys outlined?

Rex Geveden: I don't think so, Andre. I think we've got multiple ways of achieving that guidance, as we said, and we've mapped in some modest success in commercial orders for new builds. And yes, we've got multiple ways to win, and we intend to do so.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Pete Skibitski with Alembic Global.

Peter Skibitski: Rex, I'd love to get a sense for the revenue opportunity with this New Brunswick Prodigy win, I guess, we can call it. It looks like my simplistic math, it looks like it could be maybe 2 or 3 BANR reactors. And this one in Canada, of course, is a purely commercial endeavor. And we've got multiple other commercial opportunities around BANR. But it's super early days on that one, right? We've been selected for technology. The financing has got a line up behind it. New Brunswick has committed to an MOU for a power purchase agreement. So there's some government strength behind it, but there's a long road ahead on this one. And I'd like to offer you more details, but I just can't right now.

Peter Skibitski: Understood. So time lines, so you do Fort Campbell first and then would Tata be the first kind of commercial deployment and maybe then New Brunswick?

Rex Geveden: I mean, certainly, Fort Campbell's first in line. But yes, opportunities in Wyoming, opportunities in Poland, Canada, those are all kind of to me sort of running in parallel for second place.

Peter Skibitski: Okay. Okay. Got it. If I can ask one last one just because it just popped up. Obviously, Army and Janus is together, but now the Navy is talking about microreactors. I was wondering if you guys are going to do the reactor for the Navy at NSWC Crane in Indiana.

Rex Geveden: No. That's a smaller microreactor and being done by one of our competitors. And by the way, Pete, if I could just add a footnote to this whole discussion. A lot of these microreactors are out there in the sort of megawatt range, let's call it. There is one 5-megawatt reactor. And what we have, of course, with our product, the BANR reactor on the Janus program and elsewhere is a 20-megawatt electrical output, 22-megawatt actually, 75 megawatts thermal. So -- and it's a very high temperature reactor. So it's suitable for some large-scale applications, even though it's a microreactor. You can run large military bases with that. You could provide industrial heat at a large chemical plant, for example.

And so we have -- we're seeing a range of opportunities that are completely unavailable to our competitors in that space because of the scale of that reactor. That said, it still fits on a train. This is a rail shippable actually modular reactor. When we talk about small modular reactors, those are not small. And frankly, they're not modular. They're built in the field. These things are actually literally built in the factory just as our naval reactors are. And so we've got the largest scale microreactor that's capable of addressing some very big problems, and that's one of the reasons why we're bullish on it.

Joshua Korn: It's Josh Korn on for David. I wanted to ask about the free cash flow guidance. I guess, what's weighing on cash in the fourth quarter? And then you seem to be implying a pretty big working capital headwind into next year. Just kind of anything you could provide there?

Michael Fitzgerald: Yes. I think -- so fourth quarter is just the timing. We had a really strong third quarter. So you're seeing some of that just on overall timing coming into the third quarter. But we feel good about where we're guiding for the year. And I think we have a great opportunity to execute on that. When you look at 2027, there's a couple of things that are going on. One, we got about a $10 million headwind to pension contributions. This is normal course, primarily associated with the Kinectrics acquisition.

We have a little bit of working capital investment for some of the growth opportunities, and there is some timing of just overall milestones, specifically on the HPDU and kind of our newer enrichment programs. But I think at the end of the day, we're seeing -- if you look at kind of the underlying true performance from an OCF perspective, we're still seeing good conversion on our core businesses. So a little bit of headwind as we invest for growth and some other kind of unique items, but we still ultimately feel good about where we're going to land for the year.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Peter Arment with Baird.

Peter Arment: A lot of questions asked. But Rex, maybe just a quick one on the budgets. If we don't have any budgets resolved post midterms here and things linger into next year, does that have any impact on your thoughts on '27? Or is that not really an issue regarding for you guys?

Rex Geveden: Peter, historically, we've been able to work through those continuing resolutions in pretty good shape because almost everything in our portfolio is program of record and those get funded at 95% of the prior year or whatever. And we typically have some uncosted carryover that's able to sustain us. We sort of got to the end of our rope on some TSG programs last year when that one ran extra long. But broadly speaking, we've been a little bit immune to CRs. And so I don't think it certainly doesn't influence how we think about the forecast right now.

Operator: And our final question comes from the line of Michael Ciarmoli with Guggenheim Securities.

Michael Ciarmoli: Rex, we get this question a lot from investors on the AP1000, the Westinghouse. And you guys have, I guess, sized it already as a couple of hundred million dollars of content. But just given the comments you made, I mean, how much blood are you willing to lose on that content if risk is going to be spread around? And I guess I think about it from a margin standpoint, are there any terms or any potential content or undertaking that would be too risky for you guys?

Rex Geveden: I think -- so Mike, component manufacturing is something that we understand very, very well, right? And the opportunities we'll go after would be things like RPVs and steam generators and those kind of components that we understand how to make. I think that's a very, very different category of risk than delivery risk. Project delivery risk is what it's all about. And I've been saying of late that, that we need more innovation on the delivery side because these final investment decisions ultimately in the commercial sense are driven by the capital cost and the cost of capital. So we, the industry, have to deliver these reactors more quickly and more reliably.

So it's not -- yes, I don't see that component manufacturing bears the same kind of risk as delivery. Now we'll certainly have -- we'll certainly experience price pressure. We always do that. But we know how to make steam generators, heat exchangers, control rod drive mechanisms, reactor pressure vessels, just bring it on, right? We can accept that risk, and we do every day.

Michael Ciarmoli: Got it. And presumably, that's all contemplated in your 2030 forecast in terms of a margin profile?

Operator: And with no further questions in queue, I will now hand the call back to Chase Jacobson for closing remarks.

Chase Jacobson: Thank you to everyone for joining us today. We look forward to seeing and speaking with many of you at upcoming investor events. You can all feel free to reach out to us at [email protected], and we look forward to talking to you and seeing you soon. Thanks for the support.

#3182. GM’s $220M Payout Shows How Cars Can Secretly Sell Your Driving Data

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The automaker must now obtain express consent before collecting or sharing driver data.

GM has settled a multistate suit over selling customer data without consent.

In 2024, The New York Times published a damning investigation into the program, revealing that, in some cases, data on drivers’ habits could be used by insurance companies to set rates. Some drivers saw significant premium increases after GM sold their driving history, and one owner was told a 22% premium increase resulted from driving information supplied by a data broker, according to a statement from the New York attorney general’s office.

The data collection was described as “spying,” and GM quickly ended the program that year. In 2025, GM settled with the Federal Trade Commission over Smart Driver and OnStar location data, agreeing to a five-year ban on selling driver data.

Attorneys general in many of the states involved in the $220 million settlement posted announcements about it, including Anthony G. Brown of Maryland.

The settlement requires GM to obtain affirmative express consent from consumers before collecting or disclosing consumer driving and location data.

“Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” the spokesperson said.

Automobiles have evolved into computers on wheels over the last few decades, collecting vast amounts of data on drivers, including contacts and song lists, location data and diagnostic information. For GM, the issue was less about collecting data than about breaking its promise to customers that it wouldn’t sell it.

There may be more action to come on illegal or unethical data-collection practices in the auto industry.

“GM was the biggest case and, in some ways, presented the most egregious set of facts. But collecting and selling driving data is an industry norm, not an aberration,” said Peter Cassat, technology partner at CM Law and a former general counsel for Cox Automotive and New Country Motor Group.

“The difference now is that regulators have a template, and every state attorney general has seen a $220 million settlement, so I think we can expect more enforcement actions and settlements,” Cassat said.

“Vehicle providers should ask for driver consent feature by feature in plain English,” he said, not simply prompt buyers to check a box.

Beyond the touchscreen on your dashboard, modern vehicles run background systems that transmit data straight to the manufacturer, and drivers have little to no control over what gets collected or who buys it.

“Unfortunately, there isn’t a lot consumers can do,” he said. “Opt out wherever possible and don’t agree to unnecessary data sharing. Review your own Customer Disclosure Report to see whether driving data appears. And if your car has a modem that can be disabled, consider disabling it.”

#3181. Your public Discord messages may soon appear in Google search results – how to opt out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Discord announced a new feature that can make your server messages discoverable on Google. Here's how to opt out.

Also: My 5 favorite Discord alternatives – no ID verification required

Normally, in order to join a Discord server, you need an invitation link that has been generated by a current admin or member. These links usually have a very short lifespan, expiring after just a few minutes to help protect private groups from bad actors looking to cause trouble. However, for very large Discoverable Servers, Discord has an internal search function called Server Discovery that allows users to join communities without an invite link. The new policy will create a Server Web Page for each of these very large servers, discoverable in search engines like Google or DuckDuckGo, that will show a short description of the server and a summary of conversations in its public channels. New members can join servers directly from their Server Web Pages.

As for what exactly is shared on Server Web Pages, Discord’s related support page says, “From mid-December 2026, answers to questions your members sent in public channels can be found in a web search, in their own words.”

Server Web Pages will begin to go live on Nov. 16, 2026, but server admins have already been given access to tools for opting out entire channels from the program:

Once you’ve accessed the controls, you can either pick which channels will be shown in your community’s Server Web Page (something like a general chat for a content creator’s community server, or a hobby community’s rules page) or opt out of all channels so that only a server description will be visible. And even the server description can be disabled if you’re trying to keep your community as private as possible.

Discord plans to start adding chat summaries and individual example messages in mid-December, and regular users will be able to opt out of having their part of conversations shown.

Along with toggles to opt out of personalized ads and data collection (which I strongly suggest you turn off as well), you’ll see a button to block your message text and data from being used in Server Web Pages. And one toggle will cover permissions in every Discoverable Server that you belong to, so you won’t have to waste time updating your preferences for every community.

Also: Strangers can find your info with a 5-minute search – delete it ASAP

Don’t worry, the private server you have set up for playing games and chatting with friends, and even larger communities not designated as Discoverable Servers, aren’t affected by this announcement. Only official Discoverable Servers with at least 1,000 members, that are at least eight weeks old, and meet Discord’s activity and safety standards will have the new web pages and message summary features.

The move seems to position Discord as an alternative to Reddit in the market of obscure tech questions with answers that were previously only available on now-defunct Q&A forums market. Discoverable Servers will be analogous to sub-Reddit communities, offering vital information to hobbyists and pros alike that might otherwise be locked behind paywalls or “walled garden” private servers.

#3180. Lightbridge (LTBR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

DOE LaunchPad selection accelerates pilot factory development at Idaho National Laboratory.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Lightbridge Corporation (LTBR -8.46%) reported that its selection for the Department of Energy's LaunchPad program establishes an accelerated path for manufacturing lead test assemblies through a dedicated pilot facility at the Idaho National Laboratory. Management stated that this facility, designated as SHED, will operate under Department of Energy authorization to potentially shorten commercialization timelines. Executives noted that the recent agreement for loop irradiation testing in the Advanced Test Reactor allows for fuel rodlets to be tested under conditions representative of commercial pressurized water reactors. The company also reported progress in licensing its intellectual property, including a patent allowance in Japan for its multi-zone fuel design and additive manufacturing techniques. Management confirmed that the current liquidity position provides flexibility to fund expanded research and development as the company enters a more resource-intensive phase of its development program.

Operator: Thank you for standing by, and welcome to the Lightbridge Corporation Business Update and Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. Please note that today's call is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce Matthew Abenante, Senior Director of Investor Relations and Capital Markets for Lightbridge Corporation.

Seth Grae: Hello, Matt, and thank you all for joining us to discuss Lightbridge's Third Quarter 2026 business update. The third quarter brought what we believe is the most significant advance to date in Lightbridge's path from fuel testing to commercial development. In August, Lightbridge was selected to participate in the Nuclear Energy LaunchPad INL program administered by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Research Innovation Center (sic) [ National Reactor Innovation Center ] at Idaho National Laboratory. Selection provides an accelerated pathway toward DOE authorization for us to design, build and operate a pilot facility at INL to manufacture lead test assemblies of Lightbridge Fuel for demonstration in U.S. commercial power reactors.

We now call that facility, the Lightbridge Fuel Pilot Facility, which we informally referred to as SHED. By establishing a dedicated manufacturing facility under DOE authorization, we expect to shorten the time line for producing lead test assemblies for operation in commercial U.S. reactors. That gives us a two-pronged approach. The pilot factory is designed to produce lead test assemblies under DOE authorization while we continue to develop a conceptual design for our future commercial scale plans, the Lightbridge Fuel Factory, formerly referred to as the Lightbridge Expandable Fuel Facility. The Lightbridge Fuel Factory will still be expandable even though it doesn't have that word in its name. Alongside that milestone, we advanced in other key areas during the quarter.

In August, we entered into a new Project Task Statement with Idaho National Laboratory that gives us access to the Loop Facility of the Advanced Test Reactor where we will irradiate clad Lightbridge Fuel rodlets under the conditions of a fuel rod would experience in a commercial light water reactor. And in September, we received notice of -- allowance of a patent from the Japan patent office covering our multi-zone fuel element and 3D printing method. I will now turn the call over to Andrey Mushakov, Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer, to walk through our fuel development program highlights in detail. Andrey?

Andrey Mushakov: Thank you, Seth. As Seth mentioned, our focus since the launch pad selection has been on preparing the pilot factory. We're currently working with NRIC and INL to negotiate the applicable agreements and project scope. The authorization to construct and operate the pilot factory remains subject to additional DOE and INL agreements, reviews, authorizations and other prerequisites before construction can start. And as of September 30, 2026, we had not entered into any material binding commitments for its construction. We plan to design the pilot factory as a multipurpose fuel manufacturing and R&D platform rather than a facility dedicated solely to the single fuel research project and it will have a dedicated research and development laboratory.

The pilot factory will operate under an NQA-1 Nuclear Quality Assurance Program from the outset. I also want to be clear the DOE authorization of the pilot factory does not constitute authorization for lead test assemblies to be used in commercial power reactors. Any such use would remain subject to U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing, review and approval of lead test assemblies as well as any required approvals by the host utility. The pilot facility will only ever be DOE authorized and not subject to NRC licensing. Development of the pilot factory and our planned fabrication of lead test assemblies will require qualified source of uranium feedstock, including high-assay low-enriched uranium and uranium metal.

We are evaluating potential supply sources, alternative supply arrangements and related infrastructure requirements to support these activities. Separately, we continue to build the organization at Lightbridge. Idaho Falls is now home to more Lightbridge employees than any other location, and we expect to hire additional engineering and technical personnel as the pilot factory and our fuel development work progress. Approach remains disciplined and aligned with program needs so that we attract top talent and build a world-class team while maintaining capital efficiency. With that, I'll turn the call over to Scott.

Scott Holcombe: Thank you, Andrey. I will start with the Advanced Test Reactor Loop, which is the milestone Seth mentioned. In August, we entered into Project Task Statement #2 under our cooperative research and development agreement with Battelle Energy Alliance, the DOE operating contractor for Idaho National Laboratory, which we announced in September. It gives us access to the loop testing facility of the ATR. Unlike other in-core positions, a loop irradiates fuel within its own independently controlled environment, the coolant chemistry, temperature, pressure and flow a fuel rod experience in a commercial light water reactor. There are a limited number of positions in the world where that is possible, and we're now able to place our fuel into one of them.

Under this task statement, we will test enriched uranium and zirconium fuel rodlets with cladding, both cylindrical and multi-lobe geometry. The scope of work includes experiment design, provision of materials, assembly, irradiation and shipment and disposition of materials. Samples from this irradiation are later intended for further testing under transient conditions in INL's transient reactor test facility. The rodlets for that test build on our fabrication work with INL under SPP Project Task Statement #6 which supports the development of co-extruded fuel rod components for future loop irradiation testing in the ATR and transient testing. That program begins with depleted uranium and upon successful demonstration is expected to move to enriched uranium to produce fuel rod segments for irradiation experiments.

Turning to the first batch of fuel material samples removed from the ATR in May, postirradiation examination has begun. That examination will collect data on fundamental material properties at various burn-up levels which is what is required to validate and verify our field performance models, and it becomes part of the basis of our licensing work. Back to you, Seth.

Seth Grae: Thank you, Scott. The policy environment continues to move towards the market Lightbridge fuel is designed for. In June, I represented Lightbridge at the White House, launch of UPRISE. The Department of Energy initiative targeting approximately 5 gigawatts of additional nuclear capacity from reactors that are already operating. Lightbridge Fuel is designed to increase the power output of an existing reactor by up to 10% with no change to the plant's steam generators and up to 20% for plants that move to a high-capacity steam generator. New build reactors equipped with higher capacity steam generators could see an increase of roughly 1/3. Our testing and licensing program exists to confirm those design targets.

Commercial deployment also requires fuel material, and that supply must be arranged years in advance. In July, we signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Quadrant Nuclear Industries to establish a framework for discussions regarding potential long-term supply of HALEU from QNI's planned Vanguard facility at Idaho National Laboratory. The memorandum is nonbinding and does not establish pricing, quantity or exclusivity commitments and any binding terms will be subject to a definitive agreement. We continue to believe the prospects for growth in nuclear power are the strongest they have ever been.

There are approximately 440 operating power reactors worldwide today to triple nuclear power globally and quadruple it in the United States by 2050, the world will need more power from reactors already operating, not only from those still to be built. Lightbridge Fuel is designed to deliver exactly that within the same-sized cores of new reactors and plants that exist today with even greater safety and also in new reactors. I will now turn the call over to Larry Goldman, Chief Financial Officer, for a summary of the company's financial results. Larry?

Lawrence Goldman: Thank you, Seth, and good afternoon, everyone. I'd like to remind listeners that our detailed financial results are included in our earnings release issued this morning before the market opened and in our Form 10-Q that will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission later this week. Those materials will also be available on the Investor Relations section of the Lightbridge Corporation website and on the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's website. I encourage everyone to review these documents for a full discussion of our financial statements, management discussion and analysis of financial condition, Risk Factors and other related disclosures.

As of September 30, 2026, we held approximately $236.7 million in cash and cash equivalents compared to approximately $201.9 million at December 31, 2025, and we have no debt. Our balance sheet provides us with significant financial flexibility as we continue to expand our organization, invest in the infrastructure and capabilities required to support our fuel development program and advance key technical and commercialization milestones. We are now moving into a more resource-intensive stage of our development program with both head count growth and the supporting infrastructure needed to execute our R&D programs at a larger scale.

As we advance the planning and development activities associated with constructing our Lightbridge Fuel pilot factory, we expect this initiative to represent a significant multiyear investment. Expenditures are expected to be phased over the pilot factory development period and managed in a disciplined manner, taking into account technical progress, program priorities, and available financial resources. Additional information regarding our current estimated cost and development time line for the Lightbridge fuel pilot factory is included in our Form 10-Q this quarter. For the first 9 months of 2026, we used approximately $13.2 million of cash in operating activities compared to $8.1 million for the same period last year, an increase of $5.1 million.

This increase was partially offset by higher interest income earned, reflecting our increased average cash and cash equivalent balances following our equity financing. During the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, we sold in aggregate 4.3 million shares under our at-the-market or ATM sales agreement with Jefferies resulting in an aggregate net proceeds of $48.9 million. During the third quarter, ATM activity was more limited with approximately $4.5 million of net proceeds raised. As of September 30, 2026, approximately $91.4 million remained available under our $150 million ATM program.

While our current liquidity position provides us with substantial financial flexibility, we expect that development of our Lightbridge fuel pilot factory and the continued advancement of our broader fuel development program will require additional capital over time. We continue to evaluate other funding opportunities in a disciplined manner to support our long-term fuel development activities. Our potential funding sources include strategic partnerships, government grants and contracts and as appropriate, additional capital market transactions. Our capital allocation strategy remains disciplined and milestone driven. We direct resources toward the activities that advance our fuel toward regulatory licensing and commercialization, expansion of our in-house team, irradiation testing, postirradiation examination, fabrication development, computational infrastructure, safety analysis development and now deployment of our pilot factory.

I will now turn the call over to Lesli Mills, our Controller, who will review our P&L for the third quarter and first 9 months of 2026. Lesli?

Lesli Mills: Thank you, Larry. Net loss was $20.4 million or $0.62 per share for the first 9 months of 2026 compared to $12.4 million or $0.55 per share for the first 9 months of 2025. Total operating expenses were $25.6 million for the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, compared to $14.5 million for the 9 months ended September 30, 2025, an increase of $11.1 million. For the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, total R&D expenses amounted to $12.6 million, compared to $5.3 million, an increase of $7.3 million.

The increase was primarily due to a $4.3 million increase in employee compensation and stock-based compensation, reflecting an increase in new hires, increased employee bonuses and several new stock-based awards, partially offset by a reversal of previously recognized stock-based compensation for a performance milestone no longer deemed probable of achievement. A $1.7 million increase in IT expenses comprised primarily of computer software, operating expenses related to the company's high-performance computer and co-development, a $0.6 million increase in INL project labor costs, a $0.4 million increase in R&D project development costs primarily related to critical heat flux testing and safety analysis and a $0.3 million increase in other outside R&D expenses.

Total other income was $5.2 million for the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, compared to $2.1 million for the 9 months ended September 30, 2025. Other income consisted of interest income earned from treasury bills and our bank savings accounts driven by higher cash balances. Back to you, Seth.

Seth Grae: Thank you, Lesli. And with that, I will take questions. Thank you, everyone, for submitting your questions.

Matthew Abenante: Our first question, as postirradiation examination of the initial Lightbridge fuel samples progresses, when does the company expect to be able to disclose the first meaningful quantitative results to investors?

Seth Grae: We expect to be able to announce in the first half of 2027, the first meaningful results following post-irradiation examination of the initial batch of Lightbridge fuel test samples.

Matthew Abenante: One more question. Does management believe a utility can make a conditional commitment to host Lightbridge Fuel lead test assemblies before completion of the full ATR loop irradiation program subject to satisfactory irradiation and regulatory results or does management believe completion of that testing is likely to be necessary before a utility would make such a commitment?

Seth Grae: Yes, we believe it is possible that a utility could make a conditional commitment to host Lightbridge Fuel lead test assemblies before completion of the full advanced test reactor loop irradiation testing program. It is likely that the host utility would want to see the results of postirradiation examination of partially irradiated rodlets of Lightbridge Fuel in the ATR loop before inserting Lightbridge Fuel lead test assemblies. But we believe it is possible for the lead test assembly demonstration program to proceed in parallel with loop irradiation testing of the remaining rodlets of Lightbridge Fuel in the Advanced Test Reactor. I want to thank everyone for participating in today's call.

We appreciate the continued support of our shareholders and dedication of our growing team and partners. We look forward to updating you on our progress in the coming quarters. In the meantime, you can reach us at [email protected]. Stay safe and well. Goodbye.

I’m trying out some of these apps to see just how they work, but if you or people in your neighborhood use Ring devices, you should know what they’re capable of. These mini apps range from casual fun to Flock-like levels of surveillance. Most require a Ring subscription and an additional monthly fee, typically a few dollars. Here are popular examples of those apps, how they work, if they’re legal and what they could be doing in your neighborhood.

For those annoyed by illegal trash dumping or other waste violations, the DumpWatch app promises to watch for trash miscreants using Ring’s AI for about $8 per month. The app records footage whenever it detects large amounts of waste being left in the camera’s field of view and creates a timestamped PDF that can be used to submit a complaint or file a police report.

Note that some examples DumpWatch uses show trash bins left on the sidewalk, a common occurrence on collection days, or extra trash placed beside bins, which may be allowed by local waste companies. It’s not guaranteed to capture only illegal activity.

Yes, these little apps can also serve as tools for homeowners associations if your neighborhood has strict rules about what’s permitted. One example is the $3 per month LawnWatch app, which is trained to monitor properties for HOA violations such as leaving toys cluttering a lawn, dog owners not cleaning up poop and so on. A somewhat more benevolent app, Greenlapse, tracks grass and plant growth over time, and is primarily designed to monitor your own landscaping projects.

Ring’s app store includes a slew of monitoring apps made specifically to track tenants and short-term rental guests, collecting info for landlords to use. One example is the $5-per-month ZoneGauge app, which continuously tracks how many people are in a space, letting owners know when someone is throwing a party, for instance.

Another option is the GuardCat app. It’s $8 per month and it summarizes guest check-outs, cleaner visits, “house rule violations” and more based on what Ring security cameras pick up using AI detection.

A quick reminder here: Companies such as Airbnb have banned indoor security cameras entirely. Apps like these shouldn’t be used indoors at all.

Using AI to monitor pets for unusual behavior that could signal health problems is nothing new. We’ve reviewed quite a few pet cameras and smart tracking collars that do something similar. But apps such as Pet Vet AI can use Ring cams as an alternative for $10 per month. Here, the app analyzes pet snapshots for issues such as limping, throwing up food, sleeping in unusual spots and more, then summarizes any problems for pet owners. The app says it works with birds, reptiles and fish, too, but I’ve never seen pet AI advanced enough to get any worthwhile analysis from the non-mammals in our homes.

Ring’s mini apps extend beyond the home and into many aspects of the workplace, too. Apps such as ProofClock and TimeStack are designed for construction, freight and similar industries to monitor when teams arrive at a location and how long they work, even when the Ring camera owner isn’t present. Some of these apps can also generate uptime and service-level agreement reports, although I’m dubious about tying Ring AI, which isn’t always reliable, so closely to payroll.

We’ve tested plenty of bird feeder cameras that can identify bird species with varying degrees of success. But if you’d like to point a Ring camera at a feeder or birdbath, an app such as What’s That Bird.AI can do something similar for $5 per month. It captures screenshots of nearby birds and attempts to identify them so you can see which species are stopping by.

There’s a small problem here: Feeders from Birdbuddy and similar brands give you bird recognition for free, so if you don’t mind buying a dedicated bird watching camera, there’s no need to pay a subscription at all.

No. Each app has its own requirements, displayed on their download pages. Some will work with nearly any Ring device that uses a camera. Others require a wired-in Ring device or a more recent Ring camera from the past year or so, or both.

Keep in mind that tools like these aren’t perfect and shouldn’t be the sole basis for filing a complaint or taking other action. They’re also expensive for what they do — such as charging $5 per month just to tell you when your mail arrives — so I don’t think they’re worth the cost for the average user. One exception may be pet AI, which could replace more expensive pet camera services. Either way, it’s important to know your options — and which apps your neighbors may be using.
