#3178. Apple’s new touchscreen MacBook Pros may be late, but they have one big advantage

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple finally revealed its new MacBook M5 Pro and Max with a touchscreen OLED display, bringing the best features from the iPhone to its laptops.

Steve Jobs might be rolling over in his grave, but at long last, Apple announced a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen display. The new MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max features a tandem OLED display Apple is calling “ProLED XDR”, scaling up to 2,000 nits of brightness and a 120Hz refresh rate. For the first time, the MacBook Pro will feature touchscreen capabilities and the Dynamic Island — a feature first introduced on the iPhone.

Also: Forget the touchscreen MacBook – Apple’s new M6 is the laptop I recommend for most people

The display and controversial form factor aren’t its only draws: it features a thinner, lighter design and brings back the illuminated Apple logo on the back — some of the most significant changes to the MacBook chassis in years. The new MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips will come in both 14- and 16-inch sizes, with up to 128GB of unified memory, and weigh less than ever: the smaller model at three pounds and the 16-inch at four pounds.

The company, under new CEO John Ternus, is on a spree with new products, with its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, earlier this month (another product that’s been in development for years), and an all-new lineup of smart home products aimed at challenging Amazon’s dominance in that market.

The MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max feature new ProLED XDR displays that control color and pixel luminance at the sub-millisecond level, while monitoring and adapting usage over time, Apple says. The panels feature a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and cover both the P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts, high-end specs indeed for a laptop display.

To reduce glare, Apple says it etched the nano-texture directly into the glass, since the touch sensor is built directly into the panel rather than layered on top of it.

The displays work with Apple’s ProMotion technology, which adjusts refresh rates based on what the device is actively doing: scaling down to 10Hz while idle for better power efficiency and ramping up to 120Hz during gaming or graphics-heavy tasks.

In terms of software and usability, Apple says apps should be ready to go on the new MacBook Pros, since they’re set to register touches as clicks.

Touchscreen laptops are nothing new, having been standard fare on laptops of all kinds for years now. Apple’s entrance into the market is notable because the company took such a hard-line stance against them for years (Jobs famously called them “ergonomically terrible“), but honestly, the everyday consumer in 2026 may struggle to see the big deal.

Either you like using your finger or a stylus on a screen, or you don’t. Can Apple really deliver a touchscreen experience that is worlds better than what’s available on Windows PCs or Chromebooks (or Googlebooks)? It’s debatable.

However, there are a few things Apple has up its sleeve that set it apart from the competition, and they have to do with its most successful product of all time (which also happens to have a touchscreen): the iPhone.

Also: iPhone Duo hands-on: The $2,000 foldable has some magical touches

Apple smartly made the iPhone’s usability wins core to its approach to the new MacBook. For example, it features a Dynamic Island cutout, doing away with the notch in favor of a dynamic multitasking hub. This allows it to adapt through unique touch-based interactions that were previously impossible on a MacBook.

The Dynamic Island serves as the new home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri, changing how you interact with these features by putting them front and center. The design intent here appears to be to keep dynamic, time-sensitive events and apps in close view for quick reference, an interesting merge of how we use both our iPhones and laptops.

Also: Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook is days away – with another OLED surprise

Plus, with Apple’s vast App Store library, there is already a host of touch-optimized programs for Apple’s ecosystem. It doesn’t look like Apple is interested in bringing these directly to MacOS — this is still very much a MacBook Pro — instead, folding in the touch functionality as part of the feature set of these laptops’ premium displays.

In that sense, this is already well-trodden ground for Apple. Bringing the best features of the iPhone to the MacBook Pro isn’t even that revolutionary when you think about it; it’s a smart way to improve its product line.

You already know these new MacBooks aren’t going to be cheap. The base model with the lowest configuration starts at $2,899: the 14-inch M5 Pro with 24GB of unified memory and 1TB of local storage. The prices only scale up from there to seriously astronomical figures, particularly for the ultra-high-end storage options. 16TB of storage will start at $14 grand.

We haven’t seen these laptops in person yet, but I have no doubt the new ProLED XDR screens look fantastic. However, it’s a lot of money for a touchscreen laptop. These devices come hot on the heels of Microsoft and Nvidia’s recent RTX Spark devices, which also target the high end of the market, with AI enthusiasts looking for local AI performance to be front and center.

These laptops are niche, to be sure, but they also don’t speak to such a specific subset of users; instead, they focus on their impressive hardware and implications for creators, artists, and power users.

Also: Apple’s touchscreen Mac event: 3 things I’m excited for – and my one concern

Apple isn’t showcasing a reinvention of the MacBook Pro, but rather a bonus feature for its most powerful ultra-premium laptops. With the recent announcement of the M6 MacBook Pro, consumers looking for an accessible workhorse MacBook already have that option. This is for someone else entirely.

The new MacBook Pros with M5 Pro and M5 Max are now available for preorder, with general availability beginning Friday, Nov. 6.

There's something new on the ballot this time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI data centers are powering everything from ChatGPT to Google's Gemini, but the enormous facilities that make these tools possible are facing growing resistance across the country.

On Tuesday, November 3, voters in 10 states will decide on 41 local ballot measures involving data centers, according to Ballotpedia. Twenty-eight measures would restrict development if approved, while 13 would make it easier for projects to move forward.

The votes come as Americans face rising electricity costs and questions about how much power AI infrastructure should consume, who pays for new energy infrastructure and whether communities benefit enough from having these facilities nearby.

For households already struggling with higher utility bills, the debate has become about more than where technology companies build their next server farms.

Data centers are essential to the AI boom. They power cloud storage, streaming services, internet applications and the sophisticated AI systems used by millions of people every day.

But they also require enormous amounts of electricity to operate servers and cooling systems around the clock. A June 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, with projections ranging from 9.5% to 15.3%.

That growing demand is putting pressure on utilities to expand generating capacity, transmission lines and other infrastructure.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

And consumers are growing concerned about whether they'll be asked to help pay for those upgrades.

According to Reuters, residential electricity prices have increased more than 10% nationally since 2024, with increases exceeding 20% in Ohio.

Not every increase can be attributed to data centers. Rising fuel costs, aging infrastructure and other factors also contribute. But rapid growth in electricity demand is raising questions about how utilities allocate costs between large commercial customers and existing households.

Ohio is at the center of the debate. According to Ballotpedia, the state accounts for 21 of the 41 measures appearing on November 3 ballots.

Several communities, including Sunbury, Defiance and Oregon, will vote on proposals to prohibit data centers that consume more than 25 megawatts of electricity.

In Sunbury, the restrictions could affect a proposed $2 billion Amazon data center project, according to Reuters. But the issue goes well beyond Ohio. California, voters in Alhambra will decide whether to prohibit data centers within city limits. In Edgewater, Florida, residents will consider an amendment restricting new data center development and expansion.

Several Maine communities will vote on temporary moratoriums, potentially pausing projects while local officials establish development rules.

In Illinois, some voters will will weigh advisory questions about whether their communities should support or restrict data center construction.

And in New Jersey, residents of Downe Township will answer a straightforward question: Do they support data centers in their community? The New Jersey vote is advisory, meaning it measures public sentiment rather than directly authorizing or prohibiting construction.

The measures across the country differ significantly. Some establish outright bans, others would restrict only the largest facilities, and some would impose additional approval requirements. The common thread for all is that more communities want a greater say in how AI infrastructure is built.

Electricity markets operate across large regions, meaning power demand in one community can affect costs well beyond its borders. The PJM regional electricity market, for example, serves New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia and other states. According to a recent FactCheck.org analysis, PJM's independent market monitor has identified data centers as a primary driver of higher capacity market prices.

The monitor estimates that data center demand will add billions of dollars in capacity market charges over the current and following delivery years.

Those charges are shared across the regional electricity market, although the impact on individual household bills varies. Even if a community blocks a new facility, demand from AI companies could shift to another location. Existing infrastructure costs and broader electricity-market conditions would remain.

Likewise, approving a project doesn't automatically mean household bills will increase. The outcome depends partly on whether utilities and regulators require developers to cover the infrastructure costs their facilities create.

Technology companies and development supporters argue that data centers create construction jobs, generate tax revenue and attract investment.Amazon, which has major expansion plans in Ohio, has emphasized the employment opportunities, economic benefits and technology services associated with its facilities.

Supporters also argue that data centers are necessary to support the digital services that households and businesses depend on, including AI tools that are rapidly becoming part of everyday life.

Restrictions, they warn, could move those investments to communities with more favorable development policies.

Opponents raise concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, noise, land use and the possibility of households subsidizing infrastructure built primarily for large technology companies. The issue crosses traditional political lines, with local opposition emerging in communities across the country.

Tomorrow's election results could affect where major technology companies build new data centers, how local governments regulate them and the conditions developers must meet before construction begins.

For consumers in the U.S., tomorrow may determine how communities and utility regulators will manage the growing electricity and infrastructure demands of AI without placing unnecessary costs on existing customers.

#3176. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#3175. Will the iPhone Duo Fit in Your Pocket? Here’s How It Compares to Other iPhone Sizes

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The iPhone Duo has a palm-size build, but how does that measure up against Apple's other current phones?

The iPhone Duo is designed to be compact, but that hasn’t stopped some from wondering how its size compares with other iPhone models.

Fortunately, we have all the current iPhone devices on hand to show how the Duo, when folded shut, stacks up against the dimensions of everything from the iPhone Air to the iPhone 18 Pro Max. This should give you a better sense of how easily the Duo might fit into a pocket or bag.

The iPhone Duo is a $1,999 phone that, in case it wasn’t obvious from the price, isn’t for everyone. With a 5.4-inch cover screen and 7.6-inch inner display, it serves as a phone-tablet hybrid that’s ideal for multitasking, watching movies and working on the go. The Duo isn’t especially light or thin, but it’s also not too bulky. It measures 5.2 millimeters when unfolded and 11.3mm when folded, and it weighs 254 grams.

As a first-generation device, it has its shortcomings. The Duo doesn’t support FaceID, opting for TouchID instead. Its multitasking capabilities are limited compared to other foldable phones, and the cameras are more scaled back than the iPhone 18 Pro’s. But other details make the Duo feel refined and intuitive, from the matte texture of the inner display that reduces glare to dynamic software integration across both screens. The Duo can be a tempting option for anyone looking for a phone that feels refreshingly different.

Here’s how the iPhone Duo’s size compares to all current iPhone models.

Starting with Apple’s biggest nonfolding phone, the $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max has a 6.9-inch display. It measures 8.75mm thick and weighs 249 grams, making it just slightly lighter than the iPhone Duo, though that difference is negligible. What you will notice is how much shorter the Duo is, making it easier to slip into a pocket — even smaller women’s pockets.

Meanwhile, the $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display and, like its Pro Max counterpart, is 8.75mm thick. The 18 Pro weighs a noticeably lighter 211 grams, so the Duo does start to feel a little more hefty in comparison.

Apple has yet to unveil a baseline iPhone 18 model, which is expected early next year. In the meantime, here’s how the Duo compares to the $899 iPhone 17, which has a 6.3-inch display and measures 7.95mm thick. The iPhone 17 weighs 177 grams, making it significantly lighter than the iPhone Duo.

The $1,099 iPhone Air has a slightly larger 6.5-inch display compared to the iPhone 17. It measures a sleek 5.6mm thick, and it weighs a featherlight 165 grams. If you’re jumping from the Air to the Duo, you’ll definitely feel the biggest difference compared to other current iPhone models.

And finally, the slightly more budget-friendly $699 iPhone 17E has a 6.1-inch display, measuring 7.8mm thick and weighing 169 grams.

If you’re thinking about making the leap to the iPhone Duo, be sure to check out CNET’s in-depth review for more on using Apple’s first foldable phone.

#3174. The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

From a new smart alarm clock to an Alexa-powered 3D map of your home, here's what's new from Amazon, including prices and release dates.

Amazon announced several new smart home devices today, including two all-new device categories: the $200 Echo Time smart alarm clock and the $230 Alexa Photo Frame. Both are available now, along with an upgraded Echo Dot for $100 and a new Echo Studio with a built-in Home Camera for $250.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

The company’s smart home lineup also now includes a redesigned $500 Echo Show 16, which is available for preorder, with devices shipping in mid-December. Finally, Amazon announced the Alexa Home Map, which lets you create a 3D interactive map of your home’s interior and exterior.

Here are all the biggest updates to know.

The Amazon Echo Time is a new bedside companion and a definite upgrade over the Echo Spot. It’s a rounded speaker with a display and no camera, designed to be the smartest combination of alarm clock and hub available.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

The Echo Time doubles as a smart home hub, since it supports Zigbee and Matter and acts as a Thread border router. It costs $200, so it’s a definite price hike compared to the Echo Spot, but it’s also a more capable speaker with hub capabilities.

The Amazon Alexa Photo Frame is another first for Amazon, arriving just in time for the holidays. The photo frame consists of a 10.1-inch matte display with Alexa+ built in, made to cycle through your own collection of photos. It also allows you to search for specific photos by voice, as well as record voice notes associated with individual photos.

The Alexa Photo Frame comes in three frame finishes, including Birch, Walnut, and Black, so it can fit in with your home decor. It costs $230 and is already available for purchase.

Amazon also announced some big upgrades coming to the Echo lineup. They include a redesigned Echo Show 16, a new Echo Dot, and an upgraded Echo Studio with Home Camera.

The new Alexa Home Map lets you create a 3D interactive map of your home’s interior and exterior, allowing you to navigate floors, zoom into rooms, and see the locations of all your devices while controlling them in real time.

The concept isn’t a novel idea for Amazon, but the Alexa Home Map elevates the experience offered by the Amazon Alexa app’s Map View feature, which we covered at launch three years ago. Map View lets you create a basic layout of the rooms inside your home to place and tap device icons.

Unlike Map View, which focuses on indoor smart devices within four walls, the new Alexa Home Map offers a 360-degree aerial view of your property. It uses your Ring cameras to generate animations of people and cars moving around your yard and uses the controversial Familiar Faces feature to let you know who was detected.

Also: Alexa Tablet 12 Pro review: Forget everything you knew about Amazon tablets

You create the 3D interactive map of your home by using a compatible smartphone with a lidar feature to scan each room and then putting them together. You can then place Alexa-compatible smart home devices in each room and interact with them in real time, like turning on a light or lowering the volume on a speaker.

For the exterior of your home, enter your address, and the app will generate an Alexa Home Map of your residence using existing map data.

Using integrations with compatible Alexa devices, including Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV devices, and other “Works with Alexa” smart home devices, will improve your home security, Amazon says. But it also opens the door for a whole lot more surveillance of your home, both for potential bad actors and for Amazon itself.

Amazon claims that the Alexa Home Map will update dynamically in real time, gathering data from your smart devices in and around your home. As a result, it can show the color of your smart twinkle lights during the holidays, as well as animations of people and cars moving around your property.

A vulnerability in a single third-party smart device could theoretically be used to pivot deeper into your home network or manipulate the map interface, not to mention that the data in this 3D map will include sensitive and private behavioral patterns, like when the family leaves the home or when children return.

#3173. Why Arm Holdings Stock Lost 29% Last Month

Chip stocks walloped on concerns about CoreWeave

During a weak month for semiconductor stocks, Arm Holdings (ARM -4.46%) was one of several losers in the sector.

While there was no major company-specific news out on Arm, the company is highly sensitive to future expectations of CPU demand due to its upcoming launch of the Arm AGI CPU, its first chip. With sentiment turning against the AI infrastructure sector, investors seem to be dialing back expectations for the potential of its new chip business, as well as the growth of its traditional IP business.

According to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, the stock lost 21% last month. As you can see from the chart below, the stock fell steadily over the course of the month, reflecting concerns in the broader chip sector.

The only major piece of company-specific news out on Arm last month was the verdict in its legal dispute with Qualcomm over a charge that Arm breached its license agreement. Arm said the jury awarded Qualcomm just $1 in damages, and the stock finished the day, Oct. 13, bouncing back from a 5% sell-off.

Elsewhere, a combination of factors sent the stock spiraling. Interest rates continued to rise at the beginning of the month, with the yield on the 10-year Treasury note reaching a peak of 5.3%.

Relatedly, a post on a chart of CoreWeave's bond yield set off a panic in the neocloud stock and the broader AI infrastructure as investors panicked that higher interest rates would freeze demand and eventually lead to insolvency for companies like CoreWeave.

CoreWeave finished the month down 37%, and its descent paralleled that of Arm. While Arm doesn't have direct exposure to CoreWeave, Arm is dependent on long-term demand for AI chips, especially those built on Arm-based CPUs and its new Arm AGI CPU. The negative sentiment around CoreWeave not surprisingly spread to Arm then.

Meta Platforms was the named partner for the AGI CPU, and that stock tumbled after its earnings report as its free cash flow turned negative for the first time.

We'll get an update from Arm when it reports third-quarter earnings on Wednesday. Analysts are expecting revenue growth of 21.4% to $1.38 billion, and for adjusted earnings per share to improve from $0.39 to $0.48.

However, investors will want to pay attention to any commentary on the new CPU, which is supposed to start shipping this calendar quarter. While investors shouldn't expect to get any numbers on it, even a sign that production is going according to plan and that the chip has begun shipping would be a positive.

‘Resident Evil,’ ‘Primetime’ and more are streaming this week

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After a couple of quiet weeks, November is starting with a packed slate of new movies across the best streaming services. There’s plenty to watch in the coming days, including new arrivals on Netflix, Hulu, Peacock and AMC+. Plus, there are new picks on premium streaming.

Starting with the latter, this week on PVOD you can buy or rent acclaimed movies like “Resident Evil,” “Primetime” and “Bad Apples.” Meanwhile, Netflix debuts its first Christmas movie of the season, and if you're not ready to deck the halls yet, it's also adding an overlooked romantic crime thriller. Alternatively, Hulu has a farcical comedy sequel, and Peacock has a historical action movie starring Andrew Garfield.

These are just some of the most noteworthy new movies on streaming this week. Below, I’ve rounded up the highlights to save you from having to scroll through each platform to find out what’s new this week. And don’t forget to check out our guide to the top new TV shows, too.

Saoirse Ronan stars in this darkly funny thriller that centers on a school teacher pushed to her breaking point by a disruptive pupil. Ronan is the movie’s biggest asset, with the Oscar-nominated actor delivering a strong leading performance. Where the movie stumbles is progressing beyond its initial setup; the middle portion goes through the motions before a finale that takes a big leap in logic. How that swing lands is a matter of personal opinion; it's definitely divisive.

Maria Spencer (Ronan) is a good-natured primary school teacher fighting a daily battle with rebellious student Danny (Eddie Waller). When Danny pushes her too far, she impulsively locks him in her basement. At first, she regrets her rash decision. However, when her other students start flourishing in the classroom with Danny’s negative influence removed, she resolves to keep the troublemaker trapped.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 3

Director Zach Cregger (“Weapons,” “Barbarian”) delivers the definitive “Resident Evil” movie. The survival horror series has been adapted numerous times. There are the Paul W. S. Anderson movies starring Milla Jovovich, the quickly canceled Netflix series, and several animated efforts, too. None have managed to convey the feeling of playing a Resident Evil video game as well as Cregger’s intense, fast-paced action-horror.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Rising star Austin Abrams plays a courier, tasked with delivering vital medical supplies to a remote hospital in the franchise’s iconic Raccoon City. Once on location, he finds the place overrun with mutated creatures. “Resident Evil” does lean a little too heavily on comedy at times, but this is the blockbuster movie the series has long deserved.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 3

2026 is the year of Robert Pattinson. Having already starred in “The Drama” and “The Odyssey,” two of the year’s very best, he’s rounding out the year with a role in “Dune Part 3,” but before that, you can enjoy his latest performance in “Primetime.” A dramatic biopic that chronicles the controversial television show “To Catch a Predator.” Pattinson plays host Chris Hansen, and as always, the British actor fully commits to the role.

Directed by Lance Oppenheim, “Primetime” forgoes the conventional biographical movie approach and instead handles Hansen’s obsession with ratings and unearthing the most immoral sexual deviants possible through the lens of a psychological thriller. “Primetime” has a lot to say about both Hansen, the Dateline NBC show, and the millions of viewers who consumed every second with glee. Like it or loathe it, “Primetime” is most definitely a bold biopic.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 3

Writer/director Bassam Tariq and star Mahershala Ali team up for this action-thriller that, according to the actor, only came together because Marvel’s “Blade” movie fell apart. The duo met when they were both attached to the MCU project, but after multiple delays and production woes, both moved on, and instead teamed up to make “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.” It would seem we got the better movie in the end.

Rated 96% on Rotten Tomatoes, it’s been labeled an “inventive and tonally unique action flick where Mahershala Ali's soulful performance cuts deepest of all.” In the movie, Ali plays a devoutly religious contract killer who is trying to balance his work, faith, and fatherhood. However, when his wife dies, he’s left as the sole carer for three children and must protect them from the consequences of his murderous profession.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 3

Netflix’s holiday slate starts rolling out this week, and first up is “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas,” a family-focused comedy-drama based on the novel by W. Bruce Cameron, author of “A Dog’s Purpose.” This holiday movie certainly doesn’t look to be doing anything new in the genre, but any flick with an adorable dog at its core is sure to be popular.

It stars Dennis Quaid, Milo Ventimiglia and Jennifer Tilly. Curiously, Quaid actually starred in the movie version of “A Dog’s Purpose,” but this isn’t a sequel. Quaid is playing a new character here.

Netflix’s Christmas crowd-pleaser focuses on the Goss family, whose festive season is thrown into disarray by a medical emergency. With the humans rapidly losing their holiday spirit, it’s up to the family’s wise basset hound, Winstead (voiced by Thomas Haden Church), and a new arrival, an adorable Corgi puppy, to bring the Goss clan back together.

“Super Troopers” fans had to wait 17 years between the first movie and its sequel, so a mere eight-year wait for the trilogy capper, “Super Troopers 3,” probably felt comparatively fast. The cult comedy series from the Broken Lizard crew is a real underdog franchise, and this second sequel is definitely one for the dedicated fans. Its critical reception was lukewarm, but “Super Troopers 3” is sure to delight anybody who’s been watching the antics of this bumbling group of highway patrol troopers since the very start in the early 2000s.

This time there’s love in the air as Farva (Kevin Heffernan) gets engaged to Sarita (Hannah Simone), sister of fellow trooper Thorny (Jay Chandrasekhar). As the wedding approaches, Thorny is desperate to break up the relationship by any means. At the same time, the gang must crack a new drug ring. Expect silly gags and outrageous hijinks.

“Carolina Caroline” is one of 2026’s best movies you (probably) missed in theaters. The crime thriller starring Samara Weaving and Kyle Gallner takes clear inspiration from genre classic “Bonnie and Clyde,” depicting two lovebirds on a criminal spree across the Southern United States. Despite strong reviews, it made little impression at the box office, but could be set to break out now that it’s arriving on Netflix this week.

Looking to escape her small Texas town where she feels unsatisfied with her life, Caroline Daniels (Samara Weaving) impulsively runs away with a charismatic con man (Kyle Gallner), and the two become a notorious criminal duo, engaging in everything from quick hustles to more elaborate heists. As Caroline (Weaving) slips further into the role of a scam artist, she becomes seduced by a world where she can pretend to be anybody she wishes.

“Jason Bourne” director Paul Greengrass’s new historical action movie “The Uprising” found itself at the center of a bizarre marketing campaign over the summer. The movie is based on the 1381 English Peasants' Revolt, which is said to have inspired the stories of Robin Hood. For a brief period, it was claimed “The Uprising” was actually an origin story for the famous (fictional) outlaw, before this was hastily walked back. As for the movie itself, it’s a serviceable historical drama, let down by an ill-conceived ending and a slow middle portion.

In 14th-century England, the ordinary folk are besieged by a plague sweeping Europe and a harsh new tax imposed by King Richard II (Woody Norman) and his inner circle of advisors. Andrew Garfield plays an unnamed rural farmer who leads a full-scale revolt against the established order. Banding together with his fellow commoners, they march on London, with plans to free the young King from the oligarchic influence they believe has led him astray.

“Reacher’s” Alan Ritchson stars in this action-thriller film from director Potsy Ponciroli. On the surface, it looks and sounds like your typical revenge movie. However, there is a wrinkle here that makes “Motor City” a little more interesting. Dialogue is kept to a minimum, with the plot instead driven by a rocking soundtrack and over-the-top action sequences. It’s an experimental approach to storytelling that isn’t wholly successful, but is certainly unique.

Set in 1970s Detroit, John Miller (Ritchson) is a Vietnam veteran and factory worker framed for a crime he didn’t commit by a ruthless gangster named Reynolds (Ben Foster). Adding insult to injury, Reynolds also steals Miller’s girlfriend (Shailene Woodley). After breaking out of prison, Miller embarks on a quest for revenge, and with nothing left to lose, he will stop at nothing until he gets his vengeance.

Rory is a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom’s Guide based in the UK. He covers a wide range of topics but with a particular focus on gaming and streaming. When he’s not reviewing the latest games, searching for hidden gems on Netflix, or writing hot takes on new gaming hardware, TV shows and movies, he can be found attending music festivals and getting far too emotionally invested in his favorite football team.

#3171. Daylight Saving Time Ends Sunday. Get Ready to Change Your Clocks

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Most of the US gains an hour of sleep this weekend, but Hawaii and most of Arizona won’t change their clocks.

It’s time to change your clocks: Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, when clocks across most of the US move back to 1 a.m.

The timing lines up neatly with Halloween — trick-or-treaters on Saturday still get the later sunset, and the extra hour of sleep arrives overnight. Phones and computers update on their own, but oven, microwave and car clocks usually don’t.

The time shift is notorious for disrupting sleep patterns and schedules. Some politicians are advocating for the abolition of time changes and the permanent adoption of daylight saving time, or DST. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July, but it still needs Senate approval and the president’s signature to become law — meaning that, for now, we still have dark winter hours coming.

If you, too, dislike how early it gets dark each day through winter, just remember that brighter evenings will return in mid-March. Here’s what else to know about the switch, including which states skip it — and when the clocks spring forward again.

Daylight saving time in the US ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday. It will return at 2 a.m. local time on March 14, 2027. The end of DST is when we “fall back,” whereas in March, we “spring forward.”

The US isn’t alone in observing daylight saving time. Check out this list of other countries that use DST, along with their start and end dates. The UK, for example, fell back last weekend.

The official US time website shows where time zone boundaries are located.

The exact start dates for daylight saving time and standard time float a little. DST kicks off on the second Sunday of March and ends on the first Sunday of November with the return of standard time.

We spend about eight months of the year in DST. We can thank the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for bringing some order to what had been a complicated history of time changes in the US.

“Motivated by transportation improvements, this act mandated standard time within the existing time zones and established a permanent system of uniform DST, including the dates and times for twice-yearly transitions,” the Bureau of Transportation Statistics states in a history of time zones.

The country’s time zones date to the railroad boom of the late 1800s. DST formally entered the chat in 1918, but its application was inconsistent until 1966. The country tried year-round daylight saving time in January 1974 under President Richard Nixon to address the energy crisis. It didn’t go over well. Congress and President Gerald Ford restored standard time in October 1974.

If you truly hate time changes, then consider moving to Arizona (except for the Navajo Nation) or Hawaii. Those states are on standard time all year long, and their residents don’t have to deal with the physical and mental health impacts of the change. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands also skip DST.

Read more: Why Is NASA Working on a Time Zone for the Moon?

Organizations such as the National Sleep Foundation, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms are united in calling for permanent standard time, saying it’s better for human biology.

“There’s a mismatch between the outside world and our internal clocks during daylight saving time that can result in some negative health consequences,” says Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation.

Dzierzewski cites mental health concerns and upticks in cardiovascular events and drowsy driving. He also calls out safety issues with young children walking to school or sitting at bus stops in the dark. Those safety issues were a big reason why permanent DST didn’t last in 1974.

Time changes aren’t popular. An October 2024 YouGov poll (PDF) of more than 1,100 US adults found that 63% would like to see the changing of the clocks eliminated. Only 17% wanted to keep time changes, and 20% weren’t sure.

Efforts to end the time changes have so far failed to pass into law. The bipartisan Sunshine Protection Act, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, passed the Senate in 2022 — the new version of the bill passed the House earlier this year and was sent on to the Senate to review in July.

While many people agree on eliminating time changes, the schism between daylight saving time and standard time remains. Standard time may have a bit of an image issue compared to DST.

“Part of the issue is that people associate daylight saving time with summer. People love summer, right?” Dzierzewski said. “But the simple fact of the matter is, it would still be summer if we were on permanent standard time.”

President Donald Trump criticized time changes in a 2024 Truth Social post: “The Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn’t! Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient and very costly to our Nation.”

Bills and resolutions at the state level haven’t had real-world impacts yet. Politicians are still split on whether they want permanent daylight saving or standard time. Dzierzewski is hopeful that permanent standard time will win out.

“This is the first time in several years where I’ve seen more legislation introduced at a state level in support of permanent standard time as the solution,” he said.

If you’d like to see time changes end and want to advocate for either daylight saving or standard time, contact your state and national representatives and express your opinion.

Daylight saving time is happening, so now it’s a matter of figuring out how to deal with it. It’s not just about the day of the time change.

“You’re in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally,” Dzierzewski said. He recommends exposure to bright light in the morning, physical activity during the day, eating meals at regular times and practicing a relaxing wind-down routine at night.

The majority of Americans struggle to get the National Sleep Foundation’s recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep for most adults. A CNET survey found that more than half of US adults use some method to cope with sleep-related challenges. Check out some expert-backed tips for improving your sleep quality.

“If you’re doing these healthy sleep behaviors, you’re probably more resilient to some of these changes,” Dzierzewski said. “If you have poor sleep to begin with, you’re probably going to feel it a little bit more.”

Establishing a better sleep routine can take time. There are two things you can do in direct response to the time change. Dzierzewski suggests adjusting your bedtime and wake-up time gradually ahead of the change. For example, you could shift your schedule by 15 minutes per day and ease yourself into DST. He also recommends getting a good dose of bright morning light on the day of the time change to help set your internal body clock.

Think of DST as another kind of wake-up call, one that can motivate you to evaluate your sleep routine and quality and make positive changes. Start with these six simple habits. And don’t forget to change your clocks. Do it the night before, and you won’t have to worry about it later.

#3170. Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding, ranking alongside Codex GPT-6.1 Terra

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Mistral has released the weights for Large 4, along with some impressive Artificial Analysis scores.

French AI lab Mistral shipped its latest model, Mistral Large 4 (ML4), nicknamed “Le Chonk” for its trillion-parameter size, in preview on Oct. 6. As promised, the lab has released the model’s weights, alongside some new benchmark scores that show Western open models gaining ground over their Chinese peers.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

After three weeks of testing with a select group of partners, Mistral’s model sets a new standard for Western-made open models, ranking at the top of Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index among open models globally. The model also comes with three reasoning modes now (low, medium, and high), as is common for heftier models to give users more options based on their level of task complexity.

ML4’s score on the agentic coding benchmark Terminal-Bench 4.0 jumped to 41% from its preview version’s 28% to 41%, beating Opencode’s GLM-5.3 by one small but important point. On the overall Index, however, which shows a model’s composite score across three relevant benchmarks, ML4 is a point behind GLM-5.3, scoring a 48 to GLM-5.3’s 49. Codex GPT-6.1 Terra also scores a 48 overall.

As a reminder, benchmark scores themselves should be taken with a grain of salt, especially considering how many models cheat.

Still, that improvement in performance is meaningful for just a few weeks of extra training. As proprietary AI remains expensive to use, economical models that don’t sacrifice performance are eye-catching. ML4 “rivals top open models such as GLM-5.3 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index while using 47% less tokens per task on average,” Mistral said.

When Mistral released ML4 in preview earlier this month, it touted how the model prioritizes cyber defense capabilities, advertising customizable control and data sovereignty. The company has spent the last few weeks working with developers and leaders to assess the model’s cybersecurity capabilities, a practice that’s becoming commonplace for proprietary American labs like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic as concerns about model security mounts.

Similarly to Anthropic’s Project Glasswing and OpenAI’s rollout of Astra, Mistral’s initial testing partners got access to a less guardrailed version of ML4 with “expanded cybersecurity capabilities.”

At least by some measure, ML4’s promises seem to have come true: Le Chonk scored just above DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the CyberGym benchmark for defensive cybersecurity, which measures how well models find “real memory-safety vulnerabilities in C/C++ open-source projects, reproducing them with proof-of-concept inputs, and patching them without breaking the projects’ tests.”

Recent AI security incidents have somewhat pitted open and proprietary models against each other. Initially framed as less safe because of their malleability, open models are viewed as a new option for cyber defense after proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI proved just as risky.

Mistral said ML4 is built for security that stays under user control — unlike proprietary models, which frontier labs can technically rescind access to at any time.

“The cyber defense capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks,” Mistral co-founder Guillaume Lample said during a briefing for the Oct. 6 preview release.

Following the Hugging Face breach, Mistral was one of many companies that signed Nvidia’s Open Secure AI Alliance, a cross-industry partnership that argues open models are crucial to democratizing defenses against increasingly common AI security incidents.

Also: This new ChatGPT scam tricks you into installing malware

By Nvidia’s logic, and its Alliance that aims to democratize AI security tools, the race is between Mistral and other open models to achieve state-of-the-art security prowess.

Training a competitive model in a compute shortage is no small task for a trimmer lab like Mistral, which doesn’t have the same resources as a pre-IPO giant like Anthropic.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“ML4 was trained from scratch on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months, deployed in Mistral’s own data centers in Europe,” the company said. For context, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said on X that OpenAI trained GPT-6 Astra on roughly 100,000 GPUs.

#3169. Allison Transmission (ALSN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Legacy transmission business hit record quarterly revenue amid Off-Highway integration.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Allison Transmission Holdings, Inc. (ALSN +4.67%) reported record quarterly revenue for its legacy transmission business while integrating its newly acquired Off-Highway Drive & Motion Systems unit. Management reported that the company is transitioning from a component manufacturer to an integrated propulsion systems provider, which allows for increased content per vehicle across conventional, hybrid, and electric platforms. The company increased its full-year 2026 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, citing accelerated demand for North American vocational trucks and robust activity in global mining markets. Despite inflationary pressures in raw materials such as steel and aluminum, the company maintained positive price-cost realization and focused on debt reduction following the significant acquisition at the beginning of the year.

Despite near term headwinds from increased raw material costs, and other inflationary pressures, our margin outlook remains positive. Allison's ability to generate substantial cash flow is hard to overstate.

#3168. November 2026 Skywatching Guide: Meteors, Planets, Stars and a Full Moon

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

This month, you'll find three meteor showers and a planetary alignment starring four planets.

Autumn is marching right along, and so are the objects in the night sky. November is the final full month of fall, and with daylight saving time ending Nov. 1, the sun will set even earlier. That’ll give skygazers more time to see some cool sights without staying up horribly late or waking up unbearably early.

This month of fall is arguably the most active for amateur astronomers, with things to see as early as Nov. 2 and as late as Nov. 30. While there aren’t any major celestial events, a series of smaller ones makes up for it.

Every planet is visible during the month of November, though depending on the time and day, you’ll get a better or worse view of them. Mercury and Venus are the most difficult to see due to their proximity to the sun.

Mercury: Mercury was at its eastern elongation during October, so it starts November a bit too close to the sun to see safely. It reaches western elongation on Nov. 20, where it’ll be easily visible just before sunrise for the rest of the month.

Venus: Venus starts the month just ahead of the sun at sunrise, technically making it possible to see every morning in November. It gets further from the sun as the month goes on, making it easier and safer to see toward the end of the month.

Mars: Mars is high in the sky all month. It rises out of the eastern horizon shortly after midnight at the start of November and rises earlier as the month progresses. Early morning is the best time to see it, or right around midnight toward the end of the month.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are close pals for all of November, rising at roughly the same time and right next to each other in the sky. The star Regulus joins in to form a trio, which is visible to the naked eye the entire month.

Saturn: Saturn is also visible every night in November. It’s in the eastern sky when the sun sets, and sets on the western horizon shortly before sunrise. Right after dark is the best time to see it, but you’ll need binoculars or a telescope to capture its glorious rings.

Neptune: Neptune and Saturn are teamed up for November, with both of them being very close in the sky and following a similar trajectory. Bring binoculars or a telescope.

Uranus: Uranus is in the night sky every day in November, rising in the east shortly before sunset and setting in the west right around sunrise. It reaches opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s as far away from the sun as it can get, and will be the most visible. You’ll still want to bring some binoculars or a telescope for best results.

The month begins with a meetup among Mars, Jupiter and the moon. The three will appear close together in the night sky, making them easy to spot: The moon is easy to find, and both planets are visible to the naked eye. On Nov. 2, the moon will be closer to Mars, and the trio will follow one another across the sky throughout the night. Regulus will also be in tow and readily visible to the naked eye.

Nov. 3 continues the good vibes. The moon slides over to the other side of Regulus on that night, but all four celestial bodies are still quite close together and easy to spot. Mars, Jupiter and Regulus will get even closer to each other as November progresses, but the moon moves even further away after Nov. 3.

The Southern Taurids have technically been active since Sept. 20, and continue until Nov. 20. This long-running meteor shower peaks during the evening of Nov. 4 and morning of Nov. 5. It’s not a terribly strong meteor shower and should average about five meteors per hour. However, it often tosses bright fireballs, so what it lacks in quantity, it makes up for in quality.

The moon is 22% illuminated that night, which the American Meteor Society calls “favorable conditions” for viewing a meteor shower. You want to get as far away from light pollution as possible to give yourself even better odds, and make sure to dress for the weather. The Southern Taurids will appear to originate from the Taurus constellation, which rises in the east shortly after sunset and moves across the sky before setting in the west right before sunrise.

It’s no secret that the full moon is usually the most popular celestial event to happen every month, but skygazers also value the new moon. This is because the moon is a significant source of light pollution, making many stars and planets, such as Uranus and Neptune, harder to see. With the new moon on Nov. 9, it’ll be the darkest night of November — and perfect for stargazing and night-sky photography.

Nov. 9 also happens to be Carl Sagan Day, an unofficial holiday to honor the visionary astronomer. If you’re stuck inside that night, you can always use the occasion to watch Sagan’s legendary Cosmos series, which is available for free on the Internet Archive or through various user uploads on YouTube.

Most of the planets are visible in the night sky almost every night in November, but on Nov. 14 there’ll be a fun little planet parade. It’ll take place just before sunrise, so it’s mostly for early risers. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter are set to line up nicely, making them easy to spot. This is especially true for Jupiter and Mars, which should be right next to each other that night.

The show will start around Nov. 14 and will last until around Nov. 25, depending on your location. The tricky part is catching Mercury in the sky before the sun comes up. It’s only about a 30-minute window since the sun closely follows Mercury up over the eastern horizon. The single best day to view it is Nov. 20, when Mercury is at its western elongation — as far from the sun as it can get.

Uranus is also visible at this time, bringing the number of visible planets to three. Saturn and Neptune are below the horizon. Uranus is on the other side of the sky, however, so it’s not technically part of the alignment.

If you miss the Southern Taurids, you only have to wait a week to catch a glimpse of the Northern Taurids meteor shower. This is another long-lasting meteor shower that started on Oct. 20 and runs until Dec. 10. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 11 and the morning of Nov. 12. The American Meteor Society notes that the moon is only 5% illuminated on Nov. 11, giving viewers even better conditions than during the Southern Taurids.

It is otherwise virtually identical to the Southern Taurids. The shower appears to originate from the same constellation, Taurus, which rises and sets at almost exactly the same times as it did a week earlier. The Northern Taurids promise about five meteors per hour under optimal conditions, with an increased chance of fireballs. Both showers are even fueled by the same comet, 2P/Encke. It’s the space equivalent of a sitcom rerun airing just one week later.

Leonids is usually the most active meteor shower in November. It starts on Nov. 6 and runs until Nov. 30, making it shorter than both Taurids meteor showers. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 16 and the morning of Nov. 17.

The good news is that the meteor shower is very easy to find. Meteors from it will appear to originate from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars and Jupiter, which are visible in the night sky.

The bad news is that this part of the sky doesn’t rise until around midnight, making this a meteor shower for night owls. It should produce about 15 meteors per hour under optimal conditions, though you can expect slightly fewer because the 41%-illuminated moon will create enough natural light pollution to obscure fainter meteors.

The Leonids have produced exceptional meteor storms in the past, with hundreds of meteors per hour. That isn’t expected to happen in 2026, but the odds aren’t zero. They may improve after the comet loops around the sun again in 2031.

A micro moon is noticeably smaller and less bright than a supermoon or even a regular full moon.

November’s Beaver Moon takes place just two days before Thanksgiving. It is also the first of a string of four consecutive supermoons that will close out 2026 and begin 2027. This happens when the moon is within 90% of perigee — its closest point to Earth. The phenomenon makes the moon appear about 7% larger than a regular moon and 14% larger than a minimoon — and noticeably brighter than both.

Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the Beaver Moon reaches its peak illumination on Nov. 24 at 9:53 a.m. ET, which is after sunrise for most people in the US. That means the best time to see it is either the night before (Nov. 23) or the evening after (Nov. 24). The moon remains over 90% full from Nov. 22-27. If you plan on going skygazing, avoid those days like the plague, since the moon creates a ton of light pollution.

It’s not often that the same event happens twice in a single month, but it turns out Jupiter, Mars and the moon just can’t seem to get enough of each other. The trio closes out the month the same way it started: hanging out very close together in the night sky. And yes, Regulus will once again tag along.

Unlike the prior meetup, this one only lasts for one night before the moon dashes away. Since all four of them are visible with the naked eye and the moon is still mostly full, people shouldn’t have any trouble finding them. Eagle-eyed stargazers may see Algieba nearby as well. It’s the second brightest star in the Leo constellation (behind Regulus), and it’s also visible without binoculars or a telescope.

The constellations continue their summer-to-winter shakeup. Prominent constellations in the sky include Taurus, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquila, Pisces and Aries. Mainstays such as the Big Dipper and Little Dipper are still out there, but can be difficult to see if you live too far south. As a rule, we recommend using a sky map or a tool such as Stellarium to pinpoint each object so you can find it.

There are also some lesser-known asterisms to seek out, such as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters), the Great Square of Pegasus and the Circlet of Pisces. The Summer Triangle is still visible, while the Winter Triangle becomes much easier to spot as it rises above the horizon earlier in the evening.

#3167. Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents, Bank of America warns customers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The bank's message follows a trend among financial institutions that are restricting third-party AI agent access.

The age-old warning “don’t share your passwords with anyone” applies to AI agents, too.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

The second-largest bank in the US is urging its customers to stop sharing their banking login credentials with AI. In an email blast titled “Protecting your finances in the AI world,” Bank of America advised customers against sharing their passwords with AI agents.

This follows a trend across banking institutions, where some of the top banks in the country, including Citi, Morgan Stanley, and Wells Fargo, are restricting third-party AI agent access.

AI agents like Meta’s Muse, Anthropic’s Claude, and OpenAI’s Dots work on behalf of the user and across apps and services to make purchases, send messages, and fulfill to-dos. But the agents can pose a great risk to your banking portfolio if, for example, they make a financial decision on your behalf or compromise your information in a data leak.

Just last week, Axios reported that AI agents are gaining unauthorized access to their user’s bank accounts and acting independently of user instructions, sending some of the biggest US banking institutions into a frenzy.

(SNDX -4.03%) management reported a significant expansion in total revenue during the third quarter, driven by the commercial success of its lead therapies, Revuforj and Niktimvo. The company is experiencing a shift in treatment paradigms, particularly in relapsed/refractory leukemia, where an increasing number of patients are bridging to stem cell transplants and subsequently resuming therapy as maintenance. Management stated this trend creates a favorable long-term tailwind for therapy duration and franchise growth. Syndax remains focused on transitioning its pipeline into front-line indications for acute myeloid leukemia and chronic graft-versus-host disease while advancing two new assets into the clinic next year. With a cash position of over $550 million, the company indicated it is well funded to reach profitability through its existing product and collaboration revenue streams.

Nicholas Botwood: Thank you, Steve, and I would like to start with revumenib, which is on Slide 8. We have made excellent progress advancing our lifecycle management program designed to unlock the full potential of revumenib. In partnership with leading researchers around the world, we continue to advance the pivotal front-line trials of revumenib and remain well positioned to be the first to deliver a menin inhibitor for newly diagnosed AML. Global site activation and patient enrollment is well established in these pivotal trials, informed by an extensive body of clinical evidence, allowing for optimization of our endpoint assumptions and other aspects of the study designs.

We are also advancing an industry-leading portfolio of studies in partnership with clinicians at the forefront of menin research. These studies will provide important practice-informing and potentially guideline-enabling evidence across the acute leukemia treatment continuum and multiple patient populations with high unmet need. We will share the latest results from a number of these studies in the fourth quarter. The upcoming presentations will highlight the unique breadth and depth of clinical evidence supporting revumenib and the vast experience clinicians have established with our medicine. We expect new data in the fourth quarter across 3 key themes. First is the potential for revumenib to benefit patients earlier in the treatment paradigm.

Second, the ability of revumenib to bring patients to transplant and its potential in the post-transplant setting. And third, real-world evidence supporting the effectiveness and safety of revumenib, particularly in combination therapy. So I would like to walk through each of these areas separately. So firstly, we expect new front-line combination data that will provide strong support for our ongoing pivotal front-line trials of revumenib. Updates from the BEAT AML and SAVE trials will provide additional evidence supporting the potential for revumenib in combination with venetoclax and a hypomethylating agent in NPM1 and KMT2A patients who are unfit to receive intensive chemotherapy.

Notably, compared to the landmark BEAT AML data published in June, the upcoming analysis will have significantly longer follow-up and report outcomes in a larger cohort of patients. These updated data will build on the previously reported BEAT AML and SAVE data showing overall response rates approaching 90% and 100% MRD negativity among responders by flow cytometry, along with encouraging early survival data. Additionally, we will provide an update from our Phase I front-line trial of revumenib in combination with intensive chemotherapy in NPM1 and KMT2A patients. These data will build on the previously reported results showing high rates of remission and MRD negativity with the triplet, along with encouraging durability and tolerability.

We also look forward to updated results from INTERCEPT. This is the first trial studying the use of a menin inhibitor as a so-called MRD eraser. A research area of high clinical interest, INTERCEPT explores using revumenib to intervene early at MRD or early relapse, rather than waiting for morphological relapse, which can trail rising MRD by 3 to 4 months in NPM1 patients. Results presented at ASH 2024 from the first 11 NPM1 patients were encouraging, 54% of patients achieved a reduction in MRD, including 36% who actually achieved MRD negativity. We anticipate the presentation of more mature data from a larger cohort in the fourth quarter.

Positive results could support the use of revumenib to intervene earlier in the acute leukemia treatment journey. Now turning to the pre- and post-transplant setting, we will present results that highlight the relationship between the robust overall response rate observed with revumenib and its ability to enable a meaningful number of relapsed/refractory KMT2A and NPM1 patients to proceed to stem cell transplant. We also expect the first data from a Phase I multicenter trial evaluating revumenib as a post-transplant maintenance. This dataset will build on the encouraging data from MD Anderson presented at ASCO and EHA earlier this year.

They reported a 2-year overall survival rate of 90% among heavily pretreated KMT2A, NPM1 and NUP98 patients who resumed revumenib post-transplant, nearly double the historical rate observed prior to the introduction of revumenib. And then additionally, we will expand the body of real-world evidence supporting clinical decision-making with new data from multiple centers. To date, Syndax is the first and only company to report real-world data supporting the effectiveness and safety of our menin inhibitor as a monotherapy or in combination with other therapies in NPM1, KMT2A and NUP98 patients with relapsed/refractory or MRD-positive disease. Previously reported results were encouraging. Those data showed high rates of response, MRD negativity and transplant, along with evidence of durable, ongoing remissions.

Prior datasets also underscored revumenib's predictable and manageable safety profile, including in combination therapy. Turning to Slide 9 now and the other programs in our pipeline, in partnership with Incyte, we are advancing a robust lifecycle management program for axatilimab. Two trials of axatilimab in newly diagnosed chronic GVHD are underway. We now expect the top line results from the Phase II trial of axatilimab in combination with ruxolitinib to be reported at a medical meeting in the first quarter of 2027.

The updated timing reflects the goal of presenting a mature and comprehensive dataset that includes not only the primary endpoint of overall response rate, but also key secondary measures such as event-free survival, which will be important for understanding the profile of the regimens. We expect top line results from the Phase 3 trial of axatilimab in combination with corticosteroids in early 2028. Both of these trials have the potential to impact the treatment paradigm for front-line chronic GVHD. We also recently published data from AGAVE-201 supporting the safety and feasibility of reduced frequency dosing of axatilimab in patients with recurrent or refractory chronic GVHD in Blood Advances.

These data show that transition from axatilimab 0.3 mg/kg every 2 weeks to 0.6 mg/kg every 4 weeks was feasible and well tolerated. Patients had a long duration of therapy after the switch, with a median of 21 months, and 84% remained on treatment at data cutoff, suggesting ongoing clinical benefit. This is an important publication that provides physicians with evidence that can inform their treatment decisions. Turning now to our pipeline assets, SNDX-4321 and 62122. 4321 is a novel, mutant-selective, allosteric inhibitor in development for EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer. 62122 is a next-generation menin inhibitor in development for myelofibrosis, or MF. Like revumenib and axatilimab, these assets have first- and best-in-class potential in areas of high unmet need.

We expect both molecules to be in the clinic next year and remain on track to submit the IND for 4321 by the end of 2026 and the IND for 62122 next year. Both of these clinical development programs are designed to efficiently generate clinical data that could validate the target and the potential for these 2 approaches. Our development of 62122 will be supported by a Phase I/II proof-of-principle trial of revumenib in MF that we expect will initiate in the fourth quarter of 2026, with initial data anticipated in the second half of next year.

This trial, conducted in partnership with a group of leading MF researchers, will be the first to explore the potential for menin inhibition in MF. With 4321, we expect to get the first assessment of monotherapy in lung cancer in early 2028. We look forward to sharing more details on both programs as we get closer to advancing into the clinic next year. So in summary, we are executing on a bold R&D vision that aims to deliver novel therapies that transform cancer care. With world-class R&D capabilities, strong partnerships with leading scientists and clinicians and the resources to drive innovation, I have great confidence we will deliver on this vision.
