But the NPM1 patient, if we looked at the clinical trials, about 11% of patients went to transplant.

So we are seeing earlier stage patients, about 75% are first and second line, combination treatment is in 40% of patients, and I think physicians were unlocking. And this may not be just a menin effect; this could be a Revuforj effect in that NPM1 patient. So 40%, first time we have revealed that in a quarter, so that is new information, of patients moving to transplant that are NPM1 patients, and 50% returning post. So as Michael mentioned, short headwind now, but the tailwind is going to be significant. Either you're seeing patients stay on much longer, the longest duration of treatment is going to be that transplant, post-transplant start.

That group will grow, and as mentioned, if they are not fit to go to transplant, that duration is also increasing over time. So we feel like we are in a very, very, very good spot heading into the end of the year and into next year.

Operator: The next question is from Stephen Willey with Stifel.

Stephen Willey: Yes, congrats on the quarter. And also, just want to say, great working with Keith and wishing him all the best in his work. Quick question on the NPM1 transplant rate that you are seeing. I know that you kind of alluded to it. This 40% is higher than what was thought for this patient population. I know it's probably more than 2x what most of the KOLs have told us. Do you think that this is a durable trend? Do you think this has something to do with just the onboarding of new patients just having a certain phenotype?

We would just be kind of curious how you think about the durability of this 40% getting transplanted, and then just have a follow-up.

Michael Metzger: Yes, Steve, thanks for the question. No, actually, what I think is happening, what we hear from physicians, is that we are treating patients earlier, we are treating them in combination, and they are getting to response. And so I think that's essentially true for KMT2A, but it is also true for NPM1. We are having great success in getting them to a response. Remember, in our trial, we treated later-line patients and we had a 50% overall response rate. We believe that's by treating them earlier and treating them in combination, you can drive a higher percentage of patients into response.

And I think that's what's getting patients to a transplant, the ability to bridge that and get them there quickly. And then ultimately, the fact that they have received less therapy over time, meaning like if you treat them earlier, they do not get as worn down from subsequent therapy, you can get them on to maintenance. And so I think that is that coupled with the fact that physicians have told us that transplant techniques have improved, and that allows for more flexibility in how you treat these patients. So the openness to transplant and maintenance seems to be quite real to us and encouraging. I don't know, Nick, if you have anything to add on that front?

Stephen Willey: Okay. And then just a quick follow-up. I know the extension of the front-line Niktimvo rocks for steroid data was pushed into the first quarter. I know it sounds like that was a byproduct of wanting to be able to present durability data. Can you just remind us what the kind of benchmark durability data is in terms of response duration with steroids in the front-line, and I guess just kind of any ballpark estimate of what you think would be clinically meaningful in terms of exceeding that?

Michael Metzger: Yes, thanks for the second question, Steve. So I'm going to turn it to Nick.

Nicholas Botwood: Yes, thank you, Steve. So yes, we're going to -- as you heard, we have moved it into Q1 and hope to present it in Q1 in order to present the totality of the data. We've talked previously about the primary endpoint, which is the response rate at 6months, where we're anticipating a benchmark historical for steroids of around 40%, the alternative hypothesis being around 60%, so we'll be able to present that. But then I think it's important to present both the duration of response and the EFS.

Now it's not built into the statistics, but if you look at roughly what you'd expect for the EFS for steroids alone, it's probably of the order of 6 to 7 months. And I would anticipate that an increment of that of the order of 3 to 4 months would be quite clinically meaningful to physicians and patients to avoid them having to have a steroid regimen and all of the morbidity associated with having to take dexamethasone. So that's the sort of order of magnitude we would be hoping to see a difference in. But obviously, we'll look forward to reporting those data in totality in Q1.

Operator: The next question is from Etzer Darout with Barclays.

Gustave Diep: This is Gustave on for Etzer. Two quick ones for us. The first one is on the AGAVE-201 data that showed the transition from 0.3 to 0.6 Q2 to Q4 weeks. What's the significance of this data moving forward? And then number two is around the combination use, it's to about 40% still. At this point, are you able to tell whether the combination use is associated with higher transplant rate, or longer duration of treatment, or deeper responses in the commercial setting?

Michael Metzger: Maybe I'll turn it over -- thanks for the question, Gustave. Let me turn it over to Nick about the AGAVE-201.

Nicholas Botwood: Thank you for the question. I think this is a very patient-centric approach. I mean, I think the simple clinical benefit is that you are able to transition a patient from a 2-weekly IV to a monthly IV with comparable tolerability and prolonged duration of therapy. That's what we have shown in the manuscript and in the publication. And I think that's a benefit to patients. That's something that could ultimately inform guidelines and potentially even inform labeling in due course, which is a consideration. But again, I think it's a patient-centric approach just requiring less health care burden and importantly less burden for the patient to have a 4-weekly infusion as opposed to 2-weekly.

Michael Metzger: And the second question, I guess, was about combo use and the 40% that we are seeing, and really what's the breakdown in that percentage, and I guess, what's driving them there. I don't know, Steve, do you want to make any comments?

Steven Closter: I would probably pass to Nick. I think the claims data does not really give that subset, but we haven't shared data previously, but I think...

Nicholas Botwood: We've seen, I mean, I think there's a drive. Because we've presented such compelling data of revumenib in combination, I think particularly with Ven/Aza combinations, there is a desire for physicians to use revumenib in a combination with a variety of different chemotherapies. We will be updating later this quarter some 2 to -- a few real-world series from multiple centers that I think really emphasizes the desire of centers to use revumenib in combination when they can, because you get much higher response rates. And the much higher response rates, including responses like MLFS, give the patients the opportunity to go to transplant.

And again, we're hoping to present data demonstrating revumenib bridging patients from responses into transplant and then potentially onto maintenance. And that's really the best opportunity to give patients a durable remission and outcome. So that's really the drive that you are seeing to combination.

Operator: The next question is from Yigal Nochomovitz with Citi.

Joohwan Kim: This is Joohwan Kim on for Yigal. On the 20% sequential increase in new Revuforj patients, was that growth broad-based across newer accounts or primarily concentrated within the established high-volume centers? And just wondering, are you seeing meaningful repeat prescribing among the newer accounts?

Michael Metzger: Thanks for the questions. First, the 20% quarter-over-quarter growth, where accounts is that kind of falling into, Steve?

Steven Closter: Yes, I think the exact question was 20% increase in new patients: where are we seeing that from?

Michael Metzger: Right. Where is it rising from?

Steven Closter: It's coming from all over. I mean, 2/3 of our business comes from what we will call Tier 1, Tier 2, and then the rest of the business comes from, we'll say, smaller accounts of which there are hundreds. We have had over 620 accounts prescribed to date. That is most of the Tier 1s and Tier 2s, about 90%, the rest are smaller community practices. That continues to grow. I think we had 8% growth in new accounts. So the business is being spread, and that's how you want it. You want a large foundation of users, treating a wide range of patients.

That's how you build a big brand, and that's exactly what is happening today, and that will continue over time.

Michael Metzger: And how would you characterize the repeat business?

Steven Closter: High repeat business. We'll say this, the patients like this are, in general, challenging to treat. Even from early on in the launch, we've got a multifunction-type team, including nursing support care, to make sure clinicians and their entire staff know how to treat patients successfully with Revuforj. So from the launch, and that continues today, from a customer and account that prescribes for the first time, they are going to get the care. So the repeat rate is incredibly high, assuming they are seeing patients. Even smaller accounts will continue to use the drug on multiple occasions.

And as we know, Revuforj has been the standard of care in KMT2A and established itself in NPM1 patients to treat more patients on a continual basis.

Joohwan Kim: Got it. And if I could just ask one more quick one. On EVOLVE-2 and REVEAL, should we be thinking that the 2 studies complete enrollment on broadly similar time lines, or are you seeing that one is perhaps tracking ahead of the other?

Michael Metzger: Thanks for the final question. We haven't updated our guidance on either one of them, so I don't want to get into that at this point. But both are moving along well and on our schedule, so we feel encouraged.

Operator: The next question is from David Dai with UBS.

Xiaochuan Dai: Great. So very encouraging new patient starts where there is about 20% quarter-over-quarter growth versus decline in 2Q that you characterized as temporary. I mean, help us understand a little more around whether the improvement reflects a normalization of patient flow, better patient identification, broader account penetration or share gains from other menin inhibitors? And more importantly, what gives you confidence that this growth rate can remain positive next several quarters?

Michael Metzger: Thanks, David. Steve, you want to tackle the new patient start question?

Steven Closter: Yes, we can, David. Appreciate the question, and question, right, reasonable question to ask where the growth come from and why. I think, as we described last quarter, which Q2 was a somewhat down quarter for the entire market, things happen. I mean, there is just variability quarter-to-quarter. There's not any one thing that drives this. I think what we are seeing in Q3 for us, encouraged by the 20% increase in new patient starts, there was growth in both KMT2A and NPM1. We continue to see the number of our accounts expand. Formulary coverage is still holding. We -- obviously, we talk to clinicians and market research and gain insight.

So we're encouraged overall by what we see in the business. And just to reiterate, even the dynamic we see in the NPM1 patient moving from transplant, patients coming back, these are all good things that are based in the trust in the clinical profile. We talk about use, there is over 2,000 patients that have used the drug commercially, hundreds more in clinical trials. ASH is going to be great. There's so much new data coming. So in the forward, we're optimistic. We are not going to really comment on this quarter, but we gained a lot of steam in Q3 and that will continue for the rest of this year.

Michael Metzger: Right. And I would just add that, look, remember, we have 80-plus percent of this business, right? Relapsed/refractory is really ours, and we are continuing to build on that momentum. KMT2A, NPM1, we kind of have the dominant share across all age groups. So I think that is a very good place to be as we enter the last part of the year here.

Operator: The next question is from Salim Syed with Mizuho.

Salim Syed: Congrats on the progress. I guess one from us on the CFO transition. And thanks to Keith for all his help, and welcome to Aaron. Keith, so the press release was worded today as retiring. Just curious here why you felt like -- first of all, is this the loose definition of retirement that we should be thinking about here, and you plan on doing something else? And why did you feel like right now was the right time to -- I guess it looks like it was your decision, why was it the right time to make that transition out of Syndax and maybe to something else?

Keith Goldan: Yes. Salim, thanks for the kind words and the question. So yes, this was purely a personal decision that I made along with my family. Maybe the time was probably right a little earlier in the year. I care tremendously about this company, the patients that we treat, the teams that we have built, and wanted to ensure that the transition was as smooth as it could be, so there was -- to minimize any adverse impact on the business, on the team, on patients. So worked with the leadership team, the board to find a great replacement.

And yes, this is not a retirement in the loose setting, so I'm looking forward to spending more time with my family, with my friends, pursuing some of my hobbies, doing some philanthropic work. So it has been a good run. I have been a CFO for 26 years, and just looking ahead to the future.

Salim Syed: Okay. All right. Well, we wish you well, and congratulations. And thanks for the additional color, Keith.

Operator: The next question is from Andres Maldonado with H.C. Wainwright.

Andres Maldonado: Keith, I wish you the best as well. Maybe circling back to some of the commentary on the transplantation eligibility. In the context of what you guys gave us today, the 40% in NPM1 versus the 50% in KMT2A, was curious on how much of that gap reflects age and fitness versus essentially cohort maturity? And I guess how realistically can that signal go? And my second question is on combination use. Given the roughly you stated today that 40% of the use is in combinations. I guess, can you provide a little bit more color about which regimens are driving that outside of the usual suspects?

And are they essentially -- how should we think about the breakdown of whether they are extending treatment duration or just primarily getting those patients to transplant?

Michael Metzger: Great, Andres. Thanks for the questions. So in terms of what we are seeing with transplant, and where is -- essentially took your question as where is it really going here? The 40% for NPM1 with 50% of the patients returning for maintenance, 40% is a lot higher than we had expected. And so could it get to 40%, 50%? I expect it could, just given the momentum we are seeing. And at 50% of those patients resuming, we expect maybe 60%, 70% of those patients to resume maintenance. So that is sort of how we see that.

And again, it's more of a projection than a hard and fast rule; it is based on physician conversations and some research that we have done and what we are seeing in the real world. Then if you look at KMT2A, that has been creeping up over time, also much higher than we have seen in clinical trials, now at 50% transplant rate, 60% resuming maintenance, up from about 55% or 50% last quarter. So it's really moving up on the patients returning for maintenance, which is quite encouraging.

We have said that the transplant rate for KMT2A could probably go up to maybe 60%, probably not a lot higher, and we expect 70% to 80% of those patients with KMT2A to come back on for maintenance. Again, thinking about how long they can stay on maintenance therapy and reflecting from what physicians have told us and what we've seen in some of our real-world work that we'll report on even at this upcoming meeting, you see that the desire is to treat them for 1 to 2 years in maintenance. And that would be a very good outcome for patients, keep them in remission for a long time and hopefully move them forward.

And that is, I think, the paradigm that we are pursuing, again with some estimates for what the rates could be. But Nick, maybe I'll pass to you for the combination question.

Nicholas Botwood: Yes, just a few additional comments on that, including in combination. I mean, one is, I think the drive to transplant, remember in relapsed/refractory is really the best chance a patient can have of a durable remission. So it's a little different from a consideration front-line. Once you have relapsed, you really want to get a patient to transplant if you can. We are hoping to update some data in the fourth quarter which looks at our patients that have gone on to get a transplant and looks at the role of revumenib as a sort of bridge to transplant. How do you get them there?

What kind of response do you need to see, including all of the contributors to overall response rate, which we know we have the highest overall response rate in the class. So that would include MLFS, and this makes these patients eligible for transplant, which I think is quite promising for patients. Combination use varies. I think what we see most commonly is Ven/Aza or single-agent Ven, occasionally other sorts of chemotherapy. Only rarely do we see combinations with targeted agents. It's not a high priority for our program. They tend to be sequenced more, but occasionally it might be a combination. And then maintenance of course is really important.

And again, I think we have the most mature and significant data really trying to elucidate how to optimally treat a patient with maintenance revumenib. We will be updating some data from a Phase I we are doing with Dr. Ball, which I am excited about, which looks at optimization of dose and managing patients, and then a variety of real-world data again optimizing patients with revumenib in the maintenance therapy. And as Michael said, physicians tend to want to keep them on if they can for one to two years.

Again, we are hoping to update data on the MRD -- erasing MRD, which is really exciting, and I think that will be the first data to be presented showing that. And then perhaps the last thing I would say, as the data continues to mature, we are hearing from physicians now, if the patient has done really well and tolerating the drug well at 2 years, sometimes they don't even want to come off at 2 years. And so we are having discussions now with physicians who want to keep a patient on because they are just happy to be relapse-free at 2 years after their transplant and doing well.

So that's also a trend we are beginning to see as the data matures.

Operator: The next question is from Jason Zemansky with Bank of America.

Unknown Analyst: This is [ Jackie ] on for Jason. Congrats on the progress. So you've talked about transplant creating a near-term headwind, but ultimately becoming a meaningful tailwind as the post-transplant population stacks. So with the KMT2A restart rate now at 60% and NPM1 already at 50%, how should we think about the timing of that inflection? Is that something you expect to become a more meaningful driver of Revuforj growth over the course of 2027?

Michael Metzger: Jackie, thanks for the question. I think you hit it on the head. Honestly, I think this is a really important phenomenon that takes some time to play out. Basically, it's because you have patients who are going to transplant within, call it, 3 months of being put on Revuforj, and then they pause treatment for a number of months, call it, 2 to 4, to 5 months in some cases, maybe even more, and they pause treatment and then they resume. And so what that means is you are going to have the tailwind that kicks in quite a bit later.

And you need time for the number of patients who drop for transplant to be kind of overcome by patients coming back, meaning in terms of revenue stacks. So again, that takes time, and it takes time for both now NPM1 and KMT2A. We are not -- we haven't been kind of thinking about how NPM1 was part of this equation until recently when we saw the data that it's really very much the same and very similar paradigm to what we are seeing with KMT2A.

That was a bit of news to us, but we think it will be ultimately a very good thing for patients as they come back on and can stay on treatment for a long time, as Nick had mentioned earlier. So yes, I think 2027 is where you'll see the greatest impact. We have started to see some of that, but we'll start to see more as it stacks in '27.

Operator: Our final question today is from Mayank Mamtani with B. Riley.

Mayank Mamtani: Yes, congrats on a strong execution quarter. And best wishes to Keith for his next chapter. Just a clarification question, and maybe if you could update us how maybe 4Q to date is progressing on the TRX versus NRX. Obviously, NRX did very well quarter-over-quarter. TRX is lagging a little bit, 20% versus 13%. Is there, again, anything you can comment on 4Q, how that is kind of progressing would be helpful, but more sort of long-term, just thinking about how, in a sustainable manner, we can see TRX accelerating? That would be just part one, commercial question. And then second, on the -- Nick, your comments on the newly diagnosed Phase III program, very helpful.

Was just wondering if you could contextualize some of the paradigm Ven/Aza, EFS and MRD data we recently saw? And how do you think about MRD-negative CR as a surrogate endpoint? And then just your expectation in fit versus unfit control arm for EVOLVE-2 also, and how do you see essentially maintenance being handled given you are getting so much deep remission in the front-line setting across fit and unfit? Sorry, that was long-winded, but would be great to hear your thoughts.

Michael Metzger: Anyway, thanks for the questions. Yes, so the good news is I get the short question, which is the first one. What are we seeing in the fourth quarter? We are not going to comment on the fourth quarter. I'll say, look, we feel good momentum coming out of third quarter, so we are very hopeful that the business will continue to really ramp from here. But that's my answer. I am going to turn to the second set of questions for Nick.

Nicholas Botwood: Yes, great questions, and we can maybe talk a little bit more about the trials when we have presented our data at ASH, or at least the abstracts are open, on the relevance of those data to inform the Phase IIIs. But what I would say is they give us a lot of confidence in the assumptions around the endpoints. And just to remind everybody very briefly, for EVOLVE-2, we have 2 dual primary endpoints. One is CR, the other is overall survival. So those are relatively simple, and we will be updating data from both BEAT and SAVE that I think is very informative to those endpoints.

And we feel very confident in the way we have designed those studies, I think is quite strategically smart. And then for REVEAL, which is in fit patients, patients eligible to receive intensive chemotherapy, again, we have dual primary endpoints. One of them is quite stringent, which is looking at MRD-negative CR, but assessed in the bone marrow. Again, look for updates for our study 708, which is revumenib in combination with intensive chemotherapy that informed that study, and the relevance of those data for that study. And then the other dual primary endpoint in REVEAL is event-free survival, which again takes a little time to mature, but is it going to be the definitive endpoint?

I would say, for potential approvals. So more on that to come, but the data are very helpful in ensuring we have got the studies designed and executed in the most efficient way we can, with the highest probability of success.

Mayank Mamtani: And how are you handling maintenance crossover in these front-line studies, Nick?

Michael Metzger: Sorry, Mayank, can you repeat that?

Mayank Mamtani: Just the final part of that question was how are you handling crossover and some of the maintenance settings given you are getting deep remissions and some of them might be even going in transplant? Was just curious how the follow-ups are handled in the 2 studies?

Nicholas Botwood: Yes, the studies do not allow for formal crossover for that reason, and recall in REVEAL, the dual primary endpoint is event-free survival, which we are not anticipating to be unduly impacted by any subsequent therapies.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I will now turn the floor over to Michael Metzger for any additional comments or closing remarks.

Michael Metzger: Thank you all. We appreciate everyone tuning in today to discuss our recent progress and the exciting milestones ahead. We look forward to seeing many of you at the upcoming investor conferences in Q4 and at ASH. And before I say good evening, I want to thank Keith Goldan for all he has done for us. We wish you all the best in your retirement.

Michael Metzger: Have a good evening, everyone.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you, and you may now disconnect.

#3165. A massive trade just happened in surging shares of Snap

Don't call it a comeback yet, but shares of beleaguered social media stock Snap Inc. are up almost 20% this month and options traders are betting it's about to go on a big run.Snap shares have traded under $10 since July 2025 following a near-complete collapse from over $80 at the stock's high in 2021 to a low of $3.81 in April. But now, as excitement swirls over social media giant Meta Platforms' AI agent, traders are pouring into Snap call options on Monday, propelling trading volume to more than four times the month-long average, Cboe LiveVol data show.Almost 140,000 options on Snap traded Monday, including about 64,000 call trades that were likely initiated by buyers, compared to under 7,000 puts. Traders sold more than 12,000 puts, and just over 34,000 calls. The net trade sentiment, as well as net directional bias according to options deltas, was positive, according to Barchart.

Nine out of the top 10 trades by volume were calls, and of the $5.5 million in premium exchanged, $5 million was tied to calls, SpotGamma data show.The most popular contract to buy was the 8-strike call expiring Dec. 18, which traded 26,000 times. That contract costs about 37 cents and needs Snap to rally 30% before expiry to pay off. If that happens, it would be the highest the stock's traded since February.The owner of photo-sharing and messaging app Snapchat also offers augmented-reality `Specs' glasses. Shareholder Blue Duck Capital issued an open letter to Snap's board of directors last week urging the company to raise dedicated capital to support the product, saying it could lead to a $12-$14 share price.

#3164. You Can End Spammy Election Phone Calls Now With This iPhone Trick

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

The election is almost over, and you can end spam calls now.

Election day is a few days away, and that means political campaigns are mounting one last push to advocate for their candidate and issue. So you might be getting more election-related phone calls than usual. While those calls are well-meaning, they can be annoying if you’ve already voted early or have made up your mind about who to vote for. Luckily, if you keep your iPhone updated to the most recent iOS version, you can enable call screening on your device.

Apple introduced call screening in iOS 26. It isn’t an Apple Intelligence feature, so any iOS 27-compatible iPhone, such as the iPhone 14 Pro, can use it. I enabled the feature over a year ago and my iPhone has diligently held back spam calls, like the Hoover Dam, ever since. But you have to enable it first.

Here’s how to enable call screening in a few easy steps and what to know about the new feature.

1. Tap Settings.2. Tap Apps near the bottom of the menu.3. Tap Phone.

Under the section Screen Unknown Callers, you’ll see three options: Never, Ask Reason for Calling and Silence. Here’s what you should know about each of these options and which one is right for most people.

Choosing Never is the default option and lets calls from unsaved numbers come through and ring on your phone. It also documents missed calls in your Recents list in your Phone app, just like before call screening was available.

If you tap Ask Reason for Calling, your iPhone will ask anyone who calls you from an unsaved number why they are calling you without ringing your iPhone. After the caller answers a few questions, your iPhone will notify you with a transcript of the caller’s answers. Then you can decide whether you want to answer the call.

You can also pick Silence, which is the nuclear option for phone calls. Any unsaved numbers that call you will be silenced and sent to voicemail, no questions asked.

Ask Reason for Calling is the best option for most people who want to screen calls. I chose it, and while it notified me when scam callers answered some questions, which they rarely did, it also notified me when my doctor’s office called to go over some test results. If I had chosen Silence, I would have missed my doctor’s office (and choosing Never would mean checking every call if I was expecting something important).

If you choose Ask Reason for Calling and dislike it, you can always follow the steps above again and choose one of the other options. And remember, you can always silence your iPhone and not be bothered by any phone calls at all. My wife has not taken her phone off silent in months, and she remains blissfully unbothered by spam calls.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27.2 and iOS 27.1 as well as our iOS 27 cheat sheet for other tips and tricks.

#3163. Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined – update both ASAP

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The latest version of Firefox fixes 167 security vulnerabilities, most of which are of high severity, while the newest version of Chrome patches 52 flaws, four of which are critical.

With security vulnerabilities continually plaguing the software we use, it’s time once again to update both Firefox and Chrome browsers to protect yourself from the latest exploits.

Also: Half of all cyberattacks start in your browser: 10 tips for staying safe

This week, Mozilla updated Firefox to version 159, not just for Windows but also for Android, MacOS, and Linux. The latest version includes fixes for 167 security bugs. Among these, 108 are rated of high severity, while the rest are considered moderate or low.

Almost 100 of them are defined as use-after-free (UAF) vulnerabilities, which are memory management flaws that an attacker could exploit to crash the browser or trigger malicious code. Several of the bugs also refer to Firefox’s Sandbox, which means that hackers could break through the browser’s protected Sandbox area to execute malicious code.

Given the nastiness of the security bugs, you’ll want to update Firefox ASAP. For that, open the browser, click the three-line icon at the upper right, move to Help and Report, and select About Firefox. The latest update will then be installed. Restart Firefox to finish the process.

Also: I dumped Firefox, but these 5 features finally won me back

Beyond the security patches, Firefox 159 adds a few handy new features.

With Firefox for the Mac, sharing a page in the browser now displays the built-in MacOS share picker. Here, you can see a preview of the page you want to share along with recent contacts and specific apps such as AirDrop and Messages.

Next up, you’re now able to access Firefox’s passwords tool in the sidebar. This lets you more easily view any website passwords that you’ve saved to the browser. To see this in action, first make sure the sidebar is visible. For that, click the Sidebar button on the Address bar and then click the key icon to display your saved passwords.

And as perhaps the most helpful new feature, Firefox’s AI-powered Smart Window can now watch specific web pages for changes and send you a notification when the page is updated. For this, turn on the option for Smart Window if it’s not already enabled. Click the Firefox icon in the upper right and select Smart Window. Navigate to the website for which you’d like to be notified of any changes. At the chat window, type /watch, fill out the form, and then click the Create Task button.

That takes us to Chrome with version 56.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac and version 156.0.8078.73 for Linux. Here, the latest update patches 52 security bugs. Out of these, four are rated critical, while 46 are rated high.

The four severe ones point to a memory corruption problem. But like some of the Firefox bugs, they also reference the browser’s Sandbox. In this case, an attacker who exploits any of these vulnerabilities could bypass Chrome’s protected Sandbox area to run malicious code. Also as in Firefox, several of the bugs point to use-after-free (UAF) issues that would allow an attacker to exploit memory management flaws to crash the browser or install malicious code.

Also: Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

To update Chrome, click the three-dot icon at the top, move to Help, and select About Google Chrome. If prompted, allow the latest update to download and then restart the browser to finish.

Beyond many of the bugs themselves, Firefox and Chrome also share an increasing reliance on AI to find and resolve security flaws. In its advisory, Mozilla cited Amy Burnett, a security research and analyst at OpenAI, for uncovering many of the bugs. In its blog post, Google attributed the discovery of several flaws to Anthropic’s Claude and a few to OpenAI.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Here’s the spine-friendly exercise you should be doing

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I suffer from sciatica, so I have to be mindful when it comes to ab exercises like crunches and sit-ups, which typically put a lot of stress on the lower back. In the run-up to my last marathon, I asked my physical therapist for an ab exercise that would build core strength and stability without stressing my back — read on to find out what he said next.

As a reminder, what works for me might not work for you or your body. If you’re a complete beginner, pregnant or postpartum, or recovering from an injury or surgery, it’s always best to seek personalized advice from a qualified professional.

When it comes to a spine-safe way to work your core, the main exercise my therapist recommended is the bird-dog. Read on to find out how to do a bird dog with perfect form, its benefits, plus two other back-friendly exercises to add to your routine.

Unlike crunches, which force your back to bend as you lift your head, neck, and shoulders off the mat, bird dog teaches your abdominal muscles to hold your spine in place while your limbs move. This helps build the functional fitness you need for everyday life, as well as during sports like running.

As you perform the bird dog, you’ll be working the deep stabilizer muscles that run along the spine and glutes, rather than the outer six-pack muscles. The deep core works as the body’s corset and helps protect your spine from injury.

Here’s how to do the bird dog exercise with good form:

Another safe exercise to try if you suffer from lower back pain is the dead bug. Again, unlike a crunch or a plank, this exercise targets those all-important deep abdominal muscles while keeping your lower back supported.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

A huge benefit of the dead bug is that it’s performed lying flat on your back, meaning there is no compressive load on your spinal discs, as you’re not having to fight gravity to hold the pose. This allows you to build core strength and train yourself to maintain a neutral spine without triggering any pain in your lower back.

If this is too much for you, start with bent-knee taps. Instead of straightening your leg, keep your knee bent and tap one heel down to the floor, then bring it back to your starting position and repeat on the other side.

For the final move in this spine-safe series, the glute bridge is a great exercise for strengthening the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back stabilizers without putting pressure on your spine.

The core isn’t just the muscles that sit on the front of your body — it also includes the erector spinae (the muscles running along your spine) and the multifidus (the deep stabilizing muscles in the lower back). This exercise works these muscles, as well as waking up sleepy glutes. If your glutes don’t fire properly, your lower back muscles can overcompensate, leading to tight back muscles.

#3161. 200,000 Folds and Counting for the iPhone Duo. How Far Can Our Fold-a-Phone Take It?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

We're folding Apple's iPhone Duo over and over -- 900 times an hour -- to test the durability of its hinge.

Happy November! The air is getting chillier, retailers are shifting from Halloween to the holidays, and the machine in CNET’s lab continues to test Apple’s first folding phone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo. We purchased this poor phone more than a week ago, and since then its only job has been to bend and flatten, bend and flatten, until it breaks.

So how many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? On Monday, Nov. 2, we passed 200,000 folds.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. Over the last week, I’ve seen a lot of chatter about the sturdiness of the Duo’s folding hinge and its potential to fail or crack. I’ve periodically examined the Duo we’re testing in our machine, and so far, I haven’t seen any signs of damage. And the crease isn’t any more visible than it was when we took it out of the box. If that changes, I’ll let you know here and on our livestream.

In the meantime, let me explain what we’re doing. My team and I designed and built a proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.
