We're pretty much done for major phone launches in 2026, certainly for devices that will be coming to the U.S. and Europe, which means it's time to start looking forward to what might be coming next year. And, as usual, we expect the first big release of the year to be Samsung's Galaxy S27 series.

The S27 series is said to be made up of four phones: The Galaxy S27, Galaxy S27 Plus, Galaxy S27 Ultra and the new Galaxy S27 Pro. We've started hearing some rumors about what those phones could have to offer, including one of the first major redesigns Galaxy phones have had for several years. Obviously there are a few things we also really want to see on these phones as well.

So here are the top seven changes we want to see on the Samsung Galaxy S27.

Galaxy battery capacity does not change much, if ever. In fact the Galaxy S Ultra batteries have been stuck on the 5,000 mAh plateau since 2020. Meanwhile companies like OnePlus have been offering over 7,000 mAh batteries without any meaningful change to the design.

Frankly, people are sick of it, and it's time the Galaxy S27 changed that. Thankfully Samsung has shown that it can do this, thanks to the introduction of silicon carbon batteries in the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series. This technology allows for greater energy density, meaning you can offer more battery capacity without increasing the size of the battery.

Rumors suggest this may be happening too, with the S27 Ultra reportedly getting a 5,700 mAh battery. The S27 Pro is tipped to get a 5,200 mAh battery, though we don't know what the S27 and S27 Plus might be getting. We hope they'll get an increase from the 4,300 mAh and 4,900mAh batteries on their S26 counterparts.

One of my biggest gripes with Android phones is how so few of them have adopted the full Qi2 wireless charging standard — complete with the magnetic charging ring. Samsung is one such offender, adding Qi2 charging technology, while relying on special cases to add the magnetic support.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Many reasons have been given over the past couple of years, ranging from issues with the S Pen to the fact the camera bump blocks where the magnetic ring should sit. Whatever the reason, it's high time that Samsung got its act together and added Qi2 magnets to its phones, and the S27 series' redesign is the perfect place to do it.

Brighter screens offer huge visibility benefits, especially in bright conditions, and that shouldn't be affected by a new screen feature. Especially if you're not actually using it.

Samsung has a habit of neglecting the camera hardware on some of its phones, particularly the cheaper models like the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy S26 Plus. 50MP main lenses are fine, but 12MP ultrawide and 10MP telephoto lenses aren't befitting a flagship device. It doesn't matter that they don't bear the Ultra branding.

At the very least the S27 and S27 Plus need a higher resolution ultrawide lens, ideally something closer to 50MP. Any extra upgrades on the telephoto lens will be a nice bonus.

As for the Galaxy S27 Ultra, it's about time we started seeing more advanced camera features. Variable zoom has been rumored for at least a couple of years, and the rumored loss of the secondary telephoto lens feels like the perfect time to offer that. Likewise, now that the iPhone 18 Pro has a variable aperture lens, it's time Samsung brought that particular feature back to its own phones.

Samsung has not been the best at improving charging speed, though it earned some goodwill by upping the Galaxy S26 Ultra's charging speed from 45W to 60W. But sadly the S26 and S26 Plus were left at their old speeds of 25W and 45W, respectively. It's high time that changed.

There's little reason to keep both phones charging so slowly, especially since the Plus and Ultra models shared the same 45W charging speeds for a few years. It's also worth pointing out that the S26 Ultra can wirelessly charge at 25W speeds, which means the standard model really should be running faster by now.

Hopefully the Galaxy S27 series will fix that particular issue, even if the Ultra model sticks at 60W for a little while longer.

I have my concerns about the prospect of a Galaxy S27 Pro, because I'm not entirely sure there's room for another Galaxy flagship to sit between the S27 Plus and S27 Ultra. Certainly not if the other three devices in the lineup are sticking around in their current forms.

What I hope is that Samsung can find some kind of niche for the S27 Pro to ensure that it's not a complete waste of time and money. Ideally without compromising features on the S27 Plus or hiking up the price of the S27 Ultra to ridiculous levels.

The Pro needs to balance the line between features and price, while justifying its own existence. Otherwise, Samsung is just going to end up cannibalizing its own customer base and making the whole endeavor pointless.

Samsung has been an absolute demon for price hikes this year. Not only were multiple S26 models more expensive than their S25 counterparts, it also increased the price of the entire line-up back in September. To the point where the Galaxy S26 Ultra now costs $1,400. Officially, anyway, since the S26 series has been on sale almost everyday since.

Prices are high due to the skyrocketing cost of RAM and storage, and that means everyone has been hiking up the cost of their devices. With that in mind it would be really nice if Samsung didn't do that with the S27 series. Even if it's just a temporary reprieve, the last thing we need is phones getting even more expensive.

These metrics, together with corresponding GAAP numbers and a reconciliation to GAAP, are contained in today's press release, which we have posted on our website and filed with the SEC on Form 8-K.

We will also discuss historical, financial, and other statistical information regarding our business and operation, and some of this information is included in the press release. Nimrod Ben-Natan: Thanks, Scott, and welcome everyone to our third quarter 2026 earnings call. AI is produced in data centers, but it is experienced over broadband. As it moves into homes, businesses, and billions of connected devices, the network has to deliver more capacity, lower latency, and higher reliability. AI agents already generate a large and fast-growing share of internet traffic. What's new this quarter is that the largest AI platforms begun launching always-on personal assistants that work around the clock, interacting with us and with the connected devices in our homes.

That's the trend we highlighted at Investor Day, and it puts us on track for Rest-of-Market to become the majority of our business. Rest-of-Market also represented over 60% of our bookings in the quarter. Reflecting this performance and the more favorable environment, we are once again raising our full-year 2026 outlook. We're also continuing to expand our customer base. In the third quarter, we added nine new customers across seven countries, spanning DOCSIS and fiber, and including telco operators. TDC, Denmark's largest telecommunication and digital infrastructure company, selected our platform for a unified DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade. We also signed a Tier 1 operator in Belgium. We continue to lead in DOCSIS and to extend that leadership position. Our deployed cOS footprint now includes 167 customers serving almost 53 million CPE devices.

Pearl-1XL introduced earlier this year is now shipping in volume, and we booked another strong quarter for it in the quarter. Oyster+ is ramping too, giving operators a compact, power-protected way to extend fiber without a street cabinet. We also acquired a vendor-agnostic fiber management and provisioning platform this quarter and rebranded it cOS Loop. Loop is performing well with its established customer base in Brazil, and we're seeing strong interest from Harmonic customers in North America and Europe. Intelligence was also a big part of our quarter. In September, we launched SensAI, an open intelligence fabric that works across any network and any vendor, turning data from every system into decisions operators can act on.

SensAI came to market after extended trials with operators, and customers' feedback has been very strong. We are now in the next stage. New wins and the migration of our existing cloud customers onto SensAI have already begun. At SCTE TechExpo, we demonstrated SensAI running live on a production network, finding issues inside the home and out in the plant on DOCSIS and fiber, regardless of vendor. It is already delivering value. At one operator, SensAI pinpointed in about 10 minutes a field issue the team had chased for 10 days, then caught another fault further down the same line. Our installed intelligence base also grew, with Beacon now live at 25 operators, up from about 20 last quarter.

Now that cOS Loop is part of Harmonic, we have integrated its data into SensAI and launched proof of concept with a handful of Loop customers. We also launched Recon, developed with Comcast, which brings fiber monitoring technology proven in Comcast network to cable and fiber operators alike. It gives operators real-time visibility across their fiber, spotting degradation and fiber cuts before customers notice and pinpointing where to fix them. Because it integrates with SensAI, small issues are stopped before they become outages.

Let me now turn to Slide five and give you our first quarterly update on the three growth engines we outlined at our Investor Day, which together represent a total addressable market opportunity of more than $7 billion by 2030. We will report on each of them every quarter. Connectivity is our core market, representing roughly $5.4 billion of that opportunity. Our strategy is to address it on one cOS platform, extend our leadership in DOCSIS, continue taking our fiber portfolio beyond cable into telco, and get ahead of the move to 50G. For telcos, our OLT portfolio, including hardened remote OLTs and our open ONT approach, provide the interoperability and supply choice they want.

#3152. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3151. Your Netgear router may be vulnerable to a security exploit – how to check and patch it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A vulnerability in some Netgear routers could allow an attacker with access to your network to run malicious commands on the device.

Do you own a Netgear router? The bad news is that the device could be susceptible to a security flaw that would leave it vulnerable to an attacker. The good news: This exploit affects only a small number of Netgear routers, and the company has already issued patches to squash the bugs.

Also: Run this 10-step security check on your phone once a year

The vulnerabilities differ slightly among the various affected models, as described in Netgear’s security advisory. In general, these flaws could be exploited by an attacker who gains access to your network, allowing them to run unauthorized and potentially malicious commands on the router.

All the flaws are ranked as medium severity but clearly still pose a threat, prompting Netgear to roll out new firmware for each impacted model. You should be able to update your router to the latest firmware directly through its settings, but you can also grab each update from Netgear’s website.

Here are descriptions of the vulnerabilities, the names and models of the affected routers, and links to download the patches.

Described in CVE-2026-11732, the first vulnerability could allow an attacker who already has access to your network, most likely through your Wi-Fi credentials, to run unauthorized commands on the device. The flaw is exploitable only if you’ve enabled the Block Sites feature, which blocks access to specific web sites based on domain name or keywords.

Also: Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined

Affected products and the firmware download pages to patch the bug:

Among these, the RAX5 4-Stream AX1600 WiFi 6 Router has reached end of service (EoS), meaning no further updates will be available after this latest one. In this case, Netgear advises owners to upgrade to a newer router.

Defined in CVE-2026-11731, the second vulnerability could allow an unauthenticated attacker with access to your local network and your router’s management service view and modify certain device details and administrative settings.

Also: Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

Affected products and the download pages to patch the bug:

Documented in CVE-2026-11730, the third vulnerability impacts two Netgear range extenders. Here, an attacker who already has local network access could hijack an authenticated administrator session on the device’s web management portal.

Affected products and their firmware download pages:

Among these two, the EX3700 AC750 WiFi Range Extender Essentials Edition has reached end of service, which means it’s time to move to a newer device.

The remaining routers impacted by security flaws have all reached end of service. Again, that means no further updates will be available, and Netgear advises owners to switch to a newer device.

Described in CVE-2026-9218, an attacker who’s connected to the router’s local network and has the administrator username and password could run unauthorized commands on the device.

Also: The best Wi-Fi routers: Expert tested and reviewed

Affected products and their firmware download pages:

With the CBR40 Orbi AC2200 Tri-band WiFi Cable Modem Router, the latest firmware will not fix the current security bug, so owners should move to a newer device to stay secure.

The remaining Netgear router impacted by security flaws is also at end-of-service, and the latest firmware won’t fix its security flaws. Again, Netgear advises owners to switch to a newer and more secure device.

#3149. Apple (AAPL) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record iPhone and Mac sales drive $114.5B revenue amid supply constraints.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Apple Inc. (AAPL -1.83%) reported record September quarter results driven by double-digit growth in iPhone and Mac revenue alongside an all-time high for its Services division. Management reported that the company achieved its best fiscal year for both revenue and earnings per share, supported by an active installed base that now exceeds 2.5 billion devices. The company stated that it is currently navigating significant macroeconomic and supply chain challenges, specifically citing unprecedented memory pricing and constraints on advanced semiconductor nodes. Strategic focus remains on the integration of Siri AI across the hardware ecosystem and expanding manufacturing partnerships within the United States to support its multiyear investment commitments.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Apple Q4 Fiscal Year 2026 Earnings Conference Call. My name is Suhasini Chandramouli, Head of Investor Relations. Today's call is being recorded. Speaking first today is Apple's CEO, John Ternus, and he'll be followed by CFO, Kevan Parekh. After that, we'll open the call to questions from analysts. Please note that some of the information you'll hear during our discussion today will consist of forward-looking statements, including, without limitation, those regarding revenue, gross margin, operating expenses, other income and expense, taxes and future business outlook.

These statements involve risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results or trends to differ materially from our forecast, including risks related to the potential impact to the company's business and results of operations from macroeconomic conditions, tariffs and other measures and legal and regulatory proceedings. For more information, please refer to the risk factors discussed in Apple's most recently filed reports on Form 10-Q and Form 10-K and the Form 8-K filed with the SEC today, along with the associated press release. Additional information will also be in our report on Form 10-K for the year ended September 26, 2026, to be filed tomorrow and in other reports and filings we make with the SEC.

Apple assumes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements, which speak only as of the date they are made. I'd now like to turn the call over to John for introductory remarks.

John Ternus: Thank you, Suhasini. Hello, everyone, and thanks for joining us. It's a privilege to be with you for the first time as Apple's CEO. It's been a remarkable time for innovation across all of our categories.

One of the greatest testaments to that is the all-new iPhone Duo, the most transformational iPhone since the original. Meanwhile, touch has arrived on Mac for the first time with the all-new MacBook Pro, and we were excited to announce the new iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. The all-new iPad Mini features a stunning new OLED display and brings a super thin design to the smallest member of the iPad family. Apple Watch now offers users the clearest window yet into their heart health.

We're really excited to have rolled all these innovations out, and there's still so much more we plan to do. I'm feeling great about the opportunities ahead for Apple from our product road map and broad range of services to promising areas like health, emerging markets, enterprise and education. As one example, we recently secured our biggest education deal ever for Mac with the Department of Education in the Philippines. They're going to deploy 170,000 MacBook Neos to teachers and staff. Opportunities like this bring more users into our ecosystem and help fuel growth across our business. Apple is the greatest company in the world.

We've assembled an extraordinary collection of talent, the best engineers, designers, developers and experts in every corner of our business, from our supply chain to our stores. Every day, we bring the right people together with the best ideas to build products and services that change lives, guided by a foundational set of values and a belief that the best technology should make a better world. We do that by making products that are powerful and intuitive and meet Apple's uncompromising standards for quality, performance, design and durability. That's the Apple experience customers love. And with our latest lineup, people have even more reasons than ever to upgrade or switch to an Apple product.

At the same time, Apple services amplify the experience of every device, helping people work, play, listen, watch and stay connected to the world around them. I'm delighted with where our services business is today and where it's going. And with an installed base of more than 2.5 billion active devices, I'm looking forward to expanding our offerings and improving the lives of users around the world. We see tremendous opportunity in AI as well. Siri AI marks a new chapter in AI at Apple. It is a completely reimagined assistant that is powerful, personal, private and deeply relevant to our users' daily lives.

Siri AI picks up what's relevant to our users, understands what's on their screen and holds a natural conversation, all to help them with the things they do every day. It's the Siri we've always wanted. We are very pleased with the reviews and feedback we've received, and we're so excited that more and more users are getting to experience it. iPhone remains at the center of our opportunity as the intelligent personal hub. It's always with you and understands your personal context from your messages to your photos, notes and apps to deliver powerful intelligence right when you need it. Then there's Mac, which is having an AI moment all its own. Mac is what brought me to Apple.

And through the years, it has opened a world of possibilities. More than 40 years after the first Mac, the category is having its biggest moment yet with every Mac in our latest lineup, a powerful platform for AI. Mac Mini and Mac Studio in particular, are pushing the boundaries of local private AI, giving users the ability to do things once considered impossible. From Mac to iPhone to iPad, we are proud that our products are the best platforms in the industry for AI for both first-party and third-party applications, and we're excited about the opportunities that creates. Ultimately, everything we do at Apple is for our users.

The success of every innovation is best measured by its impact on people's lives, and that's what drives us to keep building great products and to get them into the hands of people all around the world. Now let's take a deeper dive into our results for the quarter. As I mentioned earlier, we had an excellent quarter at Apple. In addition to September quarter and fiscal year records in total company revenue, iPhone set a September quarter revenue record, capping its best fiscal year ever. Services achieved an all-time record during the quarter to close out our best year ever there, too.

We grew in the vast majority of markets we track, setting September quarter records in the Americas, Europe, Greater China and the rest of Asia Pacific. We also set September quarter revenue records in both developed and emerging markets, in addition to an all-time record in India. Turning to our lineup. iPhone revenue was $57.6 billion for the September quarter, up 17% from a year ago despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds. We grew strong double digits in the U.S. and Greater China to achieve September quarter revenue records.

We also set a September quarter record for upgraders worldwide as well as in the U.S., China Mainland and India, helping to deliver our best fiscal year ever for upgraders globally. At the launch in September, we introduced the all-new iPhone Duo. From the very beginning, we knew what we wanted to create, a foldable form factor with a larger display that feels as natural and intuitive as iPad. We designed the hardware and software together to make it unmistakably iPhone, while enabling entirely new ways to use it. The result is a series of remarkable innovations that we believe will redefine what a foldable phone can be. We're so proud of what our teams have built.

Developers have been quickly adapting to this new form factor, and we're excited to see more and more apps optimized for iPhone Duo. We've been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers' hands as quickly as we can. We have also been thrilled with the response to iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. It's easy to see why customers are embracing them. Our latest models feature a dramatically improved camera system with breakthrough upgrades like variable aperture and all new photographic styles. The A20 Pro and next-generation vapor chamber together deliver the highest sustained performance in iPhone history.

And iPhone 18 Pro MAX delivers the biggest increase in battery life ever on an iPhone. A20 Pro also features a new dual 16-core neural engine, accelerating on-device AI and computational photography. Turning to Mac. Revenue was $10.8 billion, up 24% from a year ago despite supply constraints. We had double-digit growth in the majority of markets we track and particularly strong performance in our emerging markets, where we set a September quarter revenue record. We also set a September quarter record for customers new to the Mac.

According to IDC, we gained share globally during the quarter and for the full fiscal year, and we have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time, which is a truly remarkable testament to these incredible products. Last week, we introduced a whole new way for people to experience Mac. The all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR brings touch to the Mac for the first time. It also boasts the best Pro laptop display we have ever shipped plus all-day battery and our most immersive laptop audio. And it all comes together in a thinner and lighter design. We also brought the power of M6 to the new 14-inch MacBook Pro and the new iMac.

This latest generation of Apple Silicon includes the world's fastest CPU core to speed up everyday tasks in addition to a dual 16-core neural engine to drive private on-device AI tasks. Now turning to iPad, where revenue was $6.2 billion for the September quarter. Last week, we introduced the all-new iPad Mini with an amazing new OLED display, super thin design and the power of A20 Pro. With the newest addition, our iPad lineup is more capable and versatile than ever before. Anywhere our users go, there's a place for iPad, like a classroom where it helps students explore the world in amazing ways. We're a design studio, giving artists and creatives an expansive canvas to explore their ideas.

In Wearables, Home and Accessories, revenue was $8.3 billion for the September quarter. Apple Watch makes the simple act of wearing a watch a powerful way to help take care of your health. We were thrilled to introduce our all-new health sensing system to help our users get the most out of health tracking. Paired with the S11 chip, Apple's most powerful wearable chip, the health sensing system delivers the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable. We were also happy to unveil new features like health age and readiness, which will tell you when to push forward or hold back as well as the all-new health app redesign.

And we're excited for audio intelligence, which will be coming in a future software update and will help you remember moments you might otherwise miss. Apple Watch Series 12 brings it all together in a beautifully light design, while Apple Watch Ultra 4 goes further with longer battery life compared to the previous generation and the most accurate on-device GPS in a sports watch. Meanwhile, AirPods 5 offers best-in-class open ear active noise cancellation at an incredible price, while improving sound quality, battery life and durability.

With iPhone and Apple Intelligence, including Siri AI, AirPods allow users to do remarkable things. like connect with someone who's speaking another language with live translation or get answers with broad world knowledge entirely hands-free. And just a few weeks ago, we introduced a whole new generation of hardware for the home. That includes Apple HomeView, which was designed to be central to the home and personal to everyone in it, bringing entertainment, connection and home management together in one place. We announced this alongside the new Apple TV 4K, now smarter with Apple Intelligence, the all-new HomePod Mini and Apple Home Collection, a new program that extends Apple Home beyond our own products through deep collaboration with key partners.

We're very excited about our programming from fan favorites like Slow Horses and Ted Lasso to the upcoming film Being Heumann. To date, Apple TV productions have earned more than 900 wins and over 3,800 nominations. Turning to Apple Pay. We recently launched in India with Axis Bank, bringing a seamless, safe and secure way to pay in one of the biggest markets in the world. Today, Apple Pay is available in over 90 markets, giving customers around the world peace of mind built into every transaction. Apple Music was created to bring artists and fans closer together. And with the opening of Apple Music Hall, we have a beautiful new venue for intimate shows that bring them even closer.

And it means introducing new child safety features to make it easier for parents to manage when and how their kids can use their devices. We're also pleased to be doing more and more manufacturing in the United States. Through our American manufacturing program, we're deepening partnerships with suppliers across the country. including Perryman, a titanium producer now supplying iPhone Duo; and Qnity Electronics, which is producing the camera technology behind iPhone 18 Pro's new variable aperture system. Nearly 100 components in our newest iPhones come from American companies in more than a dozen states. All told, Apple supports more than 450,000 American jobs with thousands of suppliers and partners across all 50 states.

It's all part of our $600 billion 4-year commitment to U.S. innovation and advanced manufacturing. I am proud of what we've accomplished this quarter, and I'm excited for what's ahead. We have everything we need to be extraordinarily successful. And with this team, this vision, this mission and these values, I have no doubt that we will. With that, I'll hand it over to Kevan.

Kevan Parekh: Thanks, John, and good afternoon, everyone. Here's a quick rundown of our key financial metrics. Our revenue of $114.5 billion was up 12% year-over-year, a September quarter revenue record. This strong performance was despite sequential foreign exchange headwinds of nearly 2 percentage points as well as supply constraints on iPhone, Mac and iPad. Products revenue was $82.9 billion, up 12% year-over-year, driven by strong double-digit growth on iPhone and Mac. Our installed base of over 2.5 billion active devices has reached another all-time high across all major product categories and geographic segments. Services revenue was $31.6 billion, up 10% year-over-year.

We saw strong performance in many services categories with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services and advertising and a September quarter record in music. Company gross margin was 47.9% and products gross margin was 37.2%. These both included a benefit from tariff refunds, which had a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point in the September quarter. When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarter, both company and products gross margin would be down about 1 point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs. As of the September quarter, we have received the vast majority of the refunds related to tariffs paid. Services gross margin was 76%, up 40 basis points sequentially.

Operating expenses came in at $19.2 billion, up 21% year-over-year as we continue to make investments in R&D. Net income was $30.7 billion. Diluted earnings per share was $2.10, up 14% year-over-year and included $0.05 of favorable impact from tariff refunds. Both net income and EPS set September quarter records even when excluding the tariff refund benefit. Operating cash flow was also very strong at $28.1 billion. This performance marked our best fiscal year yet with $478.8 billion in revenue, up 15% year-over-year and a fiscal year record for EPS of $8.98, up 20% year-over-year. Now I'm going to provide some more details for each of our revenue categories. iPhone revenue was $57.6 billion, up 17% year-over-year despite supply constraints.

We grew double digits in the majority of markets we track, and we also reached September quarter revenue records across both developed and emerging markets. As John mentioned, it was a record year for the total company, and we also had our best year ever for iPhone, both worldwide and in every geographic segment. The iPhone active installed base grew to an all-time high, and iPhone had a record year for upgraders globally and in several markets, including the U.S., China Mainland, India and Japan. According to a recent survey from Worldpanel, iPhone was a top-selling model in the U.S., Urban China, India, the U.K., Germany, Australia and Japan. Mac revenue was $10.8 billion, up 24% year-over-year despite supply constraints.

This performance was driven by the strength of the MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro. We saw double-digit growth in both developed and emerging markets with all-time records in markets like India and Southeast Asia. Emerging markets continued to see strong performance on Mac, resulting in Mac's best fiscal year there, driven by record upgraders and customers new to the Mac. iPad revenue was $6.2 billion, down 10% year-over-year, driven by the supply constraints I mentioned earlier as well as a continued difficult compare against the launch of the A16-powered iPad in the prior year. The iPad installed base reached an all-time high during the quarter and over half of the customers who purchased an iPad were new to the product.

Wearables, Home and Accessories revenue was $8.3 billion, down 8% year-over-year as we faced a difficult compare against the launch of the Watch SE 3 and the AirPods Pro 3 in the prior year. The wearables installed base reached a new all-time high and over half of customers who bought an Apple Watch in the quarter were new to the product. Services revenue set an all-time record of $31.6 billion, up 10% year-over-year despite over 1.5 points of sequential FX headwinds. We set all-time revenue records in the majority of markets we track, including several emerging markets like Latin America and India. We are optimistic about the long-term future of our services business.

Organizations are continuing to expand their fleets of Apple devices to transform operations and drive productivity. Duke Health performed the first surgical procedure using Apple Vision Pro for hip arthroscopy with an FDA-authorized app from Stryker. American Airlines is deploying over 37,000 iPhone 17 devices to flight attendants for in-flight purchases with tap to pay in addition to 25,000 iPads for pilots and mechanics. And more companies are choosing Mac across a growing range of use cases, including for on-device AI. For example, Gap Inc. is running AI entirely on Mac Mini for loss prevention across hundreds of stores, eliminating cloud token costs.

Christie's, a world-leading auction house, is running local models on Mac Studio to improve core productivity workflows such as pricing estimates. Let's turn to our cash position and capital return program. We ended the quarter with $137 billion in cash and marketable securities and $80 billion in total debt. During the quarter, we returned $28 billion to shareholders. This included $3.9 billion in dividends and equivalents and $24 billion in share repurchases. As we move ahead into the December quarter, I'd like to review our outlook, which includes the types of forward-looking information that Suhasini referred to.

Importantly, the color we're providing assumes that global tariff rates, policies and their application remain in effect as of this call and the global macroeconomic outlook does not worsen from today. We expect our December quarter total company revenue to grow between 7% and 10% year-over-year, which reflects our best view of constrained supply. We expect this to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company. We expect services revenue to grow between 8% and 9% year-over-year in the December quarter. This contemplates sequential headwinds, primarily driven by third-party licensing and foreign exchange. We expect gross margin to be between 45% and 46%.

This includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs as well as some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI. We expect operating expenses to be between $20.4 billion and $20.8 billion. We expect OI&E to be around $300 million, excluding any potential impact from the mark-to-market of minority investments and our tax rate to be around 17%. Finally, today, our Board of Directors has declared a cash dividend of $0.27 per share of common stock payable on November 16, 2026, to shareholders of record as of November 12, 2026. With that, I'll hand it back to John.

Michael Ng: Great. And then my second question is just around iCloud+. So I was just wondering, what are you seeing on iCloud+? Are there any tailwinds in terms of attach rates, just particularly given the rising cost for increased storage options on iPhone and the company's push into home products?

And so anyone who needs greater capacity will be able to purchase expanded access in the future. So kind of to your point, in the beginning, iCloud tiers were largely about storage, but we've been adding more capabilities and features to it.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Awesome. Thank you, Mike. Operator, could we get the next question, please.

Operator: Our next question is from Erik Woodring from Morgan Stanley.

Erik Woodring: John, congrats on your first quarter here. So as the world of AI evolves from chatbots to consumer agents, it seems like there are growing opportunities for Apple. And just how you look at any potential risks of some of these agents trying to encroach on your services business? And then a quick follow-up, please.

John Ternus: Sure. Thanks, Erik. Look, we -- first and foremost, we are incredibly excited to launch Siri AI alongside the latest generation of Apple Intelligence features. Siri has long been popular with our users with more than 2.5 billion requests every day. And with Siri AI, we really have the kind of the Siri that we always wanted. It's primarily request-based today. But as we talked about at WWDC, it's built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time. As far as agentic capabilities, we think these are promising tools for users. We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they're giving access to.

Erik Woodring: Okay. Awesome. I appreciate that, John. And then just quickly as a follow-up, how should we -- if we take a big step back, how should we think about the durability of services growth? Just I realize that was 10% in the September quarter. We're a little bit below that in the December quarter. As certain things like search evolves and regulatory changes impact App Store monetization, are there new services that we should be looking towards that you believe can become a more sizable offset to maybe take some pressure off these historically important revenue streams?

Kevan Parekh: Erik, it's Kevan. Thanks for the question. Let me take this one. Let me start by just talking through kind of what we did -- we talked about during the December quarter. Services grew by 10% year-over-year. And we look at that relative to the June quarter, foreign exchange was the main driver in that change on year-on-year growth rate sequentially. We saw -- we continue to see strong performance in September in many of our service categories, all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services and advertising, including our first-party Apple Ads and September quarter record in music.

But I think it's important to kind of step back also and look at the progression of what we've seen in our services business over the last several quarters. I think it's an important backdrop. And so we spoke about on the last call, we expected foreign exchange to be the largest driver of the change in the year-on-year growth rate from the March to September quarter. This ended up being a significant headwind of about 4 percentage points, and we expect additional sequential headwind of about another 0.5 percentage point for the services business as we go into the December quarter. We've also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store.

And during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store. At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we've talked about before and expect to see those continue into the December quarter. And keep in mind, we also made some changes to the App Store business model in certain countries. And in the U.S., we continue to operate under a court ruling impacting the link-out transactions.

As we move ahead, we expect services growth to be between 8% to 9%, as I mentioned in the prepared remarks, in the December quarter, and this outlook contemplates our best estimates on sequential headwinds, primarily from third-party licensing and the additional 0.5 percentage point of foreign exchange I just mentioned. And I'll turn it over to John to talk about some perspectives as we look ahead.

John Ternus: Yes. Thanks. I guess I'd like to add to that, Erik. I think fundamentally, we feel really good about the long-term opportunity that we have in our services business. We see continued growth in the installed base of over 2.5 billion active devices, which is fundamentally the foundation for future growth as more customers are able to experience our products and services. Example of this during the September quarter, App Store saw a record number of nearly 1 billion average weekly visitors, and we saw growth in the number of users who are paying for at least one service, reaching an all-time high.

Another good example of this in India, we recently launched Apple Pay with Axis Bank, bringing the seamless, safe, secure way to pay to one of the biggest markets in the world. And then on top of all this, as we talked about, we think intelligence is going to be another opportunity as well. So overall, we're feeling really good about where we're headed in the long term.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Thank you, Erik. Operator, could we take the next question, please.

Operator: Our next question is from Amit Daryanani from Evercore.

Amit Daryanani: Congrats on mine as well, John, on your first earnings call here. John, you sort of described the iPhone as an intelligent personal hub in your opening comments. And as personal AI agents become more prominent, do you see the potential for the primary customer relationship to shift from the device to the agent over time? And really, given Apple's integration of silicon, hardware and software, where do you see the greatest opportunity to combine things like personal context and on-screen awareness into an agent that can perhaps move beyond answering questions? And how far along do you think Siri is in bringing those pieces together right now?

John Ternus: Yes. Thank you, Amit, for the question. Like as I said before, and we said in our announcement, we really do think of the iPhone as the intelligent personal hub. I mean if you think about it, so much of your personal data is on your iPhone, whether it's your contacts, your communications, health data, financial data, all of that. And Siri can tap into that and help you access it in a way that's very secure and private and that nobody else has access to, even Apple doesn't have access to it. And so we think that is a core kind of differentiator that we're excited about. And we're going to continue to push on that.

And so I think this is an area that we feel really, really good about.

Amit Daryanani: Got it. And then, Kevan, the December quarter gross margin, I'm wondering if you could spend a bit of time on that. I think if I exclude all the tariff refunds, you start of implying gross margins will be down about 140 basis points sequentially at least. Can you just separate how much of this is maybe commodity memory inflation versus mix versus -- you called out Siri AI ramp costs as well. Can you just talk about what the different moving parts are as we think about the sequential gross margins, that would be helpful.

Kevan Parekh: Yes, Amit, sounds good. Let me try to address that for you. So as you alluded for the December quarter, we talked about a gross margin outlook of between 45% and 46%. As you said, when you remove the benefit of the tariff refunds in September, the midpoint of the range is a decline sequentially in the magnitude you mentioned. We expect most of that decline to be driven by higher memory costs, and I'll give John kind of the mic here to give you a perspective on that, and then I'll take the balance of your question.

John Ternus: Yes. Let me give you an overall view on memory. What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. And as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So as you know, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset.

We also expect to see some benefit from carry-in inventory in the December quarter as well, as well as lower costs on certain non-memory components. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase. As we've said before, we do believe we'll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time. And there's one more thing I wanted to add, as we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from June to the September quarter, which you'll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow. Now back to Kevan for the other parts of it.

Kevan Parekh: Yes, Amit, you mentioned Siri AI and what I alluded to in the prepared remarks. So as we continue to roll out Siri AI to more customers, the associated cloud costs will be recognized through services cost of sales. And consistent with how we've always accounted for Mac, Siri and iCloud for the devices we sell that include these bundled services, we defer a portion of the revenue and recognize it over the life of the device. So our hardware deferrals as of the December quarter will reflect the addition of Siri AI. Both of these items will have an impact to the gross margin.

But as always, we look to continue to make the investments necessary to support the business. And we also see a wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time. So on the product side, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities. And we also feel there's opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities, as John highlighted earlier, with the expanded access to server side features of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features as well.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Thank you, Amit. Operator, could we have the next question, please.

Operator: Our next question is from Ben Reitzes from Melius Research.

Benjamin Reitzes: John, my first question, I wanted to ask you about your cash-neutral policy. On one of the previous calls, you guys said that you weren't going to focus on that anymore and that, that was not no longer the policy. What do you -- how -- under your leadership, what do you mean by that? Do you mean like you may go to net debt to buy back stock or do some M&A or go the opposite way and hoard some cash again? Your thoughts on that would be welcome.

Kevan Parekh: Ben, it's Kevan. Let me take that one. As you know, we did talk about the fact that we were no longer using net cash neutral as a target. I think as we explained on the last call or the last time we talked about that was the fact that we think it makes sense to evaluate our cash and debt position independently and making sure we can optimize that and giving us the right flexibility. We remain committed to our capital allocation philosophy, which is we're going to invest everything we need to put -- invest in our business and return excess cash to shareholders. And so we continue to maintain that discipline.

And we do think this removal of net cash neutral gives us flexibility to optimize so we can make the right investments for the company.

Benjamin Reitzes: All right. And then I wanted to ask about services. I realize you only guide one quarter at a time. But from the 8% to 9%, when you think long term, I was wondering if you're willing to say you think whether it can accelerate from there and whether AI could help you launch new services we haven't thought of yet that are accretive to the growth rate there?

Kevan Parekh: Yes. I think, Ben, on that one, I think you heard John talk about a lot of the long-term attributes that really feel give us optimism about the long-term opportunity in our services business. Again, I think we talked about things like the installed base of over 2.5 billion active devices. We obviously saw a record number of weekly visitors in the App Store in the September quarter. We also continue to see growth in users who are paying for at least a service, reaching an all-time high in both transacting and paid accounts. We're excited about emerging markets.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Thank you, Ben. Operator, could we have the next question, please.

Operator: Our next question is from Wamsi Mohan from Bank of America.

Wamsi Mohan: John, great to have you on the call as CEO. I appreciate the comments on memory. Clearly, you're now competing for memory more so versus historically from pretty well capitalized companies who are signing long-term agreements. So my question is, is Apple changing anything in the way that you are procuring memory? How do you think about the progression of memory over time? And if it continues to be a headwind, is pricing also going to remain dynamic and potentially move higher? And I have a follow-up.

Sabih Khan: Wamsi, this is Sabih. Let me take that one. So as you know, we have worked with many of our suppliers for decades, and we deeply value their partnership over the years. We know our products would simply not be possible without them, and we look forward to continuing to work together. We're always working hard to improve supply. And as John said earlier, we -- our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from the June to the September quarter.

Kevan Parekh: And Wamsi, maybe I'll add here because you asked the question about pricing and how we're managing it. So look, we're trying to manage through this with a number of actions. You heard us talk about the fact we're continuing to pursue lower cost and non-memory components. John mentioned the fact that we have some benefit of carrying inventory. And we did reluctantly make the decision to change pricing in a number of our products, starting with the iPad and Mac in the June time frame and then iPhone more recently in September. I think what we try to do is evaluate in doing all that, we evaluate the unit revenue and margin.

And we're really being thoughtful and deliberate at evaluating kind of the short-term and long-term considerations, and we really believe we're balancing this well.

Wamsi Mohan: Okay. And I guess my follow-up is on Siri AI. In the early days of launching this, can you give us some sense of how the token consumption associated with Siri AI is being done on-device versus private cloud compute versus GCP? And have you started to see any acceleration of usage? And if it does accelerate really fast globally, would it change your outlook on what you need to spend for compute?

Kevan Parekh: Yes, Wamsi, I can take that one as well. So we do envision Siri AI to kind of have queries that kind of are managed on device and also in the private cloud compute environment that we've outlined. The mix of that is still very early days, and so it's hard to predict exactly what the mix of those costs are going to look like. Obviously, on device -- it's very, very efficient. No real costs associated with that. But on the server side, we would have some inference costs, and that's really the connection of the Siri AI-related costs that I mentioned that will be recognized as services cost of sales.

But I think, again, we've just recently launched it and made it available to more users. And so in very, very early stages of understanding the kind of mix of those costs as well as any further requirements we might have on the compute side.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Thank you, Wamsi. Operator, could we have the next question, please.

Operator: Our next question is from Samik Chatterjee from JPMorgan.

Samik Chatterjee: John, Sabih, good to get a chance to talk to you guys and Kevan, same there. Maybe on the Duo, can I just ask in terms of maybe your thoughts in terms of our learnings from the launch of the Duo and the demand that you've seen on that front? And what are the sort of supply chain-related issues that you're facing right now that you probably need to iron out if you're trying to meet demand on that front? Any more visibility there? And when you reach supply-demand balance on the Duo as well will be helpful. And I have a quick follow-up.

Sabih Khan: Samik, this is Sabih. Let me start with that question. So we're thrilled with the initial response on the iPhone Duo. iPhone Duo is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.

Samik Chatterjee: Okay. Perfect. Got it. And then maybe, Kevan, for you, just in terms of -- you have mentioned supply chain constraints impacting September quarter and going into December, but any way to sort of help us think about whether those are getting overall for the company, are those increasing in terms of magnitude relative to sort of the impact on revenue? And if you are willing to sort of quantify those impacts for September and December?

Sabih Khan: Yes. Let me start with that. This is Sabih. So during the September quarter, we experienced supply constraints on iPhone, Mac and iPad. And this was driven by the high levels of demand. And as we have said before, we're seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal. The Q4 constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the advanced nodes our SoCs are produced on. But as we have transitioned more of our lineup to the latest 2-nanometer technology nodes, our constraints on advanced nodes are easing. And for the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory as demand has been higher than what we expected.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Thank you, Samik. Operator, could we take the next question, please.

Operator: Our next question is from Krish Sankar from TD Cowen.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan: First one is for either Kevan or Sabih. I understand the memory price inflation. Kevan, it seems like it's probably hike 1 to 1.5 or 2 percentage points. A, is that true? And Sabih, I'm just wondering, I understand that -- is there an availability issue with memory? Are you signing LTAs with memory suppliers so that availability is not an issue even though pricing could still be an issue down the road? And then I had a quick follow-up.

Sabih Khan: Yes. Thanks, Krish. So as we said earlier, we are continuing to work to improve supply, and you'll see that our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from the June to the September quarter.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan: Got it. Got it. And any comments on the margin impact to think about going forward, Kevan, or?

Kevan Parekh: Well, I think, Krish, let me maybe take that one. I know you asked about it. So when we look at the margin change from the June quarter to the September quarter and you remove the impact of the tariffs from both the June quarter and September quarter, we saw about a 1 point sequential change in margin, and that was driven entirely by memory impacts. Now we did have some offsets because the gross memory impact was larger than that, but we had some offsets as John talked about earlier, driven by the benefit of carrying inventory, some offsets from nonmemory costs as well as some of the benefits of pricing.

And so as we talked about, we expect the memory costs to continue to be a challenge for us as we look in the December quarter, and our guide contemplates that right now. If you look at the midpoint, most of the sequential decline we're expecting for the December quarter, we expect to be driven by higher memory costs.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan: Got you. And just a quick follow-up for John. And John, congrats on the first call. It seems like consumer AI agent space is seeing increasing competition with several app-based options. I'm just wondering, when you look at the agentic capability of Siri built into the OS platform versus AI agents that are confined within an app architecture, how do you see that evolving?

John Ternus: Yes. Thanks, Krish. I think as I said before, Siri right now is primarily request-based. And as we talked about before, it is built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture. So we see opportunity to expand its capabilities over time. We think fundamentally, what's most important to us is that we're giving people these capabilities that are private and secure, and we're really focused on protecting people's data.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Thank you, Krish. Operator, could we take the next question, please.

Operator: Our next question is from David Vogt from UBS.

David Vogt: Congrats, John. And maybe one to start with Kevan. Because it certainly looks like you're looking at double-digit growth across the iPhone and the Mac business. And we all know, I think, in the industry that there's been pretty strong price inflation across the PC Mac ecosystem, and you guys mentioned that you're reluctantly taking price as well. So can you help us understand kind of what's the driving dynamics in that market?

Kevan Parekh: Yes, David, thanks for the question. This is Kevan. We don't normally provide that level of detail or color as we look at the outlook other than to say, again, we did guide to the 7% to 10% year-on-year. And again, just as a reminder, that is on top of a phenomenal December quarter last year where revenue grew 16% -- and so we don't provide the level of detail, but I would say it's early to really read price elasticity at this point in time. The iPad and Mac were constrained since kind of we have made those adjustments. And again, we just recently just adjusted the price on iPhone.

So it's really early to really assess any elasticity impact at this stage.

David Vogt: Great. And then maybe just as a follow-up, going back to the investment cycle, whether it's agentic, Siri related. It looks like you guys had -- you're coming off of a year of very aggressive investments in R&D to fund the business going forward and to grow the business. If I just think about kind of the commentary on Q1 of fiscal '27, it certainly sounds like that spending is moderating a little bit. Can you maybe walk through some of the puts and takes in terms of what's driving that moderation in spend across the operating line items?

Kevan Parekh: Yes, David, again, here, we don't break out detail on our outlook, but I would reiterate the fact that for the December quarter, we do expect OpEx to grow between 11% and 13% year-over-year, which is driven by increased and continued investment in R&D, in particular, AI. This growth rate is coming down, as you alluded, from the levels of growth that we had in FY '26. But as we've said before, we continue to significantly increase our overall investments in AI while continuing to invest in the product road map. And our December guide is a continued reflection of that.

John Ternus: Yes. And I'll just add, we feel confident that we're spending what we need to spend to achieve our road map.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Awesome. Thank you, David. Operator, could we have the next question, please.

Operator: Our next question is from Richard Kramer from Arete Research.

Richard Kramer: John, your latest MacBook Pros included more iOS features like touch and dynamic island as well as obviously Siri AI. Should we anticipate further close linking of Mac OS and iOS features, maybe even pointing at some point to a single unified OS either for simplicity or to reduce costs? And then I have a follow-up.

John Ternus: Yes. Thanks for the question, Richard. Look, we are very proud of both the Mac and the iPad. And I think what you've seen over the years is we've really enjoyed the ability to bring features and capabilities across the ecosystem and create really compelling features that span things between -- handoff between iPhone and Mac and iPad. And so when we design the product, we're looking at how can we make the best version of each and every product. And if you look at what we just did last week with the MacBook Pro, we took a huge leap forward. These MacBook Pros are better in every way than the ones that came before them.

And we're really proud of that. And so we don't have any fundamentally different changes that we're planning right now nor would we talk about it anyway.

Richard Kramer: Okay. And then we saw two years of declines in China sales. And then this year, Apple obviously grew very healthy 28% in FY '26. Can you talk through to what you attribute that recovery and whether you think Greater China can sustain these sort of elevated levels of growth, which are really leading the company regionally now?

John Ternus: Yes. Let me give you some color on China. We were very pleased with the performance in Greater China, right? Revenue was up 21% during the September quarter, which was a quarterly record. The performance was primarily driven by iPhone, where we set a September quarter record and by Mac, where we saw very strong double-digit growth. And taking a step back, Greater China was up 28% for the full year. Tim and Sabih were just in China meeting with customers and developers and partners, and it has been wonderful to see the customer reaction to our latest lineup of products, including iPhone Duo.

Our installed base of active devices has reached an all-time high, and we had a record year for iPhone upgraders in Mainland China. According to a survey from Worldpanel, iPhone models were the top 3 selling smartphones in urban China. and we think we gained share on iPhone and Mac. A couple of other really compelling things. On Mac, we had a record year for both upgraders and customers new to the product. And according to Counterpoint, MacBook Air and MacBook Neo were the top 2 selling laptop models and Mac Mini was the top-selling desktop model in the September quarter. So I guess to answer your question, we think the success comes from having really great products.

Suhasini Chandramouli: Awesome. Thank you, Richard. Operator, may we have our last question, please?

Operator: We will now go to Ben Bollin of Cleveland Research.

Benjamin Bollin: John, I'm interested in your thoughts with higher device prices, how you think about the environment around affordability programs and the importance to volumes with respect to trade-ins, subsidies and other options and what Apple can do to encourage more of that independently of funding it yourselves?

John Ternus: Yes. Look, when we're building products and then when we're pricing them, we're always focused on building the best products and services in the world and delivering incredible value to our customers. Obviously, as we talked about, these memory prices are unprecedented, and so that has put pressure on our prices. But it's been great to see the success of the products. And we have been investing in programs like Apple, the Apple upgrade program, which is a great way to help affordability. And so these affordability programs are definitely an important factor.

Benjamin Bollin: And the last one for me would be, when you look at, I guess, the level of supply-demand balance, could you speak to where you see that at, not necessarily where it is, where you'd like it to be and how you're thinking about the opportunity to get there across the portfolio?

Sabih Khan: Yes. Let me take that one, Ben. This is Sabih. So for the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, and it's primarily driven by memory. And that's because the demand has been higher than what we expected. And beyond December quarter, we're not providing an outlook.

Suhasini Chandramouli: All right. Thank you, Ben. A replay of today's call will be available on Apple podcast and at apple.com/investor. Thanks again for joining us today, everyone.

#3148. I’m finally ready for a smart calendar – why the Echo Show 16 stands out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

I'm finally ready to upgrade to a smart calendar - and Amazon's newest Echo device looks like an organizational solution for my family and I.

I’ve never claimed to be the most organized person, and I’m fully aware I need to take steps to be more on top of appointments, schedules, to-do lists, and everything that comes with family life. I’ve been tempted by smart display calendars like the Skylight, but they seemed a little gimmicky and expensive for what’s essentially a large tablet. (ZDNET’s Maria Diaz argues against that gimmick notion, by the way.)

The Echo Show 16, though, might just be the device that gets me to take the leap.

Also: Echo Show 16 makes Apple’s 7-inch HomeView look puny

When I first saw this device, I admit, it wasn’t the first thing to catch my eye. But then I started learning more about what it can do — and now I’m ready to boot my Echo Show 5 for an upgrade. It won’t be a cheap upgrade (I’ll address that later), but if it does what Amazon is promising, it’ll be more than worth it to me.

The first thing I noticed was how sleek the device looks. Amazon says it has 10% more viewing area than the Echo Show 15, but a frame that’s almost 40% thinner. Since I’ll be opting for a wall mount, I wanted something that wouldn’t be too obtrusive. Since my current device is an Echo Show 5 — the small counter-top version — it’s not exactly comparable. Still, it’ll be a huge upgrade to go from an Alexa device that shows pictures to something much more capable.

The biggest appeal for me is the organization. Amazon says the new Show offers a family hub with color-coded schedules, to-do lists, meal planning, and more. My Google Calendar holds all of that now, but it’s easy to miss a notification. And if I don’t make it a priority to check my app every day (something I need to get better about), it’s easy to miss something.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from this week

My current Show can display lists and events, but it doesn’t have a permanently present display.

Another significant upgrade is the camera. My current Show has a camera, but it’s not the greatest, especially at night or in low-light conditions, since it’s 2 MP.  The Echo Show 16 features a wide-angle 13-megapixel lens, the widest field of view on any Echo Show device to date. According to Amazon, this doubles the range of Visual ID from 8 feet to 17 feet (from the previous generation). The Show 16 also adds night vision, making it much easier to keep an eye on your home when it’s dark.

I check in on my dogs several times a day, and my current Show does an OK job, but it’s pretty much useless at night. The improved camera on the Show 16 offers a whole new level of functionality.

My biggest concern? The price. The Echo Show 16 starts at $500. If you add any accessories or upgrade to the anti-glare Nanomatte display, you’re closer to $600. That’s double the price of the similarly sized 15-inch Skylight calendar. At the time I’m writing this, a $100 coupon is available, bringing the price down to $400.

I’m already heavily invested in the Amazon ecosystem, so it makes sense that I’d bring a display into the fold as my new smart home centerpiece. A purchase like this is hardly a necessity, but if it can wrangle just a little of my life’s chaos, it’ll be a worthy investment.
