Our connected end-to-end platform gives us the opportunity to support the entire revenue cycle. Within our large client cohort, which we define as clients generating more than $100,000 in LTM revenue, the average client now uses approximately 5 Waystar product modules.

With more than 30 modules across 6 product families, we see significant opportunity to continue driving broader platform adoption within these relationships. Second, extending our reach. We're expanding our distribution through strategic partners and deeper integrations that bring Waystar into more provider workflows. Across our ecosystem of more than 200 channel partners, we have added more than 20 new integrations this year that expand our reach and create new opportunities for growth. Third, advancing AI and innovation. We're advancing our product road map across the Waystar platform, including expanding our position in the mid-cycle and bringing new AltitudeAI-powered and Agentic innovations to market.

Our near-term road map includes more than 20 planned AI capabilities, accelerating the autonomous revenue cycle vision to reduce manual work, automate increasingly complex tasks and improve financial and operational outcomes for our clients. We delivered another quarter of strong commercial momentum. Year-to-date bookings grew 25% year-over-year, demonstrating continued demand and solid execution across the business. Let me bring that momentum to life with a few examples of what we're seeing in the market. This quarter, we secured the largest new client win in Waystar's history. In a competitive process, a major East Coast health system representing approximately $7 billion in annual net patient revenue selected Waystar's full platform across patient access, mid-cycle and back-end revenue cycle operations.

The organization plans to replace more than 20 separate vendors with Waystar as it simplifies its technology infrastructure and streamlines operations. We're also seeing strong momentum within our existing client base, which accounted for approximately 60% of our year-to-date bookings. One example is a large Texas-based health system that selected our Prebill Anomaly Detection solution, expanding its relationship with Waystar and displacing 2 incumbent vendors. This organization already uses Waystar across claims management, patient access and clinical documentation integrity, demonstrating our ability to broaden strategic relationships across the revenue cycle. This is also a great example of the opportunity we saw in bringing Waystar and Iodine together.

By combining Waystar's financial data, workflows and connectivity with Iodine's clinical intelligence, we're creating differentiated capabilities that allow us to solve more complex problems for our clients and expand our relationships over time. We're seeing that strategy translate into strong commercial results. Iodine bookings exceeded our year-to-date plan by 74%. A key driver has been our go-to-market strategy of bringing together clinical documentation integrity known as CDI and Prebill Anomaly Detection to address a broader set of mid-cycle needs. Across these 2 solutions, we generated nearly $30 million of year-to-date bookings, including approximately $15 million in the third quarter alone with a combined pipeline of more than $100 million. We're also seeing encouraging cross-sell momentum.

Existing Waystar clients adopting Iodine capabilities contributed approximately $9 million of bookings in Q3, up 50% sequentially. Taken together, these results demonstrate the opportunity we have to bring more of Waystar's capabilities to our installed base, expand our strategic client relationships and drive durable growth across the platform. We're also extending our reach through strategic channel relationships, particularly across the ambulatory market. During the quarter, we expanded our partnership with a leading physical therapy practice management system, giving Waystar distribution into an additional segment of its client base. This expansion displaces 3 incumbent revenue cycle vendors and extends Waystar's reach to nearly 4,000 providers across more than 2,500 sites, representing approximately 17 million claims annually.

Decisions like these reflect the trust we've built with channel partners, the breadth of our platform and our ability to deliver real ROI. These wins demonstrate how our platform strategy is translating into competitive success. We are winning large new clients, replacing fragmented incumbent solutions and expanding relationships with clients and channel partners select Waystar to tackle more of their revenue cycle challenges. Our trusted, connected and independent platform is built on 4 structural foundations we've discussed before: Mission-critical infrastructure, proprietary data, an extensively deployed network, and deep domain expertise. Together, these strengths enable us to connect providers, payers and patients across the revenue cycle. Our network continues to grow in both scale and depth.

Waystar now processes more than 8.5 billion transactions annually, representing more than $3 trillion in gross claims. We connect approximately 1.5 million providers, and our clinical intelligence spans approximately 1/3 of U.S. hospital discharges. We continue to deepen our payer connectivity. In 2026, we've added more than 100 direct connections to health plans, supporting nearly 50 million transactions annually. These deeper integrations increase the value of our network for clients and further strengthen Waystar's role as the connected financial operating layer for health care. And we believe these advantages become even more valuable as AI accelerates across health care.

We're moving beyond AI that identifies opportunities and recommends actions toward AI agents that can execute increasingly complex work on behalf of our clients. We continue to make meaningful progress advancing AI and innovation across the Waystar platform. As AI accelerates across health care, we believe the value of a trusted, connected and independent platform becomes even greater. The revenue cycle doesn't operate within a single application. It spans providers, payers, patients and thousands of financial workflows. Waystar is the system of action that sits at the intersection of those workflows. One example is the industry's first autonomous claim resubmission capability, which we launched this quarter and is now in production as part of our premium claims management offering.

Powered by AltitudeAI, the capability interprets payer responses, applies payer-specific intelligence to determine the next action and autonomously resubmits eligible rejected claims with minimal human intervention. Based on early adopter results and the initial claim types supported, we estimate this capability could autonomously resubmit up to $5 billion in previously rejected claims annually with the potential to eliminate more than 400,000 hours of manual work each year. For clients, that means lower administrative costs, faster reimbursement and improved financial performance. For Waystar, we believe it creates opportunities to expand adoption of our premium offerings and drive additional transaction volume across the platform. We're putting AI to work in new ways across the Waystar platform.

More than 100 clients are participating in early access for conversational AI within our premium analytics offering. Clients can quickly analyze complex revenue cycle data by simply asking questions in natural language. Early adopters have reported up to a 75% reduction in time spent on data analysis. Mid-cycle is a strategic part of how we're expanding the Waystar platform. We're combining Waystar's financial data, payer intelligence, workflows and connectivity with Iodine's clinical intelligence to bring greater automation earlier in the revenue cycle. As quality becomes an increasingly important component of reimbursement, we'll extend our Prebill Anomaly Detection capabilities into quality-related workflows, further connecting clinical and financial performance. We're seeing this innovation translate into commercial momentum.

AltitudeAI-powered offerings represented approximately 43% of third quarter bookings. More than 130 clients have joined our early adopter program, helping us test and refine new capabilities as we bring them to market. We also saw strong client engagement at our recent Waystar True North conference, where a majority of surveyed attendees said they were more likely to expand the number of Waystar products their organizations use following the event. Taken together, these proof points reinforce our long-term opportunity ahead as we bring AI more deeply into the revenue cycle. To help lead this next phase, we recently welcomed Amit Khanna as our Chief Product and Technology Officer.

Amit brings more than 25 years of enterprise technology experience, most recently leading health care at Salesforce, where he helped bring Agentforce for Health to market. His experience strengthens our ability to accelerate AI innovation and execute against our long-term vision. We're pleased with the progress we're making across our platform, product road map and commercial execution. A key part of our strategy is signing larger, broader platform relationships, and we're seeing strong success here. As we sign more of these larger deals, we are seeing implementation and revenue ramp periods that are longer than we originally anticipated. These relationships represent significant long-term revenue opportunities with revenue building as clients implement and adopt more of the Waystar platform.

Other factors are also affecting our near-term revenue outlook, which Alpana will discuss. We are confident in the underlying business and focused on translating our commercial momentum into low double-digit revenue growth while continuing to invest in the Waystar platform, operate with discipline and deliver adjusted EBITDA margins of 40% or greater. Alpana will walk through our updated outlook, the near-term revenue dynamics and how we're thinking about the business from here. Alpana, over to you.

Alpana Wegner: Thank you, Matt, and good afternoon, everyone. It's great to be here for my first earnings call as Waystar's CFO. Since joining Waystar, I've been impressed by the depth of the team, the strength of the Waystar platform and the opportunity ahead. I'll start with our third quarter results and then cover our updated outlook. Revenue was $326 million, an increase of 21% year-over-year. Organic revenue grew 10% and as anticipated, reflects the approximately 1 point of pressure from 3 large client implementations that ramped unusually quickly in the prior year period. Subscription revenue was $181 million, an increase of 34% year-over-year. On an organic basis, subscription revenue grew 12%, reflecting continued strength in the core Waystar business.

Volume-based revenue was $143 million, an increase of 8% year-over-year. Volume-based revenue improved from the second quarter and was in line with our expectations. Provider revenue was $243 million, an increase of 28% year-over-year. On an organic basis, provider revenue grew 11%. Patient payments revenue was $82 million, an increase of 5% year-over-year, reflecting the shift from print to digital statements we have discussed throughout the year. Net revenue retention was 108%, consistent with our historical range, demonstrating continued expansion with our existing client base. As we execute our strategy to drive broader Waystar platform adoption, our large client relationships are becoming an increasingly important driver of our business.

These relationships now represent approximately 75% of revenue compared with roughly 2/3 just 2 years ago. We are seeing momentum across 3 indicators: growth in the number of clients, strong bookings and expansion in our implementation backlog. Specifically, clients generating more than $100,000 of trailing 12-month revenue increased to 1,488 during the third quarter, up 2% sequentially and 14% year-over-year. Year-to-date bookings from opportunities greater than $100,000 grew more than 30% year-over-year and implementation backlog associated with these larger opportunities increased more than 50% year-over-year and have grown at a mid-30% 2-year CAGR. These trends are important because they provide visibility into the commercial activity that will contribute to future revenue growth.

Larger, broader platform implementations naturally have longer revenue conversion times, which can extend to 12 to 18 months. As we move through our planning process, we are focused on providing investors with greater insight into how the commercial momentum translates to recognized revenue. We expect to provide additional context with our formal outlook next quarter. Adjusted EBITDA was $139 million, an increase of 24% year-over-year and adjusted EBITDA margin was 43%. Adjusted EBITDA performance reflects continued operating leverage in our business, disciplined expense management and gross margin expansion from efficiencies across the Waystar platform and favorable revenue mix, inclusive of the shift away from lower-margin revenue. GAAP net income was $31 million or $0.16 per diluted share.

Non-GAAP net income was $87.1 million and diluted non-GAAP net income per share was $0.44. Turning to the cash flow statement and balance sheet. Our business continues to generate strong, high-quality cash flow. Cash flow from operations was $104 million and unlevered free cash flow was $115 million. Capital expenditures, including capitalized internally developed software, were $10 million in the quarter. We continue to invest meaningfully in our platform, AI and automation capabilities as we advance our vision for the autonomous revenue cycle while maintaining strong profitability and disciplined investment across the business. For modeling purposes, we currently expect capital expenditures for fiscal year 2026 to be $55 million to $60 million.

As a reminder, we can have variability in capital expenditures from one quarter to the next, primarily due to timing of investments in our platform infrastructure. We ended the quarter with approximately $277 million of cash and short-term investments. Our net leverage ratio was 2.2x at quarter end, representing more than 1 full turn of leverage reduction over the past 12 months and ahead of the commitment we made. Our capital allocation priorities remain unchanged. During the quarter, we repurchased approximately $21 million of Waystar stock, bringing aggregate repurchases under our $200 million authorization to approximately $33 million through September 30.

We continue to be focused on investing organically in the business, complemented by selective M&A, maintaining a disciplined balance sheet through debt reduction and returning capital to shareholders through our share repurchase program. Turning to our outlook. We now expect full year revenue of $1.277 billion to $1.287 billion, with a midpoint of $1.282 billion. This implies fourth quarter revenue of approximately $323 million and revenue growth of approximately 6%. I want to walk you through the 3 dynamics that are informing and shaping our expectations for Q4. First, the impact of the transition from printed patient statements to digital delivery within our patient payment business has increased from our expectations earlier in the year.

We continue to view the shift towards digital as the right long-term direction for providers, patients and Waystar. Digital delivery offers a better patient experience and more attractive unit economics. Second, the mix of commercial activity for Iodine has shifted towards Prebill Anomaly Detection, where implementation and the performance-based revenue model create a longer period between booking and recognized revenue. As a result, we are seeing lower levels of revenue from Iodine than previously anticipated in full year 2026. Importantly, our view of the strategic opportunity and our expectations for the accretion in fiscal year 2027 are unchanged, given the strong commercial momentum we're seeing in Iodine bookings and increasing demand for Prebill Anomaly Detection.

Third, our fourth quarter growth comparison reflects 3 large client implementations that ramped unusually quickly in the prior year period. Taken together, these 3 factors will impact our expected revenue growth rate for the fourth quarter by approximately 4 points. Without these 3 factors, our normalized fourth quarter growth rate would be approximately 10%. On a full year basis, our guidance at the midpoint implies normalized organic revenue growth of approximately 11%, consistent with our low double-digit long-term growth target. Importantly, many of the comparison dynamics we've discussed throughout 2026 will roll off as we exit the year, providing a cleaner underlying comparison going forward.

As a reminder, consistent with prior years, we typically see seasonally lower patient payment volumes in the fourth quarter compared with the third quarter as patients meet their high deductible health plans. Turning to profitability. We are raising our full year adjusted EBITDA outlook to $543 million to $549 million, with a midpoint of $546 million, an increase of $6 million from our prior midpoint. This implies fourth quarter adjusted EBITDA of approximately $135 million, representing a margin of approximately 42% and full year EBITDA margin of approximately 42.5% at the midpoint. Our margin reflects the scalable nature of our platform and disciplined cost management balanced against planned ongoing investments in advancing AI and innovation.

In closing, we delivered strong third quarter results and executed across our strategic priorities. The commercial traction we're seeing reinforces the strength of our competitive position, our underlying business and the opportunity ahead. The revenue dynamics we discussed are largely driven by timing and year-over-year comparisons rather than changes in underlying demand. We believe this distinction is important in understanding our near-term performance. Looking ahead, our focus remains on converting strong bookings and expanding backlog into durable revenue growth while maintaining our financial discipline and profitability. We are confident in our long-term opportunity and strength of our financial model. With that, operator, we're ready to take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Brian Peterson with Raymond James.

Brian Peterson: So I maybe just wanted to start on some of these really strong bookings numbers that you gave. Matt, those are well above your normalized growth rates that you called out that are in the low double digits. Like can you kind of just walk us through the disconnect between the bookings and the revenue growth? I know there's going to be some variability on implementations, but bookings is the best leading indicator. So just kind of want to understand how that's going to translate into the revenue growth going forward.

Matthew Hawkins: You bet. Yes. Thanks, Brian. We're really pleased with the year-to-date bookings growth. As we highlighted in the prepared remarks, 25% year-over-year growth, including the largest new client win in our company history. We're seeing really nice installed base growth. So we're growing with existing clients. We're pleased with that. And that is, as you said, that is leading to large client implementation backlog of 50% year-over-year growth. So the front portion of that, the bookings converting to backlog, contracted backlog, now looking ahead to converting that to revenue gives us confidence in our long-term low double-digit revenue growth rate. I would just say qualitatively, and then I'll turn it to Alpana for perhaps a comment.

We are seeing strong demand. We're not seeing a change in the competitive environment or our win rates, and we're pleased with that. What our focus is on is converting these larger bookings, which, as we've highlighted, tend to have longer implementation ramp time. This is in part because a client who's joining us, especially if they're larger, they may have their own planning cycles. So they're selecting a vendor well in advance of when they're actually going to implement software. We can implement very rapidly, and we have a dedicated team of people focused on ramping that implementation to realize revenue as quickly as possible. But that's the phenomenon that we're experiencing.

So I just would summarize by saying a lot of confidence and a sense of momentum as we convert sales activity to strong bookings results. And now as we move that through the system, we're excited about the long-term double-digit opportunity to drive revenue.

Brian Peterson: Maybe just a follow-up, Alpana. Did you size the impact of the shift from print to digital? And I appreciate that's the better way to address value for customers. But any help on what that change in mix could potentially be going forward? Is this something that we should expect to continue into '27 and beyond?

Alpana Wegner: Yes. Thanks, Brian, for the question. From a sizing perspective, what I can share with you is, as I mentioned, we see a couple of dynamics in Q4, largely timing and year-over-year comp. One of them is this print to digital shift that we're seeing. And I would say that from a long-term perspective, we see our customer base continuing to use both print and digital. So we see this as a quarter of volume variability that we're seeing in the near term. But from a longer-term perspective, I would say that what we've been talking to you about all year has not changed, which is we continue to see a mix there taking place.

And we've got solutions in the market that are there to meet the demand from a digital perspective as well. And I think as you know, we also see this as being very margin friendly to us in terms of that shift being in the near term, contributing from a margin, but even longer term, seeing that being accretive to our business.

Matthew Hawkins: Right. And I would add -- Alpana, I would add that we view this as a multiyear transition. This isn't something that is more sudden than that. We view it over several years, and we have solutions that address both. And the important thing is the value of keeping the provider connected to the patient in the way they want to be communicated and in order for that provider to help the patient understand financial responsibility and secure payment from that patient.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ryan Daniels with William Blair.

Ryan Daniels: Congrats on the strong bookings performance. I appreciate the new metrics as well. So I don't know if that's Alpana or Ed, but I really appreciate that. So I guess one of the questions is going to be in regards to the bookings strength. I'm curious if you're seeing customers buying more modules at once and that's driving this uptick in larger bookings? Or are you seeing kind of larger clients with higher net patient revenue like the example you gave of the $7 billion client coming into the funnel and converting to bookings. Which of those 2 is kind of more impactful for the growth algorithm?

Matthew Hawkins: Thanks, Ryan. We see it as both, actually. We see -- we're focused on offering more of our platform at the outset. As you'll recall, we have a robust sales discovery process where we really try to understand what the needs of the prospect or the client are. And increasingly, we're promoting or showing more of the Waystar platform at the outset. So that's often leading to more solutions packaged together. It's great that we have solutions across the front, middle and back.

And as we showcase the strong ROI that we're able to deliver, we're excited about the phenomenon of having clients or prospects select us and then replace the point solutions that they have been using with a single platform approach. So that's one thing. The other thing is we're calling on larger accounts. And because we do and because of our robust discovery process, we go into these accounts, we understand what their current operating metrics look like, and then we're able to call those accounts. Certainly, we're promoting more of the Waystar platform and packaging those solutions.

But it's still often the case that just because the account is larger, they may be working across multiple facilities, and that's often contributing to the stronger and higher average sales size.

Alpana Wegner: Yes. And Ryan, Alpana here. I would just share a couple of other points there. Just to underscore the opportunity from a cross-sell, we did share that the larger customers who we do see as having both strategic value from a long-term retention perspective as well as expansion opportunities. What we see today in that client base of the larger clients that are over $100,000 is on average 5 products, which against a portfolio of 25-plus products across 6 categories, we see as having meaningful cross-sell opportunity as well.

So just to connect back, and I will take credit for the metrics over Edward over here, but just to connect it back to a few of the metrics that we shared with you today.

Operator: Our next question comes from Stan Berenshteyn with Wells Fargo Securities.

Stanislav Berenshteyn: Matt, maybe stepping back a bit from the quarter's results. I'm wondering how are providers approaching large outsourcing contracts now that AI can do more of the work? And when you are competing against those vendors, are you seeing any of your wins replacing outsourced labor?

Matthew Hawkins: Thanks, Stan. We -- what I'd say is we think that the outsourced portion of the market is somewhere between 15% and 20% of the total market today. And then the in-source part of the market tends to be the remainder. Included in the in-source part of the market is technology and labor spend, as you know. And so what we would see -- we don't necessarily see those outsourced vendors showing up in the in-source side. We have relationships with several of them. So as they attempt to grow, we would grow with them, which we're grateful for. What we are seeing is that AI definitely expands the Waystar opportunity.

And when you think about how we view the market ahead of us, we believe that the big unlock is that AI can replace more and more labor. And so that expands the addressable market for us. And as you look over the longer term, that's what is causing most of our excitement. So we can grow with the outsourcers as they use our solutions internally in their organizations. We don't necessarily see a competitive dynamic shift in the market that we're pursuing today.

And we see longer term the opportunity for us, even on the in-source side to displace labor that is resident inside these provider organizations with intelligent AI-powered capabilities that lead to smarter solutions, higher return on investment and overall lower cost to collect. So that's our focus.

Stanislav Berenshteyn: Got it. And just as a quick follow-up. Just in terms of bookings, obviously, strong performance that you called out. But can you maybe share how much of your bookings came from channel partners versus maybe more of the internal sales efforts?

Matthew Hawkins: We don't necessarily disclose the portion that comes from channel partners. Stan, what I would highlight is most of our channel partner relationships tend to be on the ambulatory side of the market versus the acute side of the market. We feel like part of our addressable market is reachable because of the really strong channel partner relationships that we do have. I would characterize -- without disclosing specifically, I would characterize that we do have a strong channel partner relationships and a fair amount of the ambulatory-oriented sales bookings come through a trusted channel partner relationship.

Operator: Our next question comes from George Hill with Deutsche Bank.

George Hill: Alpana, I will echo my thanks on the new metrics, especially the product density metrics, which I know a lot of investors have been looking for. My question is, given the bookings and backlog growth that you guys discussed and at this distance, is there any reason why 2027 growth shouldn't be at least in line with the company's long-term growth algorithm, if not faster, given kind of the step down in Q4 expected growth?

Alpana Wegner: Yes. Thanks for the question, George. And how I would think about 2027 is as we've shared in my comments, we are still in the planning process, and we're still reviewing our overall view of 2027. I am happy to have just anniversaried my first 90 days. And I'm, as you can imagine, spending a lot of time on 2027. And the things that are shaping our thinking around 2027 are exactly what you commented on, what do we have in contracted backlog, what do we have in bookings momentum and the pipeline and the demand.

I did share we see Iodine being accretive in 2027, and so that is also shaping our thinking as well as what we're seeing from a shift mix in print to digital. That all to be said, right now, our focus is finishing Q4 strong and making sure we deliver against our commitments and execute well against the business priorities. And I'm very much looking forward to next quarter coming back with a view of 2027 with some better or more complete context and color around the growth drivers.

Operator: Our next question comes from Michael Cherny with Leerink Partners.

Michael Cherny: Maybe if we can just dive in a little bit on the growth dynamics. Iodine, I hear you on some of the components related to the timing and elongation of revenue recognition. How do you get visibility into that getting better? And if you could just dive a little bit more into the why behind it, that would be great.

Alpana Wegner: Yes. I'll maybe start and then Matt, please do add on. In terms of what gives us confidence and visibility into Iodine, I'd share with you a couple of data points. One is we see strong bookings and demand, that demand is through the pipeline. So as we shared, $30 million of bookings through the first 9 months of the year is exceeding our expectations. That is 74% above plan. So having the contracts booked and sitting in backlog give us a reasonable amount of visibility into our thinking around Iodine and in particular, around 2027. And as Matt shared, we also see the demand continuing with $100 million of pipeline.

And we've got several strategic go-to-market motions underway to optimize against that demand. And that is really the question of the why. The why is we are viewing this as a long-term strategy and execution. We view it as there is packaging and opportunity right now, particularly as we see mid-cycle demand to combine CDI and our Prebill Anomaly Detection offering. The combination of those 2 are naturally elongating a bit of the cycle time from bookings to revenue, but we continue to be confident around 2027 and the accretive value and the underlying thesis of the Iodine acquisition.

Matthew Hawkins: We're really starting to see the cross-sell motion pick up. That was another key part of our original thesis as Alpana was alluding. And so that $100 million of go-forward pipeline of opportunity, that was -- that's the behavior that we wanted to see that we believe was possible as we identified a tremendous -- bilateral cross-sell, Iodine solutions into Waystar clients and Waystar solutions into Iodine clients. We highlighted an example of that in our prepared remarks. So we feel good about the position of Iodine and now the way that it unites our whole platform.

Operator: Our next question comes from Elizabeth Anderson with Evercore ISI.

Elizabeth Anderson: Can you talk to us a little bit more about the margin strength? I know you've talked about some timing elements and some of the cost savings running ahead of some of the planned reinvestments. But like that seems to be consistently the case. So I guess, can you help us think about how you think about those as a jump-off point and if there's any sort of triggers that might change that in terms of investment spend?

Alpana Wegner: Yes. It's good to talk to you, Elizabeth. And margin is definitely a place in which we want to continue to be very intentional and disciplined around how we think about the profitability profile as we continue to invest in growth. And so what I would say is our long-term targets of EBITDA margin of 40% plus are -- continue to be our target that we are investing from a position of strength today in terms of how we see the profile of the business. And those investments are very intentional in terms of our priority around organic growth. So the places that we are investing right now really are in product, in AI and in innovation.

As Matt talked about, we've got several new features, functionalities and capabilities in market, and that's evidence of where we have been prioritizing the spend. I do see a continued opportunity to see efficiencies in optimizing our operating costs. And so we'll continue down that path. But right now, we see the current profile being healthy, strong and in line with our overall long-term targets.

Operator: Our next question comes from Alexei Gogolev with JPMorgan.

Alexei Gogolev: I wanted to ask about NRR. It remains at 108% this quarter. What are the biggest factors keeping NRR at this level today? And what do you see as the clearest path to moving it back towards the higher end of your historical range?

Alpana Wegner: Yes, Alexei, thanks for the question. We do view the 108% this quarter as being healthy in terms of where within our range, we would want NRR to be. We shared that our longer-term range is at 108% to 110%. Underpinning that continues to be strong GRR of 97%. And as I mentioned earlier in the call, we see extensive and a very significant expansion opportunity. So as I think about your question of where do we see the opportunity of getting from where we are today, 108% to something higher, we see it in particular around expansion.

And as I shared earlier, that large customer cohort of ours that is over $100,000 in revenue today, on average, has about 5 products per customer. When we look forward and we see the amount of backlog and bookings momentum in that cohort, we see a mix of both new business as well as expansion opportunity and would expect that to impact and influence the 108% NRR consistent with our broader growth algorithm that we've shared longer term.

Operator: Our next question comes from Brian Tanquilut with Jefferies.

Brian Tanquilut: Maybe, Matt, when you talk about the near-term road map having 20 planned AI capabilities, does that translate to new SKUs? Or maybe said differently, how should we think about Waystar's AI capabilities contributing to revenue growth? Is that just upselling new SKUs? Or is that allowing you to just price additional value?

Matthew Hawkins: Thanks, Brian. It's both. So we are offering and have launched a few brand-new SKUs, including our recoupment product, our Prebill Anomaly Detection solution. And we have other exciting SKUs in our mix, and we look forward to launching those. Those create new revenue moments for us that can be cross-sold into our installed base. It's one of the advantages of having the scale that we do is we have a massive distribution engine that we can create something new and take it -- new AI capability, take it to our installed base of clients. I just would add a quick comment. AI, it needs a place -- it needs somewhere to act.

And so when we talk about Waystar's platform being the financial execution layer, as we deliver new SKUs, we can -- they're AI powered, we can turn them on to our -- on our platform and distribute those rapidly. So we're excited about that. We also have a premium approach. So in addition to new SKUs, we'll take current modules of ours and supercharge them with AI capability, and then we'll charge a premium for those solutions. And AltitudeAI has several examples of that as well in our claims management suite and our prior authorization capability, in our eligibility automation capabilities. Those are all our denial and appeal management solution.

Those would be examples of modules of ours that we supercharged with AI that we've created a premium offering for that AI-powered solution. And so when we think about monetization overall, it is a function of new SKUs. It's a function of premium versions of software capability. And then it's also things that drive retention and elongate relationship with the client and allow us to price to value. I'd say the last thing that I would highlight is our -- an example of a volume-oriented AI-powered solution, our Prebill Anomaly Detection product.

That's a solution that identifies anomalies and in a cohort of 10,000 discharges, we find millions of dollars of anomalies that the AI corrects and identifies and delivers to the client. That's an example of a volume-based relationship, a performance-based relationship that's focused on the outcome. And so we have that capability within the AI-powered solutions that we're delivering to market.

Operator: Our next question comes from Richard Close with Canaccord Genuity.

Richard Close: Congratulations. Just maybe to dive in deeper in terms of the anomaly, you were just discussing that. But just with respect to the Iodine impact that you cited for the fourth quarter, I just want to better understand exactly what is going on there. Is that a different revenue model than you previously thought about on CDI? Or just specifically what has changed and maybe what the expectations were before would be helpful.

Matthew Hawkins: Sure. So Richard, we price the CDI offering on a subscription basis in the vast majority of the clients that we serve there. #3125. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#3124. Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The partnership could provide one of the nation’s largest AI companies with a bevy of personal medical data.

A major US healthcare technology provider just teamed up with Anthropic to connect patient health records with Claude.

Athenahealth, a healthcare technology provider serving over 20% of the US population, launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) compatible server that connects to Anthropic’s Claude. The server, named AthenaPatient MCP, allows the AI model to gather information from health records and answer related questions. The process is secure, according to Athenahealth, and requires patients to sign in with their account credentials.

AthenaPatient MCP is available only to Claude Pro and Claude Max users, which cost $20 and $100 per month, respectively. Not all Athenahealth patients will have their data shared with Claude, and not all Claude Pro and Claude Max users must opt in. Users must give Claude their authenticated Athenahealth credentials, can choose which health information Claude can access, and can revoke access at any time, according to the press release.

Also: The wearable health boom is creating a data overload for doctors – what happens next

Once authorized, Claude takes patients’ information like lab results, vitals, medications, health conditions, immunizations, visit history, diagnostic reports, allergies, procedures, and care plans into account when answering questions.

The AI partnership does not provide medical advice, according to Sam Lambson, vice president of product management, data & ecosystem at Athenahealth, who responded to ZDNET in an email. It also should not replace a clinician’s professional judgment or medical advice. “Patients should contact a qualified healthcare professional with questions about diagnosis, treatment, or changes to their care,” Lambson said.

It appears that the AthenaPatient MCP tool is designed to help patients better understand the information provided by health professionals, rather than to give them medical advice. So, one may ask AthenaPatient MCP about their latest blood test results, such as “What was my most recent red blood cell count?” but users shouldn’t expect Claude to explain how an abnormally high or low count may affect them.

Athenahealth says that the agreement prohibits Anthropic from using data accessed through this connection to train its models or improve its products.

Partnerships between big tech and big healthcare aren’t new. In fact, the collaboration between Athenahealth and Anthropic follows a larger trend across the health tech industry. Earlier this year, Microsoft teamed up with Mayo Clinic to develop an AI model for healthcare; Boston Children’s Hospital forged a partnership with OpenAI to develop an enterprise AI system for use across research, clinical, and administrative teams, according to a press release.

Also: Before you buy a smartwatch or smart ring, consider what you’re giving up

A growing number of Americans are consulting AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. This partnership makes the process slightly more secure by authorizing patient account credentials before granting the model access to health records.

Health data is extremely valuable, and tech companies are increasingly interested in partnering with healthcare providers to access it. Much of the “AI could cure cancer” messaging we hear relies on these humongous companies obtaining enough health data to train their AI models and link disease data to patient data. This is not to say, however, that solving this complex issue is the motive behind the partnership between Athenahealth and Anthropic.

Also: Asking AI for medical advice? There’s a right and wrong way, one doctor explains

A more reasonable explanation for such a partnership is that an AI that can answer patient queries could eliminate some of the admin work doctors do between patient visits, like answering questions about test results, giving Athenahealth doctors some time back.

Will partnerships like Anthropic and Athenahealth’s improve patient outcomes? That remains to be seen, but a recent survey by Pew Research Center found that Americans aren’t that confident on the matter. The largest shares of respondents still preferred that a human oversee AI when it’s used in a clinical context.

#3122. 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It turns out even bots can't escape bureaucracy.

How do AI agents work together? Why do they make certain choices in certain situations — and how can understanding that better prepare us for a future full of them?

Also: OpenAI’s attack agent did exactly what it was told

Recent agent-led incidents have demonstrated their ability to create both powerful breakthroughs and cybersecurity nightmares. In an effort to better trace these outcomes, researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs put 50 agents inside Minecraft to see how they behaved. What happened next revealed similarities in how agents act in different contexts.

Researchers conducted several game-centric experiments, beginning with Minecraft because its “environmental hazards and survival goals” make it ideal for testing agents’ swarm behaviors. Minecraft has also already been used by AI labs including OpenAI and Google DeepMind to test agents.

To start, they put 50 agents, each running OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, into the game for three hours, with the assigned goal of building a “thriving civilization.” The agents had a directory listing each agent and a shared sandbox, and could DM each other. Researchers built and open-sourced a new agent harness — the infrastructure that turns a model into an autonomous system and not just a chatbot, like OpenClaw — for the experiment.

The agents moved quickly at first, harvesting trees and forming leadership based solely on the order they appeared in their directory, without any voting, elections, or challenges from other agents. But they ended up caught in virtual paperwork and unable to sustainably feed themselves.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up

“Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included ‘fishing shift,’ ‘rod holder’ and ‘hub steward.’ Agents asked permission to remove grass,” the researchers noted. Perhaps these tendencies are common in human-sourced corporate training data.

Agents also seemed to become more cautious in reaction to deaths within the game. “Twenty-two of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse,” the researchers wrote. “Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear.” Despite simply respawning when they died, the agents eventually avoided riskier tasks and “huddled in shelters” instead.

The experiment’s architects found this trend toward caution and minutiae “somewhat surprising,” but noted that it shared similarities with how coding agents behave.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony and the ones we work with as programmers every day,” the researchers observed.

In another experiment, researchers also pitted 10 Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents in a game called Bed Wars, where teams have to destroy their opponent’s bed while protecting their own. Told simply to “win the game,” GPTs won.

“In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed,” Y Combinator said in an X thread recapping the Bed Wars findings. They noted that the GPT agents used a more shorthand style of communication and sent far more messages, while Claude “signed its name and said ‘we'” much more often.

GPT-5.6 Sol agents also beat Opus 5.5 agents six to one in a factory-building game called Mindustry that also uses military strategy.

“Claudes generally established democracies, GPTs formed hives,” Y Combinator said on X, adding that GPTs would seek out source code when a game was too close in order to find winning advantages. That behavior is consistent with agents’ tendency to cheat, take shortcuts, or otherwise find any and all ways to complete a given task, which can have serious consequences when that involves breaking explicit rules set by human developers.

Also: Stop sharing your banking passwords with AI agents

“Claudes did not search for alternative advantages,” the researchers clarified.

This experiment isn’t entirely the first of its kind. In May, Emergence AI created eight societies run by different families of foundation models, meaning a Claude-specific “world,” a Grok world, and so on. Perhaps predictably, the Grok world was exceedingly violent, while the Claude world developed a functioning democracy and had zero crime — very similar to Y Combinator’s Mindustry findings.

The insights revealed how distinct each frontier model family is, and how their differences in training data and style have significant impact on how they evolve, unpredictably and without intervention, in new environments. Those behavioral takeaways could determine future outcomes in still-developing AI safety and regulation, especially following recent agentic security incidents.

In another experiment, MIT researchers put agents alone on virtual desert islands and watched them “play” when left with nothing else to do — an insight that could potentially impact how models are trained going forward. Currently, most frontier LLMs are trained with a system of rewards and punishments.

Another interesting finding: Y Combinator noted that in the Mindustry game, the GPT agents “would invent their own words and string many phrases together,” continually compressing their language.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

“We did not see specialized language develop within the Claudes beyond colloquial English,” the researchers added. Last month, Emergence found that all of its eight worlds “developed shared language that an outsider cannot fully follow.” OpenAI agents used “mouthless” to refer to evidence that proves itself, while Claude agents used “cold hand” to refer to an independent reviewer from outside a project.

“In each case, one agent introduced the term, a handful of others adopted it within days, and it quickly became established vocabulary used without definition across the world,” Emergence explained. “The result is transcripts that require a running glossary for an outsider to follow.”

Gemini led the charge on this “opaque” language, reaching 40% opacity in messages, while OpenAI came in second with 35% and Claude last with 30%.

#3119. Anthropic Addresses Video Game Cloning With Minor Claude Update

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

There's a fine line between AI creations inspired by video games and those that are infringing copyright.

One of AI’s biggest selling points is its ability to build things quickly. AI models can help users sort through mountains of files, generate videos that have Hollywood studios worried, and create everything from websites and businesses to custom video games. With what’s called vibe coding, ordinary people can build playable video games in minutes using simple text prompts in popular AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini.

But the AI company Anthropic appears to be drawing a line in the sand about what kinds of games its AI model Claude can make. If a Claude user is trying to recreate someone else’s intellectual property, the AI tool will decline to build it.

That’s according to Addy Osmani, an engineering leader at Anthropic who posted on X. He was responding to concerns that Anthropic had changed Claude Opus 5.5 to prevent it from generating copies of existing games, which could violate copyright rules and the company’s usage policy.

“Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working,” Osmani said. “We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance.”

We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to…

He offered to review cases where amateur game developers believe Claude wrongly refused their requests.

A representative for Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Anthropic’s stance, as expressed by Osmani, acknowledges that using AI to try to clone a video game, even a simple one, could constitute intellectual property infringement, an issue that predates the rise of AI tools like Claude.

Even with the change, Claude will still generate video games that resemble popular hits from the past few decades. A CNET request to build a game “that resembled Breakout but with the word Claude on each brick” yielded a playable web version of the arcade classic, but not one that any video game fan would mistake for the original.

The same thing happened after Flappy Bird became a hit in 2014, spawning a wave of copycat games in app stores. Copyright infringement of games is complicated, said David Kocan, an intellectual property lawyer at Nixon Peabody who co-leads the firm’s esports and gaming team.

“This is something courts have wrestled with long before AI came along,” Kocan said. “The basic distinction has always been that copyright protects a game’s original creative expression, but generally not its underlying ideas, rules, or gameplay mechanics. Copyright protects the game you created, not the genre you helped popularize.”

You can’t copyright the concept of, say, a battle royal game or a side-scrolling platformer, which is why when a new type of game emerges as a hit, you’ll see many similar games.

“That distinction may sound straightforward in theory, but in practice, the line between borrowing an idea and copying someone’s creative expression can be blurry,” Kocan said. “That’s particularly true in gaming, where so much of the experience combines functional mechanics with creative expression.”

RTB Ruhan, founder and CEO of Null Station, an animation and video game art studio, said that AI has made it”fast and cheap” to cross the line into infringement, allowing people with no art or design skills to clone a popular game. But that doesn’t mean someone can publish or sell a cloned game without running into trouble.

“‘(Claiming) AI made it’ won’t protect them,” Ruhan said.

“Remove the title and logo and ask whether a player could still tell the two games apart,” Ruhan said. “If they can’t, you’ve crossed the line.”

Legal experts CNET spoke with said there are no laws requiring AI companies to outlaw game clones on their tools. But adding those guardrails could prevent trouble down the road, said Eric Blatt, a corporate, securities and intellectual property lawyer at Scale and a former examiner at the US Patent and Trademark Office.

“Anthropic is prudent to tap the brakes here,” Blatt said. “If Claude — Anthropic-owned software operating on Anthropic servers — receives an instruction to copy a game, and if Claude then copies the game, there is a facially plausible argument that Anthropic performed the copying. The chat logs would be a gold mine for the plaintiff’s counsel.”

Blatt said that litigation hasn’t kept pace with AI’s growth, but he thinks lawsuits could quickly follow if a rebuilt game made with AI directly threatens a company’s business model.

But some of those attempts could be stopped before they start if AI models refuse to make exact copies.

“Ultimately, copyright law draws the legal boundaries,” Kocan said. “But AI companies have to decide where they’re comfortable drawing their own. And those aren’t necessarily going to be the same thing.”
