#3112. Match (MTCH) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Tinder DAU returns to growth after 3.5 years; Hinge revenue surges 19% YoY.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Match Group, Inc. (MTCH +1.59%) reported third quarter results highlighting a return to daily active user growth at Tinder and double-digit revenue expansion at Hinge. Management reported that the company expects to finish the year slightly above the midpoint of its full-year revenue guidance and meaningfully exceed previous margin and free cash flow targets. The company stated that its 2027 strategy will focus on sustainable Tinder revenue growth and monetization innovation while managing higher in-app purchase fees through disciplined operational spending. Management confirmed a commitment to deploying 100% of free cash flow toward shareholder returns over time, supported by a newly declared cash dividend.

Operator: Welcome to the Match Group Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. Should you need assistance, please signal a conference specialist by pressing the star key followed by zero. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your telephone keypad. To withdraw your question, please press star then two. Please note, this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Tanny Shelburne, Senior Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Tanny Shelburne: Thank you, operator, and good afternoon, everyone. Today's call will be led by CEO Spencer Rascoff and CFO Steve Bailey. They will make a few brief remarks, and then we will open it up for Q&A. Before we start, I need to remind everyone that during this call, we may discuss our outlook and future performance. These forward-looking statements may be preceded by words such as "we expect," "we believe," "we anticipate," or similar statements. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties, and our actual results could differ materially from the views expressed today. Some of these risks have been set forth in our earnings release and our periodic reports with the SEC.

Also during this call, we will discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures. Reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures are provided in the published materials on our ir.mtch.com website. These non-GAAP measures are not intended to be substitutes for our GAAP results. With that, I would like to turn the call over to Spencer.

Spencer Rascoff: Thanks, Tanny. Good afternoon. Thanks, everyone, for joining us. We are trying something new this quarter. We have posted our full prepared remarks to the investor relations website at ir.mtch.com for you to read through, but our plan for today's call is for me and Steve to just spend a few minutes on the key highlights and then devote the majority of our time to answer your questions. A year ago, the big question you asked us was whether we could turn Tinder around. We knew we had to start by improving user outcomes, meaning we had to build better experiences that resonate with Gen Z, deliver more relevant recommendations, and improve trust and safety.

If we got those foundations right, then better user trends and ultimately revenue would follow. Tinder has had multiple consecutive quarters of improvement in the metrics that matter. This quarter, we had our strongest quarterly year-over-year performance in both Sparks, that is six-way conversations, and Sparks coverage, the percentage of users getting a Spark, since we started tracking those metrics. In September, global daily active users returned to year-over-year growth for the first time in three and a half years, and we have cut year-over-year declines in monthly active users nearly in half over the last year. The improvement is broad-based. It spans women and men, age groups, and geographies.

We are seeing growth again in parts of the business where trends were moving in the wrong direction not that long ago. In October, markets representing nearly 70% of Tinder's DAU and 50% of its revenue had growing or flat DAU year-over-year, with the U.S. crossing into positive territory exiting the month. We now have evidence that those changes are working. There is still a lot of work ahead, particularly with the youngest Gen Z users. While we made substantial progress improving the experience for existing users, the next step is reconsideration.

That means giving people a reason to come back or to try Tinder for the first time, and that is what our Better with Friends roadmap is designed to do. We are giving people more social and lower-pressure ways to meet, often with friends and in real life, because that is what users want. Events is the feature I am most enthusiastic about, but they are all geared towards creating more opportunities for people to form meaningful connections in real life. We are building with our mission always in focus, to make Tinder the most fun way to spark something new with someone new. We live and breathe this daily.

Tinder employees can recite this clearly, and it is what keeps us working hard. Turning to Hinge, the business continues to deliver strong user growth and double-digit revenue growth year-over-year. We see clear opportunities ahead too. Even in core markets where we have operated the longest, Hinge has room to reach more people beyond urban metro markets and grow with older daters. We are targeting these opportunities deliberately with more relevant marketing. The early results are strong, as registration trends across all genders and age groups improved as we exited Q3, and we think Q4 U.S. new registrations will be up year-over-year. Hinge's 2027 product roadmap is the strongest we have had in the last several years.

The depth of thinking about intentioned daters, from what they need to what helps them get out on great dates, is evident and gives me so much confidence in where Hinge is headed. At E&E, we put a more focused strategy in place, prioritizing a smaller set of brands and taking learnings from Tinder and Hinge to improve user outcomes. We are still early in this work, and it will take time to see the impact. At Match Group, we are approaching 2027 with a stronger foundation built through a lot of hard work and a clearer path to durable growth. With that, I will turn it to Steve.

Steve Bailey: Thanks, Spencer. We are happy with the Q3 results and with the momentum in the business as we close out the year and turn our focus to 2027. We expect to finish the year slightly above the midpoint of our full-year revenue guidance range and meaningfully exceed the full-year Adjusted EBITDA margin target we set back in February. We also expect to exceed the high end of our free cash flow guidance set back in February, and we remain committed to deploying 100% of free cash flow towards buybacks, dividends, and net settling of employee equity awards over time, recognizing that the pace of capital return may vary from quarter-to-quarter.

Year-to-date, we have generated $832 million in free cash flow and deployed $591 million towards buybacks, dividends, and net settling of employee equity awards. We have reduced our diluted shares outstanding by 4% year-over-year through October, and by 10% since January of 2025. Here is how we are thinking about the financial performance and expectations at each of our business units. At Tinder, we expect to achieve our goal of improving year-over-year MAU and payer trends throughout the year, and we expect further improvement in both of these metrics, as well as an improvement in direct revenue trends in Q4. That is meaningful progress towards returning Tinder to sustainable growth.

As we said last quarter, we continue to expect Tinder's full year 2026 direct revenue performance to be better than we expected in February, declining at low single-digit rates year-over-year as a result of both smaller-than-expected impact from user experience tests and stronger underlying trends. As we begin to shift our focus to 2027, while there is still more work to do, we are feeling great about the momentum, and we are confident we can deliver full year 2027 Tinder direct revenue year-over-year growth, along with year-over-year payer growth by Q4, and flat MAU year-over-year by the end of Q4.

At Hinge, performance continues to be strong, and we expect to be within the 2026 full year guidance range we provided in February. Our expectation for $1 billion in full year revenue in 2027 has not changed. E&E continues to face headwinds from Azar's app redesign, necessitated by the App Store ban earlier this year, and weakness at other E&E brands, but we expect the strategy changes Spencer just outlined to slow revenue declines over time, with the goal of returning to growth. This will take time, and we expect E&E year-over-year revenue declines to only modestly improve in 2027 compared to 2026.

Turning to Match Group profitability, we have done a good job this year executing on the Tinder turnaround while staying financially disciplined. We intend to take that same approach in 2027 as we balance making the right investments in our business to maximize long-term shareholder value with delivering near-term Adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow, which we are giving back to shareholders through buybacks and the dividend. We will give detailed Adjusted EBITDA guidance and a full year margin target on the call in February, but here is how we are thinking about 2027 profitability sitting here today. First, we expect to remain very disciplined on headcount and OpEx, including AI costs.

Second, we now expect IAP fees to be a one-point margin headwind in 2027 based on current App Store policies and expiration of our Google partnership agreement, which I will talk more about in a minute. Third, we are still evaluating the appropriate level and allocation of marketing spend across the portfolio using our PRISM framework. As a reminder, PRISM is our standardized marketing measurement framework that we recently introduced at Match Group. It gives us a consistent, rigorous, quantitative assessment of marketing effectiveness that we use to inform investment decisions across the company. 2027 will be the first time we are incorporating it into our annual planning process.

Now let me give you a little more color on IAP fees. First, an update on Apple. In the U.S., we continue to pay 0% in IAP fees on alternative payments on iOS, and we do not expect changes to this fee structure until there is a decision in the Epic Games v. Apple case. In the E.U., Apple actually raised fees on in-app purchases effective October 1st, and the fees we pay increased from the low 20% to 26%. At the same time, Apple will begin allowing alternative payments, which we plan to test, but there are a number of restrictions, and the economics are far less favorable than they are in the U.S.

We expect the increased in-app purchase fees to cost us an additional $20 million in 2027. Now on Google. In 2024, we entered into a partnership arrangement with Google that provided value exchange across our broad relationship that has effectively offset the additional fees we incurred when we adopted Google's billing options at that time. As we previously disclosed at the announcement of that deal and in subsequent filings, that partnership is set to expire in the first quarter of 2027, and we expect Play Store fees to meaningfully increase beginning in Q2 of next year.

Our expectation when we entered into the agreement was that legal and regulatory pressure would reduce Google's in-app purchase fees by the time our agreement ended. However, Google's new global fee structure announced in March provides little benefit to us. Taking into account both the Apple changes and the Google partnership agreement expiration, and making no assumptions on future fee changes, we expect IAP fees to result in a one-point headwind to Adjusted EBITDA margin in 2027. While we are looking for ways to mitigate the impact, we also need to ensure we are making the right investments in the business to drive long-term shareholder value.

We will make that determination as part of our annual planning process, and we will give you more details on 2027 revenue and margin expectations next quarter. With that, let us open it up to Q&A.

Operator: We will now begin the question and answer session. To ask a question, you may press star, then one on your telephone keypad. If you are using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. To withdraw your question, please press star, then two. At this time, we will pause momentarily to assemble our roster. The first question comes from Robert Coolbrith with Evercore ISI. Please go ahead.

Robert Coolbrith: Great. Thank you for the opportunity to ask a question. Just wondering if you could maybe talk us through the path to positive DAU that you had in the quarter, or had in September. Maybe if you could sort of disaggregate that across retention improvement, or if there's just been a case of stacking those retention gains that you've had in successful quarters across more cohorts, and then any early indications of improving levels of consideration or reconsideration. Thanks.

Spencer Rascoff: Yeah. Thanks, Robert, and thanks for your recent research note. Look, it was a big milestone this quarter. Turning DAU positive in September year-over-year for the first time in three and a half years felt great. There were a lot of high fives and just excitement around achieving that milestone. Just a couple weeks later, at the end of October, U.S. DAU turning positive year-over-year was also just felt great. Those are the DAU trends. MAU improving from -10% to -5.5% over the last few quarters also speaks to the quality of the improvements in the product, and also improvements in MAU, similar improvements in MAU across our top five revenue markets.

The reason why I'm confident about the sustainability of the turnaround is how broad-based the improvements have been. So really, any way you cut it, by age, by gender, by geography, we're seeing improvements across really every which way you look at it. So for example, looking at it by gender, our female MAU is improving at an even faster rate than male MAU in every region and every age group. Female MAU declines narrowed by eight points year-over-year and two points quarter-over-quarter. So this is not a turnaround that's just focused on male users. Quite the contrary, it's actually, we're improving among female users even more quickly.

Looking at it by age, again, this is not a turnaround focused on just adding easier to acquire older users. Our under 30 MAU trends have improved even more than our over 30 MAU trends, and we're improving across every single age group. So that's the exciting news about the MAU turnaround. I think kind of the question behind your question perhaps is, why is DAU growing faster than MAU? The answer to that is, we have made so many product improvements that help the existing experience basically improve our users' current experience, but we still have more work to do to drive reconsideration. That is where the Better with Friends social roadmap comes into play.

We had a hit in Double Date. We layered on another hit with Events. We are in the process of building a third hit with Groups. When you take those three things together and you do brand studies and ask users about their perception of Tinder, you start to see really good promising results about people changing their perception of what Tinder is. So we still have work to do. It is definitely too soon to declare victory, but I really am proud of and impressed by where we are at today. Steve, anything to add or is that

Steve Bailey: No, I think you covered it.

Spencer Rascoff: Okay. Next question, please.

Operator: The next question is from Shweta Khajuria with Wolfe Research. Please go ahead.

Shweta Khajuria: Okay. Thank you for taking my questions. Spencer, could I please ask a follow-up to what you were just talking about in terms of the delta between DAU growth and MAU growth? There is this idea of perception and bringing people back into the ecosystem, and that is why the delta. So how long do you think it takes for that lag to narrow? In other words, for that perception to change, bringing those people back, and turning around MAU growth? Then the second question I have is around next year, Steve, you spoke about Tinder expectations.

To the degree that you can speak to other segments, Hinge, E&E, that would be very helpful, or just at a platform level, the puts and takes for both revenue and EBITDA. Understood, you are not guiding just yet in terms of EBITDA. Where would the levers be coming from to offset the headwind, and how should we be thinking about overall top line growth? Thanks a lot.

Steve Bailey: Yeah. We will take this in a couple pieces. Let me talk a little bit more about the Tinder sort of metrics improvements, and Spencer, jump in as you wish. The way to think about DAU outpacing MAU, here is kind of where things stand. Of course, we are very excited that DAU crossed over to positive growth. We are just as excited about MAU improving. So we got about one point improvement on MAU from Q2 to Q3, with MAU down 6%, which is better than the 7% it was down the quarter before. We also saw an improvement in payers, which we are very excited about. So the payers were down -5% in Q2.

They were down -4% in Q3. So progress there as well. Revenue, we like to look at it FX neutral, was down 2%. That was the same as Q2. I will just stress that these metrics are not going to move completely in lockstep every quarter, but if you take a step back and look at the revenue FX neutral trends, you have got a diagram in the prepared release, you can see progress over the last few quarters, from down 5% in Q4 last year to down 2% now. What I think is also encouraging is, we expect all those metrics to improve in Q4.

We expect payers to get better in Q4, we expect MAU to get better in Q4, and we expect that FX neutral direct revenue to get better as well. We are starting to see it flow through more than just DAU, but to these other core metrics as well. Did you want to add anything to that, Spencer?

Steve Bailey: Let us talk about 2027 a bit. We are not going to give, as you sort of alluded to, full year revenue guidance or EBITDA guidance until February, which is our normal course. I tried to give some color on how we were thinking about things. The only things I would add is, if we break it down, you look at Tinder, we are feeling really good, right. We are making progress. I just told you we expect further progress in Q4, and we are really setting ourselves up well to meet the goals I laid out in terms of payers, revenue, and MAU improvement next year. Could it be sooner? Maybe.

It is hard to pinpoint exactly, but I think we are on a really good trajectory at Tinder. When you look at Hinge, that achieving the $1 billion in revenue, which we still feel very good about, I think about it this way. Revenue growth was about 19% in Q3. We expect it to be about the same, maybe a little bit better in Q4, so think of 19%-19.5%. We have got to keep the growth rate at about that same level next year, and if we do that, we will hit the $1 billion. So, we think we have got the right roadmap and strategy in place to do it.

That is going to come from improving core trends and expansion. We talked about expanding into Japan in the prepared remarks too, and so I am feeling good about the trajectory there too. E&E, what we said was modest improvement from the declines we are seeing this year. That is really in recognition of, Spencer talked about putting the right strategy in place, but it is going to take some time to get that business back to growth. We think only modest improvement, but still negative at E&E next year. In terms of profitability, the way I would think about it is, we have got the one point IAP fee headwind.

We said we would be really controlled in terms of headcount and AI costs. The really big consideration is really around marketing spend. What is the right level of marketing spend, particularly at Tinder and Hinge in 2027, to maximize long-term returns and shareholder value. We need to balance that against hitting short-term margin targets, and that is what we will do, we will think very hard about. We will do it in a very quantitative way through the PRISM framework, and we will give you a lot more details on all that in February.

Spencer Rascoff: Next question, please, operator.

Operator: The next question is from Jason Helfstein with Oppenheimer. Please go ahead.

Jason Helfstein: Thanks. Just some more color on the givebacks. I think it sounds like the full year givebacks for Tinder are going to come in below expectations. Why have they not been necessary this year relative to your plan, and any more color there? Thanks.

Spencer Rascoff: Yeah. Hi, Jason. Thanks for the question. We've been fortunate to discover that when we launch improvements to the user experience, the accompanying MAU retention mitigates revenue loss. For example, we changed our recommendation algorithms to maximize user outcomes, and we nervously wondered if it would hurt revenue, and what we found was that the benefits of improving user retention outweighed the detriment of prioritizing user outcomes over revenue. That might not always be the case, but that's what we mostly saw in 2026.

Steve Bailey: Yeah, let me just add a finer point to that too. That's all exactly right, and what it means financially is that we thought at the beginning of the year, we would need $60 million in user givebacks in 2026. What we're now saying is that we only ended up using $25 million. If you do the math, that's about 2 points of revenue at Tinder, and that's what's driving about 2 points of that improvement versus expectations we had set back in February. There's about another point of improvement in there in terms of what we think we'll actually finish the year at for Tinder full year revenue relative to what we said in February.

That other point is improving trends, so I want to be really clear about that. Really what we're seeing at Tinder is two things, the need for less user givebacks and also improving trends, so that sets us up really well for continued improvement in 2027.

Operator: The next question is from Bryan Smilek with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Bryan Smilek: Great. Thanks for taking the question. Spencer, as you enter Tinder's resurgence phase, can you just help us think about the allocation of marketing spend by channel to reignite the consideration set? I think in the prepared remarks, you had mentioned Gen Z marketing around creator and social content and event partners, so just curious anything that you can share on the LTV curves of those channels. Thank you.

Spencer Rascoff: Sure. Thanks, Bryan. We made a lot of changes to how we allocate and how we invest our marketing in 2026. Firstly, we shifted a lot of our spend towards down-funnel user acquisition instead of up-funnel brand building. Secondly, we pointed much more of our marketing spend towards actual features rather than high-level positioning about Tinder or the category, and we saw both of those changes drive really improved results in 2026. The second one, I think, is particularly important and reminds us how product and marketing work hand in hand.

For example, when we market on Instagram that Tinder has Events in your city, and we look at the cost per registration or cost per reactivation for those types of marketing creatives and compare it with a year or two ago when we were buying the same channel but promoting, "Use Tinder because Tinder is a dating app," it is really night and day in terms of the lift that we get, and in most cases, the efficacy of how far the dollar goes when we are focusing on product innovation rather than not.

As Steve alluded to, we also now have a framework where, for really the first time ever going into an annual planning process, we have a cross-brand rubric and analytics framework to decide what the right marketing spend and right marketing allocation should be between business units and brands within business units. We are deep in the midst of that right now as we finalize our 2027 plans.

We do not have any more detail to report, but we are just in a much smarter place here as we speak to you in fall of 2026 than we were in fall of 2025, coming off the heels of a really effective 2026 for marketing and also the development of these new frameworks to assess marketing efficacy. Operator, next question, please.

Operator: The next question is from Nathan Feather with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Nathan Feather: Hey, everyone. Thanks for the question. I guess, as you think about DAUs turning positive, the focus on MAUs, what are kind of the one to two key leading factors to returning to flat MAU growth from here? How do you think about the main levers you can pull to really drive that reconsideration of the brand as you continue to push the products out?

Spencer Rascoff: Yeah. Thanks, Nathan. The biggest lever is convincing people who are not already on Tinder or who maybe used Tinder two, four, five, 10 years ago to give it another shot. This Better with Friends roadmap is the best idea that we have to execute on that. As I said, Double Date is a winner. We have delivered 30 million matches on Double Date so far, which just speaks to the scale and product market fit that Double Date has. We just launched Groups in the U.S. and a couple weeks earlier in a couple other countries.

Just to give you some insight into Groups, women are twice as likely to like a group profile as they are to like a single male profile. Again, that speaks to the product market fit that we think Groups will have within our product. 15% of our users in Norway, age 18 to 22, are already in a group. The reason I mention Norway is that was the first country that we launched in, so it has been up for a couple extra weeks. We think Groups has the potential to be another hit and to change the way people perceive Tinder. Then finally, Events, which we have been very vocal about the potential that we think Events has.

Events has absolutely started to change perception of Tinder. When we look at our measures of brand health, questions that we ask users, like, "Does Tinder have people that you want to meet on it? Is Tinder an app with your kind of people? Is Tinder just for hookups or for things more than that?" All those measures of brand health have improved over the summer and into the fall as we have rolled out Events into more and more markets. I am happy to talk more about Events if there are other questions about it.

But those are the types of initiatives that we are focused on in order to drive reconsideration, which is what will take us these last couple points from -5.5% MAU to eventual MAU growth. Next question, please.

Operator: The next question is from James Heaney with Jefferies. Please go ahead.

James Heaney: Great. Thank you. You mentioned in the letter an increased focus on Tinder revenue initiatives in 2027. Curious what kinds of options you'd be looking to explore and how you think you can improve monetization without disrupting the user engagement momentum that you have. Thank you.

Spencer Rascoff: Yeah. Thanks. Good question. When I took over Tinder, I started by focusing on the user experience. We had this theory, which has proven to be true, that if you improve the user experience, then the audience metrics will improve, and then other good things will flow from that. We moved very quickly. We changed a lot of the user experience, and today, Tinder works better than it did before. We're now turning our attention towards revenue, and we're really looking at everything. We understand what we have currently and what we can learn from other brands, and we're approaching it from pretty much a blank slate in terms of a starting point.

It's a bit early to say where that will go, but I can assure you we're bringing the same level of focus, energy, vigor, urgency, innovation to monetization in 2027 that we brought to the user experience in 2026. We have a lot of ideas that we're not ready to talk about yet, but I'm optimistic that 2027 will be a year of a lot of monetization innovation. Next question, please.

Operator: The next question is from Youssef Squali with Truist Securities. Please go ahead.

Youssef Squali: Great. Thank you so much. Maybe a quick question for Steve. Can you just quantify the marketing spend that was pushed into Q4 for Q3, the reasons for it, and would you have been able to grow a little faster had you actually met that marketing spend in that quarter? Thanks.

Steve Bailey: Yeah. In terms of quantity, we pushed about $8 million or so in marketing spend from Q3 to Q4. I think we came in about $12 million better than we expected, but $8 million of that was marketing spend. It's a couple reasons. One is just timing of campaigns, and two is, we're going to stay financially disciplined, right? In any given quarter, if we're not seeing the returns that we expect on marketing spend, we're not going to go spend those dollars just to fill the budget, right? I like to see us underspend for those reasons because it means we can deploy them in a different quarter at higher ROI. It's really a combination of those two things.

How much revenue we would have generated had we not done that's a little bit of a hypothetical that I'm not going to do at the moment. But, what I would say is, and I'll repeat it again, which I think is an important fact, we're going out and saying we expect MAU, payers, and revenue, direct revenue. While direct revenue didn't improve in Q3, we do expect it to improve in Q4 from a year-over-year growth perspective relative to Q3. So, with the marketing spend in Q4 and everything else we have going, we expect to see improvement across all those metrics next quarter.

Operator: The next question is from Benjamin Black with Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.

Benjamin Black: Great. Thanks for taking my question. The recommendation system looks to be at least a big part of the foundation of Tinder's turnaround. How much better can matching outcomes become as the system moves towards more real-time personalization? What advantages does the Tinder scale really have and the data that you guys have? How much of an advantage is that for you guys? Secondly, I would be interested in hearing the learnings from Missed Connections. I think in the letter you mentioned a four times improvement in likes from women, and it seems a bit of a game-changer to me. What are some of the hurdles to broadening out in Missed Connections? Thank you.

Spencer Rascoff: Yeah. Thanks, Benjamin. Queue Unification and our Recs improvements have been really critical to our improving business results in 2026. We just rolled out Queue Unification to other user types. I think we just rolled it out to women seeking men and women seeking anyone or other different LGBTQ audiences, but we still have more to go. Real-time Recs, we have said we intend to launch by the end of the year. We are very confident in the potential that will bring, but it is also unproven. I think that event that we did, the CEO Connection event, where I spoke with Vinay and Mark, our CTO and Head of Product at Tinder, about Recs.

I think Vinay said something like he thinks it is the second or third inning, or maybe he said the third or fourth inning maybe, in terms of Recs, to try to size the amount of potential improvements that still lay ahead. I think that is probably about right. Already huge improvements, but more to come. On Missed Connections, this is a feature that we are testing in Canada right now. If you have location services turned on, then once a week, we give you specific drops that say, "Here is somebody that you have crossed paths with in the week in a given neighborhood or in a given coffee shop," et cetera. Users love it.

The serendipity and kind of excitement is really meaningful, especially for Gen Z users. The nostalgia, the sense of a meet-cute, which is what our users are really looking for, and the digital bridge between an app and an IRL experience is really powerful. We are now working to improve it. We will be assessing when and whether to roll it out more broadly. There is still a lot of work to do to improve the product, but so far, so good in what we have launched so far. Operator, next question, please.

Operator: The next question comes from Alec Brondolo with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.

Alec Brondolo: Yeah. Hey, thanks so much. Maybe two from me. First, how did you choose the new focus brands for E&E, and does refocusing on a smaller number of brands create an incremental headwind to that business beyond Azar in 2027? Secondly, on Hinge, the new subscriptions you are launching in the fourth quarter, giving users more choice and control, is there any incremental detail you could provide around the value proposition? What is the opportunity here on paid conversion? Thanks.

Spencer Rascoff: Yeah, I will take the E&E question, and Steve, you can answer the Hinge question. So, in deciding which brands to prioritize with E&E, we looked at the white space that the different brands are going after and also the size, and in order to prioritize. So, for example, Upward and BLK and HER all are going after white space in their respective user segments, where we think there is a real right to win, a reason to exist, a category white space that is not fully won by a Hinge or a Match or a Tinder or any standalone competitor.

Brands like Match, which are more general population, we think there's a reason for them to exist in the 50-plus age segment, and just the brand awareness and brand power of the term Match, and just the size and scale of that really represents something that is worthy of prioritization. The other non-focused brands, like an OkCupid, like a Plenty Of Fish, like a Salams, these are brands that are still being worked on, but only synergistically across the portfolio. For example, we have a dedicated team that is improving profile creation, and a dedicated team that is improving photo selection, and a team that's building chat, and a team that's building recommendations algorithm.

When each of those teams launch a feature or set of features, it goes out across the whole portfolio. Something like OkCupid is not left to its own devices. It's still being improved upon by these shared teams that are building E&E-wide technologies. That's how we prioritize the different brands. Steve, you want to take the Hinge question?

Steve Bailey: Yeah. I think, look, we're pretty excited about the lower price subscription tier in test right now. It's designed for women in particular, but also for price-sensitive users. Remember that Hinge is one of the highest priced products we have. The revenue per payer, for example, at Hinge is almost twice that of Tinder, around $30. It also has one of the lower payer penetrations. Its payer penetration is only slightly more than half that of Tinder. So, we think it makes sense to offer a lower priced-offering in what is otherwise a higher-priced product to get more payer conversion from more price-sensitive users.

In terms of what it includes, think of it I'm not going to get into every specific feature, but the broad brushstrokes are additional filters and custom location boundaries, features that women find valuable. What we've seen in tests is it has improved conversion for both men and women, but women's conversion has been up more than men. The other interesting thing here is that, remember, Hinge's gender balance between men and women is far better than most other apps. Women pay at far lower rates. That's true for Hinge, and that's true for everybody.

So, if we can get this feature right and a feature set that really resonates with women, that will be really potentially powerful from a monetization perspective for Hinge in particular, with a large women user base and really good gender balance. So we're going to keep testing and tweaking, but the early reads are good, and then we expect to roll it out more in Q4, so stay tuned. Next question.

Operator: The next question is from Jamesmichael Sherman-Lewis with Citi. Please go ahead.

Jamesmichael Sherman-Lewis: Good afternoon. Thank you for taking my questions. Two here, please. First, Tinder payer penetration increased sequentially and year-over-year, and MAUs are still declining faster than payers. How much additional payer conversion runway remains as we work to inflect back to MAU growth, and how do you think about the balance of conversion gains versus audience growth into 2027? Then as a quick follow-up, Hinge's opportunity in core markets, I think you noted an uptick in U.S. marketing contributing to the improving registration trends. Could you talk a little bit about the opportunity to drive MAU growth and reconsideration in mature Hinge geographies? Thank you.

Steve Bailey: Yeah, on the Tinder payer penetration, you are right. Payer penetration was up again. That is something we have consistently seen, is that the improvement in MAU is flowing through to improvement in payers, which is great. In terms of how much more room to go, while payer penetration at Tinder is higher than Hinge, which I just mentioned, it is still relatively low. It is in the low 20%. So, we are always looking to optimize not only for the payer experience, but the free experience too. But in terms of the ability to drive further incremental payer conversion, I think there is lots of room.

I think as we look ahead, what we are doing is we are not optimizing around short-term revenue growth. We are really taking a look, Spencer got into this earlier, but finding ways to add value to the experience, both for free and paid users. If we can add value, then I see no reason why we cannot increase monetization and payer conversion at Tinder going forward.

Spencer Rascoff: I will take the Hinge MAU and TAM question. In the U.S., Hinge is most highly penetrated on the coasts and in the 20 to 30 age group. If you look at smaller cities outside of the coasts and age 30 to 40, there is ample room for Hinge to grow. We think at least another one million monthly active users in the U.S. as we focus more on those other user segments and geographies. We have already started implementing that playbook with different marketing tactics and messages in order to focus on those secondary cities and slightly older age users.

We think that playbook also is extendable to other core markets outside the U.S., like the U.K., Australia, and Canada. Operator, next question, please.

Operator: The next question is from Eric Sheridan with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Eric Sheridan: Thanks so much for taking the question. My first one would be following up on, I think Benjamin Black asked earlier about the broader AI strategy. The flip side of that coin would be, how are you thinking about managing token costs or input costs within your broader cost structure as you continue to move from testing to scaling some of your AI initiatives? That would be one. In the shareholder letter, you also talked about finding ways to drive tech platform efficiencies through elements of shared technology platforms or cross-pollinating.

The second part would be, how should we be thinking about some of the efficiency dynamics that could be gained through some of those initiatives as we move out of 2026 and into 2027? Thanks so much.

Steve Bailey: Yeah, let me take the AI token costs. I think we have done a really good job here. The costs are definitely going up. Let me give you some more details around how we are managing it. We started probably with a budget this year of about $5 million for AI cost, but we had pretty low usage. We basically had engineers using AI and nobody else, and it was spotty at that. Early in the year, May timeframe, we really wanted to push AI adoption and become a truly AI-native company. We thought it was important for the overall long-term success of the business.

We gave all our employees tools like Claude, tools like OpenAI, enterprise search tools like Glean, and gave them the training, gave them the tokens to go use these tools, and our costs probably went from $5 million to about $10 million, a little more than $10 million. The way we It was unplanned doubling of costs, but we think worthwhile, and we are getting really good efficiency gains out of it. The way we offset those costs was by controlling headcount. Not reducing the employee base, but hiring less, slowing headcount growth, and saying, "Let's do more with less through the use of AI," and that has been really effective.

Right now, I would say we are maturing as a company in terms of AI token usage, and we are really in that sort of efficiency phase. We have an AI gateway that controls what models we are defaulting to and what models engineers can use. We are doing all sorts of things like making the most expensive models only available by request. We have speed bumps or soft caps. Engineers get about $1,000 a month, and non-engineers get about $250. Once you hit that cap, that does not mean you can stop. It means you have to go to your manager, and say, "Look at the work I am producing," and if it makes sense, you can keep going.

We have given all the managers really great visualization into the spend within their departments, basically real-time token spending, and I think we have done an incredible job as a company overall in this regard. We do expect costs to go up a little again next year, but the hope is, through these efficiency gains, we are now starting to look at open-weight models, we will be able to keep them under control. In terms of in the product and in the features themselves, and feel free to jump in, Spencer, there are more features that are using AI tokens and AI costs, and you want to cover how we are thinking about that?

Spencer Rascoff: Well, let me answer it from a shared tech platform standpoint and efficiencies across the company. I will give you four quick examples. We have integrated our trust and safety tooling so that features like Face Check are now built centrally across all brands. Another example of a shared service is Tinder's Events product, so the module tab two on Tinder where you can see who is going to an event and you can see the different types of events and this whole product roadmap around Events, now powers not just Tinder but also BLK, and likely in the future, other Match Group brands. Those are two examples of things that we are building centrally across multiple brands.

Then, two other potential examples that we're working towards is Tinder has built an AI prototyping tool where any employee at Tinder can enter a prompt to visualize a new feature to Tinder, and it will instantly build a prototype of it and also build code for that prototyped new feature. That's something that has really changed the software development life cycle at Tinder, made us more design-forward, just brought a higher pace of innovation, and that's something that we're looking to extend to some of our other brands, including E&E.

A fourth example is Tinder has a homegrown customer relationship management platform that manages all of Tinder's push notifications, text messages, and emails, and it's really best in class, better than what companies pay millions or tens of millions of dollars a year to SaaS providers for that type of technology, and we're considering extending that to some of our other brands. So, those are just a couple examples, Eric, of how we're building centralized technology and extending it across the whole company. Operator, next question, please.

Operator: The next question is from John Blackledge with TD Cowen. Please go ahead.

John Blackledge: Great. Thanks. For Hinge's newer markets outside of the U.S., is user growth and payer conversion following similar growth curves to Hinge's more mature markets? Then just another one on Hinge. On the RPP, should we expect that trend that we saw in 3Q to continue as you roll out the new lower-priced sub tier? Thank you.

Steve Bailey: Yeah. Let me start, and feel free to jump in, Spencer. On the MAU growth, it is an important point to make. Global MAU growth came in at around 12%. What we saw under the covers is actually core MAU improved a bit, which is great to see. Spencer talked a little bit about that. Growth in Europe slowed a little bit. Still phenomenally high growth, but to your point, there is a growth curve. As these countries scale, we expect their growth to slow over time. That is really what you saw in the headline number, was core getting a little bit better, Europe slowing down a bit, and us netting out to about 12% growth.

That is right around what we expected, puts us right in track, not only for MAU, but also for revenue for the full year 2026. We feel good about the way those curves are playing out. It is just what we expected. We are entering LATAM, that is growing faster, but still small. We have relaunched in India, where we have a pretty big MAU base today. What we are doing is we are laying the foundation for expansion into Japan in 2027.

I would not expect a lot of revenue from Japan in 2027, or users, but it is an important, first of all, it is one of our top, it is probably the top five largest markets from a TAM perspective, from a revenue perspective in the category. So an important one for Hinge to enter, and I think we will be, we think there is a nice white space for it between Pairs, which is a little bit more marriage-focused, and Tinder, which is more casual. All our research says it should do very well there, and I think it will be a growth driver for 2028 and beyond. Those are some of the Hinge growth curves.

What was the second part of the question?

Steve Bailey: What was your second question? Sorry.

John Blackledge: The RPP was down a little bit in 3Q.

John Blackledge: Just how confident you guys are about it going forward.

Steve Bailey: Yeah. Thanks for pointing that out. What you are seeing is we saw an acceleration in payers, and we saw RPP down a little bit year-over-year in Q3. That is price optimizations, a new model we rolled out at Hinge, that was playing the biggest effect. To a lesser effect is the new lower-priced tier. That could have a bigger effect down the road. Then you normally, sort of underneath all that, we naturally get some RPP pressure because the growth in these expansion markets is still so much higher than the core markets, and the RPP on average is lower there than in a market like the U.S.

I'd expect that to actually increase a bit in Q4 just because this pricing model was rolled out mid-Q3 and will be a full quarter in Q4. But it's generating net positive revenue. It's another lever for offering a paid experience to more price-sensitive users. Third, I think this is overlooked sometimes, payers help the ecosystem too. So there's indirect benefits of higher paid conversion. Payers retain longer, they respond to likes better, they are more likely to buy ALC features.

So there's a lot of reasons why having a little bit higher payer penetration at Hinge still won't be even close to the levels of Tinder, makes a lot of sense, but that's what's causing a little noise in those metrics. I'd expect that to continue in Q4.

Spencer Rascoff: Operator, next question, please.

Operator: The last question will be from Andrew Marok with Raymond James. Please go ahead.

Andrew Marok: Hi, thanks for taking my question. Maybe one more on Hinge and the international business. You called out in the shareholder letter, and I think you answered a bit of this in the last question about the momentum in Europe and the newly launched LATAM markets. I guess, what kind of common threads are you seeing between these disparate geos? On Japan specifically, what is kind of giving you the confidence that there is a space in the market which has kind of been a tricky market for everyone in the past? Thanks.

Spencer Rascoff: Yeah, thanks, Andrew. What we're seeing as the common thread in the different markets is that Hinge's slow and steady approach of customizing the product, customizing the marketing for the individual geography is working. For example, in India, having a slightly different set of features like screenshot banning, wait list for men, and a couple other unique trust and safety features like ID verification and others are particularly useful. We're taking a deliberate approach to Japan, learning from, gosh, probably 10 years of Pairs' success in the matrimony space.

We've done a huge amount of original research in Japan to identify that there is white space between the matrimony apps and the more casual apps like Tinder, so we think there's an opportunity for Hinge to succeed without cannibalizing Pairs and Tinder. We're going to customize the Hinge product and marketing in order to achieve product market fit there, just as we have in Brazil and Mexico and India over the last year or so. I think, operator, are there any other questions or is that the last question?

Operator: That was the last question, sir.

Spencer Rascoff: Okay. All right. I will just wrap up here. As a reminder for anyone who joined late, we posted the full prepared remarks to the investor relations website for you to read through, so you can find the full script there. Hopefully, you liked this new, more efficient approach. I just want to close by taking stock of my first seven quarters as CEO here. When I joined 21 months ago, Tinder users and revenue were declining, and there was skepticism that Tinder could be saved at all. Today, we have put points on the board and mostly put that question to rest.

Several quarters of improving user trends at Tinder, top to bottom, from Sparks to Spark coverage to DAU to MAU, and improvement in payers and revenue when adjusting for FX. We have demonstrated that this turnaround is real and sustainable. We also took Hinge from $150 million-ish in quarterly revenue back in Q1 2025 when I started to over $220 million in quarterly revenue in Q2 of 2026. We purchased HER. We purchased about half of Sniffies. We significantly improved employee engagement. We drove massive productivity improvements from AI. We got a lot done in a pretty short period of time.

Meanwhile, we bought back $1.2 billion of stock and paid $369 million in dividends and reduced diluted share count by 10% year-over-year as of yesterday. I am very proud of what we have accomplished in these last 21 months, and I am even more optimistic about where we will be 21 months from now. We will talk to you in early February at Q4 earnings, and I hope to see many of you at our second Tinder Sparks event on February 23rd in New York. Until then, thanks, everybody. Bye-bye.

#3111. Upwork (UPWK) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

AI initiatives and higher-value clients drive $185.6M revenue amid marketplace pressures.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Upwork Inc. (UPWK +6.23%) reported third-quarter results that reflected a strategic shift toward high-value clients and enterprise solutions through its Lifted platform. Management highlighted the acquisition of global employer of record provider WorkMotion to accelerate international expansion and contingent employment solutions. The company also introduced AI-driven initiatives, including the public beta of Upwork Now and the expansion of its Model Context Protocol server to integrate talent directly into AI workflows. Financial guidance for the fourth quarter assumes business mix shifts and the integration of new acquisitions as the platform navigates evolving digital acquisition channels.

Operator: Thank you for standing by, and welcome to Upwork's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Currently, all participants are in a listen-only mode. Unless otherwise noted, reported figures are rounded, and comparisons of the third quarter of 2026 are to the third quarter of 2025. With that, I will now turn the call over to Hayden.

Hayden Brown: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Upwork's third quarter 2026 earnings call. In the third quarter, Upwork executed against our plan as our platform continued its rotation toward higher value, more complex work, and larger clients. We generated $914 million in GSV and $186 million in revenue, both above the high end of our guidance range. Adjusted EBITDA reached $63.8 million, exceeding the high end of our guidance. We have built a strong, durable profitability engine, which will be critical to our ongoing value creation in 2027 and beyond. As we navigate through the evolution of work on our platform, our strategic growth pillars across enterprise, SMB, and AI continue to gain momentum.

Let's walk through our performance across each of these core growth pillars, starting with enterprise. Since June, we have accelerated the pace of customer migrations from legacy Upwork Enterprise onto the Lifted platform. This transition is key to unlocking deeper expansion across our existing client portfolio, while new customer demand also continues to build. In Q3 alone, we signed three net new enterprise logos across healthcare, retail, and tech, while expanding our entire pipeline. We're seeing strong customer uptake of Lifted's direct employment EOR offering in the U.S. and Canada, and offering a global solution for employment in every market has always been our goal.

With that end, today we announced the acquisition of WorkMotion, a global employer of record provider. This dramatically accelerates our roadmap of delivering comprehensive contingent employment solutions to our customers on a global scale. Lifted's growth strategy was already delivering results, and adding WorkMotion to the portfolio allows us to further improve win rates and lower Lifted's cost to serve. Inclusive of WorkMotion, we now expect Lifted GSV to exceed 30% year-over-year growth in 2026, setting the stage for sustained strong momentum into 2027 and beyond. Turning to SMB, our focus on quality over quantity continues to yield excellent results.

The rapid adoption of Business Plus is driving higher spend among new and existing clients, and it's strongly attracting and converting new clients specifically. 40% of active Business Plus clients in Q3 had their first Upwork spend using this product. Business Plus is entering its second full year in market, and in Q3, it delivered 120% year-over-year revenue growth. It continues to perform well ahead of plan, with GSV increasing 132% year-over-year. Business Plus now accounts for 8% of total GSV, exceeding the 5% goal we set late last year. GSV per active client reached another record high of $5,418, up 8% year-over-year.

This marks our ninth consecutive quarter of sequential growth on this metric, driven by increased engagement with existing clients and the ongoing shift toward higher value work. We also saw contracts of $100,000 or more increase 7% year-over-year in Q3. As a result, GSV per contract in Q3 was our highest ever, growing 9% year-over-year. On the AI front, GSV from AI-skilled talent increased 55% to $112 million in the third quarter. As clients put AI to work, they're increasingly turning to Upwork for the expertise to implement it, integrate it into their operations, and get more value from AI. AI is also changing how customers find us.

As we discussed last quarter, traditional search is being disrupted as more people turn to AI assistants for answers, recommendations, and actions. We have been adapting our acquisition strategies to these changes, investing in AI-driven discovery and new channels of client demand. We also see an opportunity that goes beyond search. A new model of collaboration between people and AI is taking shape. AI is doing more, but human expertise continues to be important. Productive collaboration between people and AI is the future of work, and we're building Upwork to power it at scale. We're doing this through both our MCP server, which we launched in August, and Upwork Now, which we announced in public beta today.

Our MCP server is already gaining meaningful traction by opening up a variety of new use cases. AI agents can now tap into Upwork's marketplace directly to take actions like drafting a job post or searching for talent. Clients can do the same from inside any AI tool, like Claude or ChatGPT. Talent can submit proposals, work, or messages to their Upwork clients without leaving the AI tools they love. MCP implementations are an important new source of demand. GSV from work started through our MCP server grew more than 150% month-over-month in October. Upwork Now adds real-time access to human expertise for any AI agent or client.

Upwork Now connects them with Upwork freelancers who are currently online and ready to start work immediately. Customers can now access the human expert they need the moment they need them within Upwork or from within their own AI tools. In early testing and release, customer feedback has been enthusiastic about the ease, speed, and value of our MCP and Upwork Now. Upwork is powering a new way of bringing human expertise together with AI-powered work. We're capitalizing on our tremendous assets of talent, technology, and trust to become essential infrastructure, enabling human and AI collaboration.

Today, we also announced that Erica Gessert will step down as CFO on January 1st and remain with the company in an advisory role for several months. Erica has been an exceptional business partner and financial leader for Upwork, and the board and I are deeply grateful for her contributions. She helped us deliver record revenue and profitability, expand margins, strengthen cash generation, and manage our capital allocation strategy. She also developed an exceptional finance team, which is why Peter Sanborn, currently our Chief Business Officer, will be Upwork's next CFO. Since joining Upwork in 2024, Peter has helped shape our strategy and identify new opportunities for growth.

He has also led our corporate development, partnership, and frontier AI product efforts, including bringing Upwork into tools like ChatGPT and Claude so businesses can connect with our talent directly where they're already working. During Erica's leave earlier this year, Peter worked closely with me and our finance organization as we managed a challenging demand environment while maintaining our focus on profitability and growth investment. That experience gave the board and me even greater confidence in his ability to take on this role. Please join me in congratulating Peter and thanking Erica on what is now her last earnings call for all that she has done for Upwork. With that, I'll turn it over to Erica.

Erica Gessert: Thanks, Hayden, and hello, everyone. Before diving into the financial results, I want to say how professionally and personally rewarding it has been to serve as Upwork CFO. I have been reflecting on what we have accomplished these past few years, and I am incredibly proud of what we have built. In particular, the levers with monetization strategies and Business Plus, as well as the cost optimization muscle that we have built into this business, create tremendous stability and optionality for revenue and for margins. This is a great business with very strong future prospects. I am also especially grateful for the opportunity to have worked with this talented team.

To my colleagues across Upwork, and particularly to our finance and business development organizations, thank you for your passion, your dedication, and teamwork. I also want to sincerely thank Hayden and the board for your trust and partnership. I am excited to pass the mantle to Peter, who is an incredible leader, and I look forward to supporting a smooth transition to him and to watching Upwork achieve even greater success in the future. With that, let's turn to our financial results. In the third quarter, Upwork executed well as we managed through our ongoing platform transformation. We delivered top-line results above the high end of our guidance range and continue to operate with discipline.

At Upwork, we have proven that we can produce strong, highly profitable business results in a wide range of operating environments, and you will see us continue to do this as we move forward. Active client count in the quarter was 717,000, reflecting our strategy to focus on acquiring and serving higher-value customers with more complex work. Our MCP server is opening up new demand channels for us by bringing Upwork into AI tools. While still early, traffic is growing rapidly, with millions of server calls from clients and talent occurring during the quarter. Notably, we saw Connects usage through the MCP server grow rapidly, reaching a more than $3 million annual revenue run rate during the quarter.

This is an important proof point that reflects the durability of our monetization model as we explore new channels for acquisition and engagement with customers. Revenue for Q3 was $186 million. Our marketplace take rate expanded to 20.0%, up 110 basis points year-over-year, driven by the ongoing adoption of our higher-margin products. Ads and monetization streams represent a key strategic capability that produce incremental revenue streams, even in a softer GSV environment. Our Connects revenue continues to grow, and Freelancer Plus subscription revenue was up 25% year-over-year. Non-GAAP operating expenses were $84 million, or 45% of revenue, compared to 50% of revenue in the third quarter of 2025.

Adjusted EBITDA was $63.8 million, representing an Adjusted EBITDA margin of 34.4%, driven by our disciplined execution and operational efficiencies. While there was some timing of expenses between Q3 and Q4, our active cost management and disciplined operational focus continue to deliver strong results and will benefit us into 2027 and beyond. We generated robust free cash flow in Q3 of $53.9 million, with free cash flow to Adjusted EBITDA conversion of 84%, at the high end of our long-term average of 80%-85%. Turning to our guidance for the fourth quarter and full year 2026. For the full year 2026, we now expect revenue in the range of $742 million-$750 million.

This guidance includes an approximately $4 million revenue contribution from WorkMotion in the fourth quarter, which is offset by a lower-margin managed services project transitioning off platform. We are actively engaged in discussions with this same client to transition them to Lifted EOR services. This is a clear proof point for the Lifted strategy, which is enabling us to replace legacy projects with higher-margin, more durable solutions. We are raising our full year 2026 Adjusted EBITDA outlook to $236 million-$240 million, which represents an Adjusted EBITDA margin of 32% at the midpoint.

The disciplined cost management muscle we have built in this business will enable us to produce strong profitability even if we continue to see low-value account rotation impacting top-line growth in 2027. We expect full year 2026 non-GAAP diluted EPS to be between $1.45 and $1.47. Our guidance assumes stock-based compensation of approximately $50 million-$53 million for the full year 2026, and we expect stock-based compensation to continue to step down next year. For the fourth quarter, we expect to generate revenue in the range of $169 million-$177 million.

Consistent with the strength in our ads and monetization products, marketplace take rate is expected to continue to advance in Q4, while business mix with Lifted will cause overall take rate to decline sequentially. We expect Adjusted EBITDA in the range of $51 million-$55 million, which represents an Adjusted EBITDA margin of 31% at the midpoint. We expect Q4 non-GAAP diluted EPS to be between $0.30 and $0.32. In closing, Upwork delivered another quarter of solid execution against our plan as we guide our business through a fundamental shift away from traditional digital demand channels and the broad rotation of work with AI.

We are managing a major business mix shift, and while we are enduring headwinds in our business, the strategic growth pillars we identified many quarters ago are showing promise. The strength we are seeing in enterprise, Business Plus, and the higher value of customers entering our platform validate our strategy. The early but strong adoption of our MCP server-enabled demand channels offer new opportunities for customer acquisition and retention. At the same time, our robust free cash flow profile provides balance sheet flexibility to fund high-return growth initiatives, execute strategic acquisitions like WorkMotion, and consistently return capital to shareholders.

Our confidence in Upwork's ability to grow and serve customers as they engage in the future of work remains steadfast, and we will continue to execute with strength and efficiency in the new world of work. With that, we will now take your questions.

Operator: Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, you will need to press star one on your telephone. To remove yourself from the queue, you may press star one again. Hayden Brown: Josh, the Lifted roadmap has always anticipated the build-out of international entities globally to support employing folks directly in market. This really gives us yet another proof point around how we're going to grow the Lifted business next year, as we both land and expand with our customers. The value prop around these global entities is something that we've already been seeing and hearing that they're very interested in.

Erica Gessert: Yeah, just to add to your question on the financials from WorkMotion. Like I said, we're going to recognize about $4 million of revenue in the fourth quarter from WorkMotion. That's before any of the synergies that we expect to get from this business that Hayden just described. This is a really great business. Super excited about what it can do to really advance the sales motion on Lifted.

Josh Chan: Okay. Appreciate the color there. Then maybe could you give us some color on the marketplace side of things? I guess, how did traffic trend through the quarter and into October? Anything that could kind of advise on the trajectory into year-end and maybe into 2027? Thanks for the color.

Hayden Brown: I'll start, Josh, by just elaborating on kind of trends in marketplace generally, and then I'll turn it over to Erica to talk about kind of the outlook there. We're also seeing our demand channels change with how digital acquisition based on Google and other kind of web-to-AI shifts are happening. That is an ongoing theme. We talked about that last quarter.

I'd say there's really no changes in those trends this quarter, and I'd say those things both really emphasize or reinforce why we're so focused on building out the new demand channels, like the MCP server, which we launched in August, and Upwork Now, which we are announcing in public beta today. All of these things are really setting us up to capture more of that demand as it's moving into AI and really kind of move up funnel to meet these bigger customers with their more complex work needs in their favorite AI tools.

Erica Gessert: Yeah. So just on 2027, Josh, obviously, we'll give guidance on 2027 when we report our fourth quarter in February, when Peter takes over. But today, I can just give you some contours around how we're thinking about the year and some of the building blocks. So, really just all in on the year, we expect our total growth rates to continue to be headwinded with some of the headwinds we're seeing right now in the first half of 2027. We do expect some improvement in the back half, and I want to tell you why. I'll break down why we have some confidence there.

So, first on the marketplace, as Hayden articulated, we're seeing the pressure that the team expressed last quarter really in two places, right? It's in the digital search traffic pressures with all the Google changes that are happening. Then, of course, the kind of AI-related pressure as low-value work is rotating off the platform. We see that continuing in the first half. As we lap kind of some of the current pressures from a growth rate point of view, we do expect that and just the effect of a slightly smaller base in the marketplace to kind of improve some of the growth rate trends there.

But overall, I guess the other piece of the puzzle here is that we do see on the revenue front, some of our highest growth is in kind of high take rate products like ads and monetization, and Business Plus with 132% GSV growth year-over-year in Q3. We're also, the focus on client quality is also really enabling us to continue to see the march of value as new customers enter the platform go up steadily. Then on the enterprise side, WorkMotion is a great addition, like I said, growing 20% a year. We do expect Lifted to grow very well next year and improve growth rates year-over-year.

So, all in the balance of between marketplace and Lifted, we expect to see, exit 2027 with improving growth rates.

Hayden Brown: The one thing I'll add to that, Josh, is because of the more limited visibility and predictability of the GSV environment specifically at this time, which we expect will be similar next year, we are very focused on delivering our revenue and margin targets. I'd say revenue and margin is just a huge focus for us as we head into 2027.

Erica Gessert: Yeah. Thanks, Stefanos. There is some timing of expenses between Q3 and Q4. Stefanos Crist: Got it. Thank you. On AI work GSV, I think there is pretty sharp acceleration there. It was 55% this quarter versus, I think, 22% last quarter. Could you just talk about what is driving that, what jobs are performing well there, and maybe if there are jobs that are not performing well as well? Thank you.

Hayden Brown: Yeah, I would say one of the important notes there is we really have started to sunset our prior metric around AI-related GSV because what we noticed, and we talked about this a little bit on the Q2 call, is that previously what we were measuring and reporting was clients explicitly stating that they had AI needs in their job posts. As a matter of fact, those needs have become much more de facto and infused in all of the work and actually not stated as explicitly by clients because now they just assume talent will be using AI skills to execute their work.

This quarter, the metric we shared with you is, we believe, a better proxy for AI-related work happening in our platform, and that is the percentage of GSV coming from talent who have AI skills specifically on their profiles as key skills that they're using to deliver work. That's a little bit of a difference in terms of the metric. It better encapsulates some of these trends. I'd say more generally to your question about, were there changes, there was nothing super notable. We've continued to see just massive increases in demand over the year for all of these AI-related skills and talent, and that's just an undercurrent that's kind of permeating the business completely at this point.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from the line of Eric Sheridan of Goldman Sachs. Your line is open, Eric.

Eric Sheridan: Thanks so much for taking the question, and Erica, wishing you the best going forward, and thanks for all the conversations and insights over the years. Hayden Brown: These are really important strategies for us, Eric, because we can all see that the landscape is changing, both in terms of what work looks like and this notion that now humans and AI are working together across more and more types of work, and that's just going to continue to be the norm. The fact that as businesses are contemplating work and starting work, increasingly they're doing it online inside of these AI tools and channels rather than offline in a meeting or in a discussion. They're actually bringing this work online.

For us, this is super important because from the MCP server standpoint, this lets us sit inside of and be operational within any AI tool that's using our MCP. Clients do not have to leave these work environments to actually invoke and hire Upwork talent and collaborate and get work done, and that is critical. It is actually moving even faster in real time with the Upwork Now launch, which really enables people and human expertise to be tapped at the same velocity that AI agents typically move.

This is key in terms of opening up demand channels for us that are really representing not just a shift of work from other digital platforms into AI, but also a shift of work from offline discussions and execution into online tools that now give us actually an increased chance of participating in those workflows, which is super exciting. The other thing I would say generally about our AI strategies is we are very focused in terms of the unit economics piece on extending the really great foundations we have around both our talent asset, trust and safety, payments, and also, to your point, our ads and monetization prowess. This all actually translates really well into these AI tools.

I think a perfect proof point on that this quarter was what we saw with the MCP server, which is, it has only been live for a couple months, since August, and already, because freelancers are very active in submitting proposals and using their Connects, which they pay for, through this MCP server, we are seeing it generate an incremental run rate of $3 million already, and that is only poised to grow as adoption continues to scale. We are really in a good position being able to translate and deploy all of our take rate and ads and other monetization strategies into these new channels without missing a beat.

Carter Parlette: Hey, guys. This is Carter Parlette on for Matt Condon. Thanks for taking my question. For the first one, Business Plus has been one of your fastest-growing offerings. In Business Plus, we actually give them what features we call like team-based hiring and multiplayer mode, basically ways for them to operate as a larger entity and get the value out of Upwork.

There is definitely a path forward to continue to both expand the Business Plus offering and enhance its value further, as well as over time potentially add more tiers.

There's certainly a lot of different client types that we serve, and they have heterogeneous needs, and sometimes those may actually create new opportunities for new products that specifically target their needs. We're excited about both the progress and the trajectory for Business Plus, and more broadly, our ability to continue to diversify our products and monetize them really healthily because we have such a large, diverse customer base.

Carter Parlette: Thank you. That's helpful. Shifting gears here to Lifted. You previously highlighted some strong pipeline growth. Can you just provide an update on how that pipeline is progressing? Thank you.

Hayden Brown: Lifted pipeline has actually continued to expand in the quarter. We feel fantastic about the momentum there. We did close three new logos, and I think that is really just starting to show the momentum we have been building since we initiated our sales and marketing efforts on this product earlier in the year. As you will recall, there are typically pretty long sales life cycles for these customers. Often it is a 6-12 month sale process. So, we feel very good that we are where we wanted to be right now and starting to close both new customers and executing the migration plan that we had for customers moving from the legacy Upwork Enterprise business over to Lifted.

This is really not just a technology change or a platform upgrade, it is a major sales opportunity for us in terms of engaging these customers around the new ways we can serve them, the broader share of wallet that we can participate in terms of their entire contingent spend budgets, which typically are in the $100 million mark or more.

We feel fantastic that this has been moving so well this year, and frankly, it has been in response to the success and the customer demand that we have seen in our pipeline for these direct employment offerings, not just in the U.S. and Canada, where we do that with Ascen, but also more globally, that really gave us conviction in moving forward with the purchase of WorkMotion, because this accelerates our roadmap pretty significantly. We were on plan to build out some of these entities over the next one to two years, but now, overnight, we are bringing in not just the entities, but a fantastic business and team that will continue to scale under our Lifted portfolio.

Operator: Thank you. Once again, to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone. Our next question comes from the line of John Byun of Jefferies. Your line is open, John.

That is really what we have done with everything from our Connects to dynamic pricing to value-added services, variable fees, et cetera. I would not call out that there is a specific pricing opportunity to AI as a category, but rather that we are approaching it with the rigor and discipline around how we monetize across the business based on really driving marketplace health first and foremost, and of course, margin capture and revenue generation where we see the opportunities to really do so. So, we will continue doing what we have been doing.

John Byun: Okay, great. Thank you. Just one quick clarification, actually. The question on monetization was really to the new Upwork Now product. I do not know if there is more you can share on how they might look going forward.
