#3104. SI-BONE (SIBN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Procedure volume surged 20% as active physicians hit record 1,770.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

SI-BONE, Inc. (SIBN -4.76%) reported 14.5% worldwide revenue growth driven by higher U.S. procedure volume and an increase in active physicians. Management reported that procedure demand accelerated for the expanded INTRA platform among interventional spine physicians and that the company achieved a record 1,770 active physicians. The company stated that the recent launch of iFuse Granite Onyx expands the total addressable market to approximately $5 billion while addressing failure points in complex spinal fusions. Management also indicated that new Medicare reimbursement levels for multilevel spinal fusion procedures became effective in October, creating a more favorable environment for the Granite platform. Financial results reflected improved operating leverage with adjusted EBITDA growth and positive operating cash flow generation year-to-date.

Operator: Good afternoon, and welcome to SI-BONE's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this call is being recorded for replay purposes. I would now like to turn the call over to Saqib Iqbal, Vice President, FP&A and Investor Relations at SI-BONE, for a few introductory comments.

Saqib Iqbal: Earlier today, SI-BONE released financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. A copy of the press release is available on the company's website. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that management's remarks today may include forward-looking statements within the meaning of federal securities laws, which are made pursuant to the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These forward-looking statements are subject to a number of risks and uncertainties, including those set forth in our SEC filings, such as our most recent Form 10-K and Form 10-Q, and actual results may differ materially from any forward-looking statements that we make today. Accordingly, you should not place undue reliance on these statements.

These forward-looking statements speak only as of the date that they are made, and we do not assume any obligation to update any forward-looking statements, except as required by law. During the call, management may also discuss certain non-GAAP measures, including adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow. Unless otherwise noted, any reference to profitability is in terms of positive adjusted EBITDA. For a reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to GAAP accounting, please see the company's full earnings release issued earlier today. Unless otherwise noted, all results are compared to the comparable period in the prior year. With that, I'll turn the call over to Laura.

Laura Francis: Thanks, Saqib. Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us. We delivered a solid third quarter with accelerating procedure demand, broader physician adoption and improving financial performance. These results reflect disciplined execution of our multiyear strategy to expand our differentiated platform into new clinical applications. By focusing on anatomy-specific solutions that enable durable fixation and fusion in patients with compromised bone, we're reaching more patients and expanding our growth opportunity. Worldwide revenue grew approximately 15% to $55.7 million. U.S. revenue increased approximately 14% to $52.8 million. U.S. procedure volume increased approximately 20%, supported by 16% growth in active physicians.

The strong double-digit volume growth across all procedure types demonstrates that our targeted platform expansion and call point diversification strategies are delivering. In addition to the strong surgeon demand in the third quarter, demand accelerated for our expanded INTRA platform from interventional spine physicians in the office space and ASC sites of care. Our decision to build differentiated solutions with applications across all sites of care has made INTRA the preferred platform for this call point. International revenue grew 27% to $2.9 million, supported by continued adoption of technologies launched in the last 12 months. We converted the revenue growth into stronger financial performance.

Adjusted EBITDA increased 32%, more than twice the pace of revenue growth, while working capital discipline contributed to stronger operating cash flow. Innovation remains a key component of our long-term growth as we develop differentiated technologies to improve procedural outcomes for high-risk patients with compromised bone quality. We pioneered minimally invasive treatment for SI joint dysfunction and applied that experience to develop breakthrough devices targeting sacropelvic fixation and complex fusion as well as pelvic fragility fractures. With the recent launch of iFuse Granite Onyx, we're now taking that proven expertise in developing anatomy-specific solutions beyond the pelvis. Onyx received FDA 510(k) clearance in September and is our third product to receive FDA breakthrough device designation.

We believe Onyx, which is designed to address the known failure points at the upper and lower ends of the spine fusion construct, represents one of the most significant product launches in our history. The addition of Onyx increases our estimated total addressable market to over 650,000 procedures, representing an annual total market opportunity of approximately $5 billion. Onyx is the first of several differentiated technologies that we plan to bring to market that address significant unmet clinical needs and where our expertise in compromised bone gives us a clear advantage. We initiated the alpha launch of Onyx in October and are extremely pleased with the surgeon interest. Early demand is tracking ahead of Granite over the comparable launch period.

While we expect a modest contribution in the fourth quarter, as we move to full launch, we see Onyx as a meaningful accelerant to long-term growth. Recent reimbursement enhancements have added another long-term growth catalyst. New DRGs for multilevel spinal fusion procedures that incorporate pelvic fixation with Granite took effect October 1. Depending on patient diagnosis and severity, the increase in the average hospital payment could be up to $50,000 per qualifying procedure. We believe the reimbursement framework will enable physicians and patients to access our Granite platform, further extending our leadership in the nearly $1 billion target market and allowing us to potentially provide additional solutions such as Onyx in these same procedures.

Together, these developments mark a defining moment for SI-BONE. We're substantially expanding our addressable market. The new DRGs have created a more favorable reimbursement environment, and we have a highly engaged physician base, all of which give us confidence in delivering durable long-term growth. That confidence is also implied in our 2026 guidance, which at the midpoint would imply over 20% revenue growth in the fourth quarter. I will now discuss our 3 key growth drivers: innovation and market development, physician engagement and commercial execution. Anshul will then cover our fourth priority: operational excellence inside of financial results and outlook. Starting with innovation and market development.

As the U.S. population ages and lives longer, osteoporosis and osteopenia are becoming more prevalent. This creates a growing need for advanced technologies that enable durable fixation and fusion in compromised bone. We believe our biomechanical expertise in developing anatomy-specific technology gives us a competitive advantage that is difficult to replicate. Our Granite and Onyx platforms are clear examples of our disruptive innovation targeting known failures and complex fusions. Granite was our first major platform targeting failures and complex fusion, starting at the base of spinal fusion procedures. In the last 4 years, we believe Granite has become the standard of care in sacropelvic fixation.

Onyx expands our complex fusion platform by addressing screw loosening at the upper and the lower instrumented vertebra, another major challenge in spinal fusion. Published literature reports screw loosening in as many as 27% of spinal fusion constructs with higher risks in patients with osteoporosis. We've done this before. In the randomized SILVIA trial, adding fixation across the SI joint alongside S2AI screws reduced new onset SI joint pain from 8.5% to 1.1% following deformity surgery. With Granite, the PAULA study showed a 3.3% pelvic fixation failure rate at 12 months compared to a 23.7% failure rate at 2 years reported for traditional pelvic screws in large deformity databases.

With Onyx, we're bringing that same osteointegrative approach with the goal of delivering similar results. Onyx is one of the most technologically advanced solutions we've developed. We believe the anatomy-specific thread design and implant stiffness tailored to varying vertebral bone density promotes early fixation, which is crucial to reducing implant loosening and also facilitates long-term bone integration. We estimate the market for Onyx at approximately 200,000 annual U.S. procedures, representing a market opportunity of approximately $1.5 billion. Combined with Granite, our total market opportunity in complex fusion now stands at approximately $2.5 billion. Onyx will also benefit from our substantial commercial footprint and large presence in complex fusion procedures.

When Granite launched in 2022, we had over 700 active physicians, and we were in the early stages of building out our third-party agent network. Today, we have approximately 1,770 active physicians and over 300 agents. In the first few weeks of the alpha launch, Onyx is already generating incremental procedures within our existing accounts, while higher implant utilization is increasing overall procedure average selling price. As more surgical capacity comes online, we're confident that this commercial reach will accelerate Onyx adoption. From a reimbursement standpoint, depending on the number of levels fused and additional technologies being used, the new DRGs I highlighted earlier may also benefit Onyx, especially in qualifying long spinal fusion cases.

Additionally, as a breakthrough designated device, Onyx is eligible for the alternative pathway for a new technology add-on payment, or NTAP. We've submitted our application to CMS and if approved, the NTAP would take effect on October 1, 2027. In SI joint dysfunction, our largest market for minimally invasive surgical procedures, our actions to broaden our portfolio and expand physician call points to also include interventional spine physicians are delivering results. Our comprehensive portfolio serves both call points across all sites of service and extends our reach to a broader subset of patients.

In the third quarter, surgeons accounted for the vast majority of procedures, but adoption of the INTRA platform among interventional spine physicians was a significant contributor to procedure growth. We believe INTRA has established a leading position in SI joint fusion among interventional physicians, supported by our comprehensive portfolio, clinical evidence and training programs. Proposed CMS reimbursement changes could also strengthen demand for our solutions in this market. Under the proposal, hospital outpatient and ASC payments would increase to more than $20,000 and $16,000, respectively, and in new office payments of $20,000 for CPT 27279 would be established. If finalized, these changes would take effect January 1, 2027, improve procedure economics and expand patient access.

We expect CMS to issue the final ruling in the coming days. In trauma, we continue to collaborate with Smith+Nephew on surgeon awareness and education to treat sacral insufficiency fractures using iFuse TORQ TNT. As we enter the busy season for trauma, our joint commercial actions over the last 6 months are starting to deliver as we're seeing growing adoption of our platform. Looking ahead, we're advancing several programs targeting large established markets with significant unmet needs and high procedure failure rates. These solutions apply our compromised bone expertise to new clinical challenges and build on existing physician relationships and commercial infrastructure. By organizing our innovation around the needs of these high-risk patients, we remain committed to improving procedural outcomes.

Now turning to physician engagement. We ended the quarter with approximately 1,770 active physicians, representing 16% year-over-year growth. We're proud of our double-digit physician growth in every quarter for nearly 6 years, which we attribute to the impact of our innovation that is improving patient outcomes, the quality of our targeting activity as well as the prudent investment in physician education and high-quality clinical research. Given our sizable installed base, we're also focused on deeper physician engagement to increase the number of cases per physician. While we continue to see steady increases in the number of physicians performing multiple procedure types, Onyx has the potential to materially accelerate this trend.

Even in this limited launch period, Onyx is already driving an increase in the number of cases as well as the increase in the number of products used per case among existing Granite physicians. Next, let's turn to commercial execution. We ended the third quarter with 93 quota-carrying territory managers. Our trailing 12-month average revenue per territory was $2.2 million, representing 7% improvement. These productivity gains reflect the operating leverage in a hybrid model strategy as our direct team focuses on physician education and relationships while third-party agents extend procedural coverage and market reach. We're targeting to exit 2026 with nearly 100 territories.

The added field capacity will allow us to capture the anticipated Onyx demand, deepen physician engagement, capitalize on the interventional momentum and prepare for future launches. Before I hand it over to Anshul, I want to thank our colleagues for their dedication and execution. I especially want to recognize our teams involved in the development and launch of Onyx. I also want to compliment our market access team whose work helped secure the new granite DRGs. Onyx marks the beginning of our next wave of innovation, and I'm excited about what we can accomplish. We're helping physicians treat thousands of patients and improve their quality of life.

Now Anshul will discuss our financial results and outlook for the rest of the year.

Anshul Maheshwari: Thanks, Laura. Good afternoon, everyone. Our third quarter results demonstrate our ability to drive strong procedure growth, improve profitability and generate operating cash while investing in future opportunities. Let me provide additional details on our financial performance. Starting with revenue growth. Worldwide revenue was $55.7 million, representing 14.5% growth. U.S. revenue increased 13.9% to $52.8 million, driven by 19.5% procedure volume growth, partially offset by lower average selling price. The robust volume in a seasonally slower quarter for the industry reflects the benefits of our strategy to build a diversified portfolio serving both surgeons and interventional pain physicians.

With nearly 650,000 annual target procedures that can benefit from our highly differentiated technologies, we believe we are in the early stages of accelerating procedure volume growth. The ASP was impacted by procedure mix, which drives the average number of implants per case as well as the site of care mix as our INTRA platform adoption increased in faster-growing ASC and in-office settings, which typically carry lower ASP. International revenue increased 27% to $2.9 million, driven by growing TORQ and TNT procedure volume. Turning to profitability. Gross profit increased 13.7% to $44.2 million. Gross margin was 79.3%, continuing to track ahead of guidance.

The minimal change in gross margin reflects the site of care and procedure mix I highlighted earlier, partially offset by the improving surgical capacity utilization and implementation of production workflow changes to reduce implant costs as well as optimize instrument costs. Operating expenses increased 9.7%, well below revenue growth of 14.5%, demonstrating our ability to scale efficiently. Higher spending reflected sales commissions, marketing activities to support new products and continued R&D investment. Based on the trends through the first 3 quarters, we believe 2026 operating leverage will be better than our expectations at the beginning of the year.

Net loss narrowed to $3.6 million or $0.08 per diluted share compared to a net loss of $4.6 million or $0.11 per diluted share. Adjusted EBITDA increased 32.4% to $3 million, representing an adjusted EBITDA margin of 5.5%. Over the trailing 12 months, our adjusted EBITDA increased approximately 140% to nearly $13.6 million, and adjusted EBITDA margin more than doubled. Going forward, we expect strong revenue growth and continuing operating leverage to drive further margin expansion and move us towards GAAP profitability. Turning to liquidity and cash flow. Our working capital discipline and asset-light operating model are converting improved operating performance into cash. We ended the quarter with $146.3 million in cash and equivalents, up approximately $400,000 sequentially.

Year-to-date, we generated approximately $4.4 million in operating cash flow compared with $2.4 million used in the prior year period, an improvement of $6.8 million. Our robust balance sheet and progress towards consistent free cash flow generation positions us to fund our planned development programs while maintaining significant financial flexibility. Turning to 2026 outlook. We are reaffirming our 2026 worldwide revenue of $231 million to $233 million as well as our gross margin expectations at 79%. While we are making growth-oriented investments related to Onyx launch and ongoing R&D projects, based on the year-to-date performance, we now expect our operating expenses to grow 10.5% versus our prior expectation of 12%.

The midpoint of our annual worldwide revenue guidance implies over 20% year-over-year revenue growth in the fourth quarter. As we enter our seasonally strongest quarter, our fourth quarter growth acceleration is anchored by the strengthening and broad-based procedure demand, a growing base of active physicians, an expanded commercial footprint and modest contribution from new products. The new branded DRGs and a broader rollout of Onyx offers additional growth potential, both in terms of volume and procedure ASP upside. Early indications from these catalysts in October reinforce our confidence in a strong finish to 2026 and significant operating momentum entering 2027. With that, I will turn the call over to Laura.

Laura Francis: Thanks, Anshul. We're entering our next phase of growth with a differentiated portfolio, deeper physician engagement and a more favorable reimbursement environment. We've built the commercial scale to capture these opportunities, and our results demonstrate the operating leverage that growth can deliver. Looking ahead, we're very confident in our ability to accelerate growth, improve profitability and help more patients achieve better outcomes. With that, we're happy to answer your questions. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question will be coming from the line of Patrick Wood of UBS.

Patrick Andrew Wood: Just 2 upfront. First one on Onyx. Obviously, an alpha launch at the moment, but I'd love any extra color you guys have from the clinician and surgeon feedback and if you're going to change anything as you go into full release, anything you're going to tweak. Just feedback there would be great. And then secondly, big picture, you mentioned several times, obviously, accelerating procedure growth. Q4, the implied guide is for a nice acceleration. How much is Onyx going to keep that momentum as we move through into next year even before the NTAP actually comes online?

Laura Francis: [Audio Gap] the answer is yes to that question. So that's number one. Number two, we wanted to see if physicians that are using Onyx, are they using Onyx when they don't go to the pelvis where they typically don't use Granite, and the answer is yes to that as well. And then finally, we want to see if nonusers of Granite are wanting to use Onyx. And the answer is yes to that question, too. So we're really excited by what we're seeing here just in the last 30 days or so.

So they're early trends and all of the things that we talked about in terms of increasing procedure volumes and seeing implant utilization per case increase with Onyx is happening in the early stages. And also what gives us a lot of encouragement is Granite has been a huge success for us. And when we compare the demand for Onyx to the early demand for Granite, it's actually tracking ahead of where Granite was as well.

So maybe not that surprising because we've built such a strong number of physicians who are using our technologies, once again, as I said in the preprepared remarks, we had around 700 physicians that were active when we launched Granite, and now we're at almost 1,800, right? And also just the footprint that we have in the United States as well with the larger number of territory managers and territory reps, but also our third-party agents as well. I think all of those things are really important. So the excitement is really evident with our commercial team. We have actually quite a bit of inbound demand already for Onyx.

And so, for us, it's really deploying additional surgical capacity out there in November and December, and then we expect the full launch in January.

Anshul Maheshwari: And then, Patrick, on the guidance side, you're correct. The midpoint of our full year guidance implies a 20% revenue growth in the fourth quarter. Now the acceleration that we expect to see in the fourth quarter is actually a buildup of all the activities we engaged in throughout the year. It started with the meaningful physician base growth that we've seen. Just comparing third quarter to third quarter, we've added nearly 250 additional physicians. The expansion into interventional, as Laura said in her prepared remarks, is actually doing well. The INTRA platform is really accelerating adoption within the interventional space, and we saw that happen in the third quarter, which tends to be a slow quarter generally.

So that bodes well for the fourth quarter. The last piece would be on the trauma side, we've been working very closely with Smith+Nephew to sort of build the foundations entering a busy trauma quarter as well. And coming into the fourth quarter, we're seeing the benefit of that as well. And then the last piece on Onyx, what's incorporated in the guidance, when we started the year, we had said Onyx would be available at some point late in the fourth quarter. We're obviously ahead of track on that, given that Onyx was in alpha launch in October. And the color Laura provided, it's actually doing quite well for us. So I think, net-net, we're positioned really well.

Now the 2 things that could provide potentially additional upside would be the impact of new DRGs on Granite. Especially as we think about the third quarter, we had more Granite cases with 2 implants. As we continue to drive awareness in the DRGs, can we move that to 4. And then as we continue to broaden our alpha launch with more surgical sets out there for Onyx, could that be additional upside for us as well. So I think we feel very good about the setup ending the year and then also what it sets us up as we look out the next few years from a growth perspective.

Operator: The next question will be coming from the line of Matthew O'Brien from Piper Sandler.

Matthew O'Brien: Maybe just to keep going on Onyx for a second here. Laura, you mentioned the 1,800 active docs roughly that you have now. How quickly can you access those clinicians? That would seem like that's the low-hanging fruit versus going after people that had not been working with you in the past. So is there any kind of metric we should think about in terms of how many you can get to by the middle of next year, by the end of next year, anything along those lines?

And then just talk a little bit about training, how quickly they can get up the curve in terms of getting accustomed to Onyx and being able to incorporate it in their practice. And then I have a follow-up.

Laura Francis: Yes. Thanks, Matt. Good questions. And in terms of Onyx, you're right. So this first quarter is really focused primarily on just the alpha launch that we're working on right now. But as we continue with every single week, we're pushing out more trades into the field as well as more inventory as well. And given just the sheer number of surgeons that are already using our Granite product, it gives us the opportunity to work with them, first of all, in these Granite cases themselves, right? So we actually have an opportunity to have a significant throughput and increase the revenue per case with adding Onyx just into existing Granite cases.

But then also, you have these 1,800 active physicians as well at the same time. And a lot of those physicians, they are doing cases that don't necessarily go to the pelvis. And so they haven't been using Granite in those cases, but they are going to be more likely to use Onyx either at the top of the construct or at the bottom of the construct. So like, for example, in cases where surgeons use both Granite and Onyx, we're seeing utilization of around 6 implants per procedure, which is going to translate to that increase in the revenue per case that I just mentioned.

But in addition to all of that, there's also the opportunity to go after new surgeons too, that had not, for one reason or another, adopted the Granite technology, and we're already starting to see cases with some of these key opinion leader surgeons in the early stages that are interested in our Onyx product. So I think your question on the commercial infrastructure being in place, and it's really just expanding the surgical capacity is what's really going to be important. You also talked about training a little bit. And the training is very straightforward, very similar to what we did with Granite. We do a similar sort of a trade review with the surgeon before a case.

They're already used to using other technologies in these cases. And so it's just a reminder of, here's our solution, here are our instruments. And so the adoption and the road to training these surgeons is a very quick one.

Anshul Maheshwari: And the only other thing I would add, Matt, there is Onyx is a line extension. So from a VAC committee approval perspective, it's actually a very seamless process for us. It's just targeting a different disease state, like Laura said, in the UIV and LIV.

Matthew O'Brien: Okay. Appreciate that. And then something in the press release really got my attention. It was talking about setting you guys up for the strongest foundation for growth acceleration in the history of the company. I mean you've done 20%, 30% growth in the past. I'm not expecting the high end of that 30% number next year. But the Street settled in at about 15.5% growth for next year on the top line. That would seem to be well below what you can likely do, given all the tailwinds. Is that a fair assessment? Or is there something else that we should be contemplating?

Anshul Maheshwari: Yes. So Matt, I can take that question. When we make that comment, and we don't make it lightly, if you look at the structural multiyear tailwinds that we have in our business, I'll just summarize the top 6 that we have. The expanded call point strategy with interventional spine is translating into faster penetration in the SI joint dysfunction market. And the proposed expanded coverage for site of care that may be announced any day at this point, assuming it's finalized, could be a further tailwind in that business for us. The Smith+Nephew collaboration is starting to gain some momentum as well.

We've talked about the new DRGs, the impact it can have on Granite adoption and more implants per case. Onyx, again, we're in alpha launch right now. We're going to put more capacity out in '27 throughout the year into 2028. And then you've got the potential benefit of NTAP at the end of 2027 as well. And then we've got other projects we're working on. So truly a lot of tailwinds in the business. Now, as excited as we are about those tailwinds, we are still in the early stages of evaluating their impact.

And we feel good about the growth prospects into 2027, but we want to get a few more months behind us from a performance standpoint before we talk about 2027. Our focus is on closing the year strong, go through our planning process, which we are under right now and then talk about guidance and expectations in late February when we announce our fourth quarter earnings. And look, we're going to consistently be thoughtful and prudent in our approach, but we do believe that these tailwinds are not just limited to '27, but even beyond.

Operator: Our next question is coming from the line of Richard Newitter of Truist Securities.

Richard Newitter: Maybe just to follow on Matt's question just now. On the bottom line, I was just wondering if you could offer any thoughts as you potentially are about to move into one of the biggest acceleration or most confident points of -- jump-off points for acceleration going forward. And on profitability, what that could look like, it looks like you're on track to potentially exit at around 9% in 2026, adjusted EBITDA margin. That's about what you did exiting last year, 4Q '25. Just curious how we should think about the ramp, especially with what seem like pretty significant drivers, both from a margin standpoint and just sheer growth dollars? And I have a follow-up.

Anshul Maheshwari: Yes. No, Richard, happy to take that question. Our profitability is an outcome of our strong top line growth. Let's just start with that. And obviously, with the way our spend -- [Audio Gap] as a result, we've reflected a reduction in OpEx growth for the year. Now, when we think about the coming years from a profitability standpoint, we do have a lot of growth-oriented investments that we want to be able to make in the business. We do remain committed to our operating leverage expectations. As we've always said, on the low end, it's 1.25x revenue growth to OpEx growth and could be as high as 1.75x over the long term.

Now, these investments, we think, are really important to continue to drive this sustained long-term growth that we'd like to see the business deliver. It's around investment in R&D personnel and our own machining capabilities to support the annual cadence of new product launches. We do expect to expand our sales force to capture the demand that we're seeing across all the call points. And then as we launch new products, including Onyx, we want to make sure we are investing in training and marketing activities. So these are deliberate investments that we want to be able to make in the business to drive growth.

But we do expect that the accelerating top line growth should allow us to drop a significant amount of dollars to the bottom line even at the midpoint of the leverage being around 1.4x, 1.5x.

Richard Newitter: And maybe just one follow-up. Look, congratulations. Really nice acceleration in your procedure growth this quarter. But the ASP took a little step back. I guess, maybe anything to call out there, Anshul or Laura? And kind of how should we think of that trend in 4Q, especially if you've got increased revenue procedure tailwinds?

Anshul Maheshwari: No, that's a great question, Richard. So again, 20% procedure volume growth in the third quarter, it's actually very encouraging. We're very pleased with that, especially when you think about all the noise around slowdown in procedure volumes. And from an ASP standpoint, when we started the year, we had talked about sort of low to mid-single-digit ASP degradation from a per procedure standpoint, especially as the business mix evolves. Now, when you think about the reach of our platform today, it now ranges from single implant procedures where INTRA is used in an ASC or an in-office setting on one end.

And on the other end, you've got cases with Granite and also now Onyx, which could be 4-plus implant cases, which are performed in inpatient settings. So both of these factors can have an impact on our ASP. And when you looked at the third quarter, what we saw was Granite continued to grow well, but we did see an increase in 2 implant Granite cases, which generally tend to be more in the degen side versus the 4 implant side. Now with the new DRG changes, we're continuing to educate people on the benefits of 2 points of fixation on either side.

And then the strong demand on INTRA from interventional spine physicians in the ASC and office-based setting, which typically carries a lower ASP was expected. But what was encouraging was it's actually allowing us to penetrate the huge multibillion-dollar untapped SIJD TAM we've been targeting for so long. So as we think about our ASP, 2 most important variables will be around where the volume growth is coming from in the site of service.

Now, Laura talked a little bit about it earlier in the comments, even in the early stages of Onyx, what we are seeing is the average procedure ASP is actually moving up coming into the fourth quarter because we're starting to see some of the benefits of Onyx and also the uptake in multi-implant granite cases go higher. Now offsetting that is going to be the interventional volume, but we think net-net, you should see an improvement in ASP in the fourth quarter given the dynamics the way they're playing out.

Operator: Our question will be coming from Caitlin Roberts of Canaccord Genuity.

Caitlin Cronin: Maybe just jumping off of Anshul, what you mentioned about the procedure volume growth and which is strong, given the noise that you've heard from others. Maybe just a little bit more color on what you are seeing as it relates to procedure volume just across your call points.

Laura Francis: Yes. Thanks, Caitlin, for the question. I mean if you look at the third quarter with the volume growth at 20%, we would say the short answer is no, that we're not seeing this concern that you're hearing from some other companies. Now it may be that we're just in a unique position in the industry. We're targeting unmet clinical needs and known failures in various fusion procedures, and it's clearly resonating with our customers. I think also the fact that we're building new TAMs and now we're at a point where we're targeting over 600,000 annual procedures, we're not fighting for market share gains. We're more identifying these new opportunities, and that's contributing to the growth that we're seeing.

So I can't necessarily speculate on the macro impact and the broader industry volumes. But just given our particular situation with multiple growth drivers, we think we're really well positioned to navigate if there are headwinds or issues that are out there and to drive strong growth. And even coming into the fourth quarter, if you look at our guidance, it's saying that our best estimate is that we will exceed 20% growth. And so what we're seeing and expecting is continued strong demand across the portfolio and especially given the tailwinds with Onyx and then the new Granite DRGs and finally, the interventional ramp as well, it bodes well for us.

Caitlin Cronin: Great. And then just on the Smith+Nephew partnership, any KPIs in terms of surgeon or facility penetration you could share? And just thoughts on maybe partnering with them or another company for any future products that don't necessarily fit your core call points?

Laura Francis: Yes. Thanks for asking about that. And actually, we're making nice progress with Smith+Nephew at this point. It does usually take some time in order to build that relationship and to see the results, especially in the case of SI-BONE, we're a pretty nimble company that is able to innovate and bring products to market and see the impact fairly quickly, but working with a larger company, it does tend to take a little bit more time. But over the last several months, we've been focused on surgeon education, training and also just expanding access to TNT at these various trauma centers.

And there is this normal onboarding period with physician engagement, hospital approvals and the initial procedures, but we're pleased with what we're seeing exiting Q3 and entering Q4, which is typically more of a seasonally stronger period for trauma, and we are starting to see the results of our joint commercial efforts.

Operator: Next question is coming from the line of Young Li of [ Jefferies ].

Young Li: All right, great. I guess maybe back to Onyx. I wanted to hear, I guess, a little bit more on like the attachment rate for Onyx versus the classic Granite cases. I guess, what are you seeing in the alpha launch group so far? How frequently are they being used together versus not? And then where do you think that can go longer term?

Laura Francis: Yes. I mean I talked a little bit about some of the measures that we're currently using. And as you're stating, the most obvious application is for our surgeons to use Onyx in the same cases as Granite, and we're seeing that come through. And it's low-hanging fruit, as you well, if you look at that opportunity. But what's also happening is, let's talk about the surgeons that are using Granite regularly when they go to the pelvis. What we're seeing is that those surgeons are actually using Onyx in the cases where they're not going to the pelvis.

So they may not be using Granite in those cases, but they are surgeons that have been using our products for an extended period of time and now really like what we're offering here with Onyx for their patients with compromised bone. And as I mentioned, the issue is really having issues with screw loosening in these patients that have compromised bone. And so the application is well understood, and there's an excitement with our surgeons that we're finally solving this problem overall. So -- and then finally, we're actually seeing surgeons who have not used Granite previously, but they actually are interested in using Onyx.

But as you said, I would say the primary use case is in those surgeons that we've been working with for an extended period of time, in many cases, in those procedures where they're using Granite, but we're seeing much more than that as well. And I did talk a little bit about implant utilization as well in these cases where what we're seeing in a case where they're typically using Granite and Onyx together is they're using 6 implants in those cases. So it's a pretty exciting opportunity, and it just gives us this significant benefit in terms of increasing surgeon density that we didn't necessarily have with our portfolio previously.

Anshul Maheshwari: And then Young, the thing I would say is if you even look at the underlying TAM, Granite's underlying TAM is about 130,000 cases, 140,000 cases, of which about 30,000 to 40,000 cases were in the deformity -- adult deformity space. And given the complexity of those adult deformity procedures, our expectation is almost all those cases where you use Granite, you might want to use Onyx at the top and the bottom of the construct. That's what's embedded in our TAM numbers. But then once you get beyond that, within the degen space, when you think about the number of fusion procedures that happen there, there's around 400,000 procedures.

Our best estimate is that 100,000 of those end at the sacrum, and that's where Granite would have been used. But UIV/LIV can extend beyond those 100,000 cases as well, especially when you think about the number of those patients that have osteoporosis, rough estimate, 1 in 3 patients. And if you look at patients who are over 50, even more patients have osteoporosis and Onyx would have application there at the UIV and LIV as well. And those end up around 150,000 cases. Now, those are bread-and-butter cases, too, for a lot of physicians that may not do Granite, because they may not be at academic centers, but do SI joint dysfunction.

And so we've got a nice overlap of physicians that can use Onyx, whether they use Granite or not.

Young Li: All right. Great. That's very helpful. I guess I wanted to follow up a little bit on that concept. I guess, what are your expectations for any potential halo effect from Onyx, where you can enable some conversion or pull-through of surgeons to the other products in your portfolio?

Laura Francis: I think there's no question that there's a halo effect. And I talked a little bit about the clinical data that we have on our Granite technology. And we recently had a surgeon that came into a Board meeting that just talked about the fact that we have really addressed the issue at the bottom of the long construct with Granite. And now we're proving it out with our SILVIA study information and then also our PAULA study information, too. And so it's well known that you have this issue with the upper part of the spine and the lower part of the spine.

So in these particular cases with Onyx, it is another major failure point at the top and the bottom of the spine. And published literature is actually reporting screw loosening in as many as 27% of spinal fusion constructs. And so there's this understanding of what the problem actually is. There's also an understanding that SI-BONE was able to address the issue at the bottom of the long construct and now we're moving to the next area that is a significant challenge for these particular surgeons and their patients. So I'm kind of -- I'm going to go back to what you said in terms of a halo effect.

I do believe that all the work that we've done on Granite does have a halo effect and that it will have an impact on Onyx sales.

Operator: Our question is coming from the line of Gracia Mahoney of Bank of America.

Gracia Mahoney: The first one I wanted to ask on was just in the prepared remarks, you talked about how the new DRGs may benefit Onyx. So just wanted to clarify if they already mapped to it today. If not, what needs to happen for that to occur? And maybe just in terms of an NTAP strategy, if you do that, what sort of the application filing timeline process would be like and what you're doing to prepare hospitals for reimbursement around the product?

Laura Francis: Yes. Good questions, Gracia. And we are excited about the new Granite DRGs. We've been working for an extended period of time with CMS on this particular topic, and we're really pleased that they created these new DRGs, recognizing the clinical complexity and the additional costs associated with treating these patients. And so from a Granite perspective, these new DRGs went into place on October 1, 2026. And so it's going to have an impact on the Granite business. And if you think about where we were previously, the NTAP expired October 1, 2025. So for the last 12 months, there has not been a Granite NTAP in place.

But now with these new DRGs and these new DRGs, if you look at the reimbursement, they pay up to an additional $50,000 more for qualifying cases. It does provide the opportunity for hospitals and surgeons to feel confident in using Granite. And if you think about the NTAP, the NTAP is specific to Medicare cases, whereas the new DRGs are going to cover all payers, not just Medicare but also commercial payers, too. So we think that all of that is really important just for our Granite business. Now, you asked about the impact on Onyx as well.

And as I said, a lot of the cases that we're seeing currently with Onyx are being done in conjunction with Granite. And so those cases are going to be accessing the new higher-paying DRGs. And so in terms of cost, the new DRGs are helping to address the higher costs associated with these technologies. We have -- you also asked about the NTAP for Onyx. We have already applied for an NTAP with CMS. And given that this is a breakthrough device, we should be able to follow an alternative pathway with our Onyx technology, and we'll know for sure, October 1, 2027.

And earlier than that, I think April already, we'll get some information on the NTAP for Onyx specifically. But we do think that there's another opportunity there for Onyx in the future with the NTAP, but also currently in conjunction with granite cases.

Gracia Mahoney: Okay. Super helpful. And then I guess just how to think about maybe all these product launches and any incremental impact to gross margin? I think Street is modeling gross margin down a little bit versus this year. So any sort of puts and takes to consider there as we go into 2027?

Laura Francis: Yes, I think it's a good question. And I'll have Anshul talk a little bit about the gross margin impact. But the question about additional product launches is an important one. We really are looking at a compromised bone opportunity here.

And what it's done is it's created this opportunity to significantly expand our product road map and for us to be regularly putting out products in order to meet these new opportunities and address them, very similar to what we've done already with Granite, for example, with pelvic fixation, very similar to what we've done with TNT, with pelvic trauma and now finally, with Onyx with the top and the bottom of the spine construct, we have more opportunities to further expand and regularly launch products. And I'll let Anshul talk about the gross margin impact.

Anshul Maheshwari: Yes. So thanks for that question. We really feel great about our industry-leading gross margins. Year-to-date, we've actually tracked ahead of what we guided. And part of that is just our focus on asset utilization and implant and trade cost reduction initiatives. As our business scales with that strong top line growth, we are focused on driving more incremental revenue dollars to the bottom line and improving towards -- and progressing towards improving GAAP profit dollars now. When you think about 2027, and I'll provide a couple of years expectations there. Going into 2027, we do anticipate some modest gross margin pressure.

Most of that is from the higher noncash depreciation expenses associated with the additional Onyx surgical capacity we plan to deploy and to support the procedure demand that we expect from Onyx. As Laura said earlier, beyond Onyx, we do expect to bring additional platforms to market in the next few years, which we know will meaningfully accelerate top line growth given how differentiated they are and they're going after known unmet needs. As we launch these technologies, we've talked about it historically that we expect gross margin to be in sort of that 78% area as you go beyond 2027.

Most of that is going to be driven by the subscale nature of the new products and higher noncash costs from trade depreciation. Now, what that does not include is our expectations to work on cost reduction initiatives with our manufacturing partners on our existing portfolio as well as our internal operational efficiency efforts, which include driving higher utilization through setting up loaner operations and things like that. So again, very focused on gross margin profitability. We think even at that 78%, 79%, it will be industry-leading, and that should translate well into operating profit at the adjusted level and also GAAP profitability in the not-too-distant future.

Operator: Our next question is coming from the line of Matt Blackman of TD Cowen.

Mathew Blackman: Great. I'm just going to leave it to one. And Laura, shockingly, the question will be on Onyx. Just I'm curious, some of the early feedback we've been hearing from clinicians is focused on them wanting to see some commercial clinical and economic outcomes data before putting Onyx into their armamentarium. That doesn't strike me as an unusual request with a new product. But just curious what you're hearing from physicians, and to the extent you do need to build, we'll call it a commercial data dossier, what's the pathway to do that? How big do you think that needs to be? How long out do you think that data need to be?

Laura Francis: Yes. As you know, we're very used to putting together high-quality clinical data. We have over almost 200 peer-reviewed published papers, including 4 randomized controlled trials and many more prospective studies as well. And so the approach that we're taking here is very similar to what we did with our Granite technology. So we have bench data and then we have all of the information on the high rate of failure at the upper and lower ends of the long spinal constructs. And so in a lot of these cases, these surgeons actually don't have a good alternative solution.

And so what we're seeing is given how well we handled the situation with Granite and addressed the issue at the bottom of the long construct, and the quality of the bench data and the product itself and the osseointegrated nature of the product, it already is lending itself to surgeons that are interested in using the product now. And so what we're doing is we're working with those particular surgeons. With that said, we're also looking at the opportunity to build that additional clinical data. And so in terms of how we're thinking about Onyx, what we're doing is we're leveraging the benchtop in animal studies that we have currently. It's compared to conventional screws.

It compares very well to those. But then we're also going to launch a prospective multicenter clinical study to evaluate Onyx safety and clinical performance as well. So very similar to what we've done in the past. Finally, one of the other ways that surgeons do address these issues in patients is they use bone cement along with pedicle screws. But in these particular cases, cement, it can improve initial fixation, but it comes with trade-offs. So the cement can leak outside the vertebra. You can have the potential for nerve injury, pulmonary embolisms, creates a rigid interface that doesn't integrate with bone. And then it can even raise the risk of fractures at the adjacent level.

So the alternatives that surgeons have right now, they are not good alternatives. So getting back to your question, I do think that there are going to be the early adopter surgeons that understand that there are no good solutions for these patients right now. And then there are going to be others that are going to wait. In terms of the amount of time that they'll look, typically 6 to 12 months, they're going to want to see some information that shows how these particular patients did. And so -- but typically, we'll run our clinical data out at least 2 years, if not 5 years. I hope that's helpful.

Operator: Our next question is coming from the line of David Saxon of Needham & Company.

David Saxon: I'll keep it to one as well. Just wanted to follow up on the revenue per case commentary. So I mean, it sounds like you'll start to see a benefit from Onyx here in the fourth quarter. And just given how early it is in the launch and I guess that's going to offset what you're seeing with INTRA, like, is it fair to expect some pricing tailwind or revenue per case tailwind as we go into 2027? Just any color there would be helpful.

Anshul Maheshwari: Yes. I mean I'll talk about 2027, David, once we close out the fourth quarter on a strong note, get through our planning and come on the other side. Historically, we've always assumed coming into the new year some ASP degradation, again, because of the portfolio mix evolving. What you've got in our story right now is you've got an exciting opportunity within interventional with SI joint dysfunction, where we are becoming the market leader in that space with the most comprehensive solution set. Reimbursement changes there could be another tailwind as assuming 27279 gets approved for office-based or in-office procedures. So you've got that on one side, which will be a big volume driver.

On the flip side, you've got Granite and Onyx with the new DRGs, but also the symbiotic nature of these products being used together in the same procedure, you should get a tailwind from that. So I think net-net, we'll talk about more on the ASP assumptions when you get into 2027. But all indications are you've got the volume benefit on both sides with Granite Onyx and Interventional, but you will have additional ASP upside from Onyx Granite.

Operator: Our next question is coming from the line of Daniel Stauder of Citizens.

Daniel Stauder: I'll try to keep it to one as well. Just thinking about operating expenses, I appreciate you giving those op leverage bands as we think about 2027 and beyond. But I think you mentioned that you expect to expand the sales force as well to try to keep up with some of this demand. So first, how much of an investment could that be? Is it fair to assume that they'll be mostly focused on Onyx and Bedrock? And then how should we think about any cadence in terms of spend in '27 with the potential rep adds and any incremental spend as you get the Onyx launch going?

Anshul Maheshwari: Yes. No, happy to take that question, Dan. So when we think about our operating leverage in the business, like I've always shared, it's driven by top line growth and our profitability performance reflects that inherent operating leverage that we've built. Now with a lot of the untapped opportunities that we see ahead of ourselves, both with the existing portfolio as well as new product launches, we do think the investments we want to make, whether it's on the R&D clinical side, like Laura talked about on the Onyx clinical side, we believe, is really important to continue to drive penetration and adoption there. In terms of the expansion of the sales force, we're going to be very thoughtful.

The reason to expand the sales force is going to be because we see specific markets where there are huge opportunities, whether it's within Interventional or whether it's with Granite Onyx to be able to drive growth there or in the SI joint fusion business as well. So we're not going to sacrifice productivity at the sales per territory. As we expand, we're going to be very thoughtful about it. And that's what gives us confidence in the continued operating leverage in the business of on the low end, the 1.25x, on the high end, the 1.75x, which should translate into expanded profitable dollars falling to the bottom line.

Operator: Thank you. And that concludes today's Q&A session. I would like to turn the call back to Laura for closing remarks. Please go ahead.

Laura Francis: I just want to say thank you to everyone for participating in today's call, and we also really appreciate your interest in SI-BONE. And finally, we look forward to seeing you all at upcoming conferences as well as non-deal roadshows. Thanks again. Goodbye.

Mortgage rates have mostly recovered today after yesterday's jump scare.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.18% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and two basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Traders expected that the Fed would vote to hold the federal funds rate steady on Wednesday, so that wasn’t much of a factor for mortgage lenders as they set rates.

In his post-meeting press conference, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that September’s rate increase is “starting to work some” toward moving inflation down to the Fed's 2% goal, but that central bankers don't have any firm conclusions yet. He also acknowledged that the Fed’s monetary policy actions hadn’t achieved price stability yet, but that they’re “working on it.”

This hints that if inflation data continues to trend upward, central bankers might raise the federal funds rate again at their December 8-9 meeting.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, dropped yesterday— a day too late for central bankers to consider it in their decision-making process.

The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on November 25.

Next week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build an even stronger case for the Fed to raise the federal funds rate again in December, because it would suggest that the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.68% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

» Stay informed: Check out NerdWallet's mortgage news hub for all our latest coverage.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

Maybe — but even personalized rate quotes can change until you lock. That’s because lenders adjust pricing multiple times a day in response to market changes.

#3100. How to Make a $50 Holiday Gift Feel Like $100

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Trade time and a little extra thought to enhance gifts this holiday season.

Each month, NerdWallet suggests one wallet win to help you feel more confident about your money. This month’s topic is making holiday gifts feel more valuable, and we’re going to show you ways to elevate a gift without overspending.

Making an inexpensive gift feel fancy is a winter challenge I relish.

As a relatively frugal person who often gets sticker shock when shopping for gifts, I’m always looking for creative ways to save money without diminishing the present. Over the years, I’ve developed a few strategies to make a $50 gift feel like it’s worth at least double that.

In the spirit of the season, I’m sharing these strategies with you. I hope you — and your recipients — find them as celebratory as I do.

What does your gift recipient love to do? It helps if they have a favorite hobby, sports team or other interest.

Let’s say your recipient likes to fish. Giving a gift card to a niche fishing store makes it feel far more valuable than the standard Amazon card because it shows that you considered who they are. And there are specialty stores for every hobby these days.

Maybe gift cards aren’t your go-to. You can easily enhance other gifts, too.

Paying $5 extra to engrave or embroider their name on the gift — whether it’s stationery, jewelry or a backpack — makes the item feel far more valuable than its price tag because it’s customized to the individual.

If you choose a gift that couldn’t have been given to anyone else, it increases its value.

Time required: A few extra minutes to think about your recipients’ preferences and apply them when shopping.

A vintage or thrifted scarf can be a wrapping paper alternative that also functions as a gift. Similarly, you could wrap a gift in tea towels, artwork or online prints that can be reused by the recipient.

Another idea: Wrap a gift in printed sheet music that contains a special meaning for the recipient.

Customizing the presentation of the gift elevates it without adding much to the expense.

Time required: Since you have to wrap the gift anyway, this method doesn’t need to take extra time. You’ll just need to find the cloth or paper you plan to use.

One of my favorite gifts in recent memory involved turning a family photograph into a Jane Austen-era image set on a bucolic English estate with the empire-waisted gowns to match. My mom is a big fan of Jane Austen, so I knew she would appreciate seeing the family in a Regency-style photo.

I hired an Etsy artist to transform my original image, but you may be able to do it yourself with a photo app. Similarly, you could create a custom song, illustration or other form of art made specifically for your recipient.

Adding your own creative spin on a gift shows you spent extra time thinking about the recipient to make something extra special for them.

Time required: Applying your own creativity can be time-intensive, but the process is enjoyable so it goes quickly.

I like to call this technique the hybrid gift approach: You buy something, then get crafty to transform the gift into something one-of-a-kind.

One of my favorite ways to do this is with a photo. I’ll buy a nice but inexpensive frame and then put a photo of the recipient, or the recipient alongside loved ones, inside it.

If the person you’re buying for posts on social media, you might not even have to ask them for a photo in advance. Instead, you can find a favorite one that they already shared and surprise them.

The options are endless, especially with online tutorials to help hone your crafting skills. Adding your own customization to a purchased gift makes it feel special, but doesn’t have to cost much.

Time required: Baking, crafting or creating can take several hours, but again, it’s an enjoyable process.

Experiential gifts tend to go over well, and you may even get to have some fun, too.

One year, I gave my mom a membership to a nearby art museum and tacked on an offer to attend an exhibit with her. We had something on the calendar to look forward to together, and she got the option to visit more times throughout the year.

My parents have given me memberships, too. More recently, they gave me one to a local nature center. It’s great because I can visit on my own or attend kid-friendly events at a discounted rate. It makes me feel part of the community, and I love supporting an organization that helps kids learn more about nature.

Another option is to donate to charity in a loved one’s name and then make plans to volunteer at the organization together.

Experiential gifts help create more family memories together, which is one of my favorite ways to celebrate the holidays.

Time required: Setting aside time to visit a museum or other destination can take an entire day, but it’s time well spent.

The bottom line is that giving a highly personalized gift adds value without eating too far into your own budget. Spend $50. Make someone feel like a hundred bucks.

If you’re following along with us on this monthly financial challenge, start by testing out the tips we shared today over the next few weeks. We’ll be back again next month to learn about setting money goals for the new year. And if you missed last month’s edition, take a look back at how to shop the holiday sales.
