#3092. Ichor (ICHR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Revenue surged 37% year-over-year as margins expanded and earnings doubled sequentially.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Ichor Holdings, Ltd. (ICHR -5.30%) reported third-quarter revenue growth and expanding margins driven by a rapid increase in customer demand across all semiconductor segments. Management stated the company is executing a capacity expansion plan to reach $3 billion in revenue potential within its existing manufacturing footprint, focusing on transitioning facilities in Malaysia and Mexico to high-volume production. The company reported increasing proprietary content within its systems and expanding component sales to tool platforms outside its traditional gas delivery business to drive earnings leverage. Management confirmed that 2027 is expected to be a year of sequential quarterly revenue growth, with earnings projected to grow at twice the rate of the top line.

Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to Ichor's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this call is being recorded. I would now like to introduce your host for today's conference, Claire McAdams, Investor Relations for Ichor. Please go ahead.

Claire McAdams: Thank you, operator. Good afternoon, and thank you for joining today's third quarter 2026 conference call. As you read our earnings press release and as you listen to this conference call, please recognize that both contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws. These forward-looking statements are subject to a number of risks and uncertainties, many of which are beyond our control and which could cause actual results to differ materially from such statements. These risks and uncertainties include those spelled out in our earnings press release, those described in our annual report on Form 10-K for fiscal 2025 and those described in subsequent filings with the SEC.

You should consider all forward-looking statements in light of those and other risks and uncertainties. Additionally, we will be providing certain non-GAAP financial measures during this conference call. Our earnings press release and the financial supplement posted to our IR website each provide a reconciliation of these non-GAAP financial measures to their most comparable GAAP financial measures. On the call with me today are Phil Barros, our CEO; and Greg Swyt, our CFO. Phil will begin with an update on our business, and then Greg will provide additional details about our results and guidance. After the prepared remarks, we will open the line for questions. I'll now turn over the call to Phil Barros. Phil?

Philip Barros: Thank you, Claire, and welcome, everyone, to our Q3 earnings call. We are pleased to report another quarter of strong growth and expanding profitability. The strategic priorities we laid out a year ago continue to translate into results. Third quarter revenue of $329 million grew 12% sequentially and increased 37% compared to the same period last year. Year-to-date, Q3 revenue volumes represent a nearly 50% increase from our Q4 revenue trough, which is an unprecedented demand ramp across just 3 quarters. Gross margin of 16% exceeded the high end of expectations and increased 190 basis points compared to Q2, driving significant upside to earnings. Customer demand remains robust, and our visibility extends well into 2027.

With every segment of the semiconductor market ramping in unison, the pain points within the tightly constrained supply environment have clearly risen to the surface. Some of these constraints are impacting high-end edge and deposition applications. These advanced applications require highly precise gas delivery and highly precise gas delivery also represents Ichor's primary product offering. For example, high aspect ratio dielectric etch systems shipping into gate-all-around architectures and the most advanced DRAM fabs today call for pressure-based mass flow controllers in their delivery systems. And the majority of Ichor's products support exactly these types of high-end applications, which means that Ichor's product mix is heavily weighted to one of the industry's most pressing bottlenecks.

Let me spend a moment talking about how we adjusted shipments in Q3 in response to these continued constraints affecting gas delivery. Essentially, we focused on increasing gross profit dollars and generating significant earnings leverage in the face of revenue limitations. We expanded the reach of our component business into other areas of the systems we support. We secured new component wins during Q3 across 6 new tool platforms, which reside entirely outside of the gas panel. These wins broaden our opportunities for revenue growth and diversification as these programs ramp. While components carry lower ASPs than complete systems, they deliver a stronger earnings contribution per dollar of revenue.

We are seeing this benefit in our results and the pace of our earnings growth. We are also addressing supply risk directly with our product strategy by prioritizing the components that are most constrained, namely valves, fittings, substrates and soon flow control. We are working closely with our customers and suppliers to keep pace with demand. During this unprecedented ramp, we are executing ahead of plan on all the initiatives aimed at increasing our gross profit and earnings generation. There's no question that a demand ramp of this magnitude will continue to expose pain points in the supply chain. As an industry, we have worked through these challenges before, and we will again.

What you can count on from Ichor is that we will continue to deliver strong execution on all of our key profit drivers within our control. By delivering 16% gross margin in Q3, we are effectively 1 quarter ahead of plan. Our incremental gross margin in Q3 was 33%, well above our ongoing expectations of 25% to 30% as we increase the proprietary content in the gas systems we build for our customers. Our strategy to broaden component deliveries outside the gas box in Q3 also gave us an additional gross margin tailwind of favorable product mix.

Therefore, as you evaluate Ichor's results in Q3, we encourage you to look at gross profit generation, which was $3 million above the midpoint of guidance. This was much more meaningful to our earnings than $1 million of gas panel revenue. Our guidance for fourth quarter indicates continued sequential growth in revenues, gross margin and earnings per share. With our current visibility, we expect full year 2026 revenue growth of roughly 30%. The supply chain constraints that are affecting the high-end segments of etch and deposition are fully incorporated in our expected second half growth of 24% at the midpoint compared to at least 25% growth above the first half as we forecasted 1 quarter ago.

Importantly, we have increased net income by 100% sequentially every quarter this year. And in Q4, we expect to deliver earnings growth outpacing revenue growth once again. This type of earnings leverage and operating model improvement is exactly what our strategic initiatives set forth a year ago are intended to deliver. Turning to our key strategies to scale Ichor's capacity for the growth ahead. Last quarter, we discussed our plans to scale Ichor's capacity to $3 billion of revenue within our existing manufacturing footprint.

As we expand operations to this level, we are focused on 3 priorities: completing the alignment of our volume manufacturing footprint, increasing proprietary content, making strategic investments in machining capacity and adding headcount required to support next year's demand. I am pleased to report strong progress achieved in each of the 3 priorities during Q3. First, our manufacturing footprint. Our high-volume manufacturing sites in Malaysia and Mexico continue to ramp. Both machining and welding in Malaysia are qualified by both of our largest customers. All planned moves to Mexico are now complete. We are already seeing the benefits of this in our product margin.

Malaysia will continue to ramp through the fourth quarter of 2026 with additional capacity to continue to come online in 2027. Next, increasing proprietary content. We exited the third quarter ahead of plan of over 30% proprietary content within the gas systems we sell compared to 25% in Q2. We remain on track for about 35% proprietary content exiting the fourth quarter. Every point of in-house content improves our margins and reduces our reliance on outside suppliers. We are seeing strong growth in sales of proprietary content outside gas delivery systems. This will continue to be a focus for design wins as we continue to execute our strategy.

Now turning to our plans to transition existing brick-and-mortar into finished manufacturing capacity. This will happen in 3 phases. Phase 1 is converting the shelves in the clean room space. During the third quarter, we finished building out our planned clean room capacity that supports 2027 demand as described in August. Converting additional footprint in clean room capacity to support demand in 2028 and beyond requires about 3 to 4 months of lead time. Phase 2 is completing equipment orders and installation. For gas system integration, with clean rooms now in place, the largest remaining item is to install test fixtures, which are relatively low capital cost and shorten lead time.

And we can place these additional orders here as needed. We have expanded our welding capacity by nearly 2x ahead of the coming ramp. With our current visibility, this expanded capacity of weldments will support both our internal and external needs through 2027. We expect our capital spending in 2027 to chiefly support our proprietary products and machining capacity. These include flow control, valves, fittings and substrates. We received our first wave of new machining tools from Malaysia during the third quarter. They are now being installed and will ramp through the fourth quarter. All the equipment we need to support 2027 is now on order and is on track for installation within the next 6 months.

We have also partnered with qualified third parties to help us ramp our proprietary products faster with less capital. We have been qualifying these partners throughout the year. This additional capacity keeps us agile while meeting our margin targets for each products. Phase 3 is manufacturing headcount. We are hiring and training ahead of demand. This year, we have expanded manufacturing headcount by 40% through Q3 with 320 hires in Q3 alone to support the production ramp. We expect to execute on continued aggressive hiring plans for the next few quarters. To summarize, we are executing on a steep revenue ramp.

At the same time, we're expanding gross margins every quarter and achieved 16% gross margin, a full quarter earlier than expected. The operating model improvements we planned a year ago are delivering significant earnings leverage with greater than 100% growth in net income achieved every quarter year-to-date. Customer demand remains robust, and we are investing today to support our customers' growth into 2027 and beyond. We expect the structural improvements in our operating model to drive continued strong earnings leverage as revenues grow. As we look ahead in 2027, all evidence available today indicates that it will be a strong revenue growth year for all OEMs and subsystem suppliers within WFE.

While pain points in the supply chain are going to continue to emerge from time to time, we expect every quarter in 2027 will be a growth quarter for Ichor. We expect to deliver continued gross margin expansion as we move through the year, and we expect Ichor's earnings growth in 2027 will outpace revenue growth by over 2x. To sum up, within a WFE environment that supports solid revenue trajectory for all suppliers, it is Ichor's earnings growth story that truly sets us apart. And we look forward to continuing to deliver strong earnings leverage through this historic ramp. And with that, I will turn the call over to Greg to discuss our financials in greater detail.

Greg Swyt: Thanks, Phil. Before I begin, I would like to emphasize that the P&L metrics discussed today are non-GAAP measures. These measures exclude the impact of share-based compensation, amortization of acquired intangible assets, nonrecurring charges and discrete tax items and adjustments. There is a useful financial supplement available on the Investors section of our website that summarizes our GAAP and non-GAAP financial results, as well as a summary of the balance sheet and cash flow information for the last several quarters. Third quarter revenues of $328.7 million increased 12% sequentially and were up 37% year-over-year. Revenues came in within 0.4% of the midpoint of our guidance.

With Q3 product mix shifting more toward high-margin component sales, gross margin exceeded the high end of our guidance at 16%, up 190 basis points sequentially. Gross margin flow-through exceeded 30%, reflecting strong execution and increasing proprietary content in addition to the more favorable mix profile. Stronger gross margin drove the majority of upside in operating income. Q3 operating expenses came in below forecast at $24.4 million with a portion of expected spending increases now expected in Q4. Operating margin improved to 8.6%, up from 5.5% in Q2. EPS was $0.63, well above the high end of our guidance based on 38.2 million diluted shares outstanding. Both interest expense and tax expense were favorable to our earnings forecast.

Turning to cash flow. Adjusted EBITDA in Q3 was $33.9 million and after interest and taxes, cash generation from the P&L was roughly $30 million, a new 4-year quarterly record. In the current steep ramp of demand, we are quickly generating significant earnings leverage and cash flow from the P&L. At the same time, we must continue to invest in working capital to support the continued growth ahead. Total use of cash from operations was $29 million, reflecting $75 million of increase in inventory and receivables. These increases closely aligned to the revenue ramp with both inventory turns and DSO similar to Q2 at 3.6 turns and 39 days, respectively.

Capital expenditures were $10.7 million, supporting the expansion of clean room space and our next wave of new machining equipment. We ended the quarter with cash and equivalents of $213.5 million. Total debt at quarter end was $119 million, and our net debt coverage ratio was 0.8. Now turning to fourth quarter guidance. We currently anticipate Q4 revenues in the range of $345 million to $365 million. At the midpoint, this represents sequential quarterly growth of 8% and full year 2026 revenue growth of 30%. We expect Q4 gross margin will increase sequentially to 16.5%, plus or minus 0.5%. Our operating expense forecast for Q4 is $26 million, plus or minus $500,000.

Our EPS guidance of $0.65 to $0.75 assumes total interest and other expenses of $1 million, an estimated effective tax rate of approximately 15% and 38.5 million diluted shares outstanding. As we look to 2027, I will share a few parameters to give an early indication of how we are framing the shape of the year. We expect our revenue growth in 2027 to be aligned with our customers' growth in systems. Based on current visibility, those plans support sequential revenue growth every quarter. Given our expectation for another year of strong revenue growth ahead, we expect to deliver on continued gross margin expansion aligned with our new higher incremental gross margin model of at least 25%.

We currently expect operating expenses to increase around 15% for the full year 2027 as we invest in R&D and in the people required to support our growth. Current expectations are to manage OpEx growth to about 1/2 the rate of revenue growth as volumes increase, and we'll continue to update you on spending plans. We expect the most significant step-up in OpEx will be in Q1, reflecting hiring increases, annual adjustments for payroll taxes and benefits and other seasonal increases. For modeling purposes, we currently estimate total interest and other expenses of about $1 million per quarter as we move through 2027.

Based on the expected geographic distribution of profits next year, we are currently forecasting a slightly lower tax rate than the previous 20% to 25% rate. For now, we are estimating an effective tax rate of approximately 15% in Q4 and a range of 15% to 20% for fiscal 2027. Our acceleration of CapEx in 2026 currently estimated at approximately 4% of revenues will continue into 2027. We expect significant investments over the first half of 2027, given expected equipment deliveries. We will continue to add additional machining capacity in Malaysia and Mexico as well as complete the final build-out of clean room space in our Singapore facility.

While the investment may be skewed to the first half of 2027, we still expect the overall spending to be within our target of 3% to 4% of revenue for fiscal 2027. Our capital position remains strong with significant borrowing capacity and a current net debt coverage ratio below 1. With adjusted EBITDA generation in 2026 estimated to exceed $100 million, roughly 5x last year's level, we have significant financing flexibility available in order to support the working capital and CapEx investments necessary to execute on the strong growth ahead. In summary, our third quarter results demonstrate the earnings leverage of our operating models. Revenue is growing with our customer system shipments.

Gross margin is expanding faster than we planned, and our incremental margins are structurally higher. We believe this positions Ichor to convert revenue growth into strong earnings growth through 2027. Finally, a reminder that periodically, we must adjust our fiscal year-end to align with the calendar end and consistent with our prior practice, this adjustment will occur in fiscal 2027, which will have 53 weeks compared with 52 weeks in the current fiscal year. Operator, we are now ready for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Brian Chin with Stifel.

Brian Chin: Maybe the first one, and I have a follow-up will be on some of the supply and component constraints. Obviously, this environment for components has gotten tighter. Semi-cap OEMs have corroborated that. I guess looking at your 4Q revenue outlook, how much does the midpoint provide maybe more cushion or risk tolerance than in recent quarters? Or maybe said another way, is your line of sight to the midpoint of this revenue range better from a component supply standpoint than in recent quarters?

I guess that part B that, I'm sorry part B of that is just when do you have an impression or indication at this time in terms of when that kind of sub-tier component constraint could begin to ease some?

Philip Barros: Yes. I'd say a couple of things there, Brian. First thing is -- first of all, both great questions. I would say sitting here on November 2, I feel very, very confident that anything we're guiding today is what we're going to hit. We're guiding that for a reason. I will give you 2 little tidbits to keep in the back of your pocket. First one would be, I would say about half of the removal of about $10 million of revenue in Q4 was due to our commercial space business, as well as the component constraints we see in the semi space.

So I do want to just highlight there that there is a little bit of a pushout from our commercial space business due primarily to launch schedules. I wouldn't say it's positioned for wins. I'd say we feel really good about the wins that we've gotten. As you can imagine, some of those launch schedules have pushed out, and that's pushed out some of those revenues. With that said, what I would talk on top of that is, obviously, clearly, components are constrained. They're going to be constrained. We're an innovative industry. I believe that we will solve this. We've solved it before in the past. We'll solve it again.

So I feel very good that at this point in time in November 2, that we will definitely hit that midpoint based on today's visibility.

Brian Chin: Got it. And in terms of maybe is it too early at the time stamp, maybe when you could see maybe some decent progress made against some of those constrained headwinds?

Philip Barros: Yes. I would say a couple of things. In terms of our revenue linearity this quarter versus last quarter, first and foremost, our revenue linearity this quarter is significantly higher than it was last quarter. So I do feel the constraints are starting to loosen. With that said, as we've talked about before in the past, Brian, we figure we're going to be part of the solution long term. So I think the more and more of our products that we can bring online, the more and more we can relieve the constraints in the supply chain.

Brian Chin: And then maybe for the real follow-up here. The -- from a gross margin standpoint, obviously, better in the quarter than the top end of the guide. Can you help to quantify how much of that was the benefit from shifting gears and shipping more components to non-gas panel applications? And do you expect that to be an expanding tailwind into Q4? And is also lithography also a tailwind in terms of mix as well?

Philip Barros: Yes. I would say a couple of things there. Obviously, the more -- and you and I have talked about this in the past as well, the more we sell on components, the higher our ceiling is for gross margin. So clearly, one of our focus areas, and I think I introduced this back in January, one of our focus areas is clearly to sell components outside of our core gas delivery systems, so at a broader range. So I would say, in general, that is a path forward, and we're pushing that. That's a major focus for us from a design win perspective. And I would say a lot of that's converting into real revenue at this point.

So I feel good about that. In terms of litho, I think I may have discussed this in the past, but I see a small step-up in Q4, a large step-up in Q1. And as we talked about in the past, obviously, our litho customer is a good tailwind from a gross margin perspective as well.

Operator: Our next question comes from Craig Ellis with B. Riley Securities.

Craig Ellis: Congratulations on the gross margin progress. So I'll start there. Guys, we had 30% fall-through with gross margins in the quarter, and we're guiding to 25%. So can you help us understand what changes? Is it that there's just a little bit more gas panels coming back into the mix? Or was there just something unusual about the components mix in the quarter that gave us that 30% in 3Q?

Philip Barros: Yes. What I would say is, foundationally, our business has always been between 20% and 25% flow-through, about 20%, 25% flow-through in general. The fact that we're showing 30% flow-through this year kind of on average is a major step forward and showing that our strategy has really taken hold. With that said, our model going forward is 25% to 30%. So I would say 25% is the low end of the range, and that's where we expect to come in. To your point, you hit it right on the head is we do expect a bit more gas boxes to come through this quarter than we had last quarter.

That will bring down that average down to about the 25% range.

Craig Ellis: Yes. And then just going over to the capacity side and the ability to turn the knobs up, we're being optimistic, it sounds like, about our ability to match our customers' growth next year. So if they're coming in 30% to 35%. What are the things, Phil, that you feel like the business really needs to manage to grow at that level? And if their demand turned up by, call it, 10 to 15 percentage points in the year, do you have the flexibility with your supply chain to meet that?

Philip Barros: Yes. That's a great question. So clearly, the first thing we need to manage is the supply chain. So we're managing that kind of hand-in-hand and hand in glove with our customers. I would say that in general, like I said to Brian's question, I feel like we're an innovative group of people in this industry, and we'll figure it out. We always have, we always will. And I feel good about that loosening up over time. So with that said, I would say, in order to flex kind of maybe a 10% to 15%, it's really going to be people. And then on top of that, it's going to be supply chain.

So I would say it's those 2 levers. I feel really good about the capacity we're putting in place in terms of both for our internal content as well as our external content from a component standpoint and as well as our system business. We have built out the clean rooms. And I would say the ability to flex within our Malaysia factory within this time frame has really given us an opportunity to grow rather quickly and have some flexibility with our customers as we go forward.

Operator: Our next question comes from Krish Sankar with TD Cowen.

Unknown Analyst: This is Eddie for Krish. You talked about outgrowing WFE next year and growing -- earnings growing 2x that OpEx 15%. So does that imply like gross margins would stay around 17.5%, which would be incremental gross margins of 45%. I mean it seems like that's in line with your view, but a deceleration from what you just reported in Q3. What can take us back to above 30% incremental gross margin if my view on 2027 gross margins is true?

Philip Barros: Yes. What I would say is the way to accelerate our gross margins back to that level to that 30% flow-through is more and more components, right? And I talked about this quite a few times. It's all about accelerating the components. So we could see flowing through 30% if we have the right component mix. I think we can definitely hit that if that's the case.

Unknown Analyst: Got it. And regarding components, do you mean like increasing insourcing of mass flow controllers specifically?

Philip Barros: Yes. So I think about it in multiple ways. That's all of our proprietary content. And kind of what I wanted to introduce on this call, and maybe I haven't talked about it a lot, but we're seeing real good traction with it is selling those same components to other areas outside of the gas delivery system. That's actually offering a new platform for us to sell those components. And the more and more of those components we sell, the higher and higher that ceiling is for gross margin.

Unknown Analyst: Got it. And just a follow-up on that on timing, when should we expect that to show up in revenues and margins?

Philip Barros: Yes. So we're already seeing that today. And actually, if you saw that -- that's actually what helped us in Q3. So that's an ongoing progress that we're going through. You asked about flow control in particular, so I'm going to address that as well. What I would say is that what I've always said, which is a 2027 revenue event. I would say I've been in this industry and doing gas delivery for 25 years, and the appetite for change and the appetite for a new entrant like Ichor in flow control is higher than I've ever seen. So I would say that there's a lot of appetite for us to get that across the finish line.

And I still believe that's a 2027 revenue event.

Operator: Our next question comes from Charles Shi with Needham & Co.

Yu Shi: Greg, maybe I have maybe a hypothetical question. Let's say, a gas box you're delivering to a customer is short of MFCs, mass flow controllers. Are you able to ship? That's first. And then are you able to recognize at least a partial revenue out of that? This is a hypothetical question, but I think there's probably some relevance here.

Greg Swyt: Yes. Hi, Charles, this is Greg. I'll take that one. The answer is we are working with the customers to get clearance from them to enable us to ship if we do not have a specific component and in your example, the MFC. So we get the customers to authorize us to ship that. Once we get that, then yes, we can ship. And at this point, there is no material impact on revenue.

Yu Shi: Okay. So let's say the customer authorized the shipment, then you are able to recognize the that authorized the shipment, you are able to recognize the revenue without...

Yu Shi: Okay. But with some discount, I would assume or no.

Yu Shi: Like you can recognize the full amount or no?

Greg Swyt: Yes. For most part, we are recognizing full revenue. It's based on the arrangement with the customer on their authorization, the short ship, whether they're paying for the full value or we're holding back a portion of it. But for the most part, it is at full value.

Yu Shi: Got it. Got it. I know we're allowed one question, one follow-up, but may I ask another question?

Yu Shi: Yes. Okay. Great. So the internal -- the component -- I mean, maybe let me not call it the internal content yet. The components, I think there are 2 different ways for you to monetize, right? Either it goes into the gas panel, doesn't help with the revenue, but it helps with your profits or it goes out of the gas box, that's the contribution to both the revenue and the profits. So can you kind of quantify that for us that what happened in Q3 and maybe what you expect to happen in Q4, how much of that component upside really is about going into gas box versus outside of the gas box Q3 and Q4?

Philip Barros: Okay. Let me try to answer that clearly. But -- and if I don't, please feel free to follow up again. But what I would say is, we talked about our internal content. So the internal content went from, call it, 25% to 30% last quarter. We'll exit Q4 at around 35%. When you look at our external sale components, that is an area that's growing rapidly. Just to put a quantification behind it, if you will, quantity around it, think of it as from Q1 to Q4, it's grown by 250%. So we've grown that business by 250% now off of a small base, but quite a bit.

And I expect that to continue to grow between Q3 into Q4 and Q4 into Q1. And that's been a revenue driver for us through this year.

Operator: Our next question comes from Edward Yang with Oppenheimer.

Edward Yang: I just wanted to follow up on Charles' question. What will be the customer benefit of taking delivery of the gas panel without the MSC? I mean would they want like unfinished subsystem?

Philip Barros: Some of our customers -- so if you think about some of our customers, they have to test the tool before it shifts as a complete unit. So the benefit to them would be to take the subsystem test so they can test the overall functionality of the equipment and make sure that they're meeting their customer requirements. So that's really the benefit there. What I would say up to now, it's been pretty hit or miss whether or not that's something that they're willing to take or that they want to take. And so it's kind of on a case-by-case basis. What I would say is, in general, we don't plan on that.

What we plan on is shipping full boxes, and that's what we plan for. That's what we contemplated in our guidance, and that's what we contemplated in our build plan.

Edward Yang: Got it. And for my follow-up, given the continued high level of demand, how are you thinking about long-term agreements? Are customers increasingly willing to make binding commitments on inventory and capacity?

Philip Barros: Yes. What I would say for the most part, what our customers are doing is they are backstopping inventory positions. That's a practice that is, I would say, newer. They've always done a bit of backstopping, but I'd say that the amount of backstopping that they're doing is much lighter and much broader than they have in the past. So with that said, I would say that in general, what they're doing is making sure that we -- when we buy inventory and we place POs that we're not overextending ourselves. And they want to make sure that, that's inventory that's going to move for sure.

And so basically, the agreements we have with our customers, if it doesn't move for a period of time, then they own that inventory.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ben Taxdahl with Craig-Hallum Capital Group.

Benjamin Taxdahl: This is Ben on for Christian Schwab here. There's a lot of internal content commentary before I got on. But can you just share a little bit about your targets for '27? Do you expect that number to keep going higher past 35%?

Philip Barros: Yes. I would say in the near term, our short-term target is to get to 40% internal content. To get much beyond that 40%, that's going to take Flow Control. Flow Control, like I said before, is a 2027 revenue event. To get above that 40% of internal content, that's what that's going to take is Flow Control. My overall goal as a company is to get us to kind of 50-50 long term, but that's a long-term objective. That's not a near-term perspective, if you will. So long term is to get the 50-50 from a components and systems. That gets us well above our forecast.

Benjamin Taxdahl: And then my last question, just quickly on the $3 billion in capacity. Is that -- would that be with 25% margins at $3 billion? Or could we get to 25% closer to $2 billion? And then how should we be thinking about the time line of that capacity coming on?

Greg Swyt: Ben, I don't think we've positioned yet that we have a 25% gross margin target. It's a 20% gross margin target with that 25% to 30% incremental flow-through, right? So our target at $2 billion to $3 billion is still 20%. We may revisit that, but it's still 20%.

Operator: Our next question comes from Nazerke Baimukan with Freedom Broker.

Nazerke Baimukan: This is Na from Freedom Broker. Congratulations on the strong margin performance. So Phil, you mentioned that supply chain constraints are affecting high-end etch and deposition applications, including revenue limitations despite strong customer demand. So could you help us understand how significant these constraints are today and which components represent the biggest bottlenecks?

Philip Barros: There's always -- I would say there's about 4 components that keep me up at night or 4 suppliers that keep me up at night in any given day, and those 4 change every single day, right? So we have to spend a lot of time with our suppliers, making sure that they have the capacities we need and making sure that they have the parts when we need them where we need them. And that's what we do as a company. That's what we've done for over 25 years, and we're going to keep doing that. So I would say I feel good that while things pop up from time to time, we figure out ways to fix those.

With that said, I would say that supply chain constraints are fully contemplated within our guidance ranges. So that, to me, is where we think the constraints are and where they sit today. So what I would say is, in general, the supply chain is starting to ramp up and get caught up to where we need it to be, and I feel a lot more comfortable today than I would have even just a quarter ago.

Nazerke Baimukan: Yes. And a follow-up question would be, as you expand internal manufacturing of valves, fittings, substrates and eventually flow control components, could these investments help unlock additional revenue opportunities? Or are they primarily aimed at reducing supply chain risks and protecting existing shipments?

Philip Barros: Yes. I think the short answer to that is yes. What I would say is our initial thought of the strategy or take on the strategy was really to increase our internal margins and our gross margins and our -- by becoming vertical in the systems that we make. As we've matured this process and we've gotten through kind of to where we're at today, we see a significant opportunity for us to sell these same components outside of the gas delivery systems that we build. So, we see a lot of opportunities to grow revenue, not just gross margin and not just vertical content by going directly after these components in different areas of the tool.

And actually, that's exactly what happened in Q3. We saw some areas where we can win qualification positions, and we did that. And those are the same proprietary components that we talked about that go into our gas systems can also be used in other areas of the tool.

Operator: We have reached the end of our question-and-answer session as there are no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn the floor back over to Phil Barros for closing comments.

Philip Barros: Thank you, operator, and thank you, everyone, for joining our call today. A year ago, we laid out our plan to build a structurally stronger Ichor. In Q3, we reached our fourth quarter gross margin target a full quarter ahead of schedule. I want to thank our employees for making that possible while taking on an exceptionally steep ramp. I have complete faith in this team, and I'm proud of what we are accomplishing together. We will keep executing on what's under our control, supporting our customers' growth, expanding gross margin and converting revenue growth into strong earnings leverage. We look forward to updating you on our Q4 call in February.

In the meantime, please reach out to Claire to arrange any follow-up meetings. Operator, you can conclude the call.

Operator: This concludes today's teleconference. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation.

#3086. 3 Genius Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks to Buy Hand Over Fist Before Year-End

While AI and memory stocks get hammered on bubble fears, these three companies just posted sold-out demand, record revenue, and raised guidance.

Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have been getting hammered for weeks now, and the headlines all sound the same: bubble fears, AI financing anxiety, investors suddenly nervous that the hundreds of billions pouring into data centers won't pay off. None of that is made up; the sell-off is real, and some of these stocks have dropped 20%, 30%, even 40% from their highs. Here's the thing I keep coming back to, though: Price drops driven by fear tend to be the ones worth paying attention to, because they often have almost nothing to do with whether the underlying business is actually struggling.

When a stock falls because its own numbers disappointed, that's one kind of signal. When it falls because the whole sector got spooked by a headline, that's a different kind of opportunity. These three companies are showing you exactly that gap right now, between what the stock price is doing and what the business is actually doing.

Micron Technology (MU -5.78%) makes the memory chips that power AI processors, and it's been caught up in the broader memory-stock rout, like the rest of the industry. Here's what that sell-off is ignoring: Micron's high-bandwidth memory is sold out for all of 2026, the company has already locked in roughly $100 billion in take-or-pay contracts and $22 billion in customer deposits, and it still can't fill half the AI-driven demand coming its way. That's not a company bracing for a slowdown; it's really a company turning away business. Micron posted record quarterly revenue of $41.46 billion and guided to around $50 billion for the following quarter. A stock sliding on bubble fears while its own order book says the opposite is exactly the kind of disconnect worth buying into.

Astera Labs (ALAB -11.22%) makes the connectivity chips that let AI processors talk to each other and to memory inside a data center rack, unglamorous plumbing that happens to be essential. Second-quarter revenue grew 104.5% year over year, and the company just unveiled a new rack-scale architecture, Orion, built to support up to 160 accelerators in a single pod, a sign it's racing to keep pace with how fast AI hardware is scaling. The honest risk here is customer concentration: a handful of hyperscalers account for most of Astera's revenue, so any pullback from one of them would sting. But a company growing revenue that fast while expanding its product line isn't the profile of a business that's run out of room, it's the profile of one that just got caught in a sectorwide mood swing.

Vertiv Holdings (VRT -3.55%) sells the power and cooling systems that keep AI data centers from overheating, which sounds boring until you remember that every AI chip ever sold needs somewhere to run and something to keep it cool. Vertiv's third-quarter results beat estimates, and management raised full-year net sales guidance to $13.5 billion to $14 billion, yet the stock still sits well below its earlier high this year, dragged down by the same hyperscaler spending worries hitting everything AI-adjacent.

The company has also been buying its way into adjacent capabilities, picking up a microgrid developer and two liquid-cooling specialists this year, building out a fuller stack of what a next-generation data center actually needs. A business raising guidance while its stock gets punished for sectorwide anxiety is the definition of a gap between price and reality.

I'm not going to pretend none of this carries risk. AI capital spending could genuinely slow, and all three of these stocks would feel it if that happens. But that's a different risk than the one the market is currently pricing in, which is closer to panic than analysis. Each of these companies backed up its business with real numbers this earnings season: record demand, raised guidance, sold-out production, while the stock price moved in the opposite direction. That gap doesn't last forever. Buying into fear only works when the fear turns out to be bigger than the problem, and based on what these three companies just reported, that's exactly where we are right now.

Micah Zimmerman has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology and Vertiv. The Motley Fool recommends Astera Labs. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates kicked off the week with a drop, but they’re still above 7%.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3080. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3069. Tactile (TCMD) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Lymphedema revenue surged 13% as Medicare prior authorization stabilized.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Tactile Systems Technology, Inc. (TCMD -0.74%) reported revenue growth for the third quarter, supported by performance in its core lymphedema business line. Management reported that stabilization in Medicare prior authorization requirements supported a return to growth in lymphedema revenue, helping to offset a decline in airway clearance sales attributed to distributor inventory transitions. The company implemented organizational updates, including the appointment of a new Chief Operating Officer and the formation of a strategic accounts team to focus on large health systems. The company stated that technology investments in order management have improved internal efficiency, while clinical evidence progress led to expanded commercial payer coverage for specific lymphedema therapies. Management raised its full year adjusted EBITDA outlook while maintaining total revenue guidance for 2026.

Operator: Welcome, ladies and gentlemen, to the Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call for Tactile Medical. [Operator Instructions] Please note that this conference call is being recorded and will be available on the company's website for replay shortly. I would now like to turn the call over to Sam Bentzinger, Investor Relations at Gilmartin Group for a few introductory comments. Please go ahead.

Sam Bentzinger: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining today's call. Sheri Dodd: Thanks, Sam. Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to our third quarter 2026 earnings call. Here with me is Elaine Birkemeyer, our Chief Financial Officer. We delivered total revenue of $91.9 million in Q3, led by a 13% year-over-year growth in lymphedema, marking our fifth consecutive quarter of above-market double-digit growth. This consistency demonstrates the durability of our leadership position and the substantial runway created by a market that remains significantly underpenetrated. Airway clearance revenue was $10 million, down year-over-year as anticipated due to the onetime DME inventory transition associated with the launch of our next-generation AffloVest system. The same DME customers we highlighted in Q2 continued to work through temporary excess inventory during Q3.

There were no material changes in the underlying dynamics of the business, and we continue to expect airway clearance revenue to improve sequentially in the fourth quarter. Across the portfolio, we continue to balance strong growth in our core lymphedema business with disciplined execution. Gross margin expanded 90 basis points year-over-year in Q3 to 76.7%, contributing to adjusted EBITDA of $14.3 million. This marks the 12th consecutive quarter of year-over-year gross margin expansion. Importantly, we have achieved this sustained improvement while continuing to invest in our product offerings to deliver greater value to patients and providers.

Based on our year-to-date performance and our expectations for the fourth quarter, we are maintaining our full year 2026 revenue guidance of $360 million to $366 million and raising our adjusted EBITDA guidance to $50 million to $52 million. This outlook reflects our continued confidence in low double-digit growth in our business and our expectation for sequential improvement in airway clearance revenue in the fourth quarter. We expect full year airway clearance revenue to decline mid- to high single digits year-over-year. I'll now turn a closer review of our lymphedema business line, including Q3 performance and recent progress against our 3 strategic priorities. Elaine will then review our financial results and the outlook for the remainder of the year.

Lymphedema remains our core business and primary growth. Our Q3 results demonstrate our market leadership in both basic and advanced pneumatic compression devices with revenue growing 13% year-over-year to $81.8 million. Sequentially, lymphedema revenue grew 11%, supported by a recovery from the Medicare ordering timing disruption associated with the April implementation of prior authorization requirements. As expected, the prior authorization process has stabilized as our teams and the MACs have gained experience with the new requirements, and we believe this timing disruption is now behind us. Medicare revenue returned to growth in Q3, up 11% year-over-year. Beyond Medicare stabilization, the quarter's performance was driven by execution across several key drivers.

Our go-to-market investments in sales reps and CRM technology are extending the reach and impact of our commercial organization. Clinic visits increased 19% year-over-year in the third quarter, and referring clinics grew more than 10% year-to-date. These results are enabled by enhanced market insights that help our teams identify and prioritize referral opportunities across our account base. Our clinician-focused marketing programs are also delivering measurable returns with select events generating 20% to 45% order growth from participating accounts in the 90 days following the event compared to the 90 days prior. And through our medical education team, we have educated more than 13,000 clinicians who treat lymphedema patients so far in 2026, already 25% more than in all of 2025.

This expands the number of providers equipped to identify patients and refer them to appropriate therapy. Additionally, broader patient access to advanced pumps remains durable following our tighter alignment with the NCD policy, and this is reflected in our product mix. As part of the next phase of our go-to-market playbook, this quarter, we established a dedicated strategic accounts team within our broader commercial organization. This team will focus on deepening engagement with larger health systems and IDNs while expanding referral opportunities within existing high-volume regional and national accounts. Taken together, these trends give us confidence in our ability to deliver sequential lymphedema growth in Q4.

We are beginning to see benefits from investments in our operating model and order process, which are improving efficiency and service quality as patients move from referral to therapy. The strong prior year comparison next quarter resulting from the initial benefit of our alignment with the NCD will moderate year-over-year growth but does not change our confidence in the underlying momentum of the business. Looking beyond our third quarter results, we are executing well on our 3 strategic priorities designed to sustain double-digit growth, expanding access to care, creating value across the patient journey and expanding treatment options. Together, these priorities form a compelling growth model, supporting performance today while strengthening the drivers for sustained lymphedema performance over time.

As with most market development opportunities, growth starts with diagnosis. Patients must first be identified, diagnosed and referred before we can help them access clinically appropriate therapy. Expanding access to care means helping more patients get diagnosed and referred into the care pathway, but a referral is only the beginning of the order process and growth also requires pulling a higher percentage of referrals through to shipments. Today, not every diagnosed patient with lymphedema makes it through the documentation and order process necessary to receive therapy. And each patient lost along the way is a diagnosed patient who potentially goes underserved.

Creating value across the patient journey is about closing the gap and converting more eligible referrals to shipments, which is where we serve the patient and how we generate revenue. And expanding treatment options supports every step of that pathway. A broader portfolio gives clinicians more solutions for their patients, supports more additional referral opportunities and extends the patient populations and disease stages we can serve. As these capabilities scale, we also expect greater productivity and operating leverage to support adjusted EBITDA growth over time. Put simply, sustained growth in our lymphedema business is not solely a function of adding sales representatives.

It comes from helping more patients get diagnosed and referred, supporting more of those referrals so they can reach therapy and expanding the range of patients and therapy needs we can address. Our first priority is expanding access to care through earlier diagnosis and broader patient coverage. The opportunity is significant. An estimated 20 million people in the U.S. are living with undiagnosed lymphedema and many diagnosed patients continue to face coverage barriers. Our LymphaTech 3D Scanner currently gives clinicians an FDA-cleared quantitative way to measure limb volume and circumference, supporting earlier and more consistent identification of the disease.

We are encouraged that LymphaTech is currently in use and generating revenue at leading academic medical centers, even ahead of an established reimbursement pathway, demonstrating its utility in clinical practice. We recently achieved an important regulatory milestone, receiving FDA 510(k) clearance for an expanded indication of the LymphaTech 3D Scanner. LymphaTech is now cleared to provide circumference and volume measurements to aid in the assessment of lymphedema. This expands LymphaTech's clinical positioning beyond measurement and surveillance alone, and this expanded indication strengthens the foundation for our broader diagnostic strategy, including our work on clinical adoption, reimbursement and further integrated diagnostics.

On LymphaTech 3D Scanner reimbursement, our application for a Category III CPT code was discussed during our Q2 earnings call and is scheduled for final review at the February 2027 meeting. While a Category III code is a tracking code rather than a coverage decision, it is an important step towards broader reimbursement. Together, these regulatory milestones are intended to support wider adoption of LymphaTech, enabling earlier and more objective identification of lymphedema and monitoring of fluid over time and ultimately helping bring more patients into the care pathway. We are also making progress in broadening payer access for patients who already have been diagnosed with lymphedema.

Following publication of the 6-month results from our randomized controlled trial of Flexitouch therapy for head and neck cancer-related lymphedema, we have begun to see movement among commercial payers with a small number removing restrictive experimental and investigational designation from their policies. Significant work remains, but these early policy changes demonstrate that our clinical evidence and payer engagement can expand coverage over time, opening access to therapy for more eligible patients and supporting additional referral opportunities. Our second priority is creating value across the patient journey. While we see opportunities to improve the experience at every stage of care, our current focus is on the highest impact stage of the journey, helping more eligible patients successfully start therapy.

By reducing friction in the upfront documentation and order process, we can improve conversion from referral to shipment and ensure more patients receive the therapy prescribed by their clinician. This benefits patients, simplifies the experience for referring clinicians and their staff and supports a more efficient and stable operating model. Ultimately, increasing access to therapy is a key driver of both patient value and sustainable growth. During the quarter, we made organizational and operating model changes to strengthen how orders move from referral to shipment. We also continue to replatform our end-to-end order process through our AI-enabled order management platform and care navigation work.

Together, these efforts are designed to reduce friction, improve visibility into patient progression and strengthen execution across the referral to shipment process. We are already seeing tangible results in medical record review, one step within the broader order process, where technology-enabled improvements have reduced average review time by approximately 50%. While meaningful work remains, this early result demonstrates the potential to improve service levels, increase capacity and support future order growth more efficiently as we extend these capabilities across the end-to-end process. Building on this progress, we are taking another important step in the evolution of our operating model. As announced today, Steve Kiewiet, is joining Tactile Medical as Chief Operating Officer.

In this newly created role, Steve will lead our order operations and patient services teams, connecting capabilities that support a patient from referral through shipment into one operating organization. This structure will enable more coordinated decision-making across the full journey and help us extend process improvements more broadly, creating a better experience, greater capacity and a more scalable operating model. Steve brings breadth and depth of experience in revenue cycle management, field-based patient educators, call center and DME operations. This is the right time to bring an executive level enterprise operations leader to our team, and we are excited to have him on board. Our third priority is expanding treatment options.

A broader innovation portfolio allows us to address more patient needs, support additional referral opportunities and serve patients across a broader range of disease stages. We are advancing opportunities that complement our core pneumatic compression therapies and expand the patient populations we can address. Consistent with our previously stated commitment, a significant milestone came in October when we filed a 510(k) application for Flexitouch Pro, a meaningful enhancement to our advanced pneumatic compression system. Flexitouch Pro is designed to improve the patient and clinician experience through usability and connectivity enhancements that simplify therapy administration while delivering the clinical effectiveness that has made Flexitouch the long-standing market leader.

Subject to completion of the regulatory process, we are targeting a commercial launch of Flexitouch Pro in the second half of 2027. This innovation is intended to reinforce our leadership in advanced pneumatic compression and increase the value we deliver through our core franchise. We are also preparing to introduce MyoSleeve in the U.S. through our partnership with ElastiMed. Our next milestone is a focused VA pilot beginning in late Q4, which will help us evaluate the patient experience, clinical fit and appropriate go-to-market model before broader commercialization. MyoSleeve is not reflected in our 2026 guidance, and we expect its contribution to build gradually over time.

Strategically, it represents an opportunity to serve additional patients and expand the range of therapy needs our portfolio can address. Overall, we remain confident in the durability of our lymphedema business and the opportunities ahead in 2027 and beyond. Each of our strategic priorities is at a different stage of development and their impact will build over time. Collectively, they are designed to strengthen the fundamental drivers of our lymphedema business, more patients being identified and referred, more eligible patients receiving therapy and a broader range of patients and care needs we can serve. That is the growth model we believe can support durable revenue growth and improving profitability over time.

With that, I'll turn the call over to Elaine to review our financial results and full year outlook.

Elaine Birkemeyer: Thanks, Sheri. Unless noted otherwise, all references to third quarter financial results are on a GAAP and year-over-year basis. Third quarter total revenue was $91.9 million, up $6.1 million or 7.1% as double-digit growth in lymphedema more than offset the expected decline in airway clearance. By product line, revenue from our lymphedema products, including Flexitouch, Nimbl and LymphaTech increased $9.5 million or 13.1% to $81.8 million. Lymphedema growth was broad-based across payer channels with Medicare revenue increasing approximately 11% and commercial revenue increasing approximately 17% year-over-year, while VA revenue was approximately flat. Revenue from our airway clearance product, AffloVest, decreased $3.4 million or 25.1% to $10 million, consistent with the DME inventory dynamics Sheri discussed earlier.

Year-to-date, total revenue increased 12% to $252.8 million, led by 15% growth in lymphedema. Moving down the P&L. Gross margin expanded to 76.7% of revenue from 75.8% in the third quarter of 2025. The increase primarily reflected lower manufacturing costs and favorable product mix and was consistent with the expectations embedded in our full year outlook. Third quarter operating expenses increased $6.9 million or 12.7% to $60.9 million. The increase primarily reflected the annualization of prior year sales force hiring and continued investment in technology and other capabilities supporting our growth. These investments are directed at the growth drivers Sheri outlined, generating referrals, converting more referrals to shipment and expanding our portfolio.

By expense category, the increase in operating expenses reflected a $3.2 million increase in sales and marketing expenses, a $0.3 million increase in research and development expenses, a $3.2 million increase in reimbursement, general and administrative expenses and a $0.1 million increase in intangible asset amortization and contingent consideration. Operating income was $9.6 million compared with $11 million in the prior year period. Net interest income was $0.5 million, consistent with the prior year period. Income tax expense was $3 million compared to $3.2 million in the prior year period. Net income was $7.2 million or $0.31 per diluted share compared with $8.2 million or $0.36 per diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.

Adjusted EBITDA was $14.3 million compared to $14.4 million in the prior year period, and adjusted EBITDA margin was 15.6% compared to 16.8%. Gross margin improved 90 basis points, while higher operating expenses, including the annualization of prior year sales force hiring and continued investment in technology and operating capabilities more than offset that improvement. Year-to-date, adjusted EBITDA has increased approximately 35% to $29.5 million, and we continue to expect adjusted EBITDA growth for the full year. Over time, as our investments mature and scale, we expect operating expenses to grow more slowly than revenue, supporting operating leverage and adjusted EBITDA growth.

On the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with $75.1 million in cash and no outstanding borrowings, up from $69.9 million at the end of the second quarter. During the third quarter, we generated $12 million in operating cash flow, which more than funded approximately $6.2 million in share repurchases. As of September 30, 2026, approximately $12.5 million remained available under our $25 million share repurchase program. Our capital allocation priorities are unchanged. We will continue to invest in the commercial, operational and strategic capabilities that support organic growth, preserve capacity for disciplined M&A and repurchase shares when we believe valuation is attractive and doing so does not constrain our strategic priorities. Now turning to our outlook.

As Sheri mentioned, we are maintaining our full year 2026 revenue guidance of $360 million to $366 million, representing growth of approximately 9% to 11% year-over-year. Stronger lymphedema performance is offsetting a lower airway clearance outlook. In lymphedema, we continue to expect low double-digit growth for the full year. For the fourth quarter, we expect meaningful sequential growth with a moderation in year-over-year growth compared to recent quarters as we lap a particularly strong fourth quarter of 2025 when lymphedema grew 16% on the initial benefit of NCD alignment. In airway clearance, we now expect full year revenue to decline in the mid- to high single digits compared with our prior expectation of approximately flat.

DME customers are taking longer than we initially expected to work through existing inventory as they transition to the next-generation AffloVest, so we now assume a more gradual normalization of ordering. This reflects ordering timing, not a change in patient demand or market leadership. We expect sequential improvement in the fourth quarter with revenue remaining below the prior year, consistent with our full year outlook. Our total revenue range mainly reflects the timing of lymphedema referrals converting to shipments in the fourth quarter, our seasonally largest quarter.

For modeling purposes, we expect the following for the full year: GAAP gross margin of approximately 76.5%, GAAP operating expense growth of 10% to 12%, net interest income of approximately $2.4 million, an effective tax rate of approximately 28% and fully diluted weighted average shares outstanding of approximately 23 million. We are raising our full year 2026 EBITDA guidance to $50 million to $52 million, representing growth of approximately 12% to 16% compared with $44.8 million in 2025.

Our adjusted EBITDA expectation includes the following adjustments: stock-based compensation expense of approximately $8.6 million, depreciation and amortization expense of approximately $7.3 million, executive transition costs of approximately $1.3 million, acquisition-related and integration costs of approximately $1.3 million and litigation-related costs of approximately $1 million. With that, I'll turn the call back to Sheri for some closing remarks. Sheri?

Sheri Dodd: Thanks, Elaine. To close, this quarter reinforced the strength and durability of our core lymphedema business. We delivered another quarter of double-digit lymphedema growth, expanded gross margins and generated strong cash flow while investing in the capabilities that can support our next phase of growth. Our opportunity extends well beyond the patients we serve today. By helping more patients get diagnosed and referred, converting more of those referrals to shipments and broadening the range of patients and therapy needs we can serve, we believe we can continue to expand the market we serve and increase the value we create along the patient journey. At the same time, we remain focused on translating that growth into greater operating leverage over time.

Our revenue guidance reflects our year-to-date performance and expectations for the remainder of the year, while our adjusted EBITDA guidance demonstrates continued financial discipline as we invest to support long-term growth. Finally, I'd like to thank our Tactile Medical employees for their continued commitment to our patients, our clinical customers and one another. With that, operator, we'll now open the call for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And our first question will come from Ryan Zimmerman with BTIG.

Sheri Dodd: Ryan, well, we're smiling here, and thanks for the shout out on the profitability piece. Definitely a lot of work has been done on that side, and appreciate you acknowledging that. I'm going to start with the last point first on the lymphedema business. We don't see any reason why there should be a slowdown. And in fact, the byproduct of more market awareness with the diagnostic coming into play with the continued, hopefully, favorable policies that support right patient, right pump at the right time.

And certainly, from our standpoint, our operating model and our footprint in the field, we believe that this is not a disease area or category or even from our business that would see a slowdown. So we're feeling very good about lymphedema as a core growth driver for our business and the market to be super favorable in that area. Your question about 2027. So we're not going to be putting any specific guides on 2027. But lymphedema business, we're feeling very confident in the durable growth, what you've seen over the past 5 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth, 13% in this quarter alone.

Ryan Zimmerman: Very helpful. And Flexitouch Pro, any considerations that we need to be thinking about whether from a price or a margin standpoint as you introduce that to the market? So there won't be any upside or anything different from what is actually the reimbursement from the code standpoint. Operator: And our next question will come from Adam Maeder with Piper Sandler.

Kyle Edward Winborne: This is Kyle on for Adam. I might just push my luck here again with a 2027 question. I know you're not providing guidance at this time. But from a P&L standpoint, 2025 was an investment year. 2026, there were a lot of investments made as well, while you were also still able to show some good EBITDA growth in both years. So just curious, maybe just at a high level, qualitatively, how are you thinking about that for next year? Should we expect to kind of continue to see some leverage while also still investing in growth? Anything around that could be helpful.

Sheri Dodd: Yes. Thanks for the question. So we have committed to operating leverage and we're -- that is our commitment, and we'll continue to see that into next year. This year, of course, we had some annualization of the sales rep head, and we continue to invest in our business, both in terms of the transformational platform for our order operations, and those investments will continue into 2028. But we expect to see ongoing leverage, and that is our goal to both grow top line as well as bottom line.

From a revenue perspective, and as I shared with my comments with Ryan, there's nothing that says anything is going to be going down, that's going to be pulling or the market becomes less attractive. There is a reality that there is a large proportion of patients that are underserved, and there's no automatic button that allows suddenly a whole bolus of patients to get diagnosed even though we have the 3D Scanner in our portfolio. There's a lot that needs to happen in order for these patients to get diagnosed. They still have to have the documentation. They still have to see their physicians.

So we believe that there is a healthy market there, but I also want to temper some expectations that there isn't just a sudden hockey stick that happens because now we will have the Flexitouch Pro and the 3D Scanner. Takes time, it's chipping, but we are in the best position to be able to demonstrate some durable, sustainable growth in a way that is going to return value to shareholders. Kyle Edward Winborne: Great. That's helpful. Yes, it did. That was great. And maybe just as a quick follow-up, congrats on the head and neck progress with payers. Just wanted to ask if you're willing to quantify how many wins you saw in removing some of that restrictive language? Sheri Dodd: Yes. And so we're not going to quantify or kind of call out the specific payers, but we did see some of those policies change that now have moved from E&I into covered. And so that gives us confidence that the evidence is resonating that payers are willing to change their policies. And then it's just kind of a block and tackle, block and tackle all the way down of getting that to change.

But that also takes some time and we'll build what we believe to be that pace into our 2027 revenue, but it won't be a hockey stick either. But the good news is more patients are going to get access to the only available therapy, compression pump therapy for the head and neck area post them surviving head and neck cancer. Operator: We'll go next to Brandon Vazquez with William Blair.
