#3059. Kosmos Energy (KOS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Production grew 6% as debt fell $500 million, signaling improved momentum.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Kosmos Energy Ltd. (KOS -13.33%) reported progress on its strategic objectives including production growth, cost reduction, debt repayment, and portfolio advancement. Management emphasized the successful completion of the infill drilling program in Ghana and the stable operational performance of its liquefied natural gas project offshore Mauritania and Senegal. The company successfully executed a farm-down of a development project in the Gulf of America to bring in a new partner and reduce capital obligations. Following the extension of its reserve-based lending facility, the company stated it is now focused on managing long-term bond maturities. Management noted that the current operational strategy prioritizes reservoir management and high facility uptime to sustain production levels ahead of future drilling campaigns.

Operator: Good day, everyone. Welcome to the Kosmos Energy's Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. As a reminder, today's call is being recorded. At this time, let me turn the call over to Jamie Buckland, Vice President of Investor Relations at Kosmos Energy.

Jamie Buckland: Thank you, operator, and thanks to everyone for joining us today. This morning, we issued our Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Release. This release and the slide presentation to accompany today's call are available on the Investors page of our website. Joining me on the call today to go through the materials are Andy Inglis, Chairman and CEO, and Neal Shah, CFO. During today's presentation, we will make forward-looking statements that refer to our estimates, plans, and expectations. Actual results and outcome could differ materially due to factors we note in this presentation and in our U.K. and SEC filings. Please refer to our annual report, stock exchange announcement, and SEC filings for more details.

These documents are available on our website. At this time, I will turn the call over to Andy.

Andrew Inglis: Thanks, Jamie, and good morning and afternoon to everyone. Thank you for joining us today for our Third Quarter 2026 Results Call. I will begin today's call by reviewing the progress we have made against the four goals we laid out at the start of the year before giving an update on each of our business units. I will then hand over to Neal to talk through the financials before I wrap up with closing remarks and a look towards 2027. We will then open the call up for Q&A. Starting on Slide 3. When we released our full year 2025 results in March, we laid out four key objectives for Kosmos in 2026, which is shown on the slide.

I am pleased to say through the first 3 quarters of the year, we have made excellent progress against all of them. We have seen strong year-on-year production growth from our core assets, namely Jubilee and GTA. We delivered significant absolute and per barrel equivalent cost reductions year-on-year, with a specific focus on operating costs. We delivered the majority of our net debt reduction target and are on track to achieve the 20% reduction target for the year, a target we increased with our first quarter results in May. We have continued to advance our high-quality growth portfolio, particularly in the Gulf of America, with minimal capital input.

By delivering this agenda, we expect to end the year with a more resilient and more valuable company, a company with higher production, lower costs, and lower debt, with significant upside from our hopper of future growth opportunities. We will also have higher exposure to elevated commodity prices as we enter 2027, which Neal will cover later in the materials. I'd now like to focus on the progress we're making in each business unit, starting with Ghana on Slide 4. We've seen a lot of progress in Ghana this year with an active drilling campaign that has delivered in line with our expectations and highlighted the potential of this mid-life asset.

The key to delivering Jubilee's full production potential going forward is demonstrating operational delivery, in particular reservoir management in the periods between drilling campaigns. In the third quarter, Jubilee gross production was 84,500 barrels of oil per day, an increase of around 17% versus the previous quarter, reflecting the new wells that came online in late 2Q and during the third quarter. Specifically, in August, the J50 producer well came online, and then in September, the J73 water injection well completed the program. Our annual guidance for Jubilee was 70,000 to 80,000 barrels of oil per day, with year-to-date production through end 3Q around 75,000 barrels of oil per day.

With the latest drilling program now complete, the partnership focuses on improving management of the reservoir to mitigate decline. This will require daily focus on operational delivery, namely sustained water injection or voidage replacement above 120%, continued production system optimization, adding gas lift to the west side of Jubilee, and high FPSO uptime of around 98% or above. As we look ahead, we're pleased to have contracted the Faye Kozack rig from Noble for the 2027/2028 drilling campaign of up to 10 wells, with the rig due to arrive in mid-2027.

The first new wells in the program will benefit from the most recent 4D seismic, with the ocean bottom node survey, or OBN, expected to play a major role in planning and high-grading the wells for the second half of the program. In Ghana, we have a government that wants to get things done. Last month at the African Energy Week in Cape Town, I shared the stage with the Chairman of the African Energy Chamber and Ghana's Energy Minister to talk about what we're doing as a partnership to help drive energy prosperity in Ghana. It was a productive and valuable discussion.

One of the key takeaways was if companies like Kosmos can help the country win through long-term investment, lower cost associated domestic gas, the transfer of knowledge and skills, then Kosmos will win, too. Ghana is a case study on how a government and a company like Kosmos can work together to get things done for the benefit of all stakeholders. Turning to Slide 5. GTA continues to perform strongly. During the third quarter, gross LNG production was around 2.44 million tons per annum equivalent, in line with expectations, with higher seasonal temperatures through the summer months as previously guided.

The partnership lifted 8.5 gross LNG cargoes, slightly ahead of guidance, which brings the total number of gross LNG cargoes lifted to the end of the third quarter to '27. The condensate cargo that was due to be lifted at the end of the third quarter was lifted in early 4Q due to bad weather in the region that prevented an earlier lifting, with Kosmos receiving just under 400,000 net barrels of condensate. For the year, the strong operational performance means we are on track to achieve the upper end of our 32 to 36 gross LNG cargo guidance. The three gross condensate cargoes for the year have now all been lifted.

Looking ahead to the expansion of the project, Phase 1 plus is making good progress with the construction of the onshore pipeline in Senegal well underway. The bottom image on the slide shows the first piece of the gas pipeline being laid in September. RGS, the operator of the gas pipeline, reported that the first phase of the onshore pipeline connecting the GTA hub to the 230 megawatt Gandon power plant is now over 25% complete. Further segments of the onshore pipeline connecting additional demand centers to the south are due to commence construction in 2027, with commissioning targeted for 2029.

As I said in my comments on the previous slide, our focus above ground is just as important as the work we do below ground. It is a core part of the Kosmos skill set as we work with the governments and national oil companies to maximize the value of the projects we undertake together. The last 2 months, we spent time with the presidents of both Mauritania and Senegal to talk about the future, as can be seen in the top image on the slide. I'm pleased to say we have a shared vision for the future that prioritizes lower-cost domestic gas alongside the LNG exports from Phase 1 and future phases.

This lower-cost domestic gas will replace higher-cost imported diesel and LNG and help both countries achieve their gas-to-power and gas-to-industry goals over the coming years. If the countries succeed in these goals, then Kosmos will also succeed. We look forward to advancing these goals in the future. Turning to Slide 6. Production in the Gulf of America for the third quarter of approximately 14,100 barrels of oil equivalent was in line with expectations, helped partly by the lack of storm activity during the quarter. This reversed in early 4Q, and Neal will talk about this in more detail shortly. During the quarter, we successfully completed a highly competitive farm-down on Tiberius, bringing Navitas into the project as a 33.33% partner.

Following the transaction, Kosmos will remain as operator with a 33.34% interest, with Oxy, owner and operator of the nearby Lucius facility, holding the remainder. As detailed on our last earnings call, the consideration was a mix of upfront cash, carry for future development CapEx, and future milestone payments. The carry is expected to cover all of our Tiberius CapEx through 2026 and fund our share of the development through the first half of 2027. Tiberius is a low-cost, high-margin development, and we now have an aligned partnership to move forward, with first oil expected in the second half of 2028. Elsewhere in the Gulf, our strategic exploration alliance with Shell is working well.

The partnership is now preparing to drill the Trailblazer ILX well in the first half of 2027, with Transocean's Deepwater Pontus rig contracted. Trailblazer is a 4-way structural trap in the Norphlet, on trend with several other discoveries, such as Shell's Appomattox field. In a success case, the discovery could be tied back to the nearby Appomattox facility, which has available capacity, with Kosmos designated development operator. Beyond Trailblazer, there are several other high-quality opportunities in the Norphlet that we expect to advance as part of the Shell Exploration Alliance.

We are excited to be getting back to exploration in the Gulf and doing it in a capital-efficient way that allows us to test meaningful resource opportunities at a relatively low cost. I will now turn it over to Neal to take you through the financials.

Neal Shah: Thanks, Andy. Turning now to Slide 7, which looks at the financials for the third quarter in detail. It has been another strong quarter for the company, with production higher year-on-year and OpEx falling sharply in line with the targets Andy mentioned at the beginning of today's presentation. All of the line items for the quarter were in line with our guidance, except for DD&A, which was slightly higher than our guidance range due to a minor accounting change to the depletion rate in Jubilee for the quarter, with our full-year DD&A guidance unchanged. Also, tax per barrel was lower in the quarter, reflecting the mark-to-market derivatives loss that offset some of the revenue during the quarter.

Excluding the mark-to-market, tax expense was in line with our expectations. Looking ahead to Q4, net production is expected to be lower quarter-on-quarter, driven by a combination of lower Gulf of America and Ghana production. In the Gulf, fourth quarter production is impacted by planned maintenance at Delta House, the host facility for the Odd Job field, a workover at the Kodiak field, and downtime associated with Hurricane Isaias. In Ghana, with the drilling campaign now complete, the partnership is focused on reservoir management to mitigate decline at Jubilee before the next drilling campaign begins in mid-2027. Also in the fourth quarter, there will be financing costs of around $20 million related to the extension of the RBL.

Turning to Slide 8. Cost reduction has been a big theme across the company this year, particularly on operating costs after similar initiatives on CapEx and G&A last year. We are making a lot of progress, and the charts on the slide show how far we have come year to date. The top left chart shows that absolute operating costs have fallen by almost $150 million in the first 9 months of the year, a reduction of around 26%. OpEx per barrel has fallen around $12 per barrel, a reduction of around 37% on a per-unit basis.

This focus on cost management and a higher commodity price backdrop has seen EBITDAX almost double in the 9 months ended September 30 to almost $800 million, which has translated into robust free cash flow with more expected in the fourth quarter. We now expect around $300 million of free cash flow in 2026, net of any hedging impact, which is expected to be around $200 million for the year, demonstrating the cash flow potential of the business. As we look forward to 2027, our hedges have been put in at much higher levels than 2026, giving us greater exposure to higher prices with a lower cost base.

Turning to Slide 9, it has been a busy year for financing, and I am pleased to report we recently closed the reserve-based lending facility extension to April 2033. The facility amendment and extension is another demonstration of the company proactively addressing its maturities and the continued confidence in Kosmos' portfolio from the banking market. I would like to thank our banks for their continued support, many of whom have been with Kosmos for well over a decade. On liquidity, the strong cash flow performance in the third quarter meant we exited Q3 with around $570 million of available liquidity. We expect this to strengthen further in the fourth quarter.

On hedging, we continue to be active, adding what are likely to be the final hedges for our 2027 program. As mentioned on the previous slide, we have been able to achieve a higher average floor and a much higher average ceiling on the collars we have put in place for next year, giving us more exposure to the upside in a higher price environment. On the debt, in 3Q, we utilized our free cash flow to repay $50 million of the 2027 bonds, $15 million of the GOA term loan, and $25 million of the RBL.

In Q4, with the RBL now complete, we plan to prioritize our free cash flow towards our bonds with a view of addressing our 2028 maturities next. Finally, on leverage, with the strong year-to-date EBITDAX performance and significant debt reduction, leverage is moving towards 2x by year-end, a significant turnaround in only 12 months. With that, I will hand it back to Andy.

Andrew Inglis: Thanks, Neal. Turning now to Slide 10. As I said in my opening remarks, we have four key objectives for 2026: grow production, lower costs, reduce debt, and advance our quality growth portfolio with minimal CapEx in 2026. This slide shows the progress we have achieved year to date against those goals. Production for the first 9 months of 2026 is up 14% versus the same period last year without adjusting for the sale of EG. As Neal said, absolute operating costs are down 26% the first 9 months of the year, driving a reduction in OpEx per BOE of around 37%.

We delivered a reduction in net debt around 70% versus year-end 2025 and are well on track to achieve our 20% target. We are advancing our growth portfolio with the Tiberius farm-down, continued progress on GTA expansion, and the exploration alliance with Shell in the Gulf of America, which will drill the Trailblazer well in the first half of 2027. Turning now to Slide 11 to conclude today's presentation. We have been clear on our targets for 2026 and are delivering on them. As we approach the end of the year, we are turning our focus to 2027, where we have a lot to look forward to.

We have a deep opportunity set across the portfolio, and in 2027, we plan to continue to invest selectively in our highest quality growth options while maintaining the capital discipline we have displayed this year. We are returning to drilling in Ghana with another high-return infill program that is being enhanced with modern seismic to drive better results and higher recovery over time. Jubilee is a world-class mid-life field, and with regular drilling and excellence in reservoir management to mitigate decline, there is a huge amount of value to chase in the future. We are making good progress on the GTA expansion, with the construction of the onshore pipeline started in Senegal.

As I said in my earlier remarks, we have an aligned agenda with the government to make this work for the benefit of all stakeholders. We are returning to exploration with a high-impact Trailblazer well in the first half of 2027, with significant potential elsewhere in the Norphlet. We believe our continued investment in people and technology will make a real difference in growing our resource base. Finally, we remain focused on enhancing the company's financial resilience, paying down more debt, targeting year-end 2027 net debt of around $2 billion at strip prices, while addressing the rest of our near-term maturities.

We are working hard to deliver stronger and more valuable Kosmos, and look forward to delivering on these plans to support long-term value creation for our investors. Thank you, and I would now like to turn the call over to the operator to open the session for questions.

Operator: Our first question comes from the line of Charles Meade with Johnson Rice.

Charles Meade: Andy, I would like to ask a question about the cargo guidance for Ghana in Q4. I think many of us on the streets, I would be in that number, we are looking for four cargoes from Ghana in 4Q, and it seems like exiting 3Q with a 1.1 net million barrels underlift position would be a good starting point to achieve that. But of course, there are other variables, too. There are the production rates from Jubilee, there is how you expect to exit the quarter on underlift or overlift.

For those of us who it looks like there is a cargo short of what we were looking for, I wonder if you could talk through that bridge from where you are entering the quarter and what you expect from field performance over the course of 4Q, and why three is the number that we should be looking for.

Andrew Inglis: Yes. Thanks, Charles. I want to start really with back to where current performance is in Jubilee. As we mentioned in our prepared remarks, we ended the drilling campaign in September. We have had strong performance from that drilling campaign, and now it is all about managing the reservoir before we restart the program in mid-2027. The big things we are focusing on with the operator is improving the water injection. We need to get that back up above 120%. I think there are opportunities on production optimization around all the wells. Again, we need to focus on that day-to-day. On the west side of the field, we have got some planned riser gas lift to install.

Again, that will help production. And then it is about maintaining the high FPSO uptime. So all of that is going to drive ultimately where we end up in 4Q. And our objective is probably to exit the quarter around the mid-70s, something around there, Charles. And ultimately, with the cargo math, you cannot be precise because it depends on the lifting schedule for each company. Yes. I think it's better to talk about ultimately, how we're managing the production, and therefore the things that we see now that are going to drive the production. The cargo math really depends on each party's underlift and overlift, yeah? Other people can be underlifted as well.

Ultimately, we believe our best view is that turns out to be 3 cargoes in the fourth quarter. But ultimately, there's a lot to be done now in the day-to-day operation of the field now to mitigate decline and deliver a good quarter.

Charles Meade: That's helpful elaboration, Andy. Turning to the Gulf, I wonder if you could talk a bit about, to me at least, it seems you've been generally quiet on your working interests at Trailblazer, although it seems like you entered the Shell JV kind of on a heads-up basis with them. I wonder if you could talk about how you are thinking about the interest you're going to carry into drilling that well, and perhaps if Tiberius is a good analog for us to think about. I think in that case, you drilled the well and then farmed down after you had a success case. But I wonder if you could just talk about your approach to Trailblazer.

Andrew Inglis: Yes, I think it's slightly reverse. I think the alliance with Shell is about establishing the equities upfront. We're pleased to be working with, obviously, with Shell. They're the leading Norphlet player. They have the infrastructure in Appomattox. So we'll be drilling Trailblazer at around a third, Charles. Yes. That, I think, is the right level for us, with success. It allows us to participate in another high-quality development and do it with a simple partnership. I think one of the things where it's analogous Tiberius to Trailblazer is you're working with essentially the owner of the infrastructure in the area. Yeah? So that's clearly Oxy with Tiberius, and it's Shell with Trailblazer.

I think, again, the important thing when you're looking at ILX is to make sure that you've got the ability with success then to quickly tie back, and that's all about driving the economics. So I think that very similar approaches, about the same risk exposure, and it's all about making sure that we've got the ability with success to move it forward at pace.

Operator: Your next question comes from Bob Brackett with Bernstein Research.

Bob Brackett: A bit of a follow-up on Trailblazer. I will make a two-part question, one above the water and one below. Above the water, you said about a third working interest and a simple partnership. That almost makes me ask the question, is not it exactly a third, and are there any sort of clawbacks or carries in the partnership, or is it just a straightforward working interest split? Then I will ask a follow-up.

Andrew Inglis: Yes. Look, just think about it as a straight interest split, Bob. I do not want to give all the details, but think about it exactly like that.

Bob Brackett: Okay. Very clear. Then sort of below the water, Trailblazer is fairly far west of some of those thickest of those aeolian deposits. What is the sort of confidence that those aeolian dunes extend that far west? Are they imageable? Is that a key risk as well?

Andrew Inglis: Look, what I would say again on that, Bob, is that we are working clearly, I think, with the company that has very good knowledge of the Norphlet. Shell have clearly high-graded it in their drilling program to bring it on to their rig slots. So, I think that we feel good about the partnership in general and working with the leading player, and clearly we bring all of their knowledge as well. So, I think that is the way you should sort of think about it, that we have got a and clearly they have created room in their program to farm into the process, to farm into the prospect.

Operator: Your next question comes from Neil Mehta with Goldman Sachs.

Neil Mehta: I just wanted to get your perspective on the progress around deleveraging. Certainly in this type of commodity price environment, you guys have done a lot on the balance sheet. So just give us a mark-to-market on where you are and you are happy with, how you are thinking about the progress that you have made, and you are happy with how it is shaping up?

Andrew Inglis: Okay. Neil, my Neal, why don't you have a go at that one?

Neal Shah: Yes. Neil, thanks for the question. It's clear, again, we have been clear around what we wanted to do in terms of tackle the near-term maturities, create some space, increase liquidity, and bring down leverage. Again, I think we are in a good place, particularly with where Brent is at this point to continue to benefit from that, both as we sort of exited 3Q, but also into early 4Q, where prices have remained quite strong. So, we feel good about sort of exiting the year at sort of less than $2.4 billion from a debt perspective. Then, as we mentioned on the call, targeting to get to sort of around $2 billion by the end of 2027.

So I think, yeah, that sort of squares where we want to get to from a net debt or leverage perspective. I think from a maturity perspective, the next thing we clearly sort of voiced is our expectation is to manage the 2028 maturity, and there are a couple different ways we can tackle that. But once we address that, we basically have, call it three and a half years without any meaningful maturities. Again, that will be a huge amount of progress in a short amount of time. Again, the team has done a huge amount of work on that, and we have got a bit more to go, but I think we are in pretty good shape.

The market has been supportive, and things are headed the right way.

Neil Mehta: Yes. Neal, once you get to that target, how do you think about what you do with the excess cash? What are the different options that you have? Do you have a long-term debt target in mind? Are we starting to think about return of capital? Or what is the optimal balance sheet, and what is the approach to excess cash once you hit your target?

Neal Shah: Yes. Again, I think in the near-term, which again, I think, yeah, we would qualify as through 2027, is getting to that sort of less than $2 billion first, right? Then, if we are generating anywhere sort of north of $1 billion to $1.5 billion of EBITDA, we are sort of at a one and a half-ish times of leverage area. Again, I think that remains the first sort of objective. Beyond that, again, I think it will be a combination of then looking at additional debt paydown, and then either funneling the capital towards growth projects, or towards capital returns. So, that sort of framework has not changed.

Again, I think, that is really a decision probably towards the end of 2027 as we get closer to that target. Again, we have a number of growth opportunities, which again, in a more constructive commodity price environment, they make sense to accelerate forward. If the share price is weaker and we're in a bit of lower environment, we may lean more into the return side of the equation. Again, I think it's a good question. Again, we're not quite there yet, but after the next 12 months or so, that's certainly the right question to ask.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of David Round with Stifel.

David Round: Andy, can I just come back to the priorities before the next Jubilee drilling campaign, or Ghana drilling campaign? Can you just talk a bit more about how important those four projects are to your production levels? I think uptime probably speaks for itself, but any context on the other three items would be good. If I do think of these as specific projects, whether there are any timing milestones to look out for.

Andrew Inglis: Yes, David. Look, I could say it's really just about daily operational excellence. Ultimately, it's about managing the reservoir pressure, which is about voidage replacement. Our view is probably to have that well above 120% to manage the decline effectively. We've been a little short of that through 3Q, and it's really about now ramping up the reliability of the water injection equipment and ensuring that we deliver that. So it's not really a project, but it's a daily grind of operational excellence.

The second item is really about production optimization, and I think some of you have heard me say there's 168 set points as you look at all of the well intervals across the producing wells and injectors on Jubilee. It's the constant normalization and optimization of those settings, again, to take advantage of the increased water injection areas of increased pressure, and therefore maximizing the delivery. Again, as I've said, I think on previous calls, AI now is making a difference there, given the number of variables that you're optimizing around. We're seeing it have quite a significant impact. The final one, which is gas lift on the west, is in your project sort of bucket, I think.

It's reconnecting a riser so that we can introduce gas lift to the west side of Jubilee. That project's ongoing at the moment and will probably come in towards the end of this month. But altogether, those are the things that are part of our armory now to maximize the production from the field through the end of the year, and then exit at the maximum rate, and then continue with that through the first half of 2027.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Christoffer Bachke with Clarksons Securities.

Christoffer Bachke: Christoffer from Clarksons here. First of all, congratulations on a solid and eventful third quarter. I have two questions today, if I may. The first is on realized pricing in the fourth quarter, especially given the exceptional strong physical crude markets in West Africa and the significant premiums that we are seeing right now. Could you provide some color on your expectations for realized prices in the fourth quarter, and perhaps also touch upon the actual realized prices achieved from Jubilee in September and October? The second one is on the refinancing of the 2028 maturity. First of all, congratulations on the successful amendment and extension. Now, naturally, the attention turns towards the 2028 maturity.

How are you thinking about the timing of a potential refinancing, and what level of leverage or further debt reduction would you ideally like to achieve before approaching the market?

Andrew Inglis: Yes. Christoffer, why don't I ask Neal just to cover those 2?

Neal Shah: Yes, sure. On realized pricing, as I mentioned when I was answering Neil's question, we've seen good pricing really continue into October. Again, I think part of why the cargo timing impacted us a bit in 3Q in terms of just the cargo pricing, but as we exited Q3 and into Q4, pricing has been clearly a lot more favorable. We've had two cargoes lift sort of net around $120 per barrel or better, one in Jubilee in the condensate cargo. So actually, timing's been pretty good. Again, I think from a realization perspective, what we'll realize out of the Gulf in October is the highest we've netted year to date. Again, I think pricing has been strong.

We've got basically a cargo a month out of Ghana, and Dated Brent still as of Friday was right under 120. So again, I think realizations both on what we're selling out of West Africa and out of the Gulf look pretty good. Clearly today's a volatile day, but we'll see. Generally, prices are still remain pretty supportive for us to deliver a strong cash flow result in the fourth quarter. On 2028, for me, it's less of an issue around paying off more debt. It's really around sort of ensuring the market's in a good place and us getting the benefit of all the work that we've put in before we look to other solutions.

So, clearly refinancing the bond is an option. The RBL was an important milestone in terms of getting the balance sheet sorted. We also would like a bit more progress on the rating side of the equation, so in terms of what we're working on to get the ratings moved in the right place. Then clearly, the yields have improved dramatically year to date. I think it still has room to run. So, it's something we're going to continue to evaluate on a regular basis, see how markets move on a sort of monthly basis, and evaluate sort of what is the right option.

I think the good part about where we are is, again, from a cash flow generation perspective, we've delivered two quarters of right under $100 million. We expect Q4 and the early part of 2027 looks pretty good as well. So we also have an option to just pay down bonds or pay down the RBL, creating more space and liquidity or different ways to address the 2028s. So, we have more tools available to us, and again, clearly, we're in a better shape. So, we'll continue to evaluate those alternatives.

Christoffer Bachke: Just as a quick follow-up here on the underlift position that you touched upon, could you quantify how much of this inventory you expect to monetize during the fourth quarter?

Christoffer Bachke: Regarding the underlift position of 1.1 million barrels going into the fourth quarter, could you quantify how much of this inventory you expect to monetize now in the fourth quarter?

Neal Shah: Yes, I think I won't give you an exact number, but a couple thousand barrels a day unwinds in the fourth quarter. Again, I think from the first quarter, it looks like, yeah, again, sort of cargo timings move, but sometime in the first, second quarter of next year, we'll unwind the rest.

Operator: Your next question comes from Mark Wilson with Jefferies.

Mark Wilson: A couple of questions from me. First, just to carry on from that RBL extension. Excellent to see that. On the 28s, one imagines that you wouldn't be looking to extend the 28s beyond that 2033 maturity of the RBL. I think previously you had the RBL at 2029 versus these at 2028. Should we expect something similar in terms of that cadence? That's my first question, I guess, to you, Neal. Andy, I would say that overall in the market, consolidation in various basins has been a theme. Certainly onshore U.S., we've seen some in the U.S. Gulf, and obviously a lot in the North Sea, both Norway and U.K. We haven't seen much in West Africa.

I'm just wondering how you would categorize the market for further consolidation in that particular basin.

Neal Shah: Mark, let me just take your first one, then I'll hand it over to Andy. Just in terms of a refinancing, again, I don't think we'd be looking at anything out of the ordinary. Again, generally, the U.S. independents are all sort of in the issuing five to seven-year new issues. Again, I think anything we look at will be within that sort of five to seven-year window, which would probably be 2033 at the outside, and 2031 at the inside. Andy?

Andrew Inglis: Yes, Mark. Yes, no, absolutely. It's interesting, isn't it, comparing the lower 48 to the internationals. I'd say one of the big drivers in the lower 48 is access to inventory. Companies, as it were, with shorter R/Ps getting access to higher quality inventory is ultimately what's driving that. Then clearly, the second big issue then is all around the synergies from those match-ups. When it comes to the international space, you look at Kosmos today, the R/P is well over 20. That's just on a 2P basis with a relatively modest contribution from the discovered resource on a 2C basis, over 30. So, for us, it's not really about trying to lengthen the portfolio.

Ultimately, any consolidation has to help us create a stronger, more resilient business. Ultimately, it's about synergies. It would have to be around synergies. It would have to be about value being created through the combination. I think there are relatively few of those around. Then, therefore, what are we doing in the interim? It's all about the organic self-help that actually gets us there today. As Neal's talked about, really every question has been around building the resilience of the balance sheet. Ultimately, it's about lowering the breakeven, taking cost out of the business, and then improving our margin.

So, the answer is, I agree with the thesis, but for Kosmos, it has to be around something that genuinely addresses the ability to create a more valuable company, because there's another access to capital, and there's a greater cash flow potential. So, that's the basis on which we would evaluate any opportunity.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Stella Cridge with Barclays.

Stella Cridge: Thanks for all the updates and the comments on the debt side. I just wonder if I follow up with one question on bonds. Obviously, you noted about the pricing in the market at the moment, obviously interest rates have moved higher, made raising debt a bit more expensive for everyone. But the one bond that has performed quite well has been your GTA bonds, which were issued perhaps before the price rally in Brent. I am just wondering, where do they sit within your thinking about the whole capital structure?

Is that a bond that you might think about refinancing at some point to lower the cost of debt, or are you just perhaps a bit more focused on the near-term maturities for the moment?

Neal Shah: Yes, Stella. I mean, clearly we put it in place at the beginning of the year to manage the 2027 maturities. It's got some time on it in terms of it's a five-year note, but clearly it's at a higher coupon than what we'd like to manage. Again, I think, yeah, we were at a pivotal point in GTA in terms of it just starting up. It's now been online for running at full rate for over a year. We'd expect it to do a pretty meaningful contribution to EBITDAX this year for the company as well. Again, I think there's been a huge amount of de-risking the asset.

I've always thought secured debt at GTA makes sense within our capital structure on a long-term basis. That note, again, I think should be lower priced at a regular time in the capital structure. It's got a 30-month call period, so again, I don't think we can call it until mid-2028. Again, I think it'd be something we could look at extending or modifying once we get to the end of the no-call period.

Operator: Your next question comes from Erik Borthen with Fearnley Securities.

Erik Christian Borthen: Congrats on a great quarter. Thanks for the update on the bond refi and outlook there. Just to follow up on the sort of growth and M&A initiatives. Your partner at Tullow at Jubilee is struggling a bit. Could you be looking at sort of increasing your stake there come sort of 2027?

Andrew Inglis: Yes. Thanks, Erik. Look, I hope I'm being clear today that our primary focus in Ghana is seeing sustained strong performance from the assets, and in particular, Jubilee. I talked in answer to David's question around the things that we need to do to improve the performance of the field, and that's clearly what we're focused on today. If there is a process which creates an opportunity to deepen our position in Jubilee, whether that's sort of directly through a deal or indirectly through preempting a deal, then it's something that we would consider in the future. But today, we're not getting distracted by that.

It's all about a focus on the daily operations, improving the flow across the items that we discussed earlier. If there is an opportunity in the future, as I said, whether directly or indirectly through preemption, we could look at it.

Erik Christian Borthen: Also, just on the 2028 maturity, you said the GTA bond is priced on the high side. With your 2031 unsecured being priced double digits, is there a threshold we should look at to gauge where it will be an attractive opportunity for you guys?

Neal Shah: Yes, Erik. What I'd say is, again, as we reduce the amount of total debt that we have, both on the RBL and the bonds, we expect the pricing to come in. We've seen a huge compression in the credit spreads, and while they're still low double digits, we still think there's room to go. Again, I think clearly, in my mind, our credit should be single-digit paper. I think, to the extent we can get the, we've moved the credit rating back to single-B. We need to move the credit rating of the issue back to single-B as well.

That should open us up to a pretty large financing market, allowing us to issue paper where we want to on a recurring basis. Again, I think we've got some luxury.

Operator: Since there are no further questions at this time, I would like to bring the call to a close. Thanks to everyone for joining today. You may now disconnect your lines at this time, and thank you for your participation.

#3058. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3054. Palantir: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

The company's shift to enterprise workflows over generic productivity tools reveals why its pricing power may compound as corporate adoption accelerates.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 2, 2026, Palantir (PLTR -3.13%) announced quarterly revenue of $2.3 billion, representing 96% year-over-year growth as enterprise demand accelerated. The company's shifting revenue mix demonstrates that corporate software adoption is eclipsing government contracts as the primary expansion engine. Three key takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

U.S. commercial revenue surged 148% year over year to $984 million, surpassing government revenue in the region for the first time. Private enterprises are shortening evaluation cycles and expanding deal sizes as demand for operational software tools accelerates across corporate workflows.

Management emphasized that generating measurable return on investment (ROI) requires embedding technology directly into operational workflows rather than chasing individual employee productivity gains. The company's Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) targets core enterprise execution to deliver quantifiable economic results.

Customizing open-source models on proprietary operational data inside the company's ontology, its central data mapping architecture, enables clients to achieve high performance without transferring proprietary knowledge to external model providers. Fine-tuning smaller models lowers compute costs while maintaining domain advantage.

Commercial software adoption is accelerating across corporate enterprises. Palantir relies on its operational software architecture to integrate deeply into client infrastructure, maintaining pricing power while management monitors enterprise contract conversion velocity.

Deploying tailored operational systems enables the business to compound cash flow as enterprise buyers pivot from generic language models to customized enterprise workflows.

#3050. 2 Unstoppable Quantum Computing Stocks to Buy Hand Over Fist Before the Next Rally

IonQ's revenue rose 287% and Rigetti's 185% last quarter, but both carry steep valuations. Here's how the two compare on risk and fit.

Quantum computing is moving closer to mainstream adoption, creating exciting opportunities for investors. With that, IonQ (IONQ -6.22%) and Rigetti Computing (RGTI -5.16%) are two promising companies making strides in quantum computing. And looking ahead, if adoption accelerates, both stocks could be well-positioned for the next major rally.

Let's start by looking at what IonQ is building.

IonQ is building a comprehensive platform that spans quantum computers, networking, and cybersecurity. That broader strategy could give it several ways to benefit as quantum technology moves closer to commercial adoption.

One of IonQ's biggest advantages is its trapped-ion approach, which is said to deliver highly accurate quantum operations. That matters because the company is working to develop more powerful and reliable quantum computers, thereby enhancing the performance and scalability of its systems.

The company's recent technical milestones are also encouraging.

IonQ demonstrated the industry's first end-to-end real-time quantum error decoder, which could make larger quantum systems more reliable. The company also demonstrated a quantum memory-enhanced interconnect, which is an important step toward connecting separate quantum processors.

IonQ is also strengthening its manufacturing capabilities. As an example, it completed its acquisition of SkyWater Technology, a U.S.-based semiconductor foundry. This gives the company greater control over the hardware manufacturing process, helping it improve production, develop specialized chips, and scale its technology more efficiently.

The commercial opportunity is also gaining traction. IonQ reported strong revenue growth in its second quarter, supported by demand across its broader quantum platform. In fact, revenue climbed 287% year over year in a record quarter.

On top of that, its partnerships with organizations like Nvidia, Sandia National Laboratories, and Anduril highlight its role in other industries, including artificial intelligence (AI), scientific research, and national security.

But of course, IonQ remains a speculative investment at this stage, as quantum computing has yet to achieve widespread commercial adoption. The company also faces many technical and execution challenges before it can become profitable. Valuation is also a concern, with the stock trading at about 42 times its price-to-sales (P/S) ratio.

Aside from IonQ, another company is taking a different approach to scaling quantum systems.

Unlike IonQ, Rigetti uses superconducting qubits, which run using electrical circuits cooled to extremely low temperatures. One of the biggest advantages of this approach is its fast gate speeds, which allow quantum operations to run much faster. The company believes its technology can provide a practical path toward building more powerful quantum systems.

Its chiplet strategy is also a key advantage. Instead of relying on a single massive chip, Rigetti combines smaller processor units into a larger system, and the company has already demonstrated this approach with its Cepheus-1-108Q system.

Meanwhile, Rigetti has also been fulfilling orders for on-premises quantum systems, including its Novera-based machines and the 108-qubit system program for India's Center for Development of Advanced Computing. These deployments matter because they give universities and research institutions direct access to quantum hardware.

And the initiatives seem to be working. Rigetti's second-quarter revenue, for example, grew 185% year over year, though from a small base, all while Rigetti works to build a more commercially scalable business.

More recently, however, Rigetti established a dedicated systems delivery organization and appointed new leadership to oversee operations and technology development.

Still, the company faces meaningful risks in its operations. Rigetti remains an early-stage business with limited commercial revenue, significant operating losses, and a long development path. The stock also trades at about 278 times its P/S ratio, so if future growth doesn't exceed investor expectations, Rigetti could see steep losses.

But despite the risks, can IonQ and Rigetti still deliver massive upside?

IonQ and Rigetti offer two ways to invest in the quantum computing race.

With an expanding technology stack and growing commercial adoption, both companies could be poised for the industry's next growth phase. If they execute on their roadmaps and benefit from accelerating demand, their stocks could still have plenty of upside.

IonQ looks like the more conservative of the two, with a broader platform and lower valuation. Rigetti is the higher-risk, higher-reward pick, given its early stage and steep valuation.

#3046. Kimberly-Clark Acquires Kenvue. Here’s What Investors Need to Know Ahead of Its Nov. 5 Earnings Report.

The enterprise value of the monster deal was estimated at almost $49 billion.

On Monday, one of the largest acquisitions of 2026 closed, almost one year to the day after it was first announced. This is Kimberly-Clark's (KMB +0.29%) purchase of consumer healthcare company Kenvue. The two companies said in their original announcement that Kenvue's enterprise value was a cool $48.7 billion or so.

That's immense, even when considering the huge size of both Kimberly-Clark and Kenvue (formerly a business owned by healthcare giant Johnson & Johnson (JNJ -0.97%)). So it'll result in significant changes to the storied Kimberly-Clark. Let's explore what that means for that company's stockholders, particularly since we're days away from its third-quarter earnings release.

In the press release on the closing of the acquisition, Kimberly-Clark and Kenvue wrote that it "brings together two iconic American companies to create a combined portfolio of complementary products, including 10 billion-dollar brands, that touch nearly half the global population through every stage of life."

This isn't much of an exaggeration. Millions of homes in this country stock products from one or both companies. The hygiene-focused consumer goods titan Kimberly-Clark is the company behind Kleenex tissue and Huggies diapers, to name only two familiar product lines. Kenvue, meanwhile, purveys everyone's favorite headache remedy (Tylenol), the Johnson's Baby product suite, and Listerine mouthwash.

In other words, at a stroke, Kimberly-Clark will be not only a significantly bulked-up consumer goods giant but also the No. 1 company in the industry focused on health and hygiene products. That makes for quite a daunting economic moat.

The deal is a mix of cash and stock. Kenvue investors were to receive $3.50 per share in cash and almost 0.15 of a share of Kimberly-Clark's equity per each of their Kenvue shares. Kenvue's stock was delisted before market open on Monday.

The ownership structure was estimated at 54% held by existing Kimberly-Clark investors, with Kenvue stockholders owning the remainder.

An enterprise value near $50 billion is huge, even for a Kimberly-Clark-sized business. The company said that much of the funding for the cash portion of the Kenvue purchase was raised through a $4.9 billion senior notes flotation and the sale of a 51% stake in its consumer paper and business-to-business (B2B) hygiene products business to Brazil's Suzano (SUZ +0.11%).

The two companies believe they can achieve annual run rate synergies of $2.1 billion within three years after the acquisition's close. This is probably achievable given the adjacent -- at times overlapping -- nature of their product lineups and geographies.

Beyond its extremely familiar leading brands, Kimberly-Clark is renowned for its impressive streak of dividend raises. It's a Dividend King, meaning it has hiked its payout a minimum of once per year for at least half a century. Its current streak is 54 years, but, understandably, some investors are worried about the dividend's future. The financing commitments are heavy with this deal.

Yet Kimberly-Clark's stated goal for years has been to maintain its Dividend King status. Besides, Kenvue isn't its first swallow of a peer company. What I think the company will do is what it's done in the past following large acquisitions: declare incremental raises for a period of years to conserve capital for buyout-related expenses. I don't think any investor should worry about management losing that hard-earned crown.

One shareholder-pleasing activity that has been jettisoned for now is Kimberly-Clark's share buybacks, which the company once effected regularly. And at a monster scale; in 2024, for example, they totaled $1 billion. These tapered off quickly around the time of the acquisition announcement last year and fell to $0 in 2026. We can expect the same for at least a few years.

It's important to note that, because the acquisition closed on Monday, Kenvue's recent results won't be included in Kimberly-Clark's third-quarter numbers (although we shouldn't be surprised if the new owner provides them anyway to show what a clever deal it engineered). In addition to digesting the usual figures, growth rates, valuations, etc., investors should pay close attention to any management updates on financing the acquisition, maintaining the dividend raise streak, and -- if the subject comes up -- an eventual restoration of share repurchases.

From what we've seen of the acquisition so far and of both companies’ performance, I’d say it’s a good move, even at that eye-watering price. The pair are more complementary than many big companies tying the knot, and, to repeat, that goes not only for product lineups but also for their geographical footprints. I think the anticipated synergies are achievable, and the Kenvue-infused Kimberly-Clark will be a global powerhouse and a tough competitor. I also think it will maintain its vaunted Dividend King status, which is especially encouraging given its high-yield dividend currently pays out at 4.7%.

Eric Volkman has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool recommends Johnson & Johnson. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

Lattice Semiconductor Corporation (LSCC +2.66%) reported record results for the third quarter, driven by accelerating momentum in data center AI infrastructure and a recovery in industrial markets. Management stated that the company is transitioning into a sustainable, secular growth entity with a target of over 30% annualized growth over the next five years. The integration of AMI has expanded the company's addressable market into secure firmware and rack-scale management solutions. Management noted that operating leverage remains a primary focus, with earnings growth expected to consistently outpace revenue growth as the business scales.

With that, I will turn the call over to our CEO, Ford Tamer.

Ford Tamer: Thank you, Rick, and welcome everyone to our third quarter earnings call. Lattice delivered record third quarter revenue of $291 million, up 45% sequentially and up 118% year-over-year. Non-GAAP EPS was $0.72, up more than 155% year-over-year, and well above the high end of our guidance, as we translated revenue growth into even stronger earnings growth. Our fourth quarter revenue guidance of $335 million at the midpoint represents approximately 130% year-over-year growth, which is an annualized revenue run rate above $1.3 billion. This exceeds the outlook we provided last quarter and reflects accelerating momentum and broad-based demand. Our Q4 non-GAAP EPS outlook midpoint of $0.84 represents 160% year-over-year growth, reflecting our operating leverage, differentiated customer value, and disciplined execution.

As we continue to scale, we expect EPS growth to remain meaningfully ahead of revenue growth over time. This outlook implies non-GAAP full-year 2026 EPS of approximately $2.50, up 140% year-over-year, a clear reflection of the earnings power we are building across the business. Our Q3 results and Q4 guidance are well above expectations. This is the result of our deliberate strategy of enabling the success of our customers and partners by offering them differentiated products, solutions, support, and supply. Our commitment to you, our valued shareholders, is to tell you what we are going to do and then do what we said. This earnings call marks my two-year anniversary with Lattice.

We have delivered on this commitment for eight quarters in a row now and intend to continue to do so in the future. Now let me share with you the details of our FPGA business, where our actual performance and outlook are much stronger today than what was expected two years ago. Growth was broad-based across all our end markets. FPGA revenue reached $252 million, up 90% year-over-year. Our Compute & Communications segment delivered record revenue, up 132% year-over-year, driven by rapid adoption in data center AI applications. This growing demand reflects AI infrastructure investment, more server deployments for agentic inference, and increasing AI content per server.

We also continue to benefit from higher FPGA attach rates in new applications, driven by more complex disaggregated architectures and growing security requirements. Demand for our Industrial & Embedded products continued to grow, with revenue increasing 35% year-over-year. We see the worldwide and geographic-specific PMIs at near record levels since the troughs of the latest downturn. We expect our Lattice Industrial & Embedded business to continue to grow faster than the overall industrial market and accelerate its growth in Q4 and into 2027. This growth is across all sectors, including factory automation, robotics, aerospace and defense, medical equipment, and autonomy.

With channel inventory at healthy levels, customer engagement accelerating, and multiple new design wins ramping into production, we expect our Industrial & Embedded business to become an increasingly important growth engine into 2027 and beyond. During the quarter, we extended our leadership in small and mid-range FPGAs. We launched Lattice Prompt, an AI-assisted development tool for Lattice FPGAs. It allows our developers to generate and validate their FPGA applications from natural language prompts. To do so, it connects our customer-preferred large language model and agentic development environment with our Lattice Radiant tools and generates tested and proven FPGA code. Lattice Prompt provides significant FPGA developer productivity benefits and represents a significant step forward for our customer base.

We also introduced the Mach-N2 family, our latest secure control small FPGA platform, featuring integrated flash, hardware root of trust, post-quantum cryptography, and enhanced connectivity with customer sampling already underway. Now, let me tell you about the continued expansion of Lattice into secure control and management leadership with the successful closing of the AMI acquisition on July 27. The AMI business also delivered better-than-expected results in Q3, and we expect continued growth in Q4. In the three months since closing, we have engaged with hundreds of customers and partners globally, and the feedback has reinforced the strategic logic of the transaction and validated the highly complementary nature of our portfolios.

Following the AMI acquisition, we launched AMI Rack Manager to simplify deployment and operations across large-scale AI data centers. We also expanded ecosystem collaboration with SK hynix to improve server reliability with our memory resilience technology. We held joint Lattice and AMI Tech Summits in Taipei and Shenzhen with over 700 attendees and over 20 customer and partner demos, reflecting our strong customer intimacy. Ecosystem keynotes included Advantech, Inovance, Intel, Mitsubishi Electric, NVIDIA, NXP, Panasonic, Qualcomm, and Sony, showcasing the power of our companionship and firmware strategy. During the Lattice and AMI keynote at OCP, we introduced the Secure Control and Management Plane Initiative, or SCMP, with seven industry leaders: AMD, Arm, ASPEED, Intel, Jabil, Microsoft, and NXP.

Since then, four more industry leaders have notified us that they intend to join this exciting industry-wide effort. This shows the relevance of secure control and management for autonomous data center infrastructure and industrial and embedded applications. Finally, let me update you on the recent launch of four joint Lattice AMI solutions for streaming rack boot, security retrofit, plug-and-play deployment, and power and cooling management. The response to these pre-integrated and pre-validated FPGA and firmware offerings was very strong. Customers immediately recognized the benefits of rapid deployment, reduced complexity, and lower implementation risk, leading a significant number of them to advance to proof-of-concept engagements.

In summary, we entered the fourth quarter with record revenue, accelerated bookings, and backlog extending well into 2027. This momentum is being fueled by normalized inventory in the channel, our leadership in small and mid-range FPGAs, and our role as companionship, firmware, and solutions for both data center and physical AI. As a result, data center demand continues to grow. Industrial and embedded is on a strong rebound, and the AMI acquisition expands the markets and application we can serve. Together, these drivers support our confidence in sustained growth and expanding profitability. Turning to the medium to longer-term outlook, we expect revenue growth of at least 60% year-over-year in 2027.

We also expect revenue to continue to grow at over 30% CAGR for the next five years. Our confidence is based on the multiple growth vectors we have just outlined. We expect that this will create a sustainable, secular growth company with diversified and broad customer base and market segments. In turn, we believe this will drive robust demand for the foreseeable future. Our focus is on converting that opportunity into long-term earnings growth for you, our valued shareholders, for many years to come. With that, I'll turn the call over to Lorenzo Flores to review our third quarter results and outlook. Lorenzo?

Lorenzo Flores: Thank you, Ford, and good afternoon, everyone. The bottom line is that Lattice is delivering exceptional financial performance last quarter, this quarter, and based on our expectations, next quarter, next year, and beyond. Revenue was well above guidance. Both the FPGA business and the AMI business exceeded expectations. Our overall revenue of $291 million was 118% over last year. FPGA revenue at $252 million is up approximately 90% year-over-year. Gross margin also exceeded guidance, again, in both the FPGA and AMI businesses. We also managed operating expenses to our guide and delivered dramatic expansion of our profitability as Q3 non-GAAP EPS of $0.72 was 2.5x the prior year's EPS. The trajectory of our business indicates a remarkable 2026.

We see our 2026 delivering almost $1 billion in revenue and $2.50 in EPS. This would be nearly double revenue from last year and about 2.4x more earnings. We have been driving this growth across the set of end markets we serve and see strong growth continuing. Now for some key highlights. Q3 revenue reached a record $291 million, up approximately 45% quarter-over-quarter. Within that, FPGA revenue was $252 million, up approximately 90% year-over-year and 25% quarter-over-quarter. This growth was driven by another record performance in Compute & Communications, up 132% year-over-year and 36% sequentially. Very importantly, we also saw Industrial & Embedded revenue growing 35% year-over-year and 7% sequentially.

AMI, for the two months after the acquisition, delivered $39 million of revenue, also above our expectations. Q3 non-GAAP gross margin was above expectations at 70.9%. We exceeded expectations as we balanced our supply chain issues with our customer needs. Q3 non-GAAP operating expense was $86.7 million, in line with our guidance and up approximately 29% sequentially. The sequential increase primarily reflects the addition of AMI and continued investments in our product roadmap. Our Q3 non-GAAP operating margin expanded 280 basis points sequentially to 41.1%, while our EBITDA margin increased 200 basis points to 45%.

Q3 non-GAAP EPS was $0.72, up approximately 160% year-over-year and 36% sequentially, easily exceeding the high end of our guidance and showing the significant leverage in our model. GAAP net cash flow from operating activities for the third quarter of 2026 was $95 million compared to $88.3 million in Q2. Free cash flow was $77.6 million in Q3. In the quarter, we had higher-than-run-rate CapEx as we invested in test capacity and R&D capabilities aimed at driving operational efficiencies and future growth. Now, a few comments on capital allocation. Our capital allocation priorities remain unchanged. Invest in the business to support long-term growth, maintain financial flexibility, reduce acquisition-related leverage rapidly, and evaluate opportunistic share repurchases.

To that end, we paid down $50 million of our debt in the quarter. We remain on track to reduce leverage faster than previously planned. We expect net leverage to be under 2x EBITDA by the end of 2026. We intend to reduce the debt aggressively in 2027 while continuing to invest in growth opportunities across our markets. Now for guidance. As you heard earlier, we expect our strong growth to continue. We expect Q4 revenue of between $325 million and $345 million. At the midpoint of the range, this represents approximately 130% year-over-year growth and 15% sequential growth. We see continued growth across our primary FPGA end markets and AMI.

We expect gross margin to remain strong at 72% ± 1% on a non-GAAP basis. We expect non-GAAP operating expense to be between $95 million and $101 million. Most of the increase in OPEX continues to support R&D investments in our product roadmap and long-term growth objectives, as well as a full quarter contribution from AMI. We estimate our income tax rate for Q4 to be between 4% and 6% on a non-GAAP basis. We expect non-GAAP EPS to be in a range of $0.82-$0.86 per share. At the midpoint of this guidance, we anticipate that we would exceed 160% year-over-year earnings growth as we continue to demonstrate the leverage in our model.

It is worth repeating that our Q4 outlook implies full year 2026 revenue of approximately $1 billion, roughly 90% growth over 2025. We expect FPGA revenue to surpass $900 million, representing greater than 70% year-over-year growth. Importantly, we anticipate full year earnings per share of approximately $2.50, up about 140% year-over-year. These results demonstrate the strength of our business model, the benefits of scale, and the significant earnings potential we are unlocking as we execute our growth strategy. Obviously, you are interested in our expectations for 2027. We have yet to finalize our 2027 annual operating plan, but we have enough visibility to provide some expectations.

As Ford has just discussed, we see a clear path to 60% or better growth from our projected 2026 revenue base of approximately $1 billion. We expect Compute & Communications to remain our fastest growing end market. We expect Industrial & Embedded to continue its strong growth trend, and we expect AMI to grow consistent with our previous expectations. While it is still early in the planning cycle, our confidence is rooted in our backlog, the ramp of design wins in I&E augmenting our demonstrated strength in C&C, and the expected contribution from AMI. In closing, Lattice enters the fourth quarter with strong momentum across all metrics.

Together, Lattice and AMI have a broad market opportunity and position us to capture more value across all of our core markets. We are focused on translating that opportunity into above-market revenue and faster earnings growth, stronger free cash flow, and debt reduction, all while investing to build long-term shareholder value. Operator, that concludes my prepared remarks. We can now open the call for questions.
